% --- p. 6 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\chapter*{Preface}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Preface}
\opage{6}It was not my intention from the first that the ``Memoirs''
which I wrote down in the winter of 1915---16, and
continued later in 1922 and 1924, should appear
before my death. Now, however, it has come
to seem to me that conditions,
not least in the field in which I
have chiefly moved, have become so different from
the time the book presupposes that no more time
ought to pass if the book is to find understanding
readers.

My wife, who was to have been the book's editor,
has come round to my view and is now helping
me with the publication.

In the Introduction I have said enough about
why I have written memoirs at all.

\textit{Carlsberg, 14 March 1928.}
\textit{Harald Høffding.}

% --- p. 7 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\mainmatter

\chapter*{I}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{I. 1843--1861}
\markboth{I. 1843--1861}{I. 1843--1861}
\opage{7}When I write down memories of my life, it is
not because I think I have experienced anything that is
remarkable in outward respects. But in every human life
that is lived in earnest there will be events and
experiences that may be of interest, even though the
frame within which it is lived is limited. And in
old age interest in this human element naturally
comes forward, above all in its inner coherence.
It is the time of memory, and there arises a wish to
give oneself an account of the motives, the leading endeavors, that
have carried one's life. Behind the traits and the fates the individual
shares with so many others there may, after all,
lie quite different individual motives, just as logic
teaches that the same conclusion can be reached from quite different
premises. That our real life is an inner
life one learns in old age, if one had not learned
it before. And with this the urge naturally joins
to trace whether there has been an inner coherence in
the life one can now look back on. I am fully aware
that any attempt at a retrospect may bring with it
many illusions. Memory may fail, both as regards
the particular events and actions and as regards
the leading motives. --- I have myself, in my book
on Rousseau, drawn attention to the difficulty of
writing autobiography, and tried to show what different
motives cross one another in a book such as Rousseau's
Confessions. Where I can, I shall lean on letters and
other documents that may be at my disposal, in order
% --- p. 8 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{8}thereby to avoid mistakes and illusory motivations.
The letters I have are for the most part written to me. Apart
from a few drafts, I have letters from myself only when
the recipients are dead; they are therefore melancholy documents,
but they throw light on many people and many things. Thus I could
not have given a tolerably reliable account
of my development between my twenty-second and my twenty-seventh year
had I not found the letters from the time of my engagement
among the keepsakes of my late [first] wife.

When I look back on my childhood and youth, the
time of those days and the way in which
life was then lived seem to me utterly different from what now presents itself
to an observer. I should very much like
to give a description that would show this difference in vivid
small touches. But I lack the gift of lively description
of outward circumstances and events. The chief physician
Nikolaj Holm, my schoolfellow in the infant school and later as a
student, has given a lively and delightful description of
life as it was lived in our childhood in well-to-do families
of the middle class. What I remember of the daily
life of that time agrees well with his description, and our outward circumstances
were much the same. But I do not trust myself to
tell it as well as he.

Holm's description stops with his student years, and
it seems, unfortunately, that he will not continue it. If
my memoirs are to have any value, that value will surely
rest chiefly on whether I can give an accessible account
of how my inner life, my faith and my outlook on life
developed from my student days and on through the years.
While I have the impression of a great difference, as regards outward
things, between the time in which my childhood and youth
fell and the present time, I nevertheless have, on
thinking back, a still far stronger impression of the
difference there is --- in my own case at least --- between
then and now as regards the inner life. And yet
it is step by step, through many nuances and in part in
% --- p. 9 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{9}zigzag, that I have come from my ``then'' to my ``now.'' This
point I shall try to make a main theme of my account.
But this development in a purely personal respect
is closely bound up with the course of my studies and with my philosophical
endeavors. And I should like to take the opportunity
to give an account, in as accessible a form as possible, of
my development in the scientific respect as well.

The course of my life has brought me into contact with not a few
remarkable people, some who have taken part in
the life of the time, and through it in my own as well, others who
in their narrow circle exercised a quieter, but not for that reason less
deep and memorable, influence --- some who stood
further from me, others whom I have loved dearly. Here is
a host of memories which I shall try to let come
into their own.

\secrule

My parents were both of good, old Danish stock.
They were first cousins, my mother's mother having been
born a Høffding and a sister of my father's father. The Høffding
family can be traced back to the seventeenth century.
A merchant in Sorø in the seventeenth century, Anders
Rasmussen, was married to a Høfding (as the name was
spelled then), and from their son, who took up his mother's
family name again, the line can be followed down to our own day.
For several generations the Høffdings were clergymen, but later
they turned to trade. My grandfather was a chandler
in Vestergade, and my father set up as a
linen-draper on the corner of Gammel Torv and Nørregade.
The house became my birthplace and is still (1916) owned by
my family. My mother, whose maiden name was Gjellerup, was descended
from a Jutland farmhand, Rasmus Gjellerup, who went to
his studies and became a parson in Zealand. Her father
was a farmer, tenant of Strandegaard by Præstø Bay.
This farm my maternal uncle later took on lease, and after
him my youngest brother, so that for nearly
a hundred years it was lived in by my family. Some of my
% --- p. 10 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{10}best holiday memories, from my childhood up to later
years, are bound up with this idyllic place.

My father was a handsome and stately man. I remember
with what pride I saw him enter the examination room of the Metropolitan School
when he came to hear
me. Later, once during my student years, I learned in a
comical way that others besides me considered him
a handsome man. We were living in the country at Skodsborg and
had our fixed bathing times in a bathing hut that was let
for hire. One day, as I went to bathe, an elderly gentleman came and
asked me whether he might not bathe with me, since
there was no room for him elsewhere. I agreed to
this, and we undressed, jumped in and swam. When we
then stood drying ourselves, the man said: ``Whose
son are you, young man?'' And when I told him, he
exclaimed in surprise: ``What? are you a son of that handsome
man!'' Fortunately I was not vain and could take
the episode with humor.

Father was a keen man of business. I still see him
before me in his gray work coat going about the shop, the office
and the warehouse. The shop trade gradually turned into wholesale
trade, especially when after 1848 Copenhagen conquered Jutland
from Hamburg in the field of trade. The office was enlarged
and moved up to the ground floor, and the shop premises were let
out. He was highly respected in the commercial world, a member of
the Maritime and Commercial Court in some of its first years. From his
young days he was an officer in the Civic Guard, at last
a colonel. He looked well in uniform and on horseback and
was very popular among his fellow citizens, who sometimes
after the end of the drills followed him home to Nørregade
and cheered him. During the two Schleswig
wars the Civic Guard manned the various guardrooms
in the town, and at fires they cordoned off the street so
that the fire brigade could work undisturbed. Often Father was
called up at night, when the shrill watchmen's whistles
announced that there was a fire.

% --- p. 11 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{11}He worked hard to get on and to
support his large family. We were seven brothers and sisters,
of whom, however, only six reached grown age. From his
childhood Father was used to frugality, and our home always
had a frugal stamp, even after a certain
prosperity had been reached. We always lived in a relatively small flat.
Father never bought himself a country house, but rented
modest houses for the summer. In his later
years, however, he took much part in social life and himself gave
splendid gentlemen's dinners.

As he stands before me, he was a man who filled
his frame entirely. I have often applied to him
Hamlet's words about his father: ``Take him for all in
all, --- he was a man!'' Self-assured and yet with a clear
understanding of his limitation, hard-working and content with little,
with a fresh and independent view of life and with a sense
for the good things it could bring --- so he stands before
me. It was so safe to know that he was there, and so splendid
to see his manly figure as the center of the home.
We children felt ourselves at a distance from him, which made
us all the gladder at a kindly smile or an encouraging
word. There could be something reserved about
him. He found it hard to speak of himself,
and he needed one to come to meet him.
Often hypochondria got the better of him. This
brings me to think of one of the proudest moments
of my life. It was in the last year I lived at home before
my marriage that he said to me one evening: ``Harald,
you must go out with me for a little; I am so heavy at heart and
do not know why.'' So we walked about the streets in the
dark winter evening until the heavy cloud had lifted. When
his sons had grown up, the relationship between
them and him became free and cordial, although the element of distance
was always there. The straightness of his character made him
stand as a model for his children. Often in difficult
situations I have asked myself: ``What would Father
% --- p. 12 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{12}do here?'' --- or: ``Would he like what
you are doing?'' Although he was conservative in both church and civic
matters, he nevertheless understood that the young
generation must in many respects see things differently
from what he was used to. And I think I may say that he
had such trust in his sons that even when they went ways
that were strange to him, or even were against him, he
could still believe that for them these were the right ways.

A beautiful and precious memory of him I keep, from
childhood on right up to the night (25 March 1873)
when I closed his eyes.

When I now come to speak of my mother, I am led
to think of what a young student once wrote to me,
that he found it hard to get a clear memory-image
of those nearest to him: ``I cannot picture my
mother.'' I understand this very well, although it does not wholly
hold in my case. Only, with every memory-image of her
that comes up, I have the distinct
feeling that it is not adequate. My memory-images of Father,
on the other hand, are clear and definite. In
part this is explained by Mother's features having been more irregular.
But it surely has to do also
with the relationship to Mother having been more intimate; she stands almost
before me as a part of myself. I was equally fond of
them both; but toward Father the element of distance was always
present. My memories of situations in which
Mother was the chief person are clearer than any
definite and particular memory-image of her alone. I
remember an evening from my fifth or sixth year. Mother
had put me and my two younger brothers to bed and
was sitting reading Andersen's fairy tales to us. We were indeed
absorbed in what we heard; but the main thing was the feeling
of safety and homeliness, the feeling that the one
we loved so dearly sat there watching over us, while
the content of the tale slowly passed over into the content of the first
dreams.

% --- p. 13 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{13}Mother was fair and rosy-cheeked. It is from her that I
have the Socratic face I have often heard of. She had
a gentle and a bright disposition, which exercised a calming influence
on Father's choleric temperament and frequent
hypochondria. When I once complained of my helplessness
in the face of dark and sluggish states, she said gently and
quietly: ``You don't have that from yourself.'' How she loved
Father and looked up to him! He had been the dream of her
youth, and she stood faithfully at his side throughout life,
until at his death she suffered the greatest sorrow of her life.
--- Much work was demanded of her. There were many
children, and the household comprised, besides the family itself,
the whole staff of the merchant's business, clerks, shop assistants,
warehousemen, hired men and coachmen. And all this she
managed in such a way that she stood as a mother to the whole staff.
Many years later still I have met former
members of the staff who spoke with kindness of
the old Mistress, or of Madam, as she was called in earlier
times, for before Father had become a captain in the Civic Guard
she was, in the usage of the time, only Madam. At
this rung lay the boundary at that time between Mistress and Madam.
At the Theater all married actresses were called Madam, with
the exception of Mrs.\ Heiberg, whose husband had a rank.

When the business went over to wholesale, the people
were put on board wages, and Mother now had only the family to provide
for.

We children came to Mother with everything, confided everything to her.
And she understood us, saw through us too when we wanted
to make ourselves out to be more than we were. Once I came home from
school having been in a fight with some schoolfellows
and got a proper thrashing. I then said to Mother (I remember
the scene clearly: I took off my satchel and sat
down, somewhat overcome, on a chair): ``I beat some
boys today!'' But at the same moment the tears came on account
of pain and indignation, and Mother said with a peculiar
smile: ``Did you, my boy?'' Her
% --- p. 14 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{14}tone made me ashamed, because I felt myself seen through. She
did not mock me, but knew how to soften what was vexing,
here as so many times later.

She had a poetic disposition, easily kindled and moved, and
without being well read in poetic literature herself, she did
undoubtedly much to give me a sense of and interest in that
direction. In her old age, when she had been left alone,
all the young ones having flown from the nest, one would usually find her
in her armchair with a book and her knitting, and she was always
much absorbed in what she was reading, even if in her last
years she quickly forgot what she had read.

Like Father she kept to the Church. They often went
to divine service, especially in winter. They kept to the Church of
Our Lady and followed, without noticing the differences, the
line of deans from the rationalist H. G. Clausen through
the speculative Tryde to the rhetorical Paulli and the kindly
Rothe. My parents never talked about religious subjects
and hardly had any grasp of dogmatic questions. When
on the day I had taken the theological degree examination
I confessed to Father, not without apprehension, that I did not want to be
a parson, he said: ``I have never set any store by that parson
business.'' He evidently took what he could use and
left the rest alone. In Mother's last days the opposition
between believers and freethinkers came more and more strongly
forward, and she took a decided stand among the former. But when
I said that she must then really believe in a
devil too, she declared most decidedly that she would
have none of it.

Mother lived to be 83 and died quite suddenly after
a few days' illness (11 November 1896).

To whom should I now go to tell what had
befallen me of joy or sorrow? I have felt the emptiness above all
when I came back from a journey. I was used to coming
to her first of all and giving an account. Only then
did I have the feeling that I had really come home.

In her last years she stood as the ancestress (mother,
% --- p. 15 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{15}grandmother, great-grandmother) of a family that looked up to
her as the gentle and venerable matriarch. Her
70th and 80th birthdays were celebrated in a cordial
and festive way in my eldest brother's house. On her 80th
birthday children, children-in-law and grandchildren danced a minuet
they had rehearsed, in her honor. It went so beautifully
that it really was an honor.

From a song I wrote for her 70th birthday
I set down here a verse which in my opinion characterizes
her quite well.

\begin{quote}
On this day a host of memories will rise\\
of what life brought to you, the dark and bright, ---\\
of every time in sorrow you must tremble,\\
each time you shouted joy on gladness' shore.\\
But through all tones it will be sounding,\\
the soul's pure and deep harmony,\\
that ennobles life, even the quiet, humble.\\
It made your foot light and your pathway bright!
\end{quote}
% Paa denne Dag vil Minders Flok sig hæve\\
% om hvad dig Livet bragte, Mørkt og Lyst, ---\\
% om hvergang du i Sorgen maatte bæve,\\
% hvergang du jublede paa Glædens Kyst.\\
% Men gennem alle Toner vil den klinge,\\
% den Sjælens rene, dybe Harmoni,\\
% der adler Livet, selv det stille, ringe.\\
% Den gjorde let din Fod og lys din Sti!

I was born on 11 March 1843. From my first years,
before my schooldays, I remember very little. Only a few
events and situations stand fairly clearly
before me. One of the first shows me a little newborn brother
lying in the cradle and the object of my wonder and
my rejoicing. I was probably four years old at the time.
Another picture is not so pleasant. For I am receiving
a bodily chastisement (the details of which I shall not
describe more closely) because I have not yet acquired the sense of cleanliness
that every good citizen of the world ought to possess. This
scene stands especially clearly before me, and I could point out
the room and the place in the room where it took place.
Just as clearly I remember seeing the railway to
Roskilde celebrate its birthday; I stood outside the farmhouse
in Valby where we were staying in the country, and saw the flower-wreathed
locomotive come. Next I remember the evening
when the body of Christian the Eighth was taken to Roskilde. The procession
passed over Gammeltorv, and we saw it from our windows
% --- p. 16 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{16}in the house on Nørregade next to the corner house. The event
gained a special interest from Father's taking part
as an officer of the Civic Guard, in the uniform then in use: white trousers,
red coat with blue breast and shako with a long
plume. I was very proud of this sight. Dimly I remember
the people's procession to Christiansborg in March; I see before
me the many people marching past in close ranks.
The same spring, I believe, I went with my parents on a
journey by carriage to Strandegaard and saw soldiers who were
on their way to the war resting at a village inn; the signal
to march off I remember clearly. From the first year of the war
I remember besides that my big brother came home
from town with a new song that everyone went about singing in
the street; it was ``den tapre Landsoldat''. Deeply imprinted
from the year after is the disaster at Eckernførde, for it was then I first
saw my parents weep; it was through their
grief that it dawned on me that one can love, rejoice and
grieve over something that lies beyond the family circle.
The same autumn my eldest brother Emil died, and of
a single episode on the night of his death I have a memory-image
of how, from the bed I shared with my younger
brother, I saw the commotion and the weeping when the moment of death had
come.

A few more small touches come up from our summer stays
in Valby. Every summer we used to make an outing
to Alleenberg to ride on the merry-go-round. Once
I was very tired on the way home. I was very smart, with
a green velvet blouse and white trousers. And on the way home
through the willow avenue I wondered greatly that the white
legs down there could keep on walking like that, although I
``myself'' was so tired. I was held by each hand by a
grown-up and could thus act as observer. Still,
after the lapse of so many years, I see the white legs move
on undaunted, as if they had not belonged to me at all.
Otherwise I remember nothing of the whole outing.

A sight that always made an impression on me was the
% --- p. 17 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{17}train disappearing out toward Glostrup, when it had
passed the level crossing near our lodging at the farmhouse.
The train gradually became a dark dot, above
which the white smoke rose toward the afternoon sun.
I had no thought of where it was going; it was
far, far away, out into the distance. It was the first
dawning of an idea of something infinite. The memory-image
has often come back to me as a symbol; from
the first I was sure that ``out there'' everything must dwell that
was glorious.

\whiteline

When I had turned six, I began school.
My entry upon the path of learning took place
in tears. It did not help that I had been given a new
winter coat, which had been made over for me from Father's cast-off
gray shop coat. I howled as Father walked with
me by the hand to Larsbjørnstræde, where an old
student, Mr.\ Fenger, kept a highly regarded infant school.
The first day at school did not turn out wholly dismal, however. In
the last lesson the oldest boys had recitation, and one of
them recited Oehlenschläger's ``In olden days, long vanished
time, there was a lovely maiden.'' I thought I had never
heard anything so beautiful. And so poetry consoled
me after the sorry beginning of my schooling.
% I gamle, længst forsvundne Tid, der var en dejlig Pige.

Mr.\ Fenger was an old student who in his younger
days had probably cultivated billiards more than learning, and now
kept a little school of about 30 boys aged from
6 to 10. He prepared boys especially for the Metropolitan School.
We were taught in two rooms and were instructed by him
in all subjects (only for French a special teacher came once a
week). While Fenger was reading with one group,
the other age classes had arithmetic, writing or composition. We
learned well, and the school gave a good preparation for further
schooling. Fenger could be strict, and it did not feel
good to be struck with a ruler on the flat of the
hand, an episode that usually ended with a stay in
% --- p. 18 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{18}the corner. But he was fond of children and liked
us to visit him on certain days in the holidays, when a
variety of toys stood ready for our pleasant use. Like
Nicolaj Holm, who was my schoolfellow at Fenger's school, I
remember clearly the long-drawn ``G'mornin','' with which
we entered the outer schoolroom in the morning;
it was answered by him from the inner room with an equally
long-drawn ``G'mornin'.'' Our greeting had of course
arisen by imitation of his.

When the weather was fine in summer, he walked
with us to Frederiksberg Garden, where we usually settled
on the parade ground, which was then open to all. We
played on the grass while Mr.\ Fenger rested
under a tree. We set great store by these outings, which
gave school time an unexpected use. On
such days Vestergade stood in a festive glow for us. Through the swarm
of farm carts and wheelbarrows the road now led out into the open.

Mr.\ Fenger ended his days in the nursing home, where
some of the families whose children he had taught had
found him a place. As a memento of him I keep
a silver cup with his name on it, which I bought from
a woman who as a child had helped her mother to
keep his rooms in order. She had been given it by him,
and when, on the occasion of my 70th birthday, she had
heard that I had been one of Fenger's pupils, she offered
it to me for the value of the silver.

When I was nine and a half I was examined for the Metropolitan School,
but was too young and had to wait a year. In the year
1853 (the cholera year) I was admitted and now began the
eight years of school in the old school on Frueplads. Shortly
before I began to write down these memoirs I had
the honor of speaking at a commemoration of the Metropolitan School's
700 years of existence. I have been fond of my
old school and owe it much, above all a good linguistic,
historical and mathematical foundation for my later studies.
And then on the school bench I won some of
% --- p. 19 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{19}my best friends, laid the foundation of friendships that have lasted
throughout life. It is very strange to think that
if I had been admitted the first time I was examined,
these friendships would not have come about. Thus our most intimate
relations to people are sometimes conditioned
by quite particular events. Yet one can also see
this in such a way that in apparently indifferent circumstances,
as here the postponement of admission to the school, there may lie
conditions for rich future possibilities. In
my old age I have pondered much on how here in
life the greatest is often bound up with the least --- how
perhaps that which for us gives life its real
value may be dependent on something we are inclined
to call ``accidental.''

\whiteline

Because of the cholera, school began late that summer.
What I remember best from the first period in the
new school is that every day after school I went to
the police station, where it was posted up how many sick
and dead there had been in the past twenty-four hours. I quickly grew used
to the new school and went through it class by class,
alternating as No.~1 and No.~2. For many years it was the
later Supreme Court judge Grüner and I who relieved each other
at the top of the class. What distinguished the school above all was
the good order there was in everything. In the first 4---5 years
the teaching was predominantly elementary. From
these years I remember best the teaching in natural history. Our teacher,
Carl Johan Fogh, was the born schoolmaster. He had
in his whole personality something that meant that as a matter of course
there was quiet and stillness in the class. With his eyes
he could reward and punish without needing stronger means.
The strongest means he used was a stern word
he whispered to a sinner; the others did not hear it, but
the effect was at once visible. The main thing, however, was that his
spirited description and characterization of botanical, zoological
and geographical phenomena awakened the
% --- p. 20 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{20}interest of most of us. He could not help it that we did not often enough get to see the
natural history collection. There was no special room
for it, but the objects were placed in cupboards in various
places. Our old headmaster, B. Borgen, we were
very fond of, which did not, however, prevent us from often reporting
a sudden headache in order to be excused from the dull
lessons in the cold and dusty gymnasium. I believe it
has harmed me that I did not get good and rational instruction in gymnastics
in my young days, so that I might have come to want to continue
with bodily exercise. We sat still too much and did not
come to know the attractions of open-air life, as a
later generation of young people has. My mother demanded that
every afternoon I should walk around three mills on
the old ramparts, which still in my schooldays stretched from
Amagerbro to the Citadel. To walk the whole way round the ramparts would
be regarded as a regular walking tour. Frederik the Seventh
liked to ride along the whole of the ramparts with his train of adjutants,
Horse Guards and lackeys. But few pedestrians thought
of walking the whole round.

Copenhagen had at that time, not least by lying behind
its ramparts, a different character from now. It was smaller, and
the difference between town and country began just outside the gate.
People stayed in the country in Frederiksberg Allé and in Valby,
moved out in the spring and in again in the autumn. The
gates were indeed no longer closed at night as in the time of Frederik
the Sixth. But there was a customs inspection outside every
gate. When in summer we boys drove to school on
the farm's milk cart, with ``Fløderikke'' as driver,
we experienced various curious things. One, which rather
bored us, but which in our naïveté we did not think about, was
that Fløderikke (I still see her with a black patch over
one eye) got down somewhere on Vesterbro and took all her
milk cans with her into a house. We thought that this was
just how it had to be, and did not consider that there must have been
a good pump inside that house. But when we were then
just outside the town gate, the customs officers came with their
% --- p. 21 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{21}iron rods and poked into the straw of the cart to see whether there
might be an attempt at smuggling. The quality of the contents of the milk cans
nobody examined. The town gate itself
was so narrow that only one carriage could drive through
at a time; it could be a long business when
there were also carriages going the opposite way. Pedestrians
had to watch their chance to slip in at the side when there
were carriages. When a load of straw had got stuck in the gate,
one could neither get in nor out. Once, when our uncle
and aunt from Strandegaard had been on a visit to Copenhagen
and were to travel home by train, they had to turn
back and wait for another occasion, because the gate was blocked
by a load of straw.

The stay in the country at Valby from May to October every year
came to mean a great deal to us boys by making us familiar
with country life and farming. We rode horses in the fields,
drove the dung carts (where the brisk ride home without the evil-smelling
load was the main thing) and took part in the harvest work,
or tried to. Valby was then a complete farming village;
there were only a few country houses. Now there is one
five-story building beside the other, and on its
fields a whole factory town rises. This change
had taken place when, in my old age, I came to live on
Valbybakke.

Before and after the stay at Valby the ramparts and the Cherry Walk,
lying between the ramparts and the moat, were places
where we could play and stroll. The bastion of the Cherry Walk
sloped with its bush-clad sides down toward the reeds of the
moat. Here were good hiding places, and here was opportunity
to acquire a sense for the idylls of nature. Merely to lie
in the tall grass between bush and reed was a glory.
Now all this has vanished; only the Ørstedspark and Østre
Anlæg recall the former time.

If one had acquaintances out in the suburbs, where there were still
large old gardens that stretched freely out
into the country, one could also move about in the open there. In one of
% --- p. 22 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{22}these large gardens or parks was the haunt of an
``order of knights,'' formed by boys from various schools,
under the leadership, naturally, of a Grand Master with his
High Steward and Marshal, and otherwise consisting of knights and squires.
My brother Valdemar, who was some years older than
I, was a knight; it was chiefly his schoolfellows from ``Efterslægten''
who formed the army. I served as a
squire and remember with what mixture of a sense of duty
and self-esteem I, armed with my cutlass, stood on
guard at the entrance to a fortified camp that had been laid out
on the edge of a large garden out on Vesterbro, and whose
entrenchment consisted of osiers woven into a wickerwork
from tree to tree. Here the order of knights withstood a siege
by the Valby boys, whose strength lay in their artillery, since they
bombarded us with stones that had to be parried with the cutlasses.

Some years later I occupied a more exalted place in
an order of knights formed by Metropolitan boys and pupils
from another school. I was Marshal, and in this
capacity came to lead in a great battle that was fought out
in Søndermarken on the hill that slopes from the large wooden pavilion
down toward Valby Bog. Our opponents
consisted of pupils from some modern schools. Our army marched
out along Vesterbro one Sunday morning and halted at
the foot of Frederiksberg Hill. From here I sent outposts
up onto the hill to see whether the enemy was there, and
it was not long before the scouts came rushing down
the hill shouting that ``they were there.'' We then advanced in good
order up the hill, but whether it was the imposing
sight of our host (we were twenty-odd), or
whether it was deeper strategic plans that came into play
--- the enemy withdrew into Søndermarken and took up position
at the foot of the slope just mentioned. They were probably
as strong as we and better armed, since they all had
cutlasses, while many of our men had only foils.
We drew up in battle order at the top of the hill; both
% --- p. 23 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{23}armies marched forward, and the clash came halfway down
the hill. We were hard pressed and had to fall back
up the hill; some --- and among them the Grand Master
--- fled very soon. I have never had so many
blows as that day. I struck out fiercely enough with
my cutlass and guarded my right side; but my foil-armed
guard could not support me, and in my left
side I was sore for a whole week after. We must, however, have made
an impression on the enemy, for most of his men proposed
an alliance to us afterwards, and the battles were continued between new
armies on a following Sunday; but I was not in that one. Then
the whole thing was forbidden both by the police and by the
schools. It could, after all, easily become a dangerous game. --- Poul
Andræ, my classmate at the time, has published, in the notes to
his mother's journals, a fragment of his
diary of the time, where he tells of these battles (though
confusing the two battles). There I am given an honor which
I really believe I deserved. First some are named
who fled, and then it continues, making use
of some newly learned Greek words: ``ἀλλά [but] Høffding,
the chieftain in facto, fought as befits a
στρατηγός [commander].''

\whiteline

But my military exploits have led me away from
the school. --- Through Krebs's thorough teaching in
Latin I had a good foundation laid for later language studies. The
strict systematics into which we were initiated through Madvig's
Grammar has in many respects been of benefit to me
in my later career. It gave, alongside mathematics,
a good formal schooling. Yet at that time one probably went
the wrong way in beginning with grammar and practice examples,
instead of leading as quickly as possible into
connected reading, through which the grammatical
system could gradually come to stand as
a natural necessity. Krebs could be strict and, like
many schoolmasters of the older time, become vehement and deliver
% --- p. 24 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{24}long reprimands. But he was on the whole well
liked, although as inspector of the school he often had to set
himself against the pupils' desires and wishes.

In my fifth year at the Metropolitan School came the confirmation classes.
--- At home we children got no direct religious
influence. We saw our parents go to church and sometimes
went with them; but religion was more a constant presupposition
than something that asserted itself as that which
made its own peculiar demands. Nevertheless it lay, as it were, in
the air, from the moment it was decided that I should go to the Metropolitan School
(my brothers all went to ``Efterslægten''), that
I should be a parson. I have been told that as a
little boy I wavered between becoming an officer and becoming
a parson; common to both was that one had to shout loudly, and
that, I suppose, I was (then!) very fond of. The main reason
why I went to the Metropolitan School was, however, that I was
very fond of reading --- and the parson's calling then lay nearest.
Later on in my schooldays I wavered between philology and
theology. But in the year of my confirmation I really entered into a religious
life of thought and feeling, and then the thought of going
the way of the Church became alive. The elder Paulli had just then
come from the Palace Church to the Church of Our Lady and was a much
sought-after preacher. He was Bishop Mynster's son-in-law, and
his sermons recalled those of this great churchman,
but were not so full of spirit. For me there was too much
rhetoric in them, and after I had become a student I
stopped being one of his hearers. In the confirmation classes
he often had an effect through the inwardness with
which he could speak of religious subjects. But very
often his teaching was purely a matter of school.

What had been founded here, however, only came to its
unfolding when in my student years I immersed myself in
Kierkegaard's writings. Then came a being-seized which
at one and the same time led me deeper into religious life and away
from theology, and which thereby became decisive for my
subsequent development. But for the time being my religious standpoint was
% --- p. 25 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{25}rather idyllic and rather closely bound up with the prospect of
a life in a parsonage in a beautiful countryside, where I could
live in quiet among my books. When on a walking tour I
passed a parsonage, I imagined myself into the life
there. (There was, however, no Juliane in the game, as in ``Øjeblikket''.)
Then at a certain point in time I was torn
violently out of this idyll. ---

At school classical languages and history were my favorite subjects.
On my own I studied the history of Denmark to
as great an extent as I could. The school's history teaching
was of importance above all in impressing on us a firm chronological
frame, within which the various phases of development
in cultural respects could find their definite
place. With much joy I used, in the last school years,
the knowledge of Greek I had gained to read the Gospel of John
in the original language. This Gospel stood for a long time from that
time on as the most perfect expression of
Christianity for me. Later I have come to a wholly different
view of its position in the earliest Christian literature.
--- Of the last school years and their importance for me
I shall speak in a moment. I must first mention three
friends whom I won in the years of transition, friends for
life, as it turned out.

From the age of fifteen I was the classmate of
% print: Ketttinge (misprint)
Hans Skovgaard\footnote[1]{B. 1844, d. 1920. --- Cand. theol. 1866, assistant master at Nykøbing F., later parson (last at Kettinge on Lolland).} and Julius Petersen\footnote[2]{B. 1840, d. 1912. --- Cand. med. 1865, general practitioner, later professor of the history of medicine at the University.}. In these years, when
so much begins to stir in soul and body --- when
the school offers chiefly elements whose significance
one only later learns to understand --- when there is an urge to
exercise the bodily and spiritual powers --- and when, then,
in the midst of this chaos religious ideas come in as
guests from a wholly different country --- in these years a refuge
with a good friend is of the greatest importance. Toward parents
and brothers and sisters a shyness often stirs that prevents
% --- p. 26 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{26}communication of what is most inward. Later in life I have
in my work as a university teacher time and again
found that young people will sooner confide in a stranger
in whom for one reason or another they have come to trust than
in those nearest them, and this has often laid a great
responsibility on me and given me difficult tasks. For me there was
at that time, outside my family, no older person I
could go to. Perhaps I might have been able to confide in
an elder sister, if I had had one. My sister was
the youngest of us brothers and sisters and at this time still a child.
She has since been the light of my eyes and the joy of my heart,
and through her gentle look and kind smile I have, especially
after Mother's death, often won peace and rest of mind. What
I did not find in older people I found in the two schoolfellows
to whom I now most closely attached myself, only in another way.
If they were a great help to me, it was not really through
what they said, or what they did for me, but through the fact
that, of the same age as I and in the same circumstances,
they nevertheless each took life in his own peculiar way, which
I did not always understand, but which precisely thereby contained
a challenge to me to let whatever peculiarity I
might possess come to expression. We were often very much
at odds, and both in the young years and later things could
get heated between us. But behind what could bring
us into opposition to each other there lay in both of them a heartfelt
sympathy, by which I felt myself enfolded again and again.
I have not been understood by other men as by them. On
so many occasions their fellow feeling and their understanding
have helped me, besides which their criticism was a constant
spur. They both had a remarkable ability to characterize,
to find and to express what was peculiar to
particular people. Skovgaard, who has not appeared as
an author, displayed this ability as a letter writer,
the best letter writer I have known. With people who did not
know him, the ability and the desire he had
to find what was characteristic in people could often lead to his being
% --- p. 27 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{27}regarded as an ironist, as a purely critical nature. Yet
there lay behind it not only a great psychological interest, but
also a great seriousness, an energetic striving to develop his
personality and to find the content of life that was meant for it.
Julius Petersen showed his gift for
characterization later in life in the excellent biographies of physicians of recent
and older times to which his studies in the history of medicine
gave occasion.

As far as I remember, a serious illness that Hans Skovgaard
went through about a year before we became students was the
outward occasion for the three of us joining together so closely.
Julius Petersen and I often went together out to Bjerregaard
on Valby Bakke to look in on our sick schoolfellow, and thus
the alliance was founded. Skovgaard's father was a well-to-do
farm owner from North Schleswig, from one of the parishes
that later came to the Kingdom. He had sold his farm
over there and bought Bjerregaard, a home farm on whose lands
a whole villa quarter and also the side of the Western Cemetery were built.
My friend thus came of the sturdy South Jutland
farming stock. Many good memories I have of the pleasant
farm, where at that time there were open fields all around,
and where one could feel oneself wholly in the country.

Julius Petersen's father had been a watchmaker in Rønne,
but settled in Copenhagen when he had become a member of the Folketing.
Julius had perhaps something of the Bornholmers'
combative, choleric nature, but alongside it an inwardness
and an urge to give himself, an immediate
sympathy, above all with the suffering and the oppressed, which later made
him a beloved physician, not least out in the poor quarters
of Nørrebro. His mind was subject to strong
swings, alternating between enthusiasm and dejection.
It was not always easy to get on with him. Suddenly
he could collapse as if in despair, and then he could
snarl at every attempt to cheer him up or merely
draw him into conversation. And just as suddenly
such dark hours could give way to a craving for festivity. And
% --- p. 28 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{28}so it went with his work too. At certain times he worked
with feverish zeal, but then there could come
times of complete idling. The teachers regarded him
as an eccentric they did not know what to do with.
Sometimes he disappeared for weeks; then he had taken
himself off on a trip to Bornholm. Already in his school years he was
in love with his future wife, who lived at Nexø on Bornholm,
and he used every opportunity the smallest
holiday offered for an excursion over there, as a rule with one
of the small sloops that carried the freight
between Bornholm and Copenhagen. Often, especially in winter, he had
rough crossings. Our old headmaster, who at bottom rather
liked him, and who, as long as it was at all possible,
took him with humor, often exacted the solemn promise from
him that he would not use a short holiday to travel to
Bornholm: ``Will you now promise me, Petersen --- I say:
\textit{promise} me! --- that you will not go to Bornholm? Will you give
me your hand on it?'' And Petersen promised and gave his hand,
but in the afternoon he went down behind
the Exchange all the same and looked for a pear boat for the passage over the Baltic.
It must have been after such a trip that he once
turned up in the middle of a lesson. The headmaster received him with
a quotation from Schiller's Piccolomini:

\begin{quote}Spät kommt Ihr --- doch Ihr kommt! der weite Weg,\\ Graf Isolan, entschuldigt Euer Säumen.\end{quote}

Toward the leaving examination he had just such a period of slackness,
but he pulled himself together in the last months
and passed with distinction. The restlessness of mind never left
him.

The third of the friends I alluded to above I made
the acquaintance of at Bjerregaard. It was the
later famous physicist Christian Christiansen. (At this
time he was called Christian Madsen, because he was a son of
the farmer Mads Christiansen at Holmsland near Ringkøbing.
But then came the regulation that surnames
% --- p. 29 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{29}in the country too were to be fixed, and so he got the name
Christiansen; for a long time, though, it was a standing joke to
add: née Madsen.) He was living with the Skovgaards
at Bjerregaard and reading privately for the student examination. Him
too I came, especially in later years, to be close to, and
here too a peculiar nature came to meet me, a young
power that early found its definite field of work, but
at the same time a mind that suffered from heaviness and needed an absolute
refuge in the faith he had grown up in, yet with an open sense
seeking out the human in all forms and at all times.
He had the Jutlander's peculiar indirect way of stating
his opinion, and there were those who could not quite
make out where they really had him. All the
greater was the effect when he really opened
up and spoke out with warmth about a cause or a person,
or perhaps gave inward expression to his friendship.

Among my classmates was Peter Jerndorff, with whom
in my old age I have come into a closer relationship.
In our student years he sometimes came to my parents'
house, but later our ways parted. He studied medicine
and afterwards went on the stage. When much later I came into a closer
relationship with him (a kind of brother-in-law-cousinship), I saw
how splendidly he had kept the bright look and the elastic
step, in good keeping with the freshness and
youthfulness that constantly show themselves in his art. At
school he was much liked, and he was admired for his
singing and his dramatic talent; but at that time I did not belong
to his circle.

One more schoolfellow is to be named, and one who became
a prominent figure in our political life, Viggo Hørup.
He was somewhat older than the rest of us and, as
the son of a village schoolmaster, felt somewhat a stranger among us,
which later gave rise to the legend that
we, as true sons of the bourgeoisie, looked down on him
as a man of the common people. There was no question of anything of the kind. And
% --- p. 30 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{30}if he himself has said anything that could support this
legend, his suspiciousness must bear the blame. In
reality we admired his gifts. They showed themselves
at school, as later in life, predominantly as criticism. He
could direct sharp attacks on acknowledged great figures in history
and in literature. I remember a debate in which he
attacked and I defended Luther. It was probably on this
occasion that in my heat I called him a Thersites,
which I often had to hear about later. At bottom I
rather liked him, and behind his criticism and his love of opposition there lay
a comradely feeling that never wholly denied
itself. There was not a little phlegm in his character, something
that is very often the case with critical talents, which
is easily understood, for they are not set in motion when
no object for criticism presents itself. But with this there was joined
in turn a bent for daydreaming, fed by dissatisfaction
with what actual circumstances offered. He was
in a certain sense the most mature of us all, the one who looked
most independently at what had been handed down, even if he could not always,
or did not care to (``gad''), shape his opposition
in definite thoughts. Later he threw himself into politics, and
then we both met and parted.

\whiteline

The last two years at school were very important for
me. A main point in this was the reading of Greek, which was conducted
with energy by Carl Berg, later headmaster of Frederiksborg
School. He was not a man of much spirit, and
his translations were not tasteful; besides, his
Jutland-Copenhagen pronunciation stood in a strange contrast to
the Greek content. But he was tireless, and he got us
to work for ourselves. He had us prepare lectures on
subjects from Greek and Latin culture. He lent us works
to get into the material. He afterwards had the lectures bound
and deposited in the drawer of the class's teacher's desk. I gave two
lectures, one on the Gracchi (we read Plutarch's Lives
of them) and one on Socrates. This last was prepared on
% --- p. 31 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{31}the basis of a volume of Grote's history of Greece, which
he had lent me in German translation. It became a two-hour
lecture and was given to both divisions of the top
class. With that the foundation was laid for my concern
with one of the greatest figures of the human life of the spirit,
a concern that has followed me throughout my whole life
up to the most recent years, and which has been of the greatest
importance to me both as a philosopher and as a human being.
We read a whole series of important Greek works in the last two
school years, from Homer, Herodotus and Plutarch, from the Anthology,
Sophocles' King Oedipus and Plato's Symposium. This last
work above all captivated me and led me into philosophical
reflection. In my student years I continued the reading of
Greek authors, and thus a good foundation had been laid
for my studies of Greek philosophy. This whole occupation became
of great importance to me, since it allowed the thought of a purely
human way of taking life, a belief in the possibility
of an independent life of personality on a human
foundation, to arise in me. But it was only very slowly
that this thought and this belief grew strong in me.
For the time being, as already mentioned, positive religious
ideas prevailed in me, and these were not only confirmed
but also sharpened in the course of my student years, as
will appear in what follows.

Besides the Greek teaching there was in the last two
school years another teaching that became of very great
importance to me. In these years we had the poet and literary historian
Kristian Arentzen as our teacher in Danish. He
was a greater poet in mind and mood than in his printed
poems. With heartfelt admiration for what was great and for the great,
he constantly had to struggle with words to express
what he felt. It was often only in single aphorisms that
he could speak of Shakespeare and Goethe, of Lessing
and Hegel, of Oehlenschläger and Baggesen. But these
aphorisms stuck in the memory, by reason of the
zeal with which they were delivered, and the enthusiasm from
% --- p. 32 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{32}which they sprang. He also had something provoking and teasing
in his nature, which perhaps wounded some, but had a
spurring effect on others. He was the first who made
me suspect that much that was current and settled
could be seen and taken in a wholly different way. On Saturday evenings
we of the top class could visit him and his wife
in their little home by Peblingesøen, and I remember
how here, together with some schoolfellows, I fought a whole
night through for Oehlenschläger's rank as a poet against
Arentzen, who already then, as later in his extensive
work on Oehlenschläger and Baggesen, was inclined
to take Baggesen's side. It was the first time
I really felt what a spiritual tournament means. In
many other questions too he awakened, directly and indirectly, the
critical faculty in me. And yet at heart he was a romantic,
if you will an epigone of the Golden Age of our literature.
But with romanticism as background, and with the security
that sprang from a heartfelt assurance that ``the Idea''
(as it was called then) or ``Spirit'' was the innermost thing
in existence, the true reality, he let his criticism
play freely. Criticism and romanticism did not enter into a real union
in him. But it was perhaps precisely for that reason
that he could mean so much to a whole circle of young people. Of
my class it was, besides me, above all Julius Petersen and
Viggo Hørup who came to be close to him, and those two stood
closer to him, I believe, than I.

Arentzen had a quite special effect through his readings aloud,
above all of Shakespeare, into whom most of us were thereby
introduced for the first time. Like several of my old
schoolfellows I always remember particular ones of his Shakespeare readings
as especially captivating, and I can still hear
his voice. A good reader in the modern, technical sense
he certainly was not. But his enthusiasm communicated itself to
us. And here too, with the introduction to Shakespeare's
poetic world, there opened a spring that right up into my old age
has refreshed me time and again.

The last year at school was, alongside what, as
% --- p. 33 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{33}just mentioned, could lift one up and point forward, a hard year.
Six hours of school and five or six hours of homework
could well tell on one's strength. I noticed already
then what I have really noticed throughout my whole
life, that my body was not suited to sitting still. My
physician and friend Julius Petersen once said to me later:
``Your constitution would be excellent if you were to
thresh or chop firewood instead of studying.'' With bodily
heaviness hypochondria was joined, and both bred
unsociability.

Now the end of the eight years of schooling at
the Metropolitan School drew near. The last month formed
a transition, in which we did the final
revision on our own. I remember this month with a certain pleasure.
It was like a foretaste of connected study,
without division into lessons, and an inner coherence came
between many things that had not hitherto been seen in their
connection. One already felt oneself a student, could
divide one's time as one wished, and in the evening drink a
glass of beer in the open air. And far off the holiday excursion
then came into view. There was talk of a walking tour in Jutland together with
Hans Skovgaard. In the midst of being absorbed in trigonometry
or in Livy, a glimpse of a
forest road or of a path over the heath could appear as in a vision.

The examination itself went like a sport. It happened so luckily
that the subject for the Danish composition was: ``To develop the significance
of the Socratic `Know thyself!'\,''\footnote[1]{As everyone read Greek at that time, the assignment had γνῶθι σεαυτόν.} This subject
I was well prepared to answer, and it did
in fact earn me the top mark. In the Latin composition there was a subjunctive I
got wrong, and I was much put out when I came home
and discovered the mistake in my draft. But fortunately there lay waiting for
me a new installment of Lembcke's Shakespeare translation,
which had just then begun to appear, and that quenched
the sorrow. --- On 15 July 1861 I became a student with distinction.

% --- p. 34 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{34}I cannot believe otherwise than that the feeling with which
one left school in those days was of a somewhat different
nature from that which stirs in the young students of our time.
Conditions were smaller then. The school was more isolated
from life than now. Nowadays one takes up at school in advance so many
ideas, views and facts that
in those days one had to work one's way toward laboriously only after one's schooldays.
And besides, there were not as
many students as now, only a seventh of what there
are now. It meant more to become a student than now, and Hostrup's
and Ploug's student songs could still be sung with a full
heart, even if misgivings were already showing over
the proclamation of lordship in the realm of spirits.

For the time being it was the freedom won that was enjoyed. We
schoolfellows had a delightful outing to the woods some days after the end.
It was before there were railways in North Zealand,
and so we hired a ``coffee mill,'' i.e.\ a five-seated
carriage, which went with us the whole day, through Dyrehaven
to Ny Holte, and from there to the Eremitage. It was the first
fresh breath after the strict time of study. Then came the Jutland tour.

It was as if it were a foreign country I was going
to. It stood quite like a fairy tale before me, as I
knew it from Steen Blicher and Carit Etlar. I had been
about a good deal in Zealand, partly on foot. The summer holidays
I usually spent with my maternal uncle at Strandegaard;
glorious times, by the way, which still stand in radiance before me!
From there I had once made a walking tour with a cousin
to Møen. But now it was a matter of a greater excursion.

So Skovgaard and I went by railway to Korsør and
from there by steamer to Vejle. For reasons of economy
we went on that same evening and spent the night in a village inn
a mile or so north of the town. The landlord here regarded us
with some suspicion. We discovered in the night that
we were locked into our room, which caused
some inconvenience, since the bedroom furnishings could by no means
% --- p. 35 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{35}be said to be complete. Perhaps the suspicion came
from our having, in the evening, as we stood talking with him
outside the inn, unfolded our astronomical knowledge
to him, but met with absolute disbelief. He
thought that all the astronomers said about the stars
was fiction and lies. How could they know anything about
the stars up there? --- The next morning we walked to
Greisdalen, where we rested in the midday hour. I had
here an inkling of what panic terror was. We had camped
in the wood, and my companion had fallen asleep. While
I now sat alone, a strange feeling of loneliness came over me,
and at the same time I had a sensation as
if I had intruded on a place where I was not
allowed to be, and as if at any moment
demonic beings might come out of the
bushes. It was surely not only classical reminiscences
that were at work, but also the contrast between the solitude of the wood
in the still midday hour and the busy life of
the town I had recently left. Even after the lapse of so
many years I can still see the scene clearly before me and call back
something of the mood. When a couple of years ago I
visited Greisdalen again, I searched in vain for the place
where Pan had threatened to show himself to me. --- In the evening
we came to Uldum, and here we celebrated the memory of Poul
Møller, whose birthplace it is. The next day the road went to
Skanderborg. It was a long day's march, 5\textonehalf{} miles, and we
were very tired when in the evening we saw the town before us and
thought we had reached our goal. Unfortunately it was an illusion,
since the road made a great bend around the Skanderborg lakes.
Our feet almost refused their service. But then we got
into a heated dispute, I think it was about the relation between
poetry and religion. It was surely one of Skovgaard's
paradoxes that had irritated me. During the discussion
the last stretch of road was covered without our noticing it,
and the next day we took a well-deserved rest. There is something
Epicurean about a day of rest on a walking tour. One enjoys
% --- p. 36 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{36}the rest as never otherwise, because one feels one has deserved
it. The desert can here, after all, be determined by the length of the road
(when this is not all too small in relation to the time
spent). Unfortunately it is not always possible to settle desert
in that way.

From Skanderborg we went to Himmelbjerget, a splendid
walk along Mossø. Up there we met our excellent natural history teacher
Fogh and had a pleasant evening together
with him. Telegraph Director Peter Faber (the author
of ``Dengang jeg drog afsted'') also came up there with his
assistants; they were on a tour of inspection. While we lay
up on ``Kollen'' (where fortunately no tower had yet been
raised), a mighty thunderstorm came up. I can still
hear Fogh say that it was surely not worth exposing ourselves
to a thunderstorm on the most exposed spot in the Kingdom. So we
all set off for Ry Inn; there was at that time no
hotel on Himmelbjerget. We were soaked to the skin and had to be
fitted out by the innkeeper before supper. Faber amused
himself at table by telegraphing to his assistants
by imitating the sound of an apparatus with his wooden shoes, and
made telegraphic fun of us before our very eyes. It was a
merry evening. We did not, to be sure, experience anything as interesting
as the hero in Steen Blicher's ``Himmelbjerget''; but it was
still a little episode on the walking tour. In the following days we lived
at a farm near Himmelbjerget and
roamed from there about the glorious countryside. By way of Silkeborg
we then walked to Hald and from there to Viborg, where we parted,
Skovgaard going to visit relatives up near
Skive, while I stayed some days with relatives in Viborg.
Viborg's old and gloomy cathedral had a strong effect on me
then. It made a more characteristic impression
than on my next visit, when it had been restored in theoretical-Romanesque
style. From Viborg I walked out to a farm a
mile or so away, where I visited a family to whom we were distantly
related. The youngest daughter, Emma Pape, I knew
from her visits to Copenhagen, and a couple of
% --- p. 37 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{37}months before I had had her as my partner at table at my eldest
brother's wedding. She was alone at home with two brothers.
I stayed there for some days. Little did I suspect that it was my
future wife I was visiting, although I was much taken
with my young hostess.

A rough steamer trip with violent seasickness from Hobro
to Copenhagen ended this glorious tour, which awakened a love
of Jutland that has never since vanished. The last
part of this unique summer holiday I spent partly
in the Sorø district with some acquaintances of my parents, partly with
my maternal uncle at Strandegaard. --- And then began
my student years ---

% --- p. 38 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\chapter*{II}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{II. 1861--1874}
\markboth{II. 1861--1874}{II. 1861--1874}
\opage{38}When as a young student I went up the stairs of the University,
it was not the first time I had gone to lectures at
the University. In my last years at school I attended for several semesters
Carsten Hauch's lectures on aesthetics. One semester
he lectured on the folk ballads, another on Ewald's
Adam og Eva, a third on a tragedy by Shakespeare.
His inquiries did not go very deep, but when he
became inspired he could say excellent things, and his
figure then became as if transfigured, as the noble upper part of the face
won the victory over the somewhat drooping lower part. I keep
a vivid memory of the mood of these lectures.
--- In my last year at school I also attended the lectures of the later
Bishop Fog on the study of theology.
They did not give me much orientation as a future
theologian. I remember only an image that was meant to illustrate
the coldness of strict science in contrast to the warmth of
faith: Athena is a lofty and noble goddess, but she
did not spring from any mother's womb and has not been suckled at
any mother's breast. This image pursued me for a long time,
until I discovered that it did not fit, because strict
science itself is an expression of the human
spirit, conceived and nourished by it. It has its mother in a
human need that is bound up with what is innermost
in the personality. But it cost much labor before
I could see the matter in this way. For the time being philosophy
and theology stood as two poles between which I felt myself stretched.
Neither of them could I let go; but how could
% --- p. 39 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{39}they exist together! Must there not, after all, in the end be
a single expression for the life of the personality? ---

It was Rasmus Nielsen and Sibbern who became my first
teachers in philosophy. Rasmus Nielsen was at that time at his
height. He was still seeking, captivated by Kierkegaard
and occupied with mathematical and scientific
studies, striving to find a way by which these different
worlds of thought could be united. His propaedeutic
lectures in my year consisted partly of a review of
Kierkegaard's ``Stadier'', on the basis of a small selection he
had had printed, partly of a short outline of the theory of knowledge.
He spoke with life and force, often with spirit and wit,
and I owe these lectures an extraordinary amount.
They set in motion a multitude of thoughts in me that
had not stirred before. Yet it went with that course of lectures
as it so often went with his books: the plan
was too large and comprehensive, or else he worked out
its first parts so diffusely that there was not
time enough for the later parts. Of the ``Stadier'' he thus
got through only the first, the ``aesthetic''. At every
possible opportunity he polemicized against theology as a science,
distinguishing sharply between faith and theology.
This polemic at first provoked my opposition.
I had come with great expectations of what the study of
theology would bring; I hoped that the isolation
in which the religious had so far stood in my mental life
would, with the help of theology, give way to a harmony between
the different spheres. I hoped to be led into
a union of the life of thought and the life of feeling, such that they supplemented
each other; I hoped that Athena and the Madonna could
be united into one. In a diary I kept in my first years as a student
I accordingly complained about those who would not
acknowledge that there is a Christian science. --- That
was soon to change.

While Rasmus Nielsen lectured on philosophical propaedeutics,
Sibbern lectured on psychology and logic. (The philosophical
% --- p. 40 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{40}course at that time took up ten hours a week. That
was perhaps too much. But one has gone too far in
limiting it to four hours, even if, now that printed
textbooks are used, not so little can be accomplished in that time. In
my opinion six hours would be suitable.) If propaedeutics
was separated from psychology and logic, it was because it
was meant chiefly to give the theory of knowledge or a general theory of science.
Rasmus Nielsen, by the way, gave much else
besides the theory of knowledge under the heading of propaedeutics; thus,
in my year, the survey of the Kierkegaardian stages.
There was a third professor, Hans Brøchner; he doubled
by turns for Sibbern and Nielsen; and in my year he lectured on
Sibbern's subject. I had chosen Sibbern, since I wished to
hear him before he retired, and since I expected much
of the author of ``Gabrielis''. He was then 77 years old.
It was a disappointment. There did come, to be sure, flashes of genius now and then,
fine thoughts and priceless remarks; but his
delivery was flat and mechanical, and his dulled senses
let him neither hear how he himself rattled his
keys while he talked, nor notice the restlessness of his listeners
and their chatter. His naïveté and his oddity could be priceless,
as when he named his ``Gabrielis'' among
``good poetic works'', or when he explained to us at length
why the four clocks of the Church of Our Lady did not keep the same time. But when,
because he was too warm on the lectern, he first took
off his skullcap and, when that did not help, his wig, one could
not demand that young people should take it with devotion.
He had outlived himself as a teacher, though his inner
life still stirred with freshness. His books were tough
to learn, all the more so since he preferred to have his own words back.
--- Only much later, when I had myself become independent in
philosophy, did I properly learn to appreciate him, and it has
been a great joy to me to bring his memory forward and characterize
him\footnote[1]{See ``Mindre Arbejder'', First Series, and ``Danske Filosofer''.}, and to help make his thoughts known
abroad as well.

% --- p. 41 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{41}In my first year as a student I also began my theological
studies, especially exegesis and church history. The exegetical
study is probably what I have had most benefit from
within theology. It accustomed one to analysis of what one
read, to exact and thorough understanding, and it gave
occasion for interesting comparisons between the New Testament
writers. And to become at home in so
great a work of the spirit as the New Testament, to be able to wander
through it crisscross and feel the connection of the thoughts
with the linguistic form, was already a great
gain, and it is above all this that has made me never
regret having studied theology, however far I have
come away from theological ways of thinking. Certainly the diffuse
German commentaries we studied were no pleasure
to get sense out of. One ploughed through a whole series of
interpretations which in the author's eyes were wrong, and
then at last reached the author's own reading, which of course
was the highest wisdom. There was a pedantry in this
that could give one a distaste for the study. And when one really reflected
that the words which were the object of so much
learning aimed at setting those who read them before
life's greatest question, the question of spiritual
life or spiritual death, then one could often be indignant at
the whole manner of treatment, all the more when one had just
read a book like Kierkegaard's ``Til Selvprøvelse''. Several times
I have flung the commentaries across the floor --- but
afterwards I went and picked them up. I meant, after all, to finish what
I had begun. ---

Through all this I nevertheless lived for the time being as a cheerful
student and had many enjoyable evenings in the old
Students' Union building in Boldhusgade in spite of its unsavoriness.
On Saturday evenings there was often ``carousing in the hall''.
One sat with one's pipe by the punch bowl; the songbook with
Ploug's and Hostrup's songs was opened, and between the songs
more or less emotional or witty speeches were made.
Debates were not held, except at general
% --- p. 42 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{42}meetings, where there was fighting to overthrow or uphold the seniorate.
In the mornings, too, one could expect to meet
comrades up there, and I had much use of the
good library.

Since there were not as many students as now, and
since they had more lectures in common, there was much occasion
to make acquaintances. I quickly came to
know the students from the Aalborg school, several of whom became
my good friends. Not many days had passed after
the lectures began before I was on intimate terms
with Andreas Faartoft\footnote[1]{Later district medical officer in Nykøbing paa Mors.}, quite a type of the young student
of that time, open and cheerful and with great zest for life.
He had a fine singing voice, which was often a joy in
my home, where he soon became a welcome guest. Another
man from Aalborg, Søren Svendsen\footnote[2]{Later head of the navigation school on Bogø.}, I also quickly made the
acquaintance of, and he and his violoncello also soon
became welcome guests in my home. My two young comrades
were regarded by my parents and brothers and sisters as belonging
at home with us whenever there was to be an enjoyable and
cozy evening. I owe them much, not least in the
following years, when I was no enlivening element
in my home, and when I myself nevertheless needed enlivening.
Faartoft later became a respected physician in his native town, Nykøbing
paa Mors, and Svendsen, who had studied physics, became
head of the navigation school on Bogø. --- A third man from Aalborg,
Poul Kierkegaard\footnote[3]{Son of Bishop P. Chr. Kierkegaard.}, I came into a closer relation with
somewhat later, and in another connection I will tell about
him and his fate. ---

On the same day I had sat the philosophicum, Norwegian
and Swedish students arrived. It was the last Scandinavian
students' meeting to be held in Copenhagen (1862).
There was great enthusiasm in the town and among the students,
and happy and enjoyable days followed, days that I
% --- p. 43 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{43}still think of as festive memories, although dark shadows soon
fell over the hopes that formed
the basis of the festive mood. I remember particularly
the excursion in North Zealand, when, after spending the night in Hillerød,
we walked the next morning along the glorious road from Hillerød
to Fredensborg. Here there was opportunity for conversation
and exchange of thoughts with the Scandinavian brothers, and one
could get information about the conditions of study at the other Nordic
universities. Already on the first
day I was quite taken with a young Swede whose name was Svartling, and
with whom I corresponded for several years. Many years later
I heard him described as a distinguished dean. At Fredensborg
we filed past through the domed hall of the palace, from whose
gallery Frederik the Seventh, surrounded by Countess Danner,
ministers and courtiers, received our homage. We marched
down into the Nordmandsdal, where a luncheon had been laid out.
But hardly had we begun to help ourselves to the dishes before
a violent thunderstorm broke loose. We ducked down under
the tables, taking with us what we could lay hold of in the way of food and
drink, especially the latter. No wonder the mood
was high when the sun came out again and we emerged once more.
A little later the King came, and in his genial way he said
that he hoped we had become just as wet inside
as outside. The excursion then continued to Helsingør.

That summer my family lived in a house on Krogerup
Allé, from which there was a glorious view over the fields to
the Sound and to Helsingborg. It is one of the best summer holidays
I have had\footnote[1]{I see from my letters to Hans Skovgaard from the summer holiday of 1862 that I occupied myself much with Aristophanes (in Danish translation), particularly in order to get clear about the relation between him and Socrates. My interest already turned on Socrates from my school days. Besides this I read Plato's ``Gorgias'' (partly in Greek, partly in Danish), Rötscher's ``Aristophanes und sein Zeitalter'', Goethe's ``Aus meinem Leben'' and Kierkegaard's religious discourses. It was the combination of these occupations with excursions in that glorious countryside that made the holidays in Humlebæk unforgettable.}. We roamed about in that glorious countryside,
now on horseback and now on foot. The tenant farmer at Krogerup
% --- p. 44 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{44}had two Icelandic horses, which he let my younger brother
and me have, and so we could get far about in
an enjoyable way. --- One day we drove to Danstrup Hegn
near Fredensborg and there saw Frederik the Seventh at the head
of his Horse Guards receive Karl the Fifteenth of Sweden,
who came driving from Helsingør and now mounted his horse,
whereupon both kings at the head of a brilliant retinue
rode to Fredensborg. This meeting of kings was thought, like
the students' meeting before it, to herald a new
time for the North. Alas, they were soap bubbles, and heavy
and dark years came for our youthful ideals.

\whiteline

There now came a heavy and dark time in my inner
life as well. I immersed myself in Kierkegaard's writings, and after
a hard struggle I had to grant that he was right in his conception
of Christianity. Christianity no longer stood as the
mild, comforting way of truth that could take up into itself all
human ways of life --- family life, art, science,
social life --- and lead them toward perfection. The idyll
was shattered. The ideal of the otherworldly came to stand in its
whole unconditional severity. Only one thing was, in the literal
sense of the word, needful: to enter into relation with the
great paradox, the miracle of God becoming man, which made all that is
human grow pale and set only one task, that of giving up
all in order to have a share in the divine powers which,
in one single place in the world and at one single point in time,
had broken through the connection of nature and of human life
and let the light of eternity shine into the darkness. Sayings
in the New Testament that I had hitherto pushed aside
or interpreted mildly and harmonizingly now came to stand in
their whole and absolute ideality. It was not the intention of Christianity
to complete what human culture had begun,
but to break off and to set aside all human
relations as indifferent, insofar as they were not hindrances
to reaching the great goal. It was as if scales fell
from my eyes when I now took up the New Testament again.
% --- p. 45 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{45}And it became clear to me that what was proclaimed there was the
highest. I cannot point to any definite moment of conversion.
It was after hard resistance that I gave up
the harmonious and idyllic faith of my early youth. That
Christianity was and would be comfort, the eternal comfort,
was true; but this comfort was bound to one condition:
full devotion to the one thing needful, full renunciation of
the human purposes of life. Only now did I really discover
that neither art nor science nor civic activity
is mentioned in the New Testament, and that there is a warning in
severe words against marriage. It was Christian ethics
that now appeared to me in an entirely new light. With dogmatics
there was for the time being nothing wrong.

How was life now to be led, after the ideal had thus
proved to lie higher than I had thought? The
time that now came brought me, it is true, moments of heartfelt enthusiasm,
but above all it brought me doubt, unrest and homelessness.
I was at my wits' end. The master, the prophet,
had after all passed away, after he had said that the Christianity of the New
Testament did not exist, if indeed it had ever
existed beyond the very first period. It was vain
to speculate about what position he would have taken
had he not been carried off so early. And besides,
he himself had taught me that each individual must solve
the problem of life in his own way, --- that one fundamentally cannot
learn from others.

And now my theological studies! I worked with zeal in
the various theological subjects, but continued my philosophical
studies too, attended Rasmus Nielsen's evening lectures regularly,
and now also Brøchner's on the history of philosophy.
