I took part in a privatissimum Brøchner held on
Kant's Kritik der Urtheilskraft. But from the purely philosophical
side it was more and more maintained that a scientific harmony
between faith and knowledge was impossible, --- that there was fundamentally
no theological science. So I went
back and forth between theology and philosophy --- also
% --- p. 46 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{46}literally speaking, since they had their lecture rooms each at its own
end of the long University corridor upstairs. There made
itself felt in me a constant intellectual discord, besides
the personal one called forth by the new conception
of Christianity.

They were the heaviest and darkest years of my life. I shut
myself up with my doubts and became unsociable and closed
toward those nearest me. However much I
loved them, I was not a good member of the family. Life in
my room and life in the living room came to stand for
me as two worlds, and I managed only all too poorly to
make the transition between them. The bright and harmonious
way in which they downstairs took everything irritated me. Just
in those years increased prosperity came into the house, and people enjoyed
in their way what it could now open access to. I was
dismissive and cold. I have many sins on
my conscience from those years, and only later have
I understood to how great a degree people had to bear
with me. My parents were, as I have later learned,
worried about me and asked my friends for advice.

Through all this there also worked a tendency to hypochondria,
which is bound up with my bodily constitution and
has followed me through life, right up into old age. Only
those nearest me have had occasion to notice this
tendency, which in the presence of strangers I as a rule find it
easy to suppress. In my book ``Den store Humor'' the
piece that deals with hypochondria (acedia) is one of the sections
built most on my own experience. Heaviness and
darkness could, without demonstrable cause, spread over the mind
and give everything a dull and misty look. For a long time
a feeling often came up as if I were hanging by a hair
that might snap at any moment. Dissatisfied
with myself, and that I accomplished nothing in the world, I often
thought that all was hopeless for me. This tendency
naturally had all the easier a time getting the upper hand as
the mind stood doubting and uneasy before the greatest
% --- p. 47 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{47}questions. What the balance of strength was between the two currents,
the one that came from bodily heaviness and the
other that came from the heaviness of the intellectual and personal problems,
I naturally cannot disentangle, and could
do so even less at that time.

But naturally it was not the case that I constantly
went about like one lost. My studies occupied me
greatly. Besides the study of my own subject, the interest in Hebrew
that had already been awakened at school led me to read Arabic
with Professor van Mehren. I got so far that I
read a couple of tales from ``Tusind og een Nat'' in
the original language, and for a while I even thought of becoming
an Orientalist, which would no doubt have had the effect of diverting me from my
absorption in philosophical and religious problems. I still read
a good deal of philosophy; in particular I followed the development
from Kant to Hegel, a period that especially at that time stood
with a peculiar luster. For not only had Kierkegaard been
strongly influenced by Hegel, but both Rasmus Nielsen and
Brøchner represented shades of Hegelianism. I also read
some dialogues of Plato in the original language. In
short, my time was well occupied.

Systematic theology I read together with Hans Skovgaard,
as a rule out at his home on Valby Bakke. Our
reading often stretched far into the night, and I then had
a walk before me in pitch darkness from the hill down through
the narrow lane that led from Langgade to Rahbeks
Allé, and straight down to Vesterbrogade, where civilization
with its lamps began. The way was not without danger, since
assaults often occurred outside the town, and since at the country house
just opposite Pilealleen (now the main building of Ny Carlsberg)
some big dogs went loose, which rushed out at the nocturnal
wanderer without his being able to see them. But it was a refreshing
walk I had out there in the afternoon.
I remember a summer afternoon when as usual I
came to read through an agreed section. I found Skovgaard's
second-youngest sister in the garden room, and she --- who was always
% --- p. 48 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{48}amiable --- showed me that day a quite special kindness
and got me involved in a long and lively conversation. Afterwards
it came to light that she was acting by arrangement with
her brother, who had not finished his assigned reading. She
often had to hear about the comedy she had played. She
was a healthy and cheerful young girl, and I often think of
her when I walk past the old Bjerregaard. Some
years ago I had her granddaughter, who very much
resembled her, among my listeners at the University.
--- It was both enjoyable and instructive to read together
with Hans Skovgaard. He was very interested,
but also very skeptical and contrary. At that time I was
fundamentally a more eager theologian than he; later it has become
the other way round. In particular he was not as eager as I to find
meaning in Professor I. A. Bornemann's often obscure words.
In my experience it is something that cannot be sufficiently recommended
to young students, to read together with comrades.
Independent thinking and criticism are developed thereby more than by
reading with a crammer, which, when the crammer is not
especially gifted as a teacher, easily takes on a mechanical character.


Besides Valby there was another place to which I often
walked out, and where I found rest and understanding. An
old uncle of mine lived in a country house in Frederiksberg
Smallegade, and his house was kept by a distant relation
of my parents, Sofie Pape, sister of the young
girl I had visited toward the end of my journey in Jutland\footnote[1]{The two sisters were daughters of the landowner H. C. Pape of the farm Heiselt in Vendsyssel. For a time he also had a tenancy near Viborg. (See above p. 36).}.
In her I found an older sister, such as I had often wished
for. She understood my interest in Kierkegaard, though
she kept essentially to his religious discourses. And
now in the winter of 1863---64 her younger sister Emma came on
a visit to her. We three came to form a little clique.
But it was soon for the younger one's sake that I came there. We
read together and we walked together. And I now thought
% --- p. 49 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{49}that I had gained a sister of my own age. That it was a feeling
of another kind that stirred in me only became clear to me
after her departure. For the time being I pushed back everything that
stirred in that direction, under the influence of the
strict religious discipline I had put myself under. And
yet, far more than I would admit to
myself, the thought of her was in those dark years a gleam of light that
kept courage and hope up. There lay here besides the germ of
something that later worked to bring me into a living
relation to life again.

The winter of 63---64 was dark and heavy for my fatherland.
People followed with suspense the events as they unfolded
after the death of Frederik the Seventh, the threatening
federal execution, the rising in Holstein and the intervention of Prussia and
Austria. Then in February the battles at the Dannevirke
and the army's sudden retreat. Grief and indignation
seized everyone, and after the fall of Dybbøl defeat stood as
inevitable. Those were bitter and dark times. But I am ashamed
to think how much, through all this, I
nevertheless was absorbed in my inner struggles and broodings and
let myself be ruled by the feeling of powerlessness that was their consequence,
without the misfortune of the country being able to rouse me to action. In
early summer, however, I decided, together with my friend
Skovgaard, to report for conscription. For some time
it thus stood before me that now everything was to be laid aside,
and it was then also clear to me that if I came back
from the war I would not return to theology.
--- Since no more soldiers were accepted, however, I went
back to my study.

I had not given up Christianity, but I made
to myself the admission that Kierkegaard (in
``Indøvelse i Kristendom'') had demanded of the representatives of the Church.
I acknowledged that I did not live under the
ethics that primitive Christianity presupposes or entails. I
recognized my distance from the ideal of primitive Christianity, although I
held fast that it was the ideal. I felt like a Catholic
% --- p. 50 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{50}who does not enter a monastery, although he admits that it is
the ideal. I thought that on these terms I had a right
to regard myself as a Christian, although I could not think
of becoming a priest.

The Church as Church could --- this I have since understood
--- not make the admission Kierkegaard demanded. It
would have been the same as admitting that it represented
a quite different religion from that of primitive Christianity,
if a religion and its ethics are acknowledged at all to belong
so closely together that they stand and fall with one another. But
the individual who makes the admission also, after all, really
avows --- this too I did not see clearly at that time --- that
he does not have the religion the Church claimed to represent.
It signified in reality a break with the Church by virtue
of one's own experience of life and thinking, and I thereby placed myself
under the principle of personality. The reach of this
dawned on me only late and slowly, in connection with
my continued experience of life and my continued studies. At
this point Kierkegaard himself, by virtue of the principle
that subjectivity is the truth, points far beyond himself.
My love for Kierkegaard and my admiration for him
have therefore been able to follow me long after I had come
away from all dogmas. It has nevertheless been said of me in German,
on the occasion of my book on Kierkegaard, by a
lightweight theologian, that I lack love for Kierkegaard
and depth of study of him. But the fact is that there are people
who do not understand a love and an admiration that do
not vent themselves in sentimental expressions, but in taking up a
problem that has been set and working at it faithfully in the way
that accords with the individual's personality. Kierkegaard's
problem has followed me from my youth, determined
the direction of my life, again and again led me to a more inward
conception of manifold relations, to a stricter testing
of myself, to a shyness of what does not have personal
truth. And while theologians and half-theologians, in the centenary
of his birth, whitewashed the prophet's tomb, I held
% --- p. 51 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{51}to the great principle of subjectivity as truth
and sought to apply it in the way that accorded with
my personality and my studies.

Purely philosophically, the study of Kierkegaard has led me to
a thought that my later philosophical study led me to deepen
and apply in detail, namely the thought that the formal
peculiarity of spiritual life lies in the unity,
the concentration, with which the content of life is gathered together,
and that the measure of the value of a spiritual life lies in the relation
between the fullness of the content and the energy of the
concentration. This thought, which has come forward in the history of philosophy
before Kierkegaard, underlies Kierkegaard's
philosophical characterization of the different stages
or types of life. This point, naturally, was not clear
to me either. It dawned on me only through a critical
study of English philosophy and through the preparatory work for
my psychology.

There was another point of view from which I was in those years
also not yet able to judge Kierkegaard's conception
of primitive Christianity. The theologians are accustomed to regard the
thought that carries the whole ethics of primitive Christianity, namely the expectation
of the imminent coming of ``the kingdom of
heaven,'' as an inessential illusion of the earliest congregation,
or they explain away the passages where it is spoken of with
particular force. And to my great astonishment I saw, when
Kierkegaard's posthumous papers were printed, that he himself
regarded the expectation as an illusion --- only that he
turned the relation around: in his opinion one could not
live by an ethics like that of primitive Christianity without that illusion:
``It is to such a degree agonizing to be the true Christian
that it would not be bearable if one did not constantly
expect Christ's return just now.'' (Efterladte Papirer.
1849, p. 248). By calling the expectation an illusion
Kierkegaard places himself in complete opposition to primitive Christianity.
From a historical standpoint the expectation is
a fact and is the constant positive presupposition
% --- p. 52 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{52}without which the ethics of the New Testament is not understood. That
I saw clearly when later I began my reading of
the New Testament over again. Yet I had already earlier
had an inkling of this connection, since already in
my student years I felt sympathy for Irvingism,
which tried precisely to build on the actual expectation
(``just now''). From the history of religion I have since learned to see
the place of the New Testament expectation in a whole series of
apocalypses or prophecies within the Jewish world.
--- But I return to my position in the autumn of
1864.

\whiteline

Besides the reason given above why I would not
be a priest, there was also another reason, which now, when
I look back, stands before me as fully as essential. I
could not imagine having to stand up at a fixed day
and hour (Sunday at 10 o'clock!) and speak about what was to me
the most inward and the highest of all. The moments in which
something of that kind stirred in me came as gifts I could not
count on beforehand and could not call forth at will. Nor
was I master of my hypochondriac states, in
which what had stood clear
and true in the good times suddenly darkened and seemed to be nothing. To this came
a shyness, I might well say a chastity, which made (and
makes) me not like to talk about what moves me
most inwardly. I have also since then all too often experienced that what
moved me most strongly in a quiet hour of preparation
made no impression when I came out with
it at a lectern.

Whatever the reason, my decision stood firm.
But since nothing was to come of service in the Church, I decided
to complete my theological studies in the course of a
year.

It was a hard year. It still stands before me in
darkness. Yet I had the experience I had already
had in reading for the university entrance examination, that there is satisfaction
in reaching the collectedness and coherence that
% --- p. 53 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{53}becomes possible by going through in a short time the whole material
that has been studied step by step. Now, too, given the
relation in which I had now personally placed myself to
theology, its whole content stood more objectively before me. My
own course of thought and my own life of mood unfolded
now on their own. I had got from theology what
it could bring me, and in quiet I looked about for
new possibilities.

Among my theological teachers I owe most, especially as regards
this year, to Hermansen. It had long since
dawned on me that his hyperorthodox interpretation
of the Old Testament was untenable, and that his
attempts to repel what he called ``the encroachments of the newer
criticism'' had failed. But I was still interested
in reading the Old Testament in the original language.
I myself taught Hebrew and had, as already mentioned,
also read a little Arabic. And as regards the last year of study,
I owe Hermansen much for his learned and
thorough review of the essays we wrote for
the exercises he held. It was the theology of the seventeenth century
that furnished the presuppositions for his expositions
concerning the topics we treated; but precisely
for that reason there was a firmness and a consistency in the line of thought
that modern theologians of Clausen's and Martensen's
school did not offer. And then it did one good to work out
something oneself, to be a little active after so much receptivity.
I still think with a certain pleasure of those
Saturday afternoons when I sat in Lecture Room No.~6 and
worked out my exercise essays. Hermansen himself
was a solid Jutlander, naïve and dryly humorous, kind and helpful.

Toward spring brighter moods came up. I
felt myself fairly master of the material and looked forward to the end
with confidence. My way of life underwent at
this time a change. Whereas before I had regarded
walks as a luxury, I now began my day with
a walk in Frederiksberg Garden, and the broad path
% --- p. 54 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{54}to the left of the entrance I seldom walk through without
thinking of the spring mood I fell into on these morning walks
when its splendid trees arched over
me. --- One morning the walk brought me a special
joy. From a comrade I met I learned that it
was Carsten Hauch's seventy-fifth birthday, and that a number of
older and younger students would on that occasion pay
him homage at his residence in Frederiksberg Palace.
I joined them, and we then went in procession into
the palace courtyard, where a song was sung, and Ploug
then made a speech to the old poet, who appeared at his
window and with emotion thanked us for our homage. I have always
loved Hauch as a poet. Some of his ``Digte og Romancer''
belong to my favorite poetry, and his sense for
the great and lofty, his noble enthusiasm for his art,
have made his figure dear to me.

From this spring dates a reform in my habits
of no small importance. I had been completely addicted
to tobacco. It was impossible for me to read a book without
having a pipe in my mouth, and if I went out the cigar replaced the pipe.
But now I began to feel disgust at it. It was probably
a slight nicotine poisoning that was on its way. From that
time on the craving for tobacco gradually fell away.
From time to time it could come back; but I, who
had hitherto been able to tolerate the strongest tobacco and liked
to take it, could now not tolerate tobacco at all. A small reaction
came when cigarettes appeared; but it lasted only a short while.
Whereas formerly anyone who came into my room could
have difficulty finding me because of the tobacco smoke,
I now had clean, good air in my study.
It was really no victory over a drive that I can
report here, for the drive fell away when it turned out again and again
that its satisfaction produced discomfort. It died of
lack of nourishment. I have not needed to apply the
self-discipline which a German friend and colleague, Friedrich
Paulsen, has told me was necessary in his
% --- p. 55 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{55}case. He set a bundle of cigars on his table and
decided that they should be the last he smoked. This
last pleasure he then put off day by day, and in the course
of a year the craving had then disappeared. ---

The examination period went by like sport, and on 19 June 1865
I walked down the University stairs as candidatus theologiæ.
In the afternoon I had the previously
mentioned conversation with my father about my future. My
wish was to take up school work and to continue
my studies. Even before I had gone
out to my family, who were staying in the country at Skodsborg, I received an offer
of lessons at ``Mariboes Skole'' (by Frederiksholms Kanal)
in history and Danish, which I had particularly thought of
as my teaching subjects. At this school I worked
as a teacher for 17 years, right until I became professor,
and I have many good memories from that time. For the time being
I took a holiday in Skodsborg, and later in the summer
I made a journey to Stockholm, from where I returned home
by the canal route via Gothenburg.

They were difficult problems that I took with me from the
period of my life that had now closed. I had kept
my personal faith, with the reservation I have described before.
But in what relation should and could this
faith now stand to whatever else occupied me in life? That was
the main question that followed me. And to answer
it, philosophical thinking was necessary. Philosophy, which
had hitherto been a subsidiary subject for me, now became a main subject.
For the answer to that question demanded an investigation
of what human knowledge is and is capable of, and in what
relation it stands to personal life. I had to
learn what the human life of the spirit is able to reach on
its own, so as then to be able to see whether a connection
between it and religious faith was possible, and on what
terms. That was the problem the Kierkegaard studies had
set before me but had not solved. I had to pursue
this question further. My future I pictured
% --- p. 56 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{56}to myself for the time being in such a way that teaching would be my
outward work, and that to it would be joined the studies
it required, --- but that I would then strive to have a
private chamber where what lay close to my heart personally
could be cultivated. That my philosophizing could have any
significance whatever for others did not occur to me.

And so after the summer holidays I began my work as a teacher.
I had been interested in historical reading ever since my school days,
and now I planned a study
of the most important historical works, from Herodotus and Thucydides
to Macaulay and Ranke. I also thought for a moment
of answering a prize essay question the University had set
on a topic from the Danish Middle Ages; but nothing
came of it. Philosophy pressed on, and as a contrast
to all the theology I had gone through, I felt
a need to immerse myself in Greek philosophy. As I wrote some
years later in my doctoral vita: ``Classical antiquity
came forward for me in a fresher and clearer light precisely
by contrast with the scholastic period I seemed
to myself to have lived through; I truly rejoiced in
reading its historians, its poets, and soon especially
also its philosophers. I thereby gained a deep conviction
of the independent significance of science and of humane
life.'' Here too Kierkegaard's guidance was constantly at work.
He had clearly held up the Socratic-Platonic
conception of thought and life as a spiritual power one
must give oneself an account of before one could, with full right and with
clear consciousness, come to a stage that was really
higher. I now read the Greek philosophical works
consecutively, and in the following years that became my main study.
In my teaching some years later I exchanged
history and Danish for Latin (in the middle forms)
and Greek (in the top forms), and there thus came a
certain connection between my life at the school and in my study.
Besides at ``Maribos Skole'' I also taught
at the ``Lyceum'' and for a short time at ``Bohrs Skole''. I was very
% --- p. 57 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{57}fond of teaching, especially in the top forms, and have
won friends there who even after their school years have
shown me faithful devotion.

\whiteline

In the autumn of 1865 the young girl Emma Pape, who
a year before had gone away as my ``sister'', came to
town again to spend the winter there. As soon as I heard
that she was coming, it was clear to me that a decision
must now come, since she was in reality
something other and more to me than a sister. I was afraid of
a decision, not only as every young man no doubt is
when he sees an Either-Or approaching, but also for
reasons connected with my religious position. I
had for my part made the ``admission''
Kierkegaard demanded, and which prevented me from becoming
a priest. But this admission did not exclude unrest
over the question whether full participation in the
interests and tasks of natural human life was compatible
with a strictly Christian conduct of life. The strong passages
in the New Testament concerning marriage, and against marriage,
I could not get away from. And there now took place, called forth
by the Either-Or that was approaching, a last
struggle within me. The seventh chapter of First Corinthians
confronted me in all its might, and Kierkegaard's ``Øjeblikke''
lay on my desk. I was not ``seeking'' in the same
sense as Kierkegaard's ``cand. theol. Ludvig From'',
but I sought, quite personally, to make clear to myself what the consequence
was of what I held fast to as the highest.
It was the most decisive turning point of my life at which I
stood. The natural, human need won, and
with that the foundation was in reality laid for my whole
later way of taking life. As I had earlier
flung the theological commentaries across the floor, so
I now flung Kierkegaard's ``Øjeblikke''. These too I picked
up again, but from now on my occupation with
Kierkegaard aimed at finding the psychological and historical
% --- p. 58 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{58}presuppositions of his appearance, and at drawing purely
human strengthening for my life by drawing the consequence
of the truth that subjectivity is the truth. ---

And so it was one afternoon in the autumn, while
I stood bent over my Thucydides, that it came to stand
before me: now or never. Without giving myself time to
close the book I hurried out to my uncle's country house in
Frederiksberg, and here, on that starry October evening,
the covenant was made which began the short domestic
happiness that was to fall to my lot [in my young
days].

My fiancée stayed the winter over in Copenhagen. In the
following five years that passed before we could marry,
she was in Copenhagen about every other year, now in my
parents' house; the other years I spent my holidays
either at her uncle's, Dean Wulff's, parsonage in
Gunderup near Aalborg, or with her parents on
their farm in Vendsyssel.

Only on reading again, many years after her death,
her letters from the time of our engagement, did it properly dawn on
me how unfortunately placed she was in those years when she
was not in Copenhagen. Her uncle and aunt in Gunderup
were good and well-meaning people. But the dean's wife
was of the old school. The whole day was taken up with
housework and needlework. Walks were a luxury, and
so was reading or writing letters. At home with her
parents Emma had more freedom to write, read and
walk; but her mother was very difficult to get along with,
and there were many painful times. Several times
Emma wished to take a position as a young lady in a stranger's house,
but I was always against it. I did not at that time really
bring home to myself how difficult her situation was.
Good times we did have, however, partly in Copenhagen, partly in summer holidays
on her parents' farm in a characteristic
Vendsyssel countryside, with a wide view over the vigorous and
hilly surroundings.

% --- p. 59 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{59}In the winter of 1865---66 a discussion was carried on in the press
about Rasmus Nielsen's doctrine of faith and knowledge as two entirely
different principles, which precisely because of their difference
were supposed to be practically and personally compatible.
I had been led to share this view through
my own personal development in religious respects, as well
as through my philosophical studies. The latter
needs a short explanation.

In this country Hegel's philosophy was still regarded around 1860
as a summit of thought. There a
magnificent attempt had been made to show that, just as in the human
mind one thought is understood only by its relation to
other thoughts, so in nature, in history, in the world of
experience as a whole, no phenomenon, no event is
isolated, but everything is connected with everything else in the most intimate way.
As one thought proceeds from another, so
one phenomenon of experience proceeds from another. And Hegel
thought it was possible to develop the mutual connection
among thoughts in such a way that it would at the same time come
to express the connection among things. From this
sprang his great confidence in pure speculation. The
human thought could not be something unique
in the world; its laws must be the laws of the world.

In this country this doctrine had been the object of searching
criticism by Sibbern and Kierkegaard. The hints
these thinkers gave of a more critical and empirical
philosophy were not heeded. For the time being
it now stood thus, that both science and religion,
each on its own, laid claim to giving an absolute solution
to the riddles of existence. For Hegel the matter stood thus,
that the religious representations contained in the form of the image
the same thing that philosophy presented in the pure form
of thought. Trusting in this view, many
Hegelians believed themselves to be in good agreement with the doctrine of the Church,
and Rasmus Nielsen for a time belonged to their number.
But there came a great reversal in his view under the
% --- p. 60 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{60}influence of Kierkegaard's writings. He broke with his former
associates, notably Martensen, and now maintained
the absolute independence of religion over against science.
They now came to stand as two different worlds, and
man had to live in both of them. This view
was attacked from two sides. Theology still demanded to
be science and saw a danger in religion being relegated
to the world of the purely personal and subjective. From
the opposite side Georg Brandes in particular came forward in various
newspaper articles and later in a small work ``Dualismen i vor
nyeste Filosofi''. I took part in the dispute in a very awkwardly
shaped work ``Filosofi og Teologi'' (1866), which in
the main was an account of the discussion that, after
the appearance of Martensen's Dogmatics (1849), had been
carried on about the relation between philosophy and theology. My relation
to the whole matter I expressed some years later in my
doctoral vita thus: ``I have always taken this view
[Rasmus Nielsen's conception of faith and knowledge]
more from the skeptical and negative side, more as a
means to a personal solution of the difficulties, than
as a positive doctrine in its own right.'' That is to say, I was more
a Kierkegaardian than a Nielsenian. Brøchner later
expressly drew attention to the opposition between
Kierkegaard's and Nielsen's standpoints. And this opposition
became (as I have shown in ``Danske Filosofer'')
more and more pronounced in the course of Nielsen's continued development
of his thoughts, until at last (in his work ``Om
Aandsdannelse'' 1877) he entirely disowned Kierkegaard and
fundamentally granted that the latter's theological opponents were right.

As far as I was concerned, the case was that I
was on the way away from theology, and that the question now was
what conception of science and of a personal view of life
I could arrive at. A new period of apprenticeship now began
for me. It was a matter of getting a foundation for my further development
both in scientific and in purely personal respects.
Of this I was naturally not conscious at that time,
% --- p. 61 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{61}but when I look back I find an involuntary striving
for a foothold. About eight years passed before such
a foothold was reached. I had to come to know the peculiar character
of the different main problems and thereby
understand both their connection and their independence.
In a short draft for a course of lectures in the autumn of
1874 on ``Indledning til Filosofien'' were contained the main features
of everything I have later set forth more or less
fully.

But I anticipate. --- My studies of Greek philosophy
concentrated, at the point in time I am now at, more and
more on a definite task, which I treated in a
work ``Den antike Opfattelse af den menneskelige Villie'',
which in the year 1870 I defended for the philosophical doctorate.
Some years before I had answered the University's philosophical
prize question (for 1867---68) and won the gold medal.
This question too concerned the human will,
since it called for an investigation of the dispute over the freedom
of the will that was carried on at one time (1824 ff.) in our
literature between the forensic physician Howitz, Sibbern, A. S. Ørsted
and others. I am not satisfied with the solution I suggested,
and the essay had, in the judgment of the examiners (Nielsen
and Brøchner), its essential significance in its thorough
characterization of the different standpoints that
had made themselves felt, of which Howitz's and Sibbern's
had particularly interested me.

From this time on I came into a closer relation with Brøchner.
When I had won the gold medal he advised me
to travel abroad, and my father then made me a present of a
journey. I wavered somewhat as to where I should
go. Alongside my other work I had sought
to orient myself regarding the development of philosophy after
Hegel's time in Germany, and here the Göttingen philosopher
Hermann Lotze had particularly attracted my attention. I
thought of the possibility of studying with him in Göttingen.
But I judged that I could come to know this subtle thinker and
% --- p. 62 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{62}witty author just as well through his books
as through his lectures, and a stay in a small
German university town would not be able to enrich me in other
areas than the purely scientific. I thought that I
would have a more many-sided gain from spending a winter
in Paris, where one could not only study, but where
art and literature and a pulsing metropolitan life offered
possibilities for a more many-sided education. I spent a
very eventful winter in Paris (1868---69), attended lectures
(among others by Taine), wrote on my dissertation, was
a constant visitor at museums and in theaters, and used my eyes
to observe life in this center of the world. Here I came
to know other directions of thought than those that stemmed
from Germany and that had hitherto had the greatest influence
on those who at home occupied themselves with philosophy. I became
particularly aware of the positivist tendency, represented
partly by the great figure of Comte, beside, and in
opposition to, Hegel the greatest systematic thinker of
the nineteenth century, partly by Herbert Spencer's bold
but magnificent generalization of the concept of evolution.
It was some time, however, before this tendency gained a more
decisive significance for me. I have always been slow
in turning. Thoughts had to ripen quietly in me
before I could work with them.

\whiteline

So far in this autobiography I have relied essentially
on my memory. But in order to give a more immediate and
documentary impression of the period of my life that is in question in this
section, I will insert some fragments of
letters to my fiancée in the years 1866 to 1870, letters I
found among her keepsakes after her death, and which --- together
with the letters from her that I had kept ---
have now, in my seventy-fourth year, made it possible for me to put
myself back into my inner and outer circumstances in those days. I
pass over family matters and other things that are of no
% --- p. 63 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{63}interest for the task I have set myself in this work. The passages from the letters
are given in chronological order.

\whiteline

30 Sept. 1866. --- If one tries to keep life going
on idyllic, contemplative harmony, one will surely
run up against reality and learn that the reconciliation was only
in thought or in fancy ... That is why I have become
a disciple of Rasmus Nielsen, because he so strongly
emphasizes the opposition between faith and knowledge. They are, after all,
two entirely different states of the soul. Faith is an ``unchanged
mind'', but knowledge belongs to the realm of contemplation.

25 Nov. 1866. --- How mildly and calmly life does not spread
out before us when we think of those to whose lot the great
struggles and temptations fell ... ``All who live godly
in Christ Jesus shall be persecuted.'' (Second Epistle to Timothy)
... For the conditions of our life to be the truth of our
life, we must surely understand ourselves before the great exemplars
and not, in unclearness, pretend that the holy sepulcher
was well guarded. What is required is humility and sincerity
... Then restoration and inward self-affirmation
will not fail to come.

1866 (the date is missing). If I seldom go to church,
it is partly because I know of no priest who is sincere
toward real Christianity. There are passages in the New
Testament that one never hears any priest speak about. It
is by no means because I believe I can be sufficient to myself
that I never go to church.

9 Dec. 1866. --- You said recently that I seldom mentioned
them at home. That does not come from my not having
lived with them, I mean not merely in outward contact, but
in real, inward living together. On the contrary, I have always felt
a heartfelt joy in them, and I believe I understand them
far better than before. A couple of years ago things were
really a little constrained for me in that respect, as you surely
know and no doubt saw yourself. I often felt so isolated and forsaken,
so different from the others. But now I am sure that
% --- p. 64 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{64}the fault must have lain with me. That there is a difference
is certain enough; but what does that really matter either, when
only the right eye is there to see it? --- I could have
become a bad one if I had been allowed to go on the way I did
a couple of years ago. But there was one who prevented
it, who made my nature more open and gentle and drove away
the coldness that for long periods could rest so heavily upon
me. It is to you I owe it that I can again go about with a free and
glad mind here at home among parents and brothers and sisters,
for whom it must often have been a torment to
look at such a killjoy as I was then. I do not mean
at all that I am quite discharged from the hospital, ---
that I will probably never be, and that is probably as it should be; but certain
it is that I become afraid of myself when I think
of how I was three years ago ...

This autumn I have come to know Marie (my sister).
The fact is probably that I have needed her more since
I did not have you. What a genuine, unadulterated,
childlike soul she is! There is gold in her, and it will stand its test.
And the test will perhaps be hard; she knows, after all, only
prosperity --- but that too is a kind of test.

1 March 1867. --- You said once at Christmas that I never
wrote anything about my studies ... So far as I can come
to clarity with myself, I am convinced that it
is the one right thing I am doing when I strive for a more
comprehensive and deeper-going knowledge and understanding in
philosophical respects. It \textit{must} lead to a goal that for me
personally will be of great importance; I feel so surely
that my life would become without bearing and wavering if I
rejected these questions and let them stand in an indefinite
mist. In that respect I harbor no doubt, although
the goal naturally often seems to hide itself from me, and I
seem to myself so powerless and so wretched. It is
another question, on the other hand, whether I shall succeed in
arriving at such a result that it would also have some significance
outwardly. One cannot get further than one's ability
reaches. But do you not agree with me that the
% --- p. 65 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{65}first consideration is the most important? (Then the practical
prospects were mentioned; I think of taking the doctorate, working
as a teacher at a school, and one day taking over one of the
private Latin schools here in town.) To become a University teacher
is something that in our small country is, after all, a sheer piece of luck, quite
apart from the demands it makes on talent and personality.


7 April 1867. --- Now I am to lose Skovgaard. You can
believe it will be a great loss to me. He is to be private tutor
with a Count Juel-Vind-Frijs on Lolland ... Then
I shall not hear his vigorous step on the stairs and loud
banging on the door, which now for so many years has announced
a dear visit to me. It is no small benefit to have someone
one can rightly call one's friend in the full meaning of the word, with
whom one can speak from the heart and feel that one is
quite understood.

16 June 1867. --- You call me ``true''. I believe that
this truthfulness in me can turn into a timidity that perhaps
slackens me not a little ... True I would indeed
be above all. This truthfulness, which is one with inwardness,
is after all the only condition for our really
being able to call anything our own ... Untruth in particular is so hard
to get at when it hides behind an inspiring
resolve.

8 Sept. 1867. --- Sometimes I have a feeling
that I am on a right way --- that is to say, on a way that
can lead me to what I believe I ought primarily to attain.

15 Sept. 1867. --- Daily life has its high points
and its great falls in respect of ideality. If
one could only hold fast to the conviction that it is by
the high points one should judge, and that the gleam that
falls from them over life is the true light in which life
is to be seen.

22 Sept. 1867. --- (About Julius Petersen). What I have often
admired as energy and strength of will in him, I believe
is really more a restless striving, which is capable of much
% --- p. 66 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{66}when the goal seems to lie near at hand, but which
collapses in on itself when patient endurance is called for.
(Because of disappointment at being passed over
in the appointment to a post as assistant physician, he thought of giving up
continuing his studies and of settling in the provinces.)
It would be painful for me to see someone in whom
I have had as much confidence as I have had
in him give way to the pressure and obstacles of life.

13 Oct. 1867. --- What I strive for, what more
and more becomes for me a matter of spiritual welfare, is to
work my way forward to a firm world-view. On that one must
of course work throughout one's whole life, but I would
nevertheless like in my youth to have carried through such a scientific
work that I could have a good foundation in it
... That is what stands before me as the work of \textit{my} life.


27 Oct. 1867. --- I always believe that it is an idyll that
is to be performed in life, and that is why things often go so badly for me.

7 Nov. 1867. --- It may perhaps interest you to
hear in what direction my reading mainly goes.
Since the question of faith and knowledge, which tormented me when I
studied theology, and which has since constantly presented itself to
me anew, led me to a closer occupation with the history of
philosophy, I gradually became convinced that
without having grasped Greek thought in its characteristic
main forms, one would not have the right idea
of what it is really about. For the Greeks had
reached the highest perfection of spiritual development
that could be reached under purely human conditions.
With Christianity faith came into the world, and new
forces were set in motion, but everything we have of
human \textit{forms of culture,} points in its main features
back to the Greeks. I have therefore already for half a year
been occupied with Plato and Aristotle, and if I
succeed in carrying out my plan, I will one day use
a topic from there for a doctoral dissertation. Alongside this
% --- p. 67 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{67}I am busy with history and Icelandic, which I need
for my teaching.

14 Nov. 1867. --- Lately I have read a good deal
aloud from Shakespeare, especially on Sunday evenings, and also --- which
is a great pleasure --- heard Poul Kierkegaard read. About
a fortnight ago he, Troels Lund and I sat here
one evening reading Shakespeare until the clock was almost
one, without our being aware of it.

24 Nov. 1867. --- A change that has taken place
in me this autumn consists in my no longer being able to
agree with Rasmus Nielsen, to whom, as you know, I had
before on the whole attached myself. Partly a wavering in him
himself, partly a telling criticism by Professor Brøchner, partly
and above all a renewed testing of the matter itself (not
least in conversations with Poul Kierkegaard) has shown me the
untenability of his view. Yet I have not thereby been led
closer to the ecclesiastical ... On the contrary, it has at the
same time dawned on me that on several points I held
opinions that had no true root in me, but
clung on as something external and handed down. Christianity
will --- of this I am fully and firmly convinced --- always
be to me the highest truth, the one in which alone I can
find the riddles of life solved. But only what I can personally
experience and appropriate can be truth for me; and I have come
to the conviction that whatever one thinks one
possesses that goes beyond that rests on unconscious hypocrisy.
The view whose untenability I have now come
to see has naturally not been without significance; it
was a stage of development that had to be gone through.

18 January 1868. --- Almost the whole of the new year I have
been so listless and hypochondriac that I have often been
at my wits' end ... It is never something outside me that I need
in those states; it is collectedness and clearing, and above all
strength to keep myself under the proper discipline,
that is lacking.

(From the year 1868 there are not many letters, since we were
% --- p. 68 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{68}together in Copenhagen from March on, until at the beginning
of December I went abroad.)

19 June 1869. --- (About ``the period that lies before
my engagement and even partly extended into it'').
I have sometimes called this period my sentimental
period, and with a certain right, but more correctly, I believe,
it is designated by calling it the ascetic period. Happiness
and joy then stood before me as unentitled
or at least suspicious guests at the table of life.
Penance and renunciation were the main thoughts on which my view of life
rested. I do not say that at that time I lived in every respect
as an ascetic; but the corresponding anxiety was
present nonetheless ... Had I lived in a Catholic country, then I would,
at any rate at certain times, not have been far from
the monastery ... If I have become more free, unprejudiced and independent,
I have also become more humble than I was then.

11 July 1869. --- This day has been good to me. I
have truly experienced what a joy it is to busy oneself with a piece of work
that lays claim to one's interest. It is a spiritual
necessity of life. However modest what one accomplishes may be,
there still come moments when one can have
the consciousness: I too have felt the great thoughts on
which existence rests, and by which it is carried forward toward
its goal. Even if I am not among those to whom it is given to
grasp these thoughts and set them forth in a new and awakening
form, my enthusiasm has nonetheless not been less. O,
if one could only once truly collect oneself, truly concentrate all
one's powers and push every hampering power aside!
Perhaps there might after all be a stone that it could fall to my lot
to add to the great building.

18 August 1869. --- We have both, each in our own way,
worked our way forward to greater clarity and firmness ... I
have often noticed with astonishment how you saw things
in the same way as I, and I am thinking then especially
of the freer religious views that gain more and more
significance and truth for me.

% --- p. 69 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{69}26 June 1870. --- We now stand at the end of our engagement.
How much has not been experienced and lived through
in that time. I really believe it is only now that I have
become properly independent and so a real man ... Independence
consists in things no longer unrolling themselves
before thought like a panorama, but in one's taking a hand oneself
to bring forth what is true and eternal.

\whiteline

In keeping with my plan of going into school work I applied
again and again for posts as an assistant master, and it was a
disappointment to me that I did not succeed in getting such a position,
since I now wished to set up house. Yet it would
probably then have turned out that I had had to give up
continuing my studies on the scale I had intended.
And after I had defended my dissertation for the doctorate in February 1870,
I applied for and received the Smith Scholarship, which
I could expect to keep for some years if I
continued my studies. On that, and on the income from my
school teaching, together with an allowance from my father, I married
in the autumn of 1870.

In the spring semester of 1871 I began to lecture as a privatdocent
at the University. My effort to orient myself
within the philosophy of the day led to the publication
of two books, ``Filosofien i Tyskland efter Hegel'' (1872) and
``Den engelske Filosofi i vore Dage'' (1874). Through a critical
examination of English philosophy, especially as it was represented
by Mill and Spencer, I was led to see the significance
of a thought that had lain behind Kierkegaard's
philosophizing and had been consciously brought forward still earlier
by Kant, namely the thought of the unifying and unity-seeking
character of human conscious life. Later
I drew from this the hypothesis I made the basis
of my psychology. In the autumn of 1874 I gave a course of lectures
on ``Introduction to Philosophy,'' in which, from the
standpoint thus won, I characterized the various
philosophical problems. From this time on it became
% --- p. 70 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{70}gradually clear to me that the chief task of philosophy is to show
how that fundamental peculiarity of human
mental life manifests itself in the various domains
of human thinking. My philosophy, if I
may use that word, became a doctrine of problems, that is to
say, of tasks that are determined by the interaction between
the manifold of observations and the unity-seeking
need and power. A closed system could not come
out of this. On the contrary, through new observations and
new energy of thought it must constantly set itself new tasks. The point
is only to show that everything that becomes a problem for the
human spirit bears its stamp and is determined by
its nature, whether or not the problem can be solved once
and for all. For me this has been a fruitful working hypothesis,
and for over 40 years I have sought to apply it to
a series of questions. I have found that it was not only
in intellectual respects that this standpoint was satisfactory
(though people have sometimes found it too
skeptical or too subjective), but that here there was also
the possibility of the harmony between science and personality
that I had sought so long. For in purely personal matters too
the point is, after all, to bring a whole out of the manifold
of experiences, impulses, and thoughts that makes up the content of our
inner life. The sharp opposition between science
and personality thereby falls away. Science is
itself a personal labor, sprung from the innermost need
of personality. And on the other hand there is nothing in
personal life that could not be made an object
of scientific consideration, at any rate of historical
and psychological inquiry.

Given this relation between science and personality
it becomes both unnecessary and impossible to harbor fear
that science should lead to results harmful
to personal life. And just as little is there reason for lyrical
proclamations that there is nothing above and nothing
beside science. Science does not let itself be frightened,
% --- p. 71 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{71}but it is too serious a matter to be the object of a
lyricism that is not backed, point for point, by work.

For my part it became from this time on more
and more clear that what was to support me in life could not
be something outside me, but had to be something
that made itself known in me, in the very best and clearest thoughts
I could win, in the very best and purest striving
that could lay claim to me. The point was not
a sight but an eye that could see, --- a central power
within me, built on experience of life and testing in thought,
--- an inner home, a chapel, built up of everything that
could give life value. The standard of truth
and of value had to be drawn from our own innermost being,
and it is in reality from there that science draws
it, without always being conscious of it. Every image, every
form, every concept by whose help we are able to
interpret this innermost, which is at the same time the highest, and by which we
try to make it an object for us, can have only symbolic
significance, and here lies the boundary between scientific
thinking and poetic analogizing.

\whiteline

In the summer of 1872 my wife and our little son traveled up
to her home in Vendsyssel, and I was to follow as soon as
the school holidays had begun. While I was thus
in my solitude, a catastrophe befell one of
my friends, to whom in younger days I had looked
with great expectation.

Poul Kierkegaard, son of Bishop Kierkegaard and nephew
of Søren Kierkegaard, has been mentioned a few times
in the foregoing. We had matriculated in the same year,
and our theological studies also brought us together, especially
after I had begun to frequent the house of his uncle, Troels
Lund's father. He was quite certainly unusually gifted,
even if it would be difficult to say in what
direction his gift really lay. In a letter from the spring of
1867 I write to my fiancée about him that his
% --- p. 72 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{72}development is advancing with vigorous and sure steps, and that he
evidently has the makings of a great thinker. He was living
at that time with his parents in Aalborg, and the letters
I received from him show independence and originality.
He himself thinks, however, that it would come more naturally to him to develop
his ideas in poetic form. But I think he has
more mood and reflection full of mood than imagination.

Alas, it was to go quite otherwise than I had
thought. --- Poul Kierkegaard had been strictly brought up.
His mother's nervous debility and his father's heavy temper made
his childhood joyless and cowed. In his student years he was
strongly stirred in spirit, partly religiously, partly poetically, and at the same time
his reflection was sharp and penetrating. It was
very rewarding to associate with him, and I owe him much
from that time. The fable that it was his uncle's
fame that weighed on him I can firmly reject. The chief reason
for his ruin as a human being I find
partly in the violent reaction with which the craving for freedom,
sensuality, and passion forced their way out after
the constraint of his childhood years, partly in what I have already hinted at in
the letter of 1867 quoted above, namely the indeterminate in his gift.
He could not settle into patient labor of thought,
and he did not have imagination enough to become a poet. He
was thrown back and forth, did not get into a work that
could become a spiritual home for him. He would have been best
suited to be a clergyman, for he had a rhetorical sense and interest.
He loved to declaim, and Virgil, who was one of his
favorite poets, he could read aloud with enthusiasm in long
passages. But a clergyman he unfortunately could not become,
since his views became more and more heretical, and other
use for rhetoric there is, after all, none under our conditions,
apart from politics and the practice of law.

He took his theological degree the year after me, and at
his father's wish he then went home to Aalborg. Here I visited
him several times when in the holidays I came to Gunderup
Parsonage, two Danish miles from Aalborg, or to my
% --- p. 73 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{73}parents-in-law's farm in Vendsyssel. In the old Bishop's Residence
one lived as in a cloister. The bishop's wife never came out of
her rooms and only sent down her greetings, accompanied by
bouquets, to the guest. All day long one heard the
old bishop walking with heavy steps up and down in his room.
At meals he liked to tell and hear witticisms
and droll stories. This breaking loose covered
over the deep melancholy and the Old Testament
cast of mind that prevailed in him. Between father and son
a distance arose as soon as the son's heresies, and probably
also his want of self-control, began to show
themselves. The bishop declared to me that he could have nothing
to do with a person who lacked self-control to such a degree.
For a long time I was then the go-between between father
and son, no easy matter between two such natures. I
imagine, moreover, that the bishop thought he saw in his son's apostasy
the effect of the curse that, according to his
and his brother's belief, rested on their family. It became a
misfortune for the son, for he loved and admired his father,
and had the father been able to open himself to Poul and show him the
love that in spite of everything lived in the father's heart, perhaps
much would have turned out otherwise.

I remember a summer day when Poul and I were sitting down
by the Limfjord, a little outside the town. Then he asked me
whether I would advise him to propose to a young lady in Aalborg
who, he believed, cared for him. I naturally answered him
that the very fact that he asked my advice showed that he
was not himself sure of his feeling. Whether he saw in her
the possibility of a rescue for himself, I do not know. But from
what I knew of his nature and tendencies, I did not dare
take on myself the responsibility of intervening here. Those nearest him
saw a means of rescue in the young girl. Once,
after Poul had gone away on a little excursion, it was arranged
that I should take her in to dinner at a party at the Bishop's Residence,
so that I might form an opinion of her. She
was fresh and healthy, childlike and cheerful, and I thought
% --- p. 74 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{74}excellently of her. But I saw the great contrast in
temper and in need, and I could give no advice. A
year or so later, when Poul was living in Copenhagen and had fallen
into all manner of dissipation, the young girl came with her
parents to Copenhagen. She had, according to what was written
to me by a lady in the bishop's house, traveled over in
glad expectation, but came back disappointed and grieved. ---
A few years ago she was still living, unmarried, in Aalborg.

Against his father's wish Poul went over to Copenhagen and
meant to make a living there by teaching. Some
time later he got into Borch's College. In the first
years we saw a great deal of each other. He, Troels Lund, and I read
Plato together, and our sessions usually ended with Poul
reading Shakespeare to us; he was especially fond of the Falstaff scenes.
He could be brilliant and full of wit when he was really
in form. But soon his time went mostly in carousing and
revelry. He used up his money at the beginning of the month
and then starved for the rest. He would come with
a wolf's hunger to my parents' supper table, or later to
my own home, and then it was masses of food and drink
he could put away. My wife liked him,
and she thought it a pity when I wanted to set a limit
to the toddies she might give him. He could also
be magnificent in wit and humor when, with long
strides, he paced up and down the floor, puffing with all his might at
his cigar (and at the same time constantly tapping the cigar, so that
fine ash was strewn over the whole room). But he was on
an inclined plane. One summer Sunday in 1872 he came up in
the forenoon home to Borch's College without a hat, after
having been away a whole day and night. The Inspector of the College stepped
in. The doctor declared that he must go to a lunatic asylum,
and a couple of days later I accompanied him down to Oringe.
It was a dismal moment when we drove in through the hospital gate
and Poul exclaimed: ``Ye who enter, abandon all
hope!'' The chief physician declared that he had long been expecting
him, after what he had heard of his conduct, which
% --- p. 75 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{75}pointed to acute dementia.
I believe it comforted Poul that
he could be regarded as ill. He stayed at Oringe
a couple of years. After that he vegetated in Aalborg. He had
some small occupations, but real work he never
took up. In his old age he was cared for with touching
solicitude by a lady who had kept his father's
house in the latter's last years. The last times I visited
him he had had strokes, but was nevertheless fully
clear in mind and could remember many a thing from old days.
There was a sadness about him, as there was sadness in the
old friend who stood by his bed. With him the male line
of that remarkable family, which reached so deeply into Danish
intellectual life, died out. --- Poor Poul! ---

\whiteline

I return to the summer of 1872. When I had come
back from Oringe, I set out on a journey to Jutland
to join my family there. I wished to use
the occasion to see the part of North Jutland I did not yet
know. I sailed to Aalborg and from there went down
the fjord to Aggersund, and from here began a little walking tour.
I walked through Hanherred up to the North Sea. I
drove part of the way with a man who had fetched some
children from the steamer. The young horses that were in harness
took fright at the rattling chains on some harvest wagons
and broke into a gallop across the embankment the road ran
along, and down into a potato field, where all of us passengers
were scattered among the potato plants. It happened in an instant,
and when I came to myself and got up, I saw the
various children and grown-ups crawling up all round the
field. Fortunately no one had come to harm, nor
the horses and the wagon either, and we continued the drive a little
further, until our ways parted. I stopped to rest at Fjerritslev Inn
and, while I rested, read in Spinoza's letters, which I
had with me in a pocket edition. Again and again I had
immersed myself in that profound thinker; but it was only
now that the whole, as it were, crystallized for me. Of course
% --- p. 76 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{76}I have not become a Spinozist in the literal sense;
one cannot be that nowadays; but from that
time on I have often repeated Lessing's words about Spinoza: if I am to
name myself after anyone, then I name myself after him! ---
To enjoy a walking tour properly also requires being able to let
thought or imagination dwell on significant subjects. For
many years I carried a little book with me, in which I
had copied out reflections and poems I was especially fond of.
But concentrated reading of a page or two in a
profound book is also a good use of part of the
time spent resting. Then later, when the march
has begun again, one lets the countryside, with its cornfields,
woods, and hills, and with the clouds above, work on one
with all the more life and freshness. My way led up toward
Bulbjerg and Skarreklit, which I reached in the early evening.
The North Sea was throwing its waves up against the solitary
rock out there, and behind the silk-blue, foaming sea
the sun was sinking toward its setting. I continued my walk
along the coast to Torup Strand, where I enjoyed hospitality and
got a night's lodging with the beach bailiff. It was still in the time when
one could take refuge in the hospitality of strangers in
these lonely regions. The next day I set off at 6 o'clock and walked
the whole day along Jammerbugten, in splendid sunshine
and a strong wind, which made the waves beat high over the
wrecks that stood at the water's edge. The whole day through
one and the same illusion of the senses repeated itself: a piece of wreckage
sticking up out of the sand I constantly took for a human being, although
I saw again and again that it was a mistake. I have used this
example in my psychology. In the evening I came, tired and
hungry, to Blokhus, after having made a detour on the way
into the lovely Fokkedal, whose shade and luxuriant
green growth formed a contrast to the sunlit beach
I had walked along the whole day. Never has a supper
and a night's sleep done me so much good. The next day
I rested, and in the afternoon I got a one-horse carriage
to drive me to Brønderslev, where I spent
% --- p. 77 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{77}the night, so as to walk the next day to my parents-in-law's
farm, where I found wife and child in the best of health.


Every such walking tour I have made has let
me live myself more inwardly into the nature of our country, feel myself
one with it, on its sandy coasts, in its luxuriant
woods, and among its hills. Before and after the time I
am speaking of here, I have walked through North, South, and West Zealand,
Møen, Bornholm, southern Funen, and great stretches
of Jutland. The nature of Jutland especially, as I
have already said, I love, and a summer holiday does not seem
normal to me if I have not renewed my acquaintance
with it. Vendsyssel with its wide views,
its hills, meadows, and streams, Mid-Jutland with heaths and
woods, heather and bogs, West Jutland with dunes and roaring surf,
East Jutland with the glories of Aarhus Bay and Vejle Fjord
--- all this not only gladdens me while I go about
there, but images in memory from these regions often come
back in my fancies. In Steen Blicher's short stories it is not
least his splendid descriptions of nature that have made him
one of my favorite poets.

\whiteline

When, after this Jutland excursion, I return to my
life in Copenhagen, there is one figure who stands out for
me in my memory of the years around 1870. It is Hans
Brøchner. I had come into contact with him in the summer of
1867, when, after hearing me speak as opponent
at a doctoral disputation, he sent me a kind and encouraging
greeting. From that time on I visited him often. I
received advice from him regarding my study of the history
of philosophy, and when I had written a critical review
of one of his books, he sent me his rejoinders
and asked me to come one evening and discuss them
with him. In the following years, until his death (1875), I visited
him regularly once a month in his
lonely home, where he lived as a widower with his
% --- p. 78 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{78}two children. He associated with none of his contemporaries, with the exception
of the friend of his youth, Privy Councillor Vedel. Of younger men
only Georg Brandes came to him besides me, after his
closest disciple, the amiable and gifted Kristian
Møller, had died. When one visited him, it was as a rule
not philosophical subjects that came up. In his
solitude he felt a wish to hear news from the academic world
and from the rest of the world. I still see him sitting in his
rocking chair or pacing up and down the floor with his characteristic
long and decided strides. His unusually handsome
face could then shine with goodwill and interest. Often he told
of his travels or of his young wife, who had died
early. Of Costanza, the young Italian woman he had
been in love with in his youth, he never spoke to me;
it was only when I published his letters that I came to know this
episode of his life. In the letters it appears,
as he describes it, as a romance full of mood.
It seems to have been a father confessor's intervention
that prevented him from bringing Costanza up to the North.
It would surely also have been a hazardous venture. ---
When one stood up and wished to take one's leave, he became
especially lively and had many things to ask and talk about;
it was as if he was loath to let go of the few links that connected
him with the world around him.

He was a philosophical hermit. The circle of thoughts
he had made his own was his spiritual home. He did not have
much ability to communicate himself in free form, varying
his expressions according to situations and personalities, and
he had once and for all summed up his ideas in definite,
very abstract forms. But both in lectures
and in conversation there could come a quivering in voice
and expression, a sign of the deep feeling
that lay behind and bore witness to the connection of thought with
the whole personality. He was a knight of thought, the last
representative among us of the idealism that, in confidence
that the innermost of existence could find and had found
% --- p. 79 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{79}expression in the form of thought, also found in this form
expression for the highest longing of personal life. For those
who followed after him in the field of philosophy the problems
have become more complex and manifold. In one of his
last lectures Brøchner declared himself an adherent
of ``the idealistic philosophy that Germany has the honor of
having produced,'' and there can hardly have been many in whom
the chief thinker of this philosophy penetrated and
ennobled the personality to such a degree as in him. The image of ``the quiet
professor,'' as he has been called, has followed me on
my way and reminded me what value the life of thought can
have, even beyond the purely intellectual domain, when
there is earnestness in the work of thought. His friendship was to me
an honor and an encouragement, and it was with deep emotion
that I took leave of him on his deathbed. It was the day
before he died that I saw him for the last time. He spoke with
complete calm of his departure, and arranged with me the settling
of various matters. When he bade me farewell and thanked
me for my friendship, I was more overcome than he.
His housekeeper related later that he had said
quite calmly, when I had gone: ``Take that glass away, for Dr.
Høffding's tears are in it.''

A little myth formed, after he had died, about
his last moments. He died on 17 December (1875)
toward afternoon, that is, in the darkest time of year. Among
the last things he said was: ``We must have light in here.'' In
the time just after his death I heard from several quarters
that he was supposed to have cried out for light, and there were those who
added that it was no wonder that that man
cried out for light! --- The myth, however, seems to have died a natural
death. For a time it got some nourishment from what happened
at his funeral. At that time no purely civil
funeral was possible. He had wished to be buried
from the University, and that a colleague should speak; but if
that could not be done, he had named a particular
clergyman, who had spoken over his young friend Kristian
% --- p. 80 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{80}Møller and had shown great tact on that occasion. But the clergyman
in question seems to have misunderstood the situation and read
more into the deceased's very conditional wish than was
justified. I thought of correcting the misunderstanding,
but gave it up when Brøchner's oldest friend, Privy Councillor
Vedel, firmly advised against it.

In the preface to my edition of the correspondence of Brøchner and Molbech
and in ``Danske Filosofer'' I have given a characterization
of Brøchner as a personality and as a thinker,
and my work ``Den nyere Filosofis Historie'' I have dedicated
``To the memory of my teacher and friend.''

\secrule

If I were to try to describe my home life after I
had set up house, I would face the same difficulty
I have mentioned earlier with regard to
forming a clear picture of those nearest to one. The few years
in which this home life lasted stand for me as an enclave
in relation to the rest of my life. Not as if it was a pure
idyll. Looking back, I call myself to account
for many an hour when despondency and low spirits, which did not
always have deep-lying causes, fell on the one I
least of all wished to grieve. But I was borne with,
here as in my old home. And we developed side by side,
as had already begun in the years of our engagement.
My wife was naturally not at home in what occupied me.
But when I succeeded in finding an expression for the human
and personal side of the subjects my studies
concerned, it was taken up with joy and understanding. I have
always found it comic when wives simply took on
their husbands' opinions, especially when they, as is not seldom
seen, come forward more dogmatically and didactically than their
male halves. And I dare say that my wife had
such a sense for what is genuine and self-acquired, and at the same time
such tact, that she went along only with what she could make
her own by the way of her own experience and reflection.
And in the land of poetry we could meet as in a common
% --- p. 81 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{81}world.
I read Homer and Plato to her or with her,
Shakespeare and Molière, besides the authors of the day, in the
first place Bjørnson and Ibsen. I remember especially how
taken she was with Homer. Many an evening, when the question
was what we should take up, she said: ``Let us
have something about the godlike heroes!'' Our family devotions now became
poetry. In the years of our engagement it had been the Bible in
its capacity as dogmatic authority. Hand in hand we had
wandered over from the land of dogmas to the land of symbols and
poetry. Now too we read the Bible, but as great poetry of life.

Glorious summer journeys we made together, to Møen, to
Aarhus and the Silkeborg country, or we met at her parents'
farm in Vendsyssel, she traveling ahead and I
usually making a little excursion, partly on foot, and ending up with
her and her family. I have mentioned the walk along
Jammerbugten. Another time I went to Skagen. That was
in the summer of 1875. Skagen had then just been discovered
by Drachmann. No hotels and villas yet waged war
on free nature. One drove by mail coach from Frederikshavn,
partly right along the water's edge, and from the post station
one had to wade through deep sand to the thatched inn.
Here I stayed almost as the only guest; a man of the Inner Mission
was staying there too. So I could go about undisturbed in the world of
sand and sea. The return journey I made by carriage
to Frederikshavn, and from there I walked the glorious road
along the shore, with the Bangsbo hills on my right hand, toward
Sæby. That bright summer afternoon still stands clearly
in my memory, and not least the moment when, a little outside
Sæby, I met my wife, who had driven out to meet me. ---

In Copenhagen we associated first and foremost with Julius
Petersen and his wife Oliva, née Munch. He was now practicing
in Nørrebro and quickly got a large practice, not
least in the poor quarters. He was restlessly active, and
already now began his studies in the history of medicine.
When he came home from sick calls in poor homes,
he could be indignant at the luxury he thought he saw in their
% --- p. 82 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{82}very meager homes, and he could sit sunk
in low spirits and discontent. But then suddenly
quite another mood could come up, and often, when we thought
the barometer stood low, an invitation could come to
take part in a little gathering. Against his restlessness and his
many fluctuations Oliva's levelheadedness, clear
understanding, and firm will were of good use. As the flock of children
grew quickly, there was enough for her to do. And always
she kept her house running well, so that it even became a gathering place
for his friends. Here we met with Kristian
Arentzen, Viggo Hørup, and Holger Drachmann and their
wives, and in many and long speeches at the festive supper table
the many questions of the time were discussed. --- Troels
Lund I had made the acquaintance of in my student years.
From philology he had gone over to theology, and after
his examination he took up, as I did, studies of
Greek philosophy and defended (1871) an interesting
dissertation on Socrates. Later he went over to historical
studies, occasioned by an appointment in the Rigsarkiv (the Geheimearchiv,
as it was then called). Troels Lund's fine,
harmonious personality was a pleasure to associate with, and
his lively wife, together with him, made their home
a place where we liked to come. And in those days one could
also have the pleasure of being surprised by a visit;
it was so pleasant when Lund and his wife came
and settled in for the evening, making do with what
the house could offer. --- To Heegaard's home too many
good memories point back. At my doctoral disputation
he was opponent, and from that time on we came to be close
to each other. After breaking with Rasmus Nielsen he
was in a searching state, taken up with eager study of Kant
and the more recent English philosophers; he also occupied himself
a great deal with mathematics. As his financial circumstances
were straitened, he had to take on wearing extra work.
Among other things he wrote anonymously a series of novels, in which
he was strongly influenced by Dickens. For some years they found
% --- p. 83 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{83}a fairly large readership. He also took on office work at a publishing house
for a time. Heegaard was, in his vigorous period,
open and jovial, full of mockery of all manner of dogmatists;
the clergy he liked to call bonzes. He declaimed
perhaps a little too much against dogmatism instead of
immersing himself, by his own activity, in positive work. But it
was fruitful and encouraging to associate with him. And in his
home his wife had a refreshing effect through her clear and
cheerful bearing in the most varied circumstances.

Outside this narrower, personal circle of friends, the
collegial life among the teachers at Mariboe's
School played a large part for me in these years. The headmaster, old Neve,
as he was usually called, was a man of what was then
called the old school. He was a man of feeling,
and a patriarchal relation prevailed between him and
his teachers, which was not dissolved even when the radical
taste for discussion of the time also found voice at our teachers' meetings.
A young radical thus raised in all seriousness the question
why one should really arrive punctually for one's
lessons. When the person in question kept on making difficulties
and objections, Neve said afterwards to one of the teachers:
``N. N. is surely under some pressure; if it is money he needs,
I will gladly help him; but won't you question
him --- if I do it myself, he will be offended.'' He often gathered
his teachers in his home for pleasant get-togethers.
He was fond of a good glass, and there was a festive mood
on such occasions, as also when we teachers
held a party at shared cost and invited him. It was a new
student life I enjoyed in these years. Among the teaching staff were
Schandorph, Otto Borchsenius, Carl Michelsen, Kaper (later
senior master at the Metropolitan School), Frederik Nielsen
(later professor and bishop), Archivist Feilberg, and others. The
questions of the restless time could give rise at our teachers' meetings
to violent clashes. I especially remember a meeting
that Neve had called to talk with us about
how the teachers should stand toward the religious and
% --- p. 84 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{84}social questions that had come up so strongly at the beginning
of the seventies. It was maintained on the side of the orthodox (Fr.
Nielsen and Kaper) that a teacher's faith or
unbelief must show itself in his teaching,
even if this concerned writing or German grammar. That
was to give the rest of us the choice between hypocrisy and agitation.
The orthodox believed they had old Neve on their side,
because he maintained that the Christian spirit should pervade
the school. But when from the other side
a closer explanation was asked of what the Christian spirit was,
he answered that he was thinking chiefly of monotheism and
morality --- whereby he also answered the question
of how the school should stand toward the Jews,
who made up about a third of the school's pupils. The
