orthodox pulled rather long faces at this explanation.
For the rest, the whole question found its natural settlement
in the simple pedagogical rule, which was surely
followed by all of us, that one should not in school bring forward problems
that there is not yet maturity to deal with.
There is, moreover, occasion enough in the school subjects themselves to
dwell on the purely human and its significance; then
it must be left to the later personal development of the young
whether they can get through life by keeping
to that, or whether they need something that claims to go beyond
it. ---

The circle I moved in at Maribo's School coincided in
part with the one that gathered around Kr. Arentzen.
The subjects of discussion in Arentzen's circle, --- to
which, besides Julius Petersen, Hørup, and me, also
Schandorph, Borchsenius, Carl Michelsen, Drachmann, and
Schwanenflügel belonged, --- were connected directly or indirectly
with Arentzen's own personality, since they turned
on the relation between romanticism and criticism, to which now also
was added the relation between romanticism and realism. Arentzen
had worked so strongly on us partly by his provocative
criticism, partly by the background of something great and
% --- p. 85 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{85}infinite that seemed to stand behind him. It was this union
that conditioned his awakening influence. When in
the year 1872 he was to travel abroad to be away for a
year, we held a farewell party for him that stands as a shining
memory for me. Drachmann had written a splendid song
and read a beautiful poem aloud. We vied with one another in expressing our thanks
for all that we owed the guest of honor. Kaalund, Arentzen's
old friend, was present and read an excellent poem,
which is printed in his collection of poems ``En Eftervaar'' under
the title ``Ved en Vens Afrejse til Udlandet,'' and in which he
aptly characterizes Arentzen, especially in the following lines:

\begin{quote}
The homage I bring you here today\\
is a debt I have owed you so long.\\
So long --- yes, since the youthful years ---\\
I think since our first meeting,\\
for no one so well as you knows how\\
to help others to give birth.
\end{quote}
% Den Hyldest, jeg bringer dig her idag,
% er en Gæld, jeg har skyldt dig saalænge.
% Saalænge --- ja, fra de unge Aar ---
% jeg tror fra vort første Møde,
% ti Ingen saa godt som du forstaar
% at hjælpe andre at føde.

\begin{quote}
We know it, who know your bright spirit:\\
on the banner that you have raised,\\
that from youth you have boldly held in your hand,\\
there stands ``Excelsior'' written:\\
Upward and onward and always up! ---\\
Your aim is as high as the goal!\\
It beckons you like an Alpine peak\\
above the fog and the bawling of the day!
\end{quote}
% Vi véd det, som kender din lyse Aand:
% paa den Fane, som du har hævet,
% som fra ung du kæk har holdt i din Haand,
% der staar „Excelsior“ skrevet:
% Opad og fremad og altid op! ---
% Dit Sigte er højt som Maalet!
% Det vinker dig som en Alpetop
% over Døgnets Taage og Skraalet!

Arentzen had grown tired of school life and used the
occasion that the closing of some classes offered to take his
retirement on a waiting allowance, and after that he and his
wife went away to spend a year or so in southern Germany. Before that
an attempt had been made to bring him into contact
with Georg Brandes, around whom, after his return
from a long journey abroad, a circle had begun to
gather. The attempt failed. At a gathering that
was arranged, Arentzen made a speech that was somewhat long-winded;
--- making speeches was on the whole not his forte. He impressed on them
that, even if one struck out on new paths, one
% --- p. 86 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{86}must not give up piety toward the old, still less mock it.
The speech was unfortunate in its form and met only with mockery from the
other side. One had to know Arentzen well to understand
his conduct, and it was in itself not strange
that people were ill pleased at being admonished to consideration
when on so many occasions such inconsiderate methods
were used by those who came forward on behalf of the
old.

When Arentzen came home from abroad, it was more and
more a romantic conservatism that gained the upper hand in
him. And he was vexed that so many of his younger
friends were so taken up with Georg Brandes. Altogether
it seemed as if he could not get used to the thought
that those who had been his pupils and had benefited so
much from his comprehensive literary knowledge as well as
from his enthusiasm now came forward more or less independently
and went other ways than his, perhaps even
directed criticism against him himself. In their younger
days he had so often driven them to the wall in discussion, and now
there were those who tried the same with him. Increasing
deafness did its part to isolate him and often led
him to misunderstand what was said. His later
years he spent, true to his old love of the
great and the great ones, reading Homer and Dante in the original languages.
Unfortunately his suspicion and his ill will
toward the new movements led several of his younger friends
(Drachmann, Schandorph, and others) to break with him outright.
I do not believe the wrong was wholly on their side. I have
had the opportunity to read Drachmann's letters to Arentzen
right up to the break, and these letters do Drachmann honor
by their warmth and sincerity, and by the attempt
to hold on, in spite of everything, to the connection with his older friend.
For my own part I could well notice an ill feeling
in him. Every time I met him, I usually got some
sarcasm. But it was only long afterwards that I learned
that the reason was something I had said one evening at the
% --- p. 87 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{87}Schandorphs' during one of the usual discussions about old
and new. Arentzen, as usual, went violently at
the younger men. I had then said that when he rejected
the new gods they believed in, it was at any rate not
because he himself believed in the old gods. The remark must
have been reported to him in distorted form; for it said only
what was true, and what in earlier days he would have acknowledged
himself. But now his romanticism, which earlier could unroll
a background full of intimations for a younger man, led him
to defend orthodoxy and reaction. It pained me, as
it did the others, to be estranged from him. In all of us, however,
the good memories have continued to prevail. In the last year Drachmann
lived, he and I had the plan of publishing a
portrait of him with contributions from a series of his former
friends. Drachmann was to write a long introductory poem.
The plan proved for various reasons impracticable.
I must content myself with expressing in these memoirs
my great gratitude toward the teacher of my youth
and the friend of my manhood. ---

\secrule

In literary and poetic respects my youth fell between
a period that can be described as the end of the Golden Age
and a new period whose signature I am not able
to give in brief. When I think back on literary events
that made an impression on me during my school years,
it is ``Hjortens Flugt,'' Bjørnson's short stories, and Kaalund's
``Et Foraar'' that especially come up for me. ``Hjortens
Flugt'' came as a fresh greeting from the land of poetry, taught
us that poetry was not something merely handed down from
the past, but that it can constantly open new springs. It
took on a special interest for me because from my childhood
on I had gone about in the part of South Zealand where the action
took place. I could fill in its fresh pictures of nature
with my memories, and conversely an increased poetic
luster came over the summer stays down there when I could
% --- p. 88 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{88}people the countryside with the figures and events of the poem.
It made a melancholy impression on me when some years
later I met Christian Winther in Paris during my stay
there. He was old and decrepit, and at the Café de la Régence
the waiters amused themselves over him when he came shuffling in
and asked for his sugar water. It was probably not of
his own good will that he made this journey to Paris; it was
his wife and daughter who wanted to go out and enjoy themselves. Life
and enthusiasm came over him only when he told of
how he had been on the point of going blind, but had been
saved by an operation, and how now the world's
glory in colors and forms had again become accessible
to him. As my journey home drew near, I promised to see to
something for him in Copenhagen and therefore went up to the
house where he lived. Outside his and his family's rooms
there was an open entrance hall, and when I came into it,
I heard, before I knocked, his voice inside. He
was speaking with much emotion to a person in there, and I heard
him say: ``I think that when I now show you that I have
confidence in you, then'' .... A family scene was evidently going on
in there, and I would rather have slipped away. But
I had asked for them from the porter's wife, so it could easily
be learned that someone had been at the door.
I then took a few firm steps and knocked. A little later
he came out in dressing gown and slippers and with tears in his eyes
and led me over into a room on the other side of the corridor,
where we talked together and where I was told what
I was to do for him. --- Poor Folmer Sanger
had had his wings clipped and could not now himself follow the
advice he had given to ``him who has sorrow in his heart.'' ---

Kaalund's ``Foraar'' I borrowed in my last school year from
Kr. Arentzen and copied out many of the poems. I used
at that time to copy out poems I was fond of, and thereby
often learned them by heart. It amused me on walks to test
whether I could bring them back. Kaalund's nature poems
I was especially fond of and still read with pleasure. Him
% --- p. 89 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{89}I came to know through Arentzen and Schandorph. More
than the cheerful and fresh, what stood out in his personality was the
enthusiastic, the pathetic, in part the sentimental. I have
had good conversations with him and was glad of a visit
he and his wife paid me one summer day in Øverrød.
Here he made an attempt to convert me to his religion,
which was a poetic theism; but he did not get the better
of my Spinozism. It was at the time when he was having
his poetic tournament with Schandorph, and I do not forget
a day I met him as he came straight from the railway station
and was on his way to the printer's with a new contribution. His
tall, lean figure with a face that could recall
Don Quixote could not but attract attention, apart from the
great cloak he was wearing. He embraced me on
the spot, led me into a café, ordered two glasses of
port, and now declaimed to me (and the whole public)
with much pathos his new poem, while the cloak flapped
under his violent movements of the arms. --- Better than
his poems to Schandorph, I think, is his poem to Drachmann.

With greater poetic gift than Arentzen, he lacked the latter's
fullness of knowledge and critical sharpness. But like
Arentzen he marks a stage where romanticism lived on
in the mind after its time of flowering was over, and where
a polemical attitude often asserted itself toward
the new that would take the place of the old. ---

Bjørnson I came to know personally only at a later time
and therefore postpone speaking of my relation
to him.

\secrule

Of my relation to what is usually called ``the Movement
of the Seventies'' I have had occasion to speak in a
``Tilbageblik'' I wrote in ``Tilskueren'' (1913) on the occasion
of my 70th birthday. I have nothing essential to
add to that statement. I still maintain that ``the Movement''
was predominantly literary, --- that scientifically and
% --- p. 90 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{90}philosophically seen it was very superficial, --- and that it had
more eye for what had to fall before criticism than
for what keeps its significance, and for the new possibilities
of positive value. For my part the
main thing was that I had enough to do in getting
firm ground under my feet in the domain where I
was personally to work. In the middle of the '70s I had arrived
at what one could call a critical positivism (and what
I have somewhere, from another standpoint, called a critical monism).
It constantly set me new tasks that I
had not been able to see beforehand, but that gave me
constant work. I had, as I have said in the ``Tilbageblik,''
a thread to spin further on, whether the current of the time
went in one direction or the other. The fluctuations
of literature, which modern literary historians believe
they can follow from decade to decade, so that each decade
gets its characterization, I have not gone along with, and I have
not really been able to trace these rhythms in the young generation
I have had to do with either. But then I am probably not
fine enough in my senses.

Georg Brandes and I had been opponents in the controversy
over faith and knowledge. Later we often met in Troels
Lund's father's house. When, together with his brother, he had
founded the journal ``det nittende Aarhundrede,'' I became
a contributor and thereby came into a closer connection with him,
very beneficial for me.

He invited me one evening after he had married, and
he and his wife also visited my home. I have always
followed him with admiration in his works of literary criticism.
For me, as for so many others, he has opened
new poetic and literary worlds, and by his power of searching
characterization and analysis he has thrown light on
so many of the great figures of literature. I felt myself
very different from him in temperament. I took everything more heavily and
more awkwardly, and I lacked the self-confidence
that is the condition of bold action. What I
% --- p. 91 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{91}have been able to accomplish is owed to long and unflagging work,
and my tasks lay further from the great public. Moreover,
I have generally held the view that what
there is to change or get rid of in the world of thought or of society
can only be recognized when the right thing is found.
It is difficult to find the right thing, but when it is found,
it becomes clear what the false is. And the forms in which
men's need for support and footing in life finds rest
can be changed only when this need itself changes; but
such change takes place very slowly if it is to
be thorough. Here too it is truth that shows what
is false, the positive that grounds the negative.
As Spinoza says: truth bears witness both to itself
and to untruth (verum est index sui et falsi). And
Comte maintained that one only displaces what one
replaces. This way of looking at things meant that I stood
differently from Brandes toward religious and moral polemics.
But his criticism has in many ways benefited my
work, since in many it awakened a need for
further orientation in the domain of thought. I have,
to be sure, seen in not a few cases how the view
arose that it was enough to have bold and brash opinions,
without one's needing to care that philosophy demanded
a penetrating inquiry.

What I am not least grateful to Brandes for from the time I am speaking of here, the seventies,
is the advice he gave
me in connection with the contributions I sent to his journal.
Thus he wrote to me on 7 June 1875: ``Allow
me, not so much as editor as in the capacity of a sympathetic
fellow striver, to put a couple of questions to you.
Have you ever made the experiment of reading what you
give to the press aloud to some man or other who has not
been to a grammar school? Have you read it aloud to a lady
who was not especially trained in philosophy? Have you put a mark
at the places he or she did not understand, and tried to rewrite
them in other words? I dare say that you have not
% --- p. 92 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{92}made this attempt. But why not?'' And thereupon he complains
in particular about a passage in an article I had submitted to
the journal, and which was undeniably expressed in a very
unpopular way. I found the complaint just; unfortunately it probably
also hits much of what I have written since, although I
really set myself to write as accessibly as
possible. But there is, after all, a difference between philosophy and literary history,
and besides, it has been my lot to develop
slowly and to come late to clarity. I could have
waited to write until everything could be expressed clearly (if
not for those who have no prerequisites at all); it
might not have harmed literature. But
I have always myself learned much by trying to set forth
my thoughts and the knowledge I had so far acquired. And
in Brøchner I had an example of what it can lead to
to wait too long to write; he often regretted that
he had wanted to wait with his writings until he had completely
worked through all his subjects, and when that
time seemed to him to have come, he was nearly fifty,
and he had grown wholly into the abstract expressions
handed down from the Hegelian philosophy, and
which in themselves could have done good service as short
formulas during his solitary thinking. --- I have, however,
often been surprised later on at how wide the circles are
that many of my books have reached.

When in the year 1876 I had published my little book ``Om
Grundlaget for den humane Etik,'' to which I shall return in
another connection, Brandes wrote to me
(24 Oct. 1876): ``You are, although on another basis, the
`transfigured' Brøchner, and it would certainly have been
a great joy to Brøchner if he had lived to see this book
of yours. .... I also congratulate you on the form of your
book. You have gained extraordinarily here in freedom and mobility.
You once said a despondent word to me about the dryness
of your style, in which you were far too severe on
yourself .... There is in my opinion still too little
% --- p. 93 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{93}temperament in your style; you do not yet write sufficiently
with your whole personality, the whole human being.
But you are on the way to doing so.'' --- Brandes, by the way, recalls
in this letter the inscription on the papers of the Committee of Public Safety:
``Liberté, Egalité, Fraternité, ou la mort!''
--- and he thinks that I have hardly ever been so
young that I could have said this. In that he is quite right.
Yet it grated a little on my ears when he added: ``You
must have been born to a certain degree old.'' Of himself he then
says: ``I am afraid that I was once very
young.'' ---

The relation in which I had come to stand to Brandes was to me
a source of much joy and encouragement. After Brøchner's death
I felt lonely, and since Brandes combined with his great artistic
sense an understanding of philosophical inquiries,
his letters were always welcome to me. Some years later
he wrote to me from Berlin: ``I am very glad
to be on such friendly terms with you; there is nothing I
would rather do than live in brotherly understanding with all my contemporaries
in the North who inquire honestly.'' What was here expressed
so warmly found a full echo on my side.
And this feeling did not disappear in me even when it
was put to the test some years later by a serious and
sharp opposition between our views on an essential
point.

% --- p. 94 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\chapter*{III}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{III. 1874--1883}
\markboth{III. 1874--1883}{III. 1874--1883}
\opage{94}In the autumn of 1874 I gave a lecture on ``Introduction
to Philosophy'', in which I set out in brief the view of the
philosophical problems and of the relation between them that had now
become settled in me. And after that my authorship proper began, as I
now set myself the task of treating the individual problems each by
itself. The short program I had given in the lecture mentioned
naturally had to undergo many changes when it was worked out in
detail, and there was great work to do in the individual fields. I can
divide my work in the following 40 years into three periods. From 1875
to 1887 it turned on psychology and ethics in the first place, from
1887---1895 on the history of philosophy, and after 1895 it is
philosophy of religion and theory of knowledge that have especially
laid claim on me. As the position of philosophy still stands, it is of
some importance that these different fields, which in so many ways
overlap one another, can be treated by the same person. It is not
certain that this will always be possible, and the problems of
philosophy would then present themselves in more difficult forms. We
must at all times take up our work as the questions present themselves
to us; we must only not forget that questions as well as answers can
take on a different character at different times. Yet I cannot
conceive of philosophy without a striving to gather human thought under
certain general points of view. And this striving is prepared within
the individual sciences, the more these themselves seek to become
% --- p. 95 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{95}conscious of their guiding ideas. There is then always a task for
philosophy as a comparative science.

The first tasks that presented themselves to me were: to write an
ethics on purely human presuppositions, and to work out a psychology by
which the study of human mental life, which had not been cultivated
here at home since Sibbern's time, could be taken up again. From this
time on I felt my work more and more as a continuation of Sibbern's,
or rather, I wished that it could be regarded so. However much I owed
Rasmus Nielsen and Brøchner, I saw nevertheless that one had to go
other ways, ways that ``old Sibbern'' had traveled over long stretches,
although a romantic-speculative background had at many points
determined the light in which he saw the questions.

In the autumn of 1876 I published a little work ``Om Grundlaget for den
humane Etik''. I sought here to show that there is a purely human
foundation for the conduct of life, which is given with the possibility
that man can bow to a law that points beyond the individual moments and
beyond the individual persons. Although I believe that I got some way
forward in clarity with that work, and that the analysis of the concept
of authority in particular may still have some interest, there remained
an indefiniteness, connected with the fact that I did not yet
distinguish between the motive that leads us to call actions good or
evil, and which I have later called the motive of valuation, and the
motive that in the individual special cases gets us to satisfy the
demand of the motive of valuation, and which I have later called the
motive of action. When I became fully clear about this distinction,
which is so often overlooked, I could proceed to the working out of a
full ethics. But that happened only several years later.

For the time being I became absorbed in psychological studies, and from
the autumn of 1876 on I treated every year one section or another of
psychology in my lectures as privatdocent. Gradually a considerable
circle of listeners gathered around
% --- p. 96 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{96}these lectures, so that from the little room in which I had begun I
had to move to the larger, and at last to the largest rooms at the
University. Now and then, for variety, I lectured on subjects from the
history of philosophy, thus on Spinoza, on the occasion of the
bicentenary of his death. This lecture I worked up into a little
popular work, which came out in the autumn of 1877.

I remember the winter of 1876---77 as an especially good time for work.
But there is sadness bound up with this memory, for it was the last
winter my wife lived. Traces of the chlorosis of her young days came
out again and again, and there appeared, as the doctor, my friend
Julius Petersen, later told me, symptoms of anemia. I believe that
already in the autumn she had had forebodings of what lay ahead. One
fine October day we had gone out to Øverød to rent a little summer
apartment for the next summer. After that was seen to, we walked in
Geel Skov, and the expression on her face when, sitting on a tree
stump, she looked down over Søllerød Sø toward the little house we were
to live in, later stood for me as the sign of a sad thought that she
perhaps would not come to live there. It is above all this remembered
image that I have kept from her later years, the one I most return to.
At New Year she gave birth to a son, and after that came a bad
phlebitis, which was however healed, so that she had a good time in the
early spring. But then the decline began, with increasing weakness and
exhaustion. And then came the day when the doctor told me that there
was no hope. A pernicious anemia had developed.

We lived in a little house by St. Jørgens Sø. In front of the house
there was a little garden; then came an embankment, over which one saw
the clear lake and in the background the towers of Copenhagen. The
scene stands clearly before me in the glow of the light nights, with
the wondrous contrast between the glorious nature outside and the
struggle with death that was fought inside. Day and night not only
glided into one another out there, but
% --- p. 97 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{97}also merged into one in there under the anxious strain. And in the
same way, in the sick woman, clear consciousness alternated with
sinking into unconsciousness. In one of the clear moments I came out
with a hint that I was aware of what lay ahead, and it turned out that
she too was clear about it. I tried to tell her all that she had been
to me, and how poor a return I had made. She was not afraid to die ---
``but it is so early, though!'' --- I asked her whether she did not
want to speak with a priest, but she would rather keep to what we had
so often talked about, and what lay at the root of the poetry we had
both set highest. She asked me to recite Paludan-Müller's
``Nattevagt'', one of our favorite poems, and I then whispered it into
her ear. And then she slipped away, away from me and my two little
boys. In the last days she lay in fantasies that did not seem to be
distressing. One of her last exclamations was: ``Lift me up into the
boat!'' --- And the boat glided slowly away, out into the great sea.
Early one morning (12 June 1877) I closed her eyes. --- ---

Some days later I moved out to the little house by Søllerød Sø. The
summer went in work on the psychology, a work that in the years now
following was a great help to me. It is good in times such as those
that had now come over me that there is always a piece of work lying
and waiting. Otherwise emptiness threatens. Besides, it was a
refreshment to me to roam about in Rude Skov, which only now I really
came to know. Here I spent the afternoons. Often I walked to Hørsholm
and had supper and then wandered home through the forest.

The support I had in my mother and my brothers and sisters made it
possible for me to live with my two little boys without having any
``lady in the house'', which I have always dreaded. It has perhaps not
been good in all respects for the sons that the comfort only a woman
can bring to a home was lacking. But it could not be otherwise.

In the following years I had special reason to
% --- p. 98 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{98}appreciate my friends, and I won new ones. Skovgaard had become an
assistant master in Nykøbing paa Falster, and I liked to visit him once
a year. Julius Petersen and his wife I was with even more than before.
I have always, not least in times of sorrow, found a heartfelt sympathy
with them, and have myself also taken part in their fortunes. It was
not always easy to get along with Julius. Precisely because he was so
fond of me, it was a sorrow to him, to which he could often give a
violent and provocative expression, when there was disagreement between
us, e.g. in literary or political questions. Perhaps it also irritated
him that there was in my nature a striving for continuity and harmony
that he did not understand, because he also did not understand how much
it could cost me to keep this striving up in spite of heaviness and
torpor. I believe that I understood him better than he understood me.
His wife Oliva had been my wife's friend, and it was a comfort to me to
talk with her about the past. When, as could happen, a hitch came in
the line between Julius and me, she stepped in as mediator. It could
happen that I met her on her way to me when I myself was on my way to
Julius after a little clash that might threaten to let grass grow on
the path. She understood her husband as no one else did and held fast
to him through all his swings, even the most violent. Steady and
faithful she was in her ways, and he always came back to her, always
understanding better what she was for him. She saw clearly that besides
his practice, which satisfied his humane mind but could often wear too
hard on him, it was a vital necessity for him to work as a scholar and
a writer, and it did him no good to resist; he always had to go back to
the desk and continue his works on the history of medicine, works that
led to his appointment in this subject at the University and gave him
well-deserved standing. After Oliva's death he broke down.

What these two people have been to me,
% --- p. 99 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{99}I keep in grateful remembrance. And their children, a row of able and
aspiring people, keep this memory alive in me in the finest way through
the kindness they show on every occasion to their old Uncle, as they
have called me since they were small.

With Troels Lund and with Heegaard too I had good support in these
years, and to these two homes I often went when I needed a pleasant and
interesting evening.

In remembering the years after my wife's death I also think with
gratitude of how Herman and Anna Trier opened their home to me at this
time. His steady and calm nature and his pedagogical interest, which
also led him to interest in and understanding of philosophy, made
association with him beneficial and strengthening. And Anna Trier's
lively, enthusiastic, and faithful nature brought me a refreshment and
an encouragement that I could well need in those years. She came from a
Grundtvigian circle, but now entered with an open mind into circles
where quite other thoughts prevailed than those she had grown up with,
and she did not lose her originality and boldness. For her the only
thing that mattered was that she felt herself before something truly
human. Illness broke her strength early, and her sudden death (in the
summer of 1888) was a heartfelt grief to me. Again something beautiful
and bright had gone out of my world. ---

\whiteline

My psychological studies went their way through all this. In the
journal ``Nær og Fjern'' I published (February 1878) an essay ``Om
Erindring'', in which some of the basic ideas of my Psychology, which
came out later (1882), were expressed in popular form. The view of
human mental life to which my studies led me had partly come about
through criticism of the presuppositions of English ``association
psychology''. This school has done psychology great service by
demanding exact analysis of each single mental phenomenon and by
rejecting the
% --- p. 100 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{100}spiritualistic appeal to ``the essence of the soul'' at every
difficult point. But it could not see the forest for the trees, and in
particular did not see that in all memory an inner connection makes
itself known, a belonging together of all mental elements with one
another. I tried to follow this connection right from the simplest
sensations to the highest thoughts and decisions. In addition there
appears in the essay mentioned a main point of my psychological
research, namely the way in which the study of morbid states throws
light on the general nature of mental life, inasmuch as states of
dissolution bear witness to the significance that collectedness and
concentration can have for the persistence of mental life.

In the same journal I published that same year a series of reviews, in
which my ethical view was brought out through criticism of various
works. First among these stands a critique of Bishop Martensen's Ethics
running through several numbers (July 1878). It was a settling of
accounts with theological ethics, especially with the ``modern
Christianity'' about which, after much inner work, I had come to
clarity for my own part. Martensen was a characteristic representative
of this modern Christianity, in that, with all his combination of
speculation, aestheticizing, and edification, he nevertheless claimed
to stand in continuous connection with original Christianity.
Kierkegaard had protested against his attempt to set up Bishop Mynster
as a Christian witness to the truth, an attempt that overlooked the
opposition between primitive-Christian and modern-Christian ethics.
Since one of my main tasks was to discuss the possibility of an ethics
built on purely human ground, it was bound to be of interest to me that
there was a spirited exposition from an opposite standpoint.
Martensen's attempt to work Christianity and humanity together appears
in a characteristic way in his criticism of Augustine's famous sentence
about the virtues of the heathen as splendid vices. He instructs the
old Church Father that the pagan virtues were not vices, but
% --- p. 101 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{101}splendid fragments, which only through Christianity could be given a
harmonious composition. Not only a Church Father, an apostle too is
corrected by the Bishop. When Paul advises against marriage because the
one thing needful is to live in expectation of Christ's return, he is
now told that one should certainly hold fast to this expectation, but
that one must not therefore give up living a healthy and abundant human
life with enjoyment of all the goods of culture. The heavenly existence
is only the conclusion of a great process of development. It is in
reliance on this view that the author of the ``kristelige Etik'' goes
through all human relations in society and state, in theater and school
(e.g. orthography!) in order to arrange them under what is for him the
fundamental Christian view. It follows of itself that he thereby goes
far outside the domain that can be illuminated from the New Testament,
whose ethics is borne throughout by the great expectation, whose
fulfilment Martensen really could not wish to come too soon, since
otherwise there would be no time for the cultural development that was
to be crowned with the ``Second Coming''. --- In spite of his defense
of the heathen, Martensen nevertheless declares that when men like
Kant, Lessing, and Schiller were not believing Christians, it came from
ill will and loathing of the holy!
--- Here the old theological barbarism broke through.

This critique of Martensen won much approval round about. There were
many older scholars, authors, and politicians who had been annoyed at
the Bishop's attempt to let theological points of view dominate science
and art, the life of the state and of society, and who now --- in all
quietness --- expressed their sympathy. Among them were e.g. Madvig and
Bille.

Some years later I again reviewed (in ``Ude og Hjemme'' 1882) a book by
Martensen, his ``Jacob Böhme''. It was the subject that interested me.
It amused me to demonstrate how little the profound and
independent-minded mystic would have put up with being shut up within
the
% --- p. 102 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{102}bounds the Bishop wanted to set between ``Christian'' and ``pagan''
thinking. --- At that time I often met the historian Caspar
Paludan-Müller at the University, as we lectured at the same hour. When
at his wish I had sent him my review, he said in his peculiar decided
way: ``Well, your opinion is really that the whole book is nonsense. I
hold to what my father said, that faith is a matter of the will and
that one should not speculate about it.'' And a little later he added:
``Besides, I would advise you against attacking Martensen so often; he
could whisper something in the King's ear, and then you will not become
professor!'' --- This warning was not needed, since I had now got said
what I wanted to say, and I was now wholly occupied with developing and
grounding my own views. --- In his ``Levned'' Martensen mentions that
his later writings were attacked from the side of the ``purely negative
tendency''. I assume that I too have here come under the concept of
``the purely negative''. I myself felt more and more positive, the more
the human in its manifold types and forms dawned on me. ---

But I have strayed from the year 1878. --- In ``Nær og Fjern'' (August
1878) I wrote a review of Heegaard's book ``Om Intolerance''. This book,
under evident and strong influence from Kierkegaard, set out to show
that a faith or view of life can only appear in the form of personal
conviction. Scientific decision of the highest questions is impossible,
and it is no use appealing to authority, for faith in an authority is
also subjective conviction. The differences between personalities make
common formulas that should fit everyone impossible. All through life
the individual has only himself to deal with. Social life concerns only
external relations and stands as a coercive, hostile power. Regarding
the religious questions, of which immortality especially lies close to
the author's heart, it is stated that we do not get beyond mere
possibilities. We live on possibilities! And in the strict school of
% --- p. 103 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{103}possibilities the very best in our nature can be developed: nobility
in ways of thinking, and conciliatoriness toward those who think
otherwise.

Against this way of looking at things I maintained that if there is no
common ground at all to build on, all negotiation between different
views of life is impossible. And the common ground must in the end be
science. We demand of every view of life that we are to respect that it
agree with itself, display inner consistency. Already here, in pure
logic, there is a common ground. But besides, we cannot have respect for
a view of life when it does not bear witness to an honest endeavor to
apply and think through the knowledge that is available. A view of life
that cares nothing at all for natural science and historical criticism
cannot gain significance beyond a quite definite circle. --- I did not
emphasize, as I would now, that every view of life comes into being
under definite inner and outer conditions and must therefore become an
object of psychological and historical investigation. But I showed the
impossibility, for one who would develop into a real personality, of
isolating himself from society, and also from acting on society. ``If
the author,'' I said, ``had only made clear to himself what kind of
feeling it was that brought him to write down the fine and energetic
statements in his book, he would know from personal experience that the
ethical demand on the personality includes the endeavor for a higher
and nobler development of life in society.''

I set great store by my personal friendship with Heegaard. He was one of
the few with whom I could then discuss philosophical subjects, and it
was a pleasure to associate with him in the good working years he had
after he had become professor. His horizon widened, and his sense for
problems sharpened. The best he gave at the University was probably the
course he held for the young students at the end of the seventies. He
% --- p. 104 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{104}treated here the concept of development and its history, and besides
often gave himself in his lectures to personal statements on the
significance and necessity of independent conviction. Many of his
listeners from these years have kept a fine and distinctive memory of
him. Unfortunately his good working years were not to last
long. ---

I wrote yet another review the same year and in the same journal (``Nær
og Fjern''. Sept. 1878). After Sibbern's death (1872) his moral
philosophy had been published, and I then used the occasion to give a
characterization of my old teacher, whom I had come to value highly
over the years. This review was a preliminary study for a fuller
characterization of Sibbern, which I wrote in ``Tilskueren'' (1885) on
the occasion of the centenary of his birth, and which is reprinted in
the first volume of my Mindre Arbejder.

When I have also mentioned an essay on philosophy in Sweden, in the form
of a review of Axel Nyblæus' work ``Den filosofiska Forskningen i
Sverige'' (Nordisk Tidsskrift, utg. af Letterstedske föreningen 1879), I
have named the most important literary works from my hand at the end of
the seventies. ---

At the end of 1879, at the urging of Madvig and Heegaard, I submitted an
application for a lectureship, which was also recommended by the
faculty. It was not only on this occasion that Madvig showed interest in
me. I had first met him when, as inspector of education, he made a
visitation at a school I taught in, and I have also had him as censor
when I examined in Greek for the Artium. Madvig took a great interest in
philosophy, and at a festive gathering on the occasion of his having
been a member of the Royal Danish Academy of Sciences for 50 years, he
gave a survey of his own philosophy, which, however, since I was not
then a member myself, I know only through a summary written down by
Fausbøll. His thoughts went
% --- p. 105 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{105}generally in the direction of the critical philosophy, concluding by
way of analogy in an atmospheric ``pantheism'', with a firm holding to
the doctrine of causality, in the domain of the will too. He sympathized
with the theory of evolution, and when I had (1874) given a talk in the
Students' Union on ``Darwinismen og Filosofien'' (printed in ``Nær og
Fjern''), he spoke very warmly of it and said that it seemed to him
that the idea of an ascending development was far more appealing than
the doctrine of a fall. He added with a sly smile: ``But I dare not say
it to my daughters!'' These excellent ladies were in fact very
orthodox, and the learned father was very considerate. Some years later
I proposed to him that he be a co-sponsor of a collection of
contributions to a statue of Spinoza in The Hague, on the occasion of
the bicentenary of Spinoza's death. Madvig at first had misgivings,
also out of ``consideration for his home'', but overcame them, and he
raised a considerable sum, so that the contribution from Denmark to the
international undertaking became relatively large. With my critique of
Martensen's Ethics he sympathized greatly, and he expressed to me in
warm words his interest in the way I had illuminated theology's attempt
to dominate the whole of life. From these (and several other) different
conversations with the great philologist I had formed an idea of his
relation to religion and church. But when, many years after his death,
his notes on philosophical and religious subjects were published, I was
nevertheless surprised at the sharpness with which he expressed himself
about the dogmas and the church. In the address given over him by
Paulli the Younger in Frue Kirke he was honored as a constant
churchgoer (``Sunday after Sunday he sat here in the church'' etc.); but
in the hours of his quiet reflection he had written that the sermon
with its obscurities and crooked conclusions spoiled for him the
elevated mood that organ playing and singing had put him in! --- His
philosophical stray thoughts often point in a direction I sympathize
with.
% --- p. 106 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{106}--- In the year 1878 Madvig obtained for me two years' support from
the newly founded Carlsberg Foundation for preliminary work on my
Psychology. And it was under his auspices that I applied to have my
privatdocentship replaced by a permanent lectureship. The Minister of
Education (Kultusminister) Fischer tracked down an unused sum in his
budget, and on 11 March 1880 I received my appointment
as lecturer in philosophy.\footnote[1]{In a letter to Hans Skovgaard of 17 April 1880 I say on the occasion of my appointment as lecturer: ``I am of course very glad of the prospects I have thereby gained of continued work in the field where I most wish to work. But on the other hand the feeling of responsibility also came up, and still more the feeling of the inadequacy of my abilities in relation to what one ought to demand of a teacher of philosophy. Until now my striving has been private, personal .... It was from the start not at all my intention to want to be an official scholar. I only wanted to sit quite still and read what I was interested in knowing. And now step by step it has come to this. Whether I would not have become happier if I had entered a more practical occupation is a question I sometimes raise. Only at certain times ... do I answer it with no.''} I now gave up most of
my school hours and set to work in earnest on the writing of my
Psychology. After I had once more gone through the subject in a series
of lectures over two semesters, the book came out in the autumn of 1882.

The main idea around which it moves, or rather the hypothesis it seeks
to ground and confirm, is this: that the fundamental law of mental life,
or of the life of consciousness, in which its essence shows itself, is
synthesis, combining activity. This hypothesis is grounded partly by
investigating the passage of the life of consciousness into the
unconscious, and conversely, its awakening out of it, partly by analysis
of important mental phenomena and processes (memory, comparison, grief,
doubt, decision). And the hypothesis is sought to be confirmed through
investigation of the conditions of sensation, as Fechner and the
experimental psychology founded by him illuminate them; further through
investigation of the association of ideas, of the activity of
imagination, of the main forms of the life of feeling, and of the stages
of the life of the will. If the law named is the fundamental law of
mental life, the will, in the widest sense of the word, becomes its
proper, central expression, since, as long as mental life
% --- p. 107 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{107}lasts, there is work to be done to hold together a more or less full
content. The feelings are symptoms of this will, and knowledge is at
first its servant, later perhaps its master. I thus attach myself most
nearly to so-called voluntarism. This standpoint is carried through with
greater consistency in the later editions, but lay decidedly and clearly
at the base of the first edition. The usual threefold division
(knowledge --- feeling --- will) is thus here first traced back to a
unity, or rather to a whole.

That this book has become so widespread that I, if I wanted to boast,
could well say that it is spread over the whole world, can be explained
by several causes. Its guiding idea was, when the book came out, not a
common one. One usually started from spiritualistic or materialistic
hypotheses. With me it had, as I have indicated in the foregoing,
developed step by step, right from the Kierkegaard studies of my early
youth, through my Kant studies, to studies of the sick mental life in
its relation to the healthy. To this came the fact that this main idea
was sought to be illuminated by contributions from all the different
sources of psychological knowledge (natural science, self-observation,
history of culture and of literature). No single person can master all
these sources; there are really many psychologies; all the more
significance it can then have to begin with a well-grounded hypothesis
and seek contributions from the various sides to illuminate it. Finally,
it happens in a small country that a philosophical author is obliged to
gather his thoughts in as easily accessible a form as possible, since
the number of experts is small. Be that as it may, the book has been
translated into many languages (German, French, English, Spanish,
Italian, Polish, Russian, Finnish, Japanese) and it has brought me
friendly approaches from the most varied people around the world. It
was a special pleasure to me that the psychopathologist Pierre Janet
wrote a preface to the French edition; precisely on account of the
significance that a comparison between sick
% --- p. 108 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{108}and healthy mental life had had for the development of the book's
underlying hypothesis, it was interesting to me that it came out in a
major language under the aegis of an eminent psychopathologist.

I am myself aware of the book's shortcomings (although I probably do not
know them all). Its time is perhaps now past. But I am sure that its
main ideas will in some form or other continue to assert themselves.
There will probably arise a greater opposition between the different
methods in psychology. One will be obliged not only, like most
experimental psychologists (who often claim to be the only proper
psychologists), to start from the relatively simple mental phenomena
that can be produced by experiment, but also to start from observation,
description, and analysis of the phenomena of complex mental life, and
from there to seek back to the simpler and more easily unraveled ones.
And sociological psychology, especially the psychology of culture and
of literature, will also more and more mark out an independent
direction. But efforts will always arise anew to find basic mental
forms that satisfy all these points of view. Such efforts will probably
be harder to carry through than it was when I worked out my Psychology
in the years 1876---1882.


For my teaching at the University the psychological way of looking at
things in which I had become practiced, and the psychological sense and
interest I believe I possess, were of great importance. Here, in face of
the intellectual movements of the time, was given a standpoint that
could meet the different tendencies with intellectual sympathy, while it
held open the concluding epistemological and ethical questions. My old
teacher Sibbern has said that just as for the botanist there are no
weeds, so for the psychologist there is nothing in the stirrings of the
life of the spirit that cannot become an object of interest and
observation. Before we can judge the intellectual or
% --- p. 109 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{109}moral value of a spiritual phenomenon, we must surely know it and
understand it, preferably from within. All too often one goes the
opposite way and stamps as stupidity or sin what has its natural root in
the coherence of life and perhaps, if it were understood rightly and
therefore taken rightly, could grow up into the world of truth and
goodness.

\secrule

The new tendency in literature that developed in the seventies collided
more and more sharply with the representatives of the older tendency.
The most violent clash was the so-called literary New Year feud of
1879---80, provoked by a powerful polemical poem against Ploug by
Schandorph. The dispute soon came to a standstill. I had no reason to
take part in it, although I was indignant at seeing the conduct of the
old champion of liberty Ploug toward the new tendencies in literature
and in politics. Both these tendencies came for a time to run side by
side, as the men of the new literature cherished sympathy for the
political Left. Ploug then also christened the new literary tendency
``the literary Left'' and doubtless believed he was thereby dealing it a
mighty blow. But the name was accepted, and for the time being
collaboration came about in various ways between the two tendencies.

On the occasion of this alliance I carried on a correspondence with my
friend Victor Pingel. It was partly at Arentzen's, partly at Julius
Petersen's, that I had come into contact with this fine, pure,
idealistic man. He lived like a hermit for his studies, which, apart
from his proper field, classical philology, extended over various
domains of nature, especially geology. He had been strongly taken with
the new tendencies, which he understood from his ideal standpoint. What
struck everyone who knew Pingel was the purity of his mind. Arentzen
once said: ``Pingel --- he is like clean linen on a Sunday morning!''
But behind his hermit ways there was a smoldering passion that
% --- p. 110 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{110}broke out into flame, as indignation at the fanatical opposition the
new tendencies met had an inflaming effect. Later, as is well known, he
threw himself with passion into political life. For the time being he
set himself a more theoretical task, namely to write a program that
should gather the literary, scientific, and political strivings for
freedom under common points of view. From a letter from Pingel from the
beginning of 1880 I see that I criticized this program. Partly I feared
that party combination would hamper individual development, and partly
I thought that the diverse strivings could be brought under the same
heading only in an artificial way. I was not glad to be enrolled and to
take others' sins upon me besides my own. I seemed to myself too
unfinished in my own field to be able to come forward with
proclamations. Only step by step could I work my way forward.

Pingel replies (26 March 1880) that as a younger man he had been bent
on complete isolation and had torn himself out of it only with great
difficulty. He thought that since a general European movement had now
reached us, had been met with ill will by a political tendency that
believed it could monopolize the whole of intellectual life, and since
that movement had obtained a sort of alliance with this party's
opponents, the nature of the new tendency must be stated unreservedly
and in a generally understandable way. ``I believe, dear Høffding, that
both you and Lange and Heegaard and perhaps almost all our younger
scholars overestimate the significance of individual independence and
misjudge party cohesion as a necessary condition for development.''
--- To my remark that Drachmann's and Schandorph's poems bear no
particular trace of the world-view that Pingel had set up as the common
foundation of the tendency, Pingel replies that this only shows that
these poets have not gone into the depths, have not caught sight of
``what underlies the age''. ---

Although I thus did not think that the political,
% --- p. 111 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{111}scientific, and poetic movement of the seventies could be brought
under a common metaphysical formula, I had nevertheless followed the
political struggle from the beginning of the seventies with keen
interest. It presented two sides, a struggle on the part of democracy
for influence on the government of the country, and a struggle over the
defense question, especially the fortification of Copenhagen. I stood
divided in this struggle, as my sympathy was more and more on the side
of democracy as far as the purely political is concerned, while I was
convinced, as I am to this day, that a vigorous, up-to-date, and
proportionate development of the defense system is a condition of life
for a people that would maintain its material and spiritual
independence, --- its honor. But it became clearer and clearer to me
that a cause like the defense question could not be carried through
except with the people's support through its lawful representation. In
a state of emergency it can be defended to act against the law, because
something is at stake that is more than the law, the very existence of
the people. But no state of emergency was at hand, at most dangers and
threatening possibilities. Experience would therefore not be able to
prove the justification of a defense arrangement carried through in
defiance of the expressed will of the people. One ought in any case to
try whether responsibility would not lead the leading men of the Left to
see the matter differently when the government was entrusted to them.
When the Estrup ministry in the spring of 1877 resorted to the desperate
expedient of issuing a provisional finance law, this step, which at once
offended my sense of justice and stood for me as a great stupidity,
made me a man of the Left, and in the following years I voted and spoke
for the opposition's candidates.

A friend I had won in these years did much for my increased interest in
politics. One day in the winter of 1879---80 the banker Laurids Bing
came up to see me. I had been his teacher in Mariboe's School, and later
I had met him in the ``Nationaløkonomisk Forening'', of which I was a
member and had even helped to found. He came to propose that I give some
popular lectures
% --- p. 112 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{112}on philosophy in his home for a small circle. He and his wife soon
became my good friends, and since we lived near each other in
Frederiksberg, I often went over to them for a good conversation,
besides giving my little lectures for several winters on Wednesday
evenings. Laurids Bing was an eager democrat and took a large part in
the political stir. Together with him I took part in the winter of
1882---83 in some meetings held in the house of Christopher Hage, later
a minister of the Left, by a circle that consisted of what were then
called liberal men of the Right, and that sought understanding and
collaboration with the Left. Among those present were Supreme Court
Justice Nyholm, presiding judge Madvig, Professors Deuntzer and Falbe
Hansen, the Supreme Court advocates Frederik Salomon and Octavius
Hansen, and others. These meetings led to the formation of the Liberal
Voters' Association in Frederiksberg, the first sign that the Right did
not hold sole power in Copenhagen and its environs. Its candidate was
Supreme Court Justice Nyholm. He was elected in the summer of 1884. On
this occasion I was one of his speaking nominators, and soon after I
became chairman of the Liberal Voters' Association in Frederiksberg, to
which liberal men of the Right, men of the Left, and Social Democrats
belonged in brotherly union. On this occasion I came to know several
worthy and able workmen.

A politician I never became. There was always much that repelled me in
politicians by trade. In their eager opposition to the Right, the Left
also attacked the University, because they believed that all university
teachers must be men of the Right. They had even wanted to deny men like
Vilh. Thomsen, Zeuthen, and Julius Lange appointment. I remember a
conversation with Hørup in which he confided to me that he looked with
irony on scholarly work, insofar as no politics could be got out of it:
``Come down to the market, for that is where we do business!'' He added,
however, in his good nature, that I presumably also took his political
activity humorously. This, however, was
% --- p. 113 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{113}by no means the case. Later on, when I had become professor, they
wanted me to stand for the Folketing in Roskilde, and a deputation came
to me from down there. I also had a meeting with Berg and Hørup in the
former's chairman's room in Christiansborg Palace. Sitting between
them, I was worked on for a good hour. But it did no good. On this
occasion Hørup said, when I had spoken of my university work not
leaving me time for political work, that once I had made my lecture I
could find time enough. So: just turn the pile over! Besides, it was
said that I need not always attend, so long as I attended for the vote!
--- These arguments had the opposite effect of the one intended.

In the political movement of the following period I took part, as will
be mentioned later, really only within my own constituency and in the
Students' Society. I often met Hørup at this time and had occasion to
observe his remarkable union, or rather rhythmic alternation, of phlegm
and skepticism on the one side, fanatical passion on the other. His
political program really aimed at the possession of power, the power of
government, as the most important thing; then one could talk afterward
about what it should be used for. He took no interest in particular
special social tasks. A brilliant journalist he was. Many of his
articles were unsurpassable, at least when one had the whole definite,
given situation present to mind. A masterly speech, and one
characteristic of him, he gave at the Constitution Day festival on
Frederiksberg Exercerplads in 1884. His skepticism about the state's
ability to solve social questions found expression here in an apt image:
One year the forest would not come into leaf. A commission was then set
up by the state to see what could be done. It inspected the forest, and
when the first green leaves appeared, it said: ``That color is good; we
adopt it!'' --- When things thus grow forth of themselves,
% --- p. 114 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{114}there is surely, by the way, not even any reason to fight over power
--- the power to set up commissions! But a certain mystical faith that
there is something in the world that grows ``of itself'' Hørup did
have. --- I once said to him that in my opinion he was more journalist
than politician. He answered: ``Yes, you can believe it is fun to be in
on things behind the scenes.''

\secrule

Besides the literary and the political world there was around the year
1880 yet another world I came into contact with. One evening I was
invited to a gathering at the wood engraver Hendriksen's, where there
was to be talk of founding an association that should consist of
artists and authors. Taking part in the gathering were Georg and Edvard
Brandes, Drachmann, Schandorph, Krøyer, Zahrtmann, Viggo Johansen, and
others. It became an enjoyable evening, especially on account of
Zahrtmann's merriment and inexhaustible humor. Sometimes we lay back in
our chairs with laughter. But we got our purpose achieved, an
association of artists and authors who sympathized with the new
tendencies in art and literature. The majority of the association's
members were painters, especially of the group that had been influenced
by modern French art. There was to be a gathering every month in the
winter, and there was the draconian rule that the meeting should be held
each time in a new place. The result was that we sometimes came to
taverns that would otherwise have remained unknown to most of us. But
the association did not last so long that we needed to resort to
repetitions. The meetings were to be arranged by the members in turn,
two each time, in alphabetical order, and the association was therefore
called ``Bogstaveligheden'', which did not, however, imply that radical
realism was to be the program. I think back with great pleasure on
these gatherings. Among the painters a common love of art made itself
felt, so that the whole circle rejoiced when one of
% --- p. 115 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{115}the comrades had done something good. One cannot say the same of the
authors, and it was indeed literary quarrels that caused the association
to cease. It was refreshing to move in artists' circles. Artists are
certainly not as eloquent as authors; but through their short and quick
remarks I got many a pointer toward a better understanding of what art
is. I have followed this circle of artists with interest in their
further development. Later tendencies I have not really been able to
understand, and in the end I have quite stopped visiting exhibitions.
Among the individual artists with whom I came into closer relations I
will especially name Viggo Johansen, Valdemar Irminger, and August
Jerndorff. With the last I later became related through my youngest
son's marriage to his daughter. And the thought of this pure and fine
human being, this enthusiastic artist's soul, this faithful friend,
belongs to the best within my world of memories.

\secrule

In ``Bogstaveligheden'' I met several times with J. P. Jacobsen, who
now, after ``Mogens'', ``Marie Grubbe'', and ``Niels Lyhne'', was the
most admired of the authors of the new age. Several years earlier (1870)
I had been in contact with him. He had not then yet appeared as an
author, but was known as an eager botanist. I met him one evening at
Poul Kierkegaard's, who then lived in a boarding house in Studiestræde,
and who had invited us so that we might make each other's acquaintance.
And when a bottle of Swedish punch had then come onto the table,
Kierkegaard declared that he liked us both so well that he wanted us to
drink to brotherhood. That we naturally did, as in duty bound. Jacobsen
read some poems aloud, which seemed to me somewhat stilted. He was very
angry with Georg Brandes, who had advised against the printing of his
poems. The evening went well. Jacobsen was then still fresh and strong
and sparkled with wit. But it turned out so
% --- p. 116 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{116}unluckily that when some time later he came up to visit me (I was
then still living with my parents), I had completely forgotten that we
had drunk to brotherhood, and that presumably had the consequence that
the visit was not repeated.

His books, especially Niels Lyhne, made on first reading a somewhat
artificial impression through the many new words and turns of phrase.
But it was striking how this fell away on repeated reading. His language
had triumphed. It is still a delight to me to hear a piece of ``Niels
Lyhne'' read aloud. Especially the chapters on Edele's death and on the
mother's stay in Clarens are pearls so genuine that time does not touch
them.

At one of the meetings of ``Bogstaveligheden'' Jacobsen read his
masterly story ``Pesten i Bergamo''. This reading, which Erik Henningsen
has rendered in a drawing that is in the Frederiksborg Museum, became
unforgettable for us all through the uncanny correspondence between
story and reader. Jacobsen was now attacked by tuberculosis, and his
face and voice, marked by death, suited in a strange way the subject he
was presenting. ---

In ``Bogstaveligheden'' Holger Drachmann was a constant guest. I knew
him from Arentzen's circle and had followed him with enthusiasm on his
poet's career. ``Dæmpede Melodier'' and ``Sange ved Havet'' still belong
to my favorite poems. His unsettled course I followed at a distance, but
did get the chance to give him a small helping hand once, when he was in
an awkward situation. In the spring of 1878 I was visiting a friend in
Lund and heard then that Drachmann was living there in hiding, after he
had gone away from North Zealand with a married woman and her (and his)
child. I sought him out, and I do not forget the expression of fright
that came over him at someone asking for him. He did not forget me this
visit, and when the next winter we met at a party in Copenhagen, he drew
me into a side room, thanked me for having sought him out, and proposed
brotherhood to me. The awkward situation he had been in had, by the
way, a comic ending, when
% --- p. 117 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{117}the lady fled from him with a Swedish doctor. --- This time I did not
forget the brotherhood, which I also had frequent occasion to cultivate
through our common circle.

Drachmann's strength and limitation was the decidedly lyrical character
of his gift. Neither as a novelist nor as a dramatist was he really in
his element. ``Der var engang'' disappointed me greatly when I saw it; it
was a series of poetic scenes, but no drama. I saw it, to be sure, only
long after it first appeared, and after the excellent actors who had
carried it at the first performances had passed away or had gone over
to other kinds of parts. --- Once Drachmann had received a state grant
to make dramatic studies abroad. A good while afterward I met him at a
party where Olaf Poulsen was also present. Olaf Poulsen teased him by
asking when the new dramas would come for which the state had given him
an advance. Drachmann snapped a little at first, but then it burst out
of him: ``Well, that I don't know. But I promise you to cover the whole
foyer of the Royal Theater with verse, if you wish it!''

\secrule

Julius Lange did not belong to ``Bogstaveligheden''. He refused to
become a member, because he thought it was a party formation that was
to take place. But I had already earlier become acquainted with him,
especially after I had, at his request, written a review of his book
``Om Kunstværdi'' (``Nær og Fjern''. 1876). Later on he asked me several
times to go through parts of the great book on the human figure in the
history of art, particularly with regard to the psychological ideas he
employed. This led, among other things, to a discussion between us, as
Lange held that it was the task of art to give the typical, e.g. the
typical in the human form at a given time, while I maintained that the
representation of the individual and characteristic was art's highest
task. Lange appealed
% --- p. 118 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{118}to Greek art, first and foremost to the Parthenon frieze. (See
Lange's letter to me of 24 January 1887). I held that the Parthenon
frieze meant a great advance in individualization in relation to
oriental (Asiatic) art, and that art had later (especially in modern
art) gone further in the same direction. A main point for me was that
only on this view does art itself appear as a characteristic form of
spirit in relation to science. --- It was a great joy to be Lange's
friend, to hear at first hand his original judgments and the outbursts
of his humor, which did not fail him even when he was succumbing to a
heart disease. ---

In the first years after my wife's death I lived in summer in the little
house by Søllerød Sø, which we had been out to rent the last autumn she
lived. After that I lived for a series of summers with a skipper on
Vemmetofte Strand by Faxebugt. Here there were good walks, and I had
only three quarters of a mile to my youngest brother, who had now
succeeded my maternal uncle as tenant of Strandegaard. I now renewed the
childhood memories of the glorious summer holidays I had once spent in
this region.

One summer I made, with three young students, my former pupils, and two
ladies, the one a sister of one of the students, the other her friend,
a glorious sailing trip to Møen. We hired a brand-new fishing boat that
lay at Faxe Ladeplads; it was manned by three skippers, of whom my host
was one; my housekeeper supplied us with provisions. On a fine starry
summer evening we sailed off before a brisk wind, and we had a splendid
night passage. In the morning we were at the cliff, but since the wind
was onshore we could not land there, but went south round the island and
put in at Klintholm Havn, from where we drove to Liselund. After
spending the day on the cliff, we went back to the harbor in the
evening; the ladies, whose number was now four, two acquaintances having
joined us at the cliff, got a room ashore, and the gentlemen lay on hay
in the boat.
% --- p. 119 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{119}The next day we sailed south of Møen, up through Grønsund and
Ulfsund and across Faxe Bugt to the Ladeplads. It was in the first days
of August, when one can sing ``Soon the time of the light nights is
past'', and there was something of this song's mood over our sailing.
--- It is said, by the way, to have caused some offense that we had
thus sailed out with young ladies. And I was indeed told by a female
relative that I must not imagine I was old enough to be a patriarch. I
believe that such things are now looked at differently. ---

This excursion is among the good memories of the summer of 1882. When I
came into town after the holidays, I received an invitation to give a
lecture in the newly founded ``Students' Society'' on its first meeting
evening. ``The Society'' had been founded in the spring, because Georg
Brandes had been refused a discussion in the Students' Union after a
lecture he had given there by invitation. To ``the Society'' there now
came the older and younger students who in literary, religious, and
political respects felt themselves in opposition to the ruling
authorities. The title of my lecture was ``Om Realisme i Videnskab og
Tro''; it is printed in the first series of my Mindre Arbejder. I sought
to show how science laid weight more and more decidedly on the definite,
factual conditions, in contrast to the idealistic interpretations of the
Romantics, and that at the same time in theology one clung to the
definite, factually given dogmas, in contrast to the symbolizing
interpretations of speculative theology. --- In the following years I
spent many Saturday evenings in ``the Society'', where in that
politically stirring time one could meet like-minded people and talk
about what one had on one's heart. In the first years there were often
lively and interesting discussions.

The following winter brought a change in my position at the University.
Of the two professors of philosophy, the one, Heegaard, had been struck
by a stroke a couple of years before, and he had not yet recovered from
the
% --- p. 120 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{120}after-effects, which, as I shall mention later, grew worse after a
great sorrow. There was talk of my holding the philosophical course in
his place in 1882---83; but Rasmus Nielsen declared himself ready to
take it over, although he too had recently had a stroke. It soon turned
out that he was too weak to carry it through to the end, and since the
number of students had now risen greatly, a division became necessary,
and Dr. Kroman and I were approached to lecture in the spring semester
of 1883. When Rasmus Nielsen then retired, the faculty recommended me
for the vacant professorship. Attempts are said to have been made with
the minister to work against my appointment, particularly on account of
my conduct in the Students' Society, perhaps also on account of my
religious opinions. I have never been able to find out who the man was
who, according to what I know from a reliable source, went on this
matter to the then Minister of Education (Jacob Scavenius). Several of
my friends were greatly concerned and doubted that I would be
appointed. But on 2 February 1883 I received my appointment (reckoned
from 1 Sept., since Nielsen's retirement was reckoned from that day).

I had long given lectures and exercises as privatdocent and as permanent
lecturer. Now I also took over the philosophical course for the young
students. My university activity consisted in the following years
(until 1916) of three things. Besides the annual course for the young
students, I held special exercises, intended for those who wished to
take the master's examination in philosophy, or for students who wished
to continue their occupation with philosophy after the first year, and
finally I often gave evening lectures, which were intended for wider
circles and which sometimes gathered a large number of listeners.

It was twelve years since I had begun to lecture as privatdocent, and
since 1883 I have then worked as professor for 32 years. But this last
section comprises different periods, each of which must have its
chapter.

% --- p. 121 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\chapter*{IV}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{IV. 1883--1894}
\markboth{IV. 1883--1894}{IV. 1883--1894}
\opage{121}It has been a great good fortune for me to be a university teacher.
The constant interplay between the study and the lecture hall, --- the fact that little by little,
facing the young, one could come to touch on or speak of everything that concerns one's chief
interest in life, --- indeed, the very fact of having to do with young people at the age when so much
is laid down in them, --- all this makes life rich. I have had very great difficulties to overcome
both as a speaker and as a writer, and I know well that I have never entirely overcome them. And I
have, especially in my earlier years, suffered from what one might call lectern fever. Just before a
lecture or an address one easily gets a feeling of emptiness; what one has worked out stands there as
uninteresting, and as something that in any case will not interest those one is to speak to; --- and
can one even bring out what one wants to say in the right way? --- In time I have no doubt gained
greater freedom and confidence. And in any case what I have been able to offer has been received and
acknowledged in a way for which I must feel deeply grateful. ---

Already during my years as privatdocent I had come into a personal relationship with some of my
listeners, and as my circle of listeners widened, this took on a larger scope. One came to seek advice
about his choice of studies, another to discuss a philosophical problem, a third to complain of his
hypochondria, a fourth to get advice concerning difficult or problematic circumstances at home. And I
also began to gather some of those who seemed to have a philosophical interest beyond the
% --- p. 122 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{122}extent to which philosophy is required for the philosophicum. At monthly gatherings various
subjects within and outside philosophy were then discussed, most often in such a way that the students
gave the introduction in turn; yet I myself also sometimes gave the introductory talk. I valued these
gatherings highly for the personal acquaintance they led to in many cases. It particularly pleased me
to learn how the foundation was laid here for many friendships among the participants. Many took part
in these gatherings year in and year out; but I sometimes had to drop the oldest age groups, so that
they should not weigh down the younger ones. For me myself, too, friendships have grown out of such
gatherings. Men like Valdemar Vedel, Georg Saxild and Niels Møller I have through them come into a
personal relationship with that will surely last through life, since it has lasted so long. Among the
dead I remember with sadness Knud Ipsen, whose posthumous work on Diderot I published with an account
of his life and personality.

Among those who for a time took part in these gatherings were also two young men who later won fine
names as poets, Johannes Jørgensen and Viggo Stuckenberg.

Johannes Jørgensen I remember as an eager young biologist who had gone over from the study of German
to natural science. He gave a talk at my home on Weismann's biological theories. But biology could no
more hold him fast than the study of the German language, and after he had for some time talked of
studying philosophy, he devoted himself entirely to literature. I liked the young man with the
beautiful eyes in the Mongolian face, but I cannot --- according to his own autobiography --- boast of
having been anything to him. What, by his own account, interested him in philosophy was really only
that it could not set up new authorities in place of the old ones, which he believed he had left once
and for all, and he then found it
% --- p. 123 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{123}justified to give himself up to his bohemian life, just as he no doubt also later, after his
conversion to Catholicism, finds it to have been the most consistent course. If there is no hell and
no purgatory, why should one deny oneself anything at all? In his first books he depicts time after
time the poor student from the provinces who comes to Copenhagen without having any foothold there and
therefore knows only the life of the streets and ends in the gutter. I once wrote to him, when he had
sent me a new book of the same content: ``Dear Jørgensen, you once traveled from Svendborg to
Copenhagen, and you never forget that journey.'' After he had left my circle, he attacked me from the
various standpoints he later took up, lastly from the Catholic one. I nonetheless kept my interest in
him and found in particular that the conversion to Catholicism not only gave him hold and support but
also made his poetry truly unfold. Yet I confess that I prefer the old Catholic poets to the modern
