ones; in the latter, it seems to me, the poetry often stands in a somewhat external relation to the
religious ideas that are professed. --- On the occasion of my sixtieth birthday he wrote to me from
Rome: ``I believe I am connected with you on more than one point, and I think that the more the years
go by, the more I shall come to recognize this. In any case I believe I can never come to be as far
from you as I was in my negative period.'' (9 March 1903). --- I do not deny that after this I was
both surprised and hurt by the cool and superior (forcedly superior) manner in which I am spoken of in
his autobiography. On the one hand he has me teach a purely negative view, without heeding that I have
always conceived and presented the human life of the spirit, its laws and its tasks, as a positive
fullness that was able in itself to give life value, and that the negations I was led to aimed only at
protecting this true and genuine positivity. A delight in mere criticism I have never felt.
% --- p. 124 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{124}On the other hand he does not mention the purely human motives that in my view could give
strength for serious self-assertion and keep one from throwing oneself away to end in the gutter.
--- Had he written his autobiography in his ``negative period'' I could have understood it, but not
after the statement in the letter. But perhaps the point was to set off in relief the conversion that
a later part of the biography is to depict.

[That it is not only I who have received this impression of Jørgensen's account of me in his
biography, I see from a letter I received in January 1917 from a former listener who was personally
quite unknown to me. He writes: ``The way in which you and your life's work are spoken of in
Jørgensen's memoirs cannot but outrage a person who has received some of his best impressions from
your human personality. There is, to be sure, nothing directly disparaging about you in these books,
but it is in a high degree dispiriting to see the complete blindness that has struck a spiritually
stirred man and outstanding poet with regard to your life's work ... You taught us respect for the
significance of the life of the spirit. You always pointed to the human, which united us all.'' --- I
could not wish for any better summary judgment of what I strove for in my work as a teacher than the
one which a listener of 1906, unknown to me, has expressed here, several years after his
participation in my teaching. In my most confident moments I pass a similar judgment myself; but it
does one good to see them come forth in a spontaneous outburst from another quarter]. ---

Viggo Stuckenberg, too, took part for a time in the monthly gatherings on Amicivej. I see clearly
before me his handsome face with the radiant eyes. When he had begun his work as an author with tales
and short stories, he once asked me for a frank opinion on one of them. I found it slight and unclear,
and in keeping with the promise I had given him, I wrote this to him
% --- p. 125 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{125}in words as kind as possible. From what I heard, my judgment nevertheless hurt him, and he
thought of ceasing to take part in the meetings. Yet he overcame his misgivings, and a short time
afterwards he read aloud at my home a fragment of a short story that was very successful. It depicted
how a young student, who sits absorbed in reading in his room with Darwin's picture on his wall and
Brandes' books on his table, receives a visit from an old uncle from the country, who is then appalled
at what he gets to see and hear. --- Stuckenberg's later production, from ``Favre Ord'' onward and
through his deeply felt and finely wrought poems, I followed with interest and sympathy. I still
admire the great poem about his mother and the even more profound poem ``Bekendelse'', in which he
settles accounts with a friend (Johannes Jørgensen) who had changed his faith. After I had not seen
him for a number of years, I met him one day up at ``Nordisk Forlag'' and took the opportunity to
thank him for his books in a few kind words. He seemed a little embarrassed by this, but I thought no
more about it. The same evening I received a letter from him, in which he thanked me in the most
touching and childlike way for what I had said to him, and apologized for his confusion that morning.
``There lies,'' he concludes, ``a kind of curse on reverence; it always keeps a barrier lowered
between the younger and the older. I would just not like to see that barrier too much gone.
Conversations matter least in this world, most the thoughts we go about with of one another. And I
shall be glad if you, from your thoughts about me, will always be able to greet me as kindly as you
met me this morning.'' --- The wish Stuckenberg expressed in these last words has been fulfilled,
though I did not get the opportunity to tell him so. Of his struggle with grief and poverty I heard
only after his death. His memory I have kept in admiration and sadness, and the letter I have
mentioned I keep as one of
% --- p. 126 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{126}the finest memories of how young people I have come into contact with on my way could feel
disposed toward me. ---

After the laboratory instruction had become more organized, it was as a rule the participants in it
whom I invited. I had grown somewhat tired of the more general subjects I discussed at the monthly
gatherings. And the laboratory hours themselves, in which a major philosophical work was as a rule
gone through (other works too, e.g. one of my own), gave occasion for closer acquaintance. I then
gathered the participants for an evening at the end of the semester, and it was then as a rule a
purely social gathering. In the years when I lived in the little apartment on Carl Bernhards Vej
(1908---14), space could be tight; we sometimes had to go out for a walk while the table was being
laid. At Carlsberg there was room enough, and it was a fine sight to see groups of young people moving
about in the garden or in ``Pompeji''. Perhaps it is on such evenings that I have especially had a
festive feeling about ``the Honorary Residence''.

\secrule

In the autumn of 1883 Heegaard resumed his work at the University after the heavy blows of fate that
had passed over him, and he lectured alongside me for the young students.

During the examinations in the summer of 1880 he had suffered a stroke, which for a time left him
unable to work, and to regain his health he traveled to Italy. I received several letters from him
that seemed to show that he was recovering. But in the spring of 1881 he had a new attack in Florence,
and his wife and daughter then traveled down to him. The daughter, a fresh and cheerful young girl who
was a great joy in the home, caught typhoid during the stay in Florence and died after a couple of
weeks' illness. After this sorrow Heegaard never rose again. There now took place
% --- p. 127 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{127}a great change in him. His former intellectual zeal, his absorption in independent and
critical inquiry, was now replaced by a sinking into brooding. It was the thought of his daughter that
occupied him. I remember conversations with him in Frederiksberg Garden, where he set out how the dead
were not far from us; he could well imagine his daughter stepping forth under the trees there in front
of us. Anyone who has lost someone he truly loved will know something of this feeling. But in Heegaard
the brooding over it became more and more dominant. At the same time his attacks recurred, and he
became more and more enfeebled. The energy for work was gone. The need for an absolute foothold in
another world than the one that experience and reflection could open became stronger and stronger in
him. And so there came the declaration (in the preface to the second edition of his Pædagogik) that
he had returned to the old faith of the Church as the only thing that could hold him up. In a very
fine way, and with the honesty that lay in his nature, he declared his changed faith, whose coming
into being I had been able to follow step by step through our conversations. He himself believed that
it was by an act of will at a particular moment that the change had taken place. But such
``mutations'' surely always have their prehistory, in the spiritual as in the material domain, and I
had been able to follow this one in its main outlines. From the belief in immortality, which sprang
from the need to feel himself near his beloved daughter, as a first beginning, his mind had been bent
more and more toward what lies beyond experience, and when the need for definitely formed ideas of
this beyond made itself felt, the content of his childhood faith lay nearest at hand.

There was something touching in the inwardness with which he spoke of his new position, and I felt
the greatest reverence for what was stirring in him. All the more did it pain me that he sometimes
harbored mistrust of me. We met almost daily at the University in the
% --- p. 128 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{128}autumn of 1883. But one day he did not come. The next day I said to him: ``You were ill
yesterday?'' He answered: ``Yes, I was ill.'' I thought no more about it; but a little after I had
come home after the lecture the bell rang, and Heegaard came into my room deeply moved and said: ``I
have come to tell you that I lied to you. I was not ill yesterday, but I was at communion, and I
feared you would mock me for it.'' To this I answered that it pained me that he could harbor such a
belief about me, especially as he had to acknowledge that I had given him no occasion for it. It ended
with both of us weeping, and we parted as good friends. --- In the course of the autumn the strokes
became more and more frequent. After the lecture I had to accompany him to the omnibus and often feared
for how he would get home. Some way into the new year he passed away.

From the orthodox side a great deal was made of Heegaard's conversion. His friends, who had known him
in his good working years and seen his best and manliest qualities unfold in them, could not be in
doubt as to where they should look for the real Sofus Heegaard. They saw him in the man who in his
full strength let his thought work on the problems, even if the world of possibilities already then
occupied his mind when it sought rest, --- in the man who looked with irony on every kind of
dogmatism, wherever it came from. Now he was weakened in mind and body. He had spent far too much of
his strength in toil for a livelihood, and then the great sorrow came on top of it. The time of his
vigorous unfolding of life was so short. But an honest man he was, wherever he stood. ---

It is of course so that what we think and believe in our strong times must stand its test in the weak
times, and precisely in them. But how many are put to such a test as Heegaard? And it holds of every
faith that it can fail when it counts. I have on my way seen several cases where people who in good
times were
% --- p. 129 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{129}churchly believers, precisely when sorrow and misfortune came upon them, had the experience
that the faith they had held to until then did not help them. These are exceedingly deep-lying
matters, hard to disentangle, that we face here. And however great a weight one may wish to lay on the
times of weakness as decisive, they can still never be what one should take as one's basis. A building
can be firmly joined and have a deep foundation, even if it cannot withstand an earthquake. The measure
of a life's value we must take from the times when it unfolds freely and luxuriantly. The free man,
says Spinoza, broods not over death but over life.

\secrule

Another friend took, at about this time, a significant step which, while it did not have the
character of principle that Heegaard's conversion had, yet came as a surprise. Hans Skovgaard, my
friend from my school years, had studied theology like me, and in our first student years I was
probably more theological than he. After his theological examination he took to studying history and
French and, after having been a teacher in Copenhagen (at the ``Lyceum'', where I also taught),
became assistant master in Nykøbing on Falster. He had, for that matter, like me come into Greek
studies and occupied himself closely with Plutarch's philosophical writings and with Stoicism. In
Nykøbing, where he was much taken up with the school and with his boarders, he got up at
4\textonehalf{} in the morning to read Plutarch and Marcus Aurelius. One of his fellow teachers said of
him that he still lived as a student, and that was right. It has also lasted into his older days. His
religious views had hardly changed. But those closest to him had the impression that he was wholly
absorbed in his school work and his studies. Then he wrote to me on 2 January 1884: ``In the autumn I
spent a great part of the time, in my room or on solitary
% --- p. 130 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{130}walks, debating pastor or not pastor, until one fine day, to a certain astonishment of my
contemporaries --- not least of my wife --- I declared that I would become a pastor.''

After he had been ordained, the same year, I wrote a letter to him whose content I do not remember,
but whose character and direction appear from his reply (3 Nov. 1884), from which I quote a longer
passage because it is characteristic of our relationship before and after: ``Thank you for your kind
letter. I had indeed expected a letter from you, and a real letter from a friend too, and that I have
also received. So I have nothing to complain of, one would think --- and yet I cannot deny that there
was something that as it were hurt inside me when I read it. Were I properly a `pastor', --- yes,
possibly I ought not to say `pastor' in quotation marks, but simply a Christian pastor (possibly, I
say, for I do not really know) --- well, were I that, then I ought presumably to say that it pained me
for your sake. But that would not be the truth, not the full truth at least. Still less does it pain
me for my own sake, --- but for both our sakes, or for the sake of a breaking harmony. Your words sound
to me as if they came from a far, far place and could reach me only faintly ringing and half broken;
--- there is something so melancholy in the echo of a farewell far away .... It is a mood that sounds
in me, not only when I look back on your path and mine, how they have slowly and surely moved away
from each other, so that we must now raise our voices to be heard, but also when I measure my own
wayward paths against the King's highway on which I ought to walk.'' --- In the following years he
often comes back to the same subject. Thus in a letter written on my birthday in 1891: ``We have
indeed talked much together, and thought or dreamed together, and taken together that comes to: we
have lived much together. And then it is so strange that we cannot live together like that and
% --- p. 131 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{131}think and talk together as before. Sometimes I cannot get it into my head: you are after all
still the old Harald Høffding, and you have the same eyes when you go to the borderline and look out
over the infinite, which \textit{is} there, whatever kind of hoarfrost may cover it ... And when you go
down into yourself to find the origin of yourself .... then I think you must see the same as I see
...... At other times it whispers inside me: `How far we have come away from each other ...' --- In
January 1894 he writes: ``Strangely enough: although, especially in the evening, when I sit alone in
my room after my usual bedtime, I not so rarely have little conversations with you (have you ever
noticed it?), which are carried on without voice and could hardly be rendered in distinct words (so
unborn are they --- unripened moods) --- yet I have never in them caught myself attempting to convert
you --- although I quite soberly think that you ought to do it. I suppose that we both (as far as I am
concerned) are still 20 years old in such evening hours, and something in us is indeed so still.''

I have visited Skovgaard in his various parsonages, --- in Ørum near Vejle, in Lynge near Sorø, in
Kettinge on Lolland. The friendship and the intimacy have lasted. We have indeed had a single clash on
account of the opposition between pastor and philosopher; but it did no harm. There was and remained,
moreover, something of a student in my old friend. I quote a passage from a letter of March 1909 which
shows how the pastor and the student in him could work together: ``I still live, then, as pastor in
Kettinge-Bregninge. Of exploits in this my capacity it is, for good reasons, quite impossible for me
to speak. The feelings that come up in me during the work --- whether I sit at home at the table here
trying to get hold of something that people may benefit from hearing, or am out on my parish rounds
--- can be of rather different kinds. Now I think that it is tough to
% --- p. 132 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{132}be a pastor, tougher than most other things, now again that no other work can be finer, so
genuinely human --- in both cases a unicum, which it certainly is, too. --- Then I have got it into
my head that it is not without danger for the pastor and the human being to grow old. And to avoid
that danger as far as possible I read some strenuous book or other --- one that lies so high up that
I must stand on tiptoe to reach it --- that is salutary, even at the risk of not understanding it. In
that respect Boutroux: `Sur la contingence des lois de la nature' fulfills all reasonable demands.''
Of other books he is reading Amiel's ``Journal intime'' and James' ``Religiøse Erfaringer''.'' From
the fragments of letters I have quoted here, one may perhaps get a small idea of my friend's gifts as
a letter writer. But the main thing for me has been to show the fine way in which he conceived our
relationship, all the while he was living himself more deeply into his churchly position. ---

There was another parsonage I visited in the '80s and '90s besides Skovgaard's. Through my cousin
Karl Gjellerup I had made the acquaintance of his foster parents, the poet and pastor Johannes Fibiger
and his wife Amalie, née Waage, --- an acquaintance that soon passed into warm friendship, on both
sides, I am sure. From 1880 on I spent a few days with them every year. At first it was in the
summertime, and I remember some glorious summer days spent in the garden or in the surroundings of
their snug parsonage. Fibiger was, when I came to know him, pastor in Valensved near Næstved, later in
Ønslev on Falster. I have received from his nephew a picture Fibiger himself painted of the garden at
Ønslev, and it awakens good and fine memories in me. Later it was mostly in the month of January that
I went down to them. Precisely in the heart of winter I needed those two people, whose spirit was as
deep as their hearts were warm. The quiet days with them helped me through many a low time.
% --- p. 133 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{133}Johannes Fibiger was, as I said, both poet and pastor, and he himself admitted that he was
not entirely clear where the one ended and the other began. Deeply religious he was in any case,
though he did not think much of theology. We sometimes had long conversations about the relation
between the figurative and the literal in people's faith. One winter evening I remember especially,
when our conversation ran so lively, and at the same time so thoughtful, a course that I later said
to Fru Amalie, who had been our interested and understanding listener, that she ought to have taken
it down in shorthand; it could have become a philosophical dialogue. It was probably in the course of
this conversation that I, when Fibiger had set out the content of his faith, said: ``For me it is
only poetry!'' --- whereupon he answered: ``Do you say \textit{only} poetry?'' Since that time I have
avoided saying ``only'' in that connection when what was in question was what I call the poetry of
life. By the poetry of life I understand a poetry that is the symbolic expression of deeply affecting
experiences and experiences of life, which the poetry of art is not always. --- Often we seemed to
draw closer in our verdicts, only then suddenly to see the opposition stand out sharply. Fibiger liked
to bring his statements to a point, and he could then perhaps hold on a little too long to the
artificial point. But his rich imagination and life of feeling and his thorough study of the history
of religion gave conversation with him great interest when he was in good form. In his later years
he could sometimes say with sadness that the calling of pastor had not really suited him, and that he
would not choose it if he had to choose now. His sermons were not delivered to many listeners. His
Bible readings, on the other hand, were well attended; here he could give himself more freely, and
there he could put his spirited independent thinking and great wealth of knowledge to more use.
Visits to the sick and the poor also suited him well.

Of his poetic work, special mention should be made of some Old Testament poems and the collection he
called
% --- p. 134 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{134}``Den evige Strid'' and published under the name of Diodorus. But his best book is his
autobiography, which appeared after his death and which gives an exceedingly interesting contribution
to the understanding of the spiritual life of the forties. The greatest interest of the book, however,
lies in its depiction of the life of two lovable and spirited people.

When his wife was mentioned above as listener at our conversations, it was by no means because she
could not give her own, independent contributions to a serious discussion. She was a finely
cultivated lady who strove to see for herself and to find her own bearings in the great questions.
When her foster son Karl Gjellerup, whom she loved dearly, began to move away from the churchly faith,
she made it her concern to examine what the reasons for such a change might be. She studied the main
works of critical theology; I often saw learned works of this kind lying on her table. Her great
modesty and her great admiration for her husband meant that she as a rule held back in the presence
of others. But in conversations alone with her I received the impression of a very considerable human
being. There was a radiance over her utterances, because they came from a stirred mind and were the
fruit of serious seeking. Perhaps she was quite as gifted as her husband. It was at bottom easier for
me to talk with her than with him, and I was and am very proud of the openness with which she
expressed herself to me. I cannot refrain here from inserting a passage from a letter of hers,
although it contains exceedingly kind words about me. I believe it gives a true impression of the
relationship between us. It is written on 7 May 1894.

``It was fine and kind of you to send me a letter for my birthday, and one so heartfelt and so full
of content! It pleased me greatly, and I thank you for it. That we have been able to be so much to
you, even I, could not but both please and surprise me; though one may hope for such a thing, it is
still something one does not really know until one
% --- p. 135 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{135}hears it from the person concerned. We have indeed both regarded you as a truly good friend,
with whom we could speak freely and in confidence and from whom we could hope for understanding, in
spite of much difference in development and opinions. Yes, it has often surprised me myself that I
did not shrink, as you remark, from speaking to you about religious questions that lay close to my
heart, and on which I knew you took a different view from mine. I, who otherwise find it hard to
speak of such things and feared any rough or mocking touch upon this inner life of mine, have never
had any such feeling with you; on the contrary, it interested me to speak to you about it. On one
single occasion I thought I offended you by it, but that this was not the case I now see, and it
pleases me. When people trust each other, it works.'' ---

After Fibiger had retired on account of infirmity, he and his wife moved to Copenhagen. He survived
the move only a short time, however. Fru Amalie lived some ten years more after his death, and it was
always a refreshment to me to visit the old lady. She for her part appreciated my visits in the most
touching way. I once called her in a letter my motherly friend, and she gladly accepted this name.
With her it was always easy to come onto subjects of interest. But just as I was looking forward to
coming to live nearer to her (she lived on Kochs Vej, and I was to move out to Carl Bernhard's Vej),
I received word of her death. For several years she had suffered from a heart ailment; her strength
declined, and life had become a burden to her. Then came a stroke, after which she passed away. ---
But often, when I come along Kochs Vej, I still look up at the windows where I had so many times seen
my motherly friend at her work, and from which I sometimes received her friendly greeting already
down on the road.

Those two people stood for me as fine and noble representatives of the generation that went before
mine.
% --- p. 136 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{136}Through them I understood much of the time to which they had belonged. But they represented
for me first and foremost themselves. ---

\secrule

In the summer of 1884 I visited both Skovgaard, who still lived in Nykøbing, and the Fibigers in
Ønslev. Julius Petersen came along to Nykøbing to visit a colleague there, and one day we three
schoolfellows went out to Pumlenakke on the east coast of Falster. The day after I went out to
Ønslev, and after some good summer days there I went on board the steamer to Rostock at Nykøbing. I
had in fact decided on a little journey abroad --- to get to know German philosophers and Swiss
mountain scenery. In Berlin I stayed some weeks, visited the museums, where Rembrandt in particular
and my special favorite Ruysdael absorbed me, and attended lectures at the University as a guest. The
most famous man I made the acquaintance of was old Eduard Zeller, author of the giant work ``Die
Philosophie der Griechen'', a neat and precise scholar whose pronounced Swabian dialect entered into
an attractive union with his guileless and kindly words. I further came to know Friedrich Paulsen and
thereby laid the foundation of a friendship that has been of much significance for me. Paulsen was a
Frisian from South Schleswig and has given in his memoirs of youth a fine and interesting account of
life in the lonely regions of southwest Schleswig. He was a broad, steady and solid scholar and
teacher. The acquaintance was continued on my later visits to Berlin, and he has also visited me in
Copenhagen. He could read Danish from his childhood, and it was owing to his urging and
recommendation that my Psykologi came out in German, where it has then drawn my other books after it.
A third philosopher I came to know in Berlin was the moral philosopher Georg v. Gizycki, an eager
follower of Bentham and Mill. Gizycki was somewhat dry in thought and speech, but an enthusiastic
adherent of utilitarianism in its specifically English form. His thoughts went more and
% --- p. 137 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{137}more in a socialist direction, and he was a great optimist, though he was a cripple. A
nervous debility had paralyzed his legs, so that he had to be wheeled in a wheelchair up to the
University and into the lecture hall, where a ramp had been laid up to the lectern. He told me that
one evening his servant was out, and he (who was then unmarried) was alone at home. He wanted a book
that stood at the other end of the room and dragged himself over there along the table, but was so
unlucky as to fall. Get up he could not, but he lay there on the floor and read until the servant at
long last came home. As a boy he had been able to walk, but run he had never been able to. In the
afternoon he liked to sit over a mug of beer in the zoological garden, and there one could have a
good conversation with him. And sometimes one Berlin colleague or another would join us, thus one day
Gustav Schmoller, famous for his works in social history. --- Besides these men's lectures I heard
Adolph Wagner on political economy and Scherer on Goethe's poems.

From Berlin the journey went to Dresden, where it was of course the museums that laid claim to me. The
Sistine Madonna struck me as a revelation. The little room where the picture hung had the character of
a chapel, and the visitors too felt seized with devotion, whether they were believing Catholics or
not. The picture stands for me in a radiance that has become, if not more brilliant, then more inward
and full of feeling on my later visits. It is the apotheosis of motherly love, of inwardness and of
enthusiasm. The cult of the Madonna is the cult I understand best, especially since sociological
studies have shown me the mother with the child as a psychological center for the development not
only of the family's feelings but of all sympathetic feelings, the hearth of altruism in the history
of the race. In later years Yrjö Hirn's fine work on the cult of the Madonna has deepened my
understanding of this at once most exalted and most inward religious figure.

% --- p. 138 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{138}A devotion of another kind I held in Weimar, where I entered into Goethe's daily round. The
little garden house outside the town, by the river Ilm, reminded me of the young Goethe's enthusiasm
for nature, when he took up his abode out there one spring evening and made his bed out in the open
air, where he was woken by the birdsong. The Goethe Museum in the town called up the memory of the old
Goethe, whose heart could yet still beat like a young man's, though resignation had to dampen its
beat. I saw him sitting in his armchair in the plainly furnished study, while Eckermann, over by the
table, was absorbed in the glorious Marienbad Elegy, the most beautiful and deepest of Goethe's poems
of his old age.

Eisenach with the Wartburg turned my thoughts again to other regions. From the high castle Luther's
eye has looked out over forests and mountain peaks. In the Thüringerwald I took glorious walks.

A little comic story from the table d'hôte in Eisenach I must tell. I happened to sit beside a
gentleman and a lady who were speaking Danish, and when they came onto private matters, I made them
aware that I understood them. They turned out to be a village pastor from Zealand and his wife. The
pastor was coming from Carlsbad, where he had been taking a cure, and complained loudly about the high
spa tax he had been assessed. This tax was set according to the person's position, and to give an
impression of something very humble and lowly he had entered himself on the list as
``Landpfarrer''; in his opinion that was to mean a simple village pastor --- but it was interpreted as
a kind of bishop, a pastor over the clergy of a whole province, and his attempt to make himself as
small as possible thus had an unfortunate outcome. At the hotel he must have made similar attempts,
for the landlord whispered to me when we talked about them: ``die Pfarrer können bisweilen sehr
praktisch sein!''

From Eisenach the journey went to Heidelberg, where I paid a
% --- p. 139 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{139}visit to the well-known historian of philosophy Kuno Fischer and spent an evening with him.
He was a stately man, felt himself a Geheimerath-Excellenz and spoke with sovereign contempt of other
authors. His books had been of much use to me in my first attempts to find my bearings in the history
of modern philosophy; later I saw how uncritical they were, in that they passed lightly over the
difficult points. A spirited man he was, and his lectures were well attended. From Copenhagen I knew
that in the autumn he was to marry a Danish lady, Fru Stilling, a very beautiful lady with radiant
eyes and chalk-white hair. I had been a guest in her house and had learned to value her kind-hearted
and lively nature. In the course of the conversation Fischer asked me, seemingly quite by chance:
``Kennen Sie eine Frau Stilling in Kopenhagen?'' It was a little sly; but even if I had not been
prepared, I would still have had nothing but good to say of her. Later I sometimes saw Fischer and
his wife in Copenhagen, where he also paid me a visit.

In Freiburg in Baden I stayed a couple of days and visited Aloys Riehl here, who was already then
known for his work on ``Den filosofiske Kriticisme''. Riehl was an energetic man, sharp in speech and
thought. A very lively evening I spent at his home together with an English guest. From Kiel, where
he later lived, he has visited me in Copenhagen. In his older days he is professor in Berlin, and I
have been in touch with him there.

My travel plan as regards Switzerland had been laid by arrangement with a younger, much-traveled
friend, the zoologist Nielsen, assistant master in Aalborg. I had met him at Brøchner's, who thought
highly of him, and I learned to do the same. He had decided scientific gifts, but was in despair over
his isolation in Aalborg. An excellent teacher he was, but that did not wholly satisfy him. He felt
happy only on his journeys, for which he
% --- p. 140 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{140}saved up the whole year. Now we met in Schafhausen and began our Swiss tour from there.
Zurich was our first station. Here I looked up the philosopher Richard Avenarius, founder of the
journal ``Vierteljahrsschrift für wissenschaftliche Philosophie'', in which I had written the year
before. He was an acute thinker whose main work, which came out some 8---9 years later under the
title ``Kritik der reinen Erfahrung'', has, despite its abstract form, an exceedingly interesting
content; in my book ``Moderne Filosofi'' I have given an account of his theory and characterized it as
the natural history of problems. The strenuous work later broke down his health; he sought relief,
among other places, at Skodsborg, where in the summer of 1894 I was together with him several times
and philosophized with him among the trees of the Dyrehave. Two years later he died. But in 1884 he
was still healthy and active, and with him and his wife I spent a good evening in their snug home.

It was on the way from Schafhausen to Zurich that I first caught sight of snow mountains (the Glarus
Alps) and at first took them for white masses of cloud. I have used this experience in the preface to
my Etik. We began our walking tours in Graubünden, from the little post station of Thusis. We walked
over the Albula Pass to get to the Engadine. Up on the top of the pass we were snowed in, to the great
joy of two German gentlemen who were staying up there to collect butterflies, but who had now begun to
grow tired of each other. In any case the one, a tall and heavy man, had grown tired of the other, a
small, thin fellow who undeniably did not seem to have much to say either. The big one expressed his
joy that we had to stay there, --- for, he said, ``zwischen mir und diesem Herrn ist der Faden schon
ausgesponnen''. The little one looked a little sheepish at that. The big one at once took it upon
himself to arrange the meal and was altogether something between a steward and a maître de plaisir
for us.

From the Albula Pass we walked the next day through
% --- p. 141 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{141}Samaden to Ponte Resina, where we settled down for some days and made excursions in the
Engadine with its glorious lights and the lovely colors on lakes and fields. And then the air one
breathed here; it was a pleasure merely to draw breath. When I later read Nietzsche, who got some of
his best thoughts up here, I understood well that he valued living up here so highly. We saw the
Alpine peaks glow in the light of evening. It was cold in Ponte Resina; but in the mornings the sun
lured the marmots out of their burrows on the mountain slopes; they sat in front of the burrows and
licked up the sunshine, while a fine piping expressed their contentment. The small and the great
alike here drew one's attention. We climbed Piz-Languard, 9000 feet high. The ascent was laborious
but not dangerous, yet I became dizzy, especially when the Alpine choughs swished past me and suddenly
shot downward. Our guide gave me moral support by taking off his trouser belt and letting me hold one
end while he himself held the other. But the toil was well rewarded. When we got up, we saw many miles
away snowy peak after snowy peak shining in the strong sunshine. It was a sight I have never forgotten.

In a return carriage we drove back to Chur, went from there to Göschenen and began here a new walking
tour,
% print: over Andernach op over Sheideck (misprint)
over Andermatt and up over the Scheidegg, past the Jungfrau and the Mönch. It was 5 days' march,
which ended in Lauterbrunnen, from where we drove to Interlaken to rest there before the journey home
began. We were very weary after the 5 days' walking, but they had been glorious days; the mountain
landscape showed itself to us in all its splendor under the radiant sunshine, which let every form
stand out in its full particularity.

We traveled home through Germany and up through Jutland. Nielsen was going to Aalborg (which he did
not at all look forward to seeing again), and I was to fetch my two boys in Vendsyssel, where they had
spent the summer holidays with their relatives. ---

\secrule

% --- p. 142 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{142}In the years 1884---85 the political tension grew. Copenhagen, which for so long had been
undividedly National Liberal and Right, was now divided, as the formation of liberal voters'
associations indicated. On Constitution Day the Opposition too now marched en masse in procession
out to their festival ground. The mass was not large, however, at any rate the mass of those who were
willing to prostitute themselves by taking part in the procession. At the festival in 1884 we
gathered behind Tivoli and were then bold enough to march out along Vesterbro, a small but perhaps
select band. But people laughed at us from the windows, and our band had the stupidity or the malice
to play ``When I lay in the cradle --- and was as big as that'' --- The festival otherwise went off
% Danish: „Da jeg i Vuggen laa --- og var saa stor som saa“
excellently. There were good speakers, Hostrup, Hørup, Bojsen and others. There was a large
assembly, for a great many of the like-minded had preferred to meet out there instead of taking part
in the procession. On the platform, where I had a place as chairman of the meeting and as president
of the Frederiksberg Liberal Voters' Association, I talked with a journalist, an old schoolfellow,
about how many people there were. I thought 10,000, he 8,000. The next day I saw that his paper, a
Right paper, gave 4,000. But he then came out to me and explained that he had written 8,000, but that
the editors had changed it without further ado. --- It is hardly the only time such a thing has
happened --- on both sides.

Although the Opposition won the election in the summer of 1884, the Estrup ministry nevertheless
continued its policy and from 1885 on governed without an appropriation act. The tension grew, and
there was great unrest in people's minds. It was a feeling of indignation and humiliation that made
itself felt among those who belonged to the Opposition. The Danish people had not deserved such
treatment.

Once in the course of the summer a political meeting was held in Holstebro, where Chr. Berg was to be
the main speaker. The chief of police had on this occasion taken a seat on the platform; but Berg
refused to speak as long as he was there, and two men (Noos and Nielsen) on the board of the
% --- p. 143 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{143}voters' association then gently led the chief of police down from the platform in spite of
his protest. The government made a great deal of this affair. The government sent a special
commission over to judge those who were thought to have offended. Noos and Nielsen were arrested and
treated as criminals. They were roughly addressed by the examining magistrate, and even their wives
were treated insolently when they sought to obtain some easing of their husbands' conditions in
prison. This aroused general indignation. The agitation was great all over the country, especially of
course in the district itself. There had even, according to what a man from the district told me
shortly afterward, been talk of taking the two men out of prison by force and of disarming the
soldiers in the Jutland garrisons, which was thought not to be difficult once men from the soldiers'
own home districts came forward. It was the local members of the Folketing who prevented the carrying
out of this plan. The sentence was 6 months' imprisonment on ordinary prison fare for Berg and the two
men from Holstebro. After the sentence Noos and Nielsen were set at liberty, since they, like Berg,
appealed to the Supreme Court.

A short time afterward all three were invited to a gathering at the Students' Society. There was no
special occasion for me to come that evening; but I remember that at dinner I said to my brother that
I would go up there to shake some brave men's hands. I had taken the gathering to be private, but by
an irony of fate it became the first evening at which everything was reported. My colleague Erslev and
I were present and both spoke. It was the two men's treatment while in custody that had aroused our
sympathy for them.

The next morning the Right papers raged and demanded that an example be made of Erslev and me for our
``friendliness to criminals''. Some weeks passed, and I was prepared to be dismissed. The tension rose
when Estrup was shot at, though only a coat button was hit. The evening this had happened, two of my
colleagues who, like me, lived in
% --- p. 144 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{144}Frederiksberg came to me and said that I must be prepared for a search of my house during
the night, as president of the liberal voters' association, and that I should therefore get all
dangerous papers out of the way. There were no such papers, and no guests came in the night either.
On one of the following days I took part in a large meeting at the Kasino, which had been arranged
beforehand, and sat, with members of the liberal voters' associations, on the stage while Hørup in a
brilliant speech presented the Copenhagen Voters' Association with a new banner. Before the meeting
there had been a dinner in common at the Hotel Kongen af Danmark, and as I made my way there, I
noticed two well-known politicians of the Right who, each from his street corner, were taking note of
who came to the meeting. In the following week there was a meeting of the Frederiksberg Voters'
Association at ``Sommerlyst'', where I was to speak. Just before the meeting began, a stenographer
from the Rigsdag came and told me that, from what he had heard, it was now to be dismissal for Erslev
and me. The fact that the decision seemed thus to have been made brought complete calm to my mind, and
I gave my address with full composure and with quite as much force as I am otherwise able to put into
it. It dealt with how powerless those in power would in the end prove to be in the face of what has
developed by virtue of a people's nature and has become its will.

I now prepared myself for how I should arrange my life if I was dismissed. A main concern for me was
how I should now gain time to complete my ``Etik'', which I had long been working on. I thought of
resuming school teaching in some form or other. But then the decision came in a somewhat different
form from the one expected, namely in the form of a severe reprimand, because we had taken part in
celebrating ``convicted lawbreakers'' and had thereby made ourselves guilty of a ``gross
tactlessness'' toward the respect owed to the courts, and it was intimated to us that a repetition of
conduct of a similar kind would not be tolerated.

% --- p. 145 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{145}It was hard enough to receive such a rebuke. It had been sent to us in copy through the
Consistory; but when some time later a meeting of the teaching staff was held, the then rector (J. L.
Ussing) considered it fitting to read it aloud there. By chance neither Erslev nor I was present. The
Right papers had, moreover, printed the text at once. --- It would of course have been tempting to
refuse to accept the reprimand and thereby bring about a dismissal. I received letters from several
of my friends who urgently advised against such a step, which I too thought of only for a single
moment. Erslev and I valued our teaching at the University highly, and we also believed that we had
the right to attach such significance to it that there was ample counterweight to what had now
befallen us. Hørup had already said to me at the Kasino meeting: ``Just stay, and don't venture too
far forward. You do the cause the best service by staying where you are.''

Some students, according to what I later heard, are said to have planned a demonstration for me at one
of the following lectures, but that day I was prevented from lecturing by a dental abscess. Some time
afterward I appeared as a speaker at a meeting in the Students' Union and was greeted here with
demonstrative applause as I mounted the rostrum. I did not take this as approval of my conduct in the
Students' Society, but as an expression of the wish to see me remain at the University.

I believed that it was the reactionary government that had thought it necessary to take action
against the ``friendliness to criminals''. But many years later I happened to learn that it was the
commission judges who had felt offended by our conduct and had lodged a complaint about us. One of
them (later Justitiarius N. Lassen) is said to have boasted that on this occasion he had upheld the
dignity of the judiciary, and he drew from this the conclusion that a judge is grander than a
professor. ---

% --- p. 146 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{146}As long as Estrup was in power, the country continued to be governed
by provisional finance acts, no matter what the outcome of the elections.
The Government issued several provisional laws besides the Finance Act,
for instance a law establishing a gendarmerie to keep watch on the
population. This law aroused particular indignation. It was offensive
that when the Government, ``in order to satisfy the requirements of the
Constitution,'' laid the Gendarmerie Act before the Landsting, it was
buried there in a committee, because it was known that the Folketing would
reject it! That the sense of justice in the country did not weaken under
these conditions, which recurred year after year, is a proof of the sound
sense of our people.

Relations between those who belonged to different parties were often very
strained. In my family, for example, politics could not be discussed at
our gatherings. My eldest brother, the wholesale merchant Victor Høffding,
and I belonged to the Opposition, but my younger brother, the tenant
farmer Otto Høffding of Strandegaard, was a man of the Right (later a Free
Conservative). Mother kept the peace with anxious caution; yet I do
believe that she gradually became liberal. The present generation can
hardly enter into the conditions of that time. In my case, the fact that I
took part in electoral life in my own constituency, and that I had
moreover once been ``prostituted,'' was enough to brand me as a fanatic
who thought of nothing but politics. It was believed that I agitated from
the lecture chair. An excellent old colonel who was to meet me at his
son's wedding is said to have exclaimed: ``What on earth am I to talk to
that man about! He is a politician, after all.'' By being a politician was
meant voting with the Opposition. The doings of the Right were naturally
not ``politics.''

The autumn of 1886 brought me a new little clash. At a discussion meeting
held jointly by the Students' Union and the Students' Society I had been
asked to preside, since I was at the time a member of both associations.
On the day the meeting was to be held, strong articles were written
against me in
% --- p. 147 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{147}various papers of the Right. The evening itself passed quietly,
until one of the Students' Society's speakers used an expression about
Goos as a politician whose ambiguity I did not catch at the moment. That
gave a man of the Right occasion to accuse the chairman in sharp words of
partiality, because the expression had not been reproved. I rejected the
accusation. But on looking more closely into what had happened after the
meeting, it became clear to me that the remark ought to have been reproved,
and I then wrote a statement to the papers, which I also sent to Goos
personally. It was painful to me that a colleague from whom I had learned
much, and who had shown me goodwill, should believe himself to have been
publicly mocked without my having reproved it as chairman. There were men
of the Left who disapproved of my having made this concession. But I have
always found it best to make amends where I had been at fault.

A short time afterward a little incident occurred which the papers of the
Right combined with my other offenses. In the Students' Union a liberal
party had formed, whose leader was the librarian Alfred Larsen. I was
invited to a gathering of the party in the small hall of the Students'
Union, where plans were to be laid for the year's meetings. We sat around
a round table, I on one side of the chairman, one of my colleagues from
the law faculty on the other side. The lists on which people were to sign
up for the coming meetings were sent round by the chairman, one to each
side, so that my colleague and I came to stand at the top, each on his own
list. Whether it had been planned so in advance, I do not know. But
``Dagbladet'' (the real old Dagblad, before the merger with
``Nationaltidende'') now carried a leading article headed ``Professor and
Agitator,'' which dealt only with my humble self and accused me of letting
myself be used as a decoy for the young students. One of the following days
I then gave a talk to the students at the University, in which I explained
my view of the relation between them and me: in my participation in student
life I proceeded, I said, on the assumption that each of them thought
% --- p. 148 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{148}for himself and took his side according to his best conviction,
not because a professor had taken that side, and that was at bottom, I
added, the presupposition on which my whole work as a teacher rested.

In spite of these experiences I became neither more nor less of a
politician in the following years, as long as the political struggle
lasted. Later on, after the ``change of system,'' my political interest has
undeniably weakened, and I gradually became a political free-lance. I cast
my vote according to the particular issue at hand. For the cause which the
Right had abused and the Left misunderstood, the cause of defense, I have
come forward in particular a few times.

I appeared as a speaker at the Left's Constitution Day celebration in
1889, and in the same year I tried, together with the banker Gotfred Rubin,
the colleague of my friend Laurids Bing, to mediate in a strike which the
furniture joiners had started. We trudged from Rømersgade to the offices of
the factory owners. I thereby gained an insight into the course of labor
disputes and acquired besides a special knowledge of price lists for
panels, moldings, window frames, etc., which unfortunately did not stay
with me long. I met interesting people on both sides, for instance the
later Mayor Jensen, who was then a journeyman painter and spokesman for the
workers' committee. Our mediation did not lead to the settlement, but it
did prepare the way for a later mediation. --- In the summer of 1890 I gave
a political lecture at a meeting at Frederiksberg. Some Social Democrats
also took part in the discussion after the lecture, and as a consequence
they spent some time on the platform. Now I had again done something a
professor must not do --- been on a platform together with Social
Democrats! In a dispatch from Copenhagen to ``Hamburger Nachrichten'' this
dreadful event was reported, and it was added that this time I would
certainly not get off as lightly as before. In Danish papers too there were
hints of my dismissal, and the reprimand of 1885 was reprinted. ``Ugeblad
for Danmarks
% --- p. 149 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{149}Højreforeninger'' discussed the matter and declared that it did
not know whether the rumor of my impending dismissal was true, but that it
went without saying that an official who appeared together with Social
Democrats could have no claim to keep his position! Some of my friends were
very apprehensive. But nothing came of the matter. It turned out later that
the Minister of Education (Kultusminister) himself, Scavenius, had trouble
enough clearing himself (though on account of other things than me). He had
to resign shortly afterward. --- Many years later I came together with him,
he being President and I Vice-President of the Association franco-danoise
(an unsuccessful attempt to bring about a livelier interchange between
France and Denmark). At a meeting for discussion with French guests, which
was held in the chamber of the Landsting, I had a seat at the chairman's
table beside him, and I said to him then: ``I would never have believed,
Chamberlain, that we two should meet \textit{here}.'' He laughed. The
former antagonisms were now forgotten. New ones had come in their place.
---

--- What I have related here are only small and insignificant features of
the strange but painful time of the eighties. I have dwelt on them only
because it is an autobiography I am writing, and I therefore naturally come
to speak of how the events of the time reached into my personal existence.
A good deal of vexation was caused me thereby, but then I did come to bear
my share of the general pressure that lay upon life here at home in those
days. Isolate myself from what was going on in my people I could not, and
even if I tried, some occasion or other would come where I was held fast
--- at least by the coat-tails.

\secrule

Through all this I had continued my philosophical work. After completing my
Psychology I resumed my ethical studies. My concern was to gain clarity
% --- p. 150 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{150}about how matters stand with the presuppositions on which every
attempt at a scientific ethics must build. This problem now presented
itself to me more sharply than before. It is in general in this way that
my books have come into being, --- not because I thought that people now
needed to learn this or that, but because tasks presented themselves to me
which I, quite personally, had to have solved. Against the otherwise so
kind account I receive in Vilhelm Andersen's ``Tider og Typer'' (Goethe
II), I have the objection to make, not an unimportant one in my eyes, that
it looks as though I had from the very first laid out a course (thus from
1876 to 1910!), in which the appearance of each individual work was
determined by ``a pedagogical regard for the attention and receptivity of
the participants.'' No, the order of the works was determined by the
difficulties and tasks that presented themselves to me myself, after I had
become clear (as mentioned above, in the year 1874) about the essential
standpoint from which I could treat the problems that might present
themselves to me. If I have had any significance as a teacher, it is
because I have had the need, and perhaps the ability, to learn myself.

In my little book of 1876 I had not posed the question of the
presuppositions of ethics in a critical way. \textit{Now} I asked: just as
logic and mathematics rest on presuppositions that are universally human,
and just as empirical science rests on the principle of causality, which
all must acknowledge, are there likewise universally human presuppositions
for ethics? I remember clearly the strenuous labor of thought which for
several days on end (in January 1886) kept me almost without interruption
at my desk, until I had seen that, when one makes duly strict demands of
justification, there is no ethics that can rationally be imposed on all, as
logical, mathematical and natural-scientific propositions can. Psychological
observation and historical experience show that human actions are judged
from widely differing
% --- p. 151 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{151}presuppositions. And since pronounced typical differences assert
themselves in the ways of thinking of men, --- since, besides, constant
shifts and changes take place in human nature and in the conditions under
which it develops, one could not expect anything else either. Ethical
judgments are passed, and must be passed, from different standpoints,
which, even if they agree in their results, do not always agree in their
justification. By logical analysis we can get back to the presuppositions
peculiar to a single standpoint, but these are bound up with psychological
and historical conditions which do not assert themselves in the same way
where other standpoints are concerned. In a lecture I gave in February 1886
in the Royal Danish Academy of Sciences, of which I had become a member two
years before, I sought to point out the main types that appear when we go
back to the first presuppositions of ethical judgments, all the way from
the standpoint of the moment through the standpoint of individuality, the
clan or family stage and the stage of nationality, to the universal stage
of humanity. Ethical judgments vary consistently with the stages or types,
even if they can meet at many points. After the lecture two Excellencies,
Madvig, the President of the Academy, and the Minister of Justice
Nellemann, raised the objection that the different stages ought to have
been derived from ``the Idea of Man.'' I answered that I did not consider
such a derivation possible. We are here on the ground of psychological and
historical experience, and moreover it is precisely ``the Idea of Man''
(man's innermost being) that appears differently at the different stages.
--- Madvig, for that matter, is said to have liked the lecture very much.
According to what Vilhelm Thomsen told me, he said that it was a long time
since a lecture so good in both form and content had been given in the
Academy.

I see the position of ethics as analogous to the position of astronomy
before Newton. Then too several different systems were possible (the
Ptolemaic, the Copernican and
% --- p. 152 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{152}the Tychonic). Whether ethics will get its Newton, I do not know;
at any rate he has not come yet. Every ethical view proceeds from definite
presuppositions, and it is of decisive importance to become conscious of
this. Every attempt at ethics that is to have significance must itself
point to the psychological and historical conditions on which it rests.
Here, as so often in science, the point is to take as one's basis the
hypothesis one can best work with. For my part, the universal human feeling
of sympathy or humanity, which broke through in the Greco-Roman world after
the time of Alexander and, after the ecclesiastical authority of the Middle
Ages had lost its absolute rule, manifested itself again in the eighteenth
century's assertion of the rights of man, stood as a significant foundation
which it was worth deepening and trying to apply in detail. What can be
justified from these presuppositions can then be compared with what can be
developed from other standpoints (individual self-preservation, family,
nation etc.). ``The Idea of Man'' does, after all, express itself through
different types, partly simultaneous, partly successive. Here we have what
Fichte called a projectio irrationalis. Even where people meet in their
results, the justification can be different, and in the end what matters in
ethics is the fundamental motive, the fundamental value, that determines the
particular valuations. One can set up a civic or social morality without
asking about the motives. But the ethical is, after all, not merely action
but the expression of a disposition. And as regards motive, one must ---
this I first saw clearly now --- distinguish between the motive of valuation
(fundamental value) and the motive of action, since they need not coincide.
Thus love of mankind as the motive of valuation can give rise to special
motives of action such as justice, courage, helpfulness etc. The motive of
valuation need not be the constant motive of action. It leads, on the other
hand, to a valuation of the various possible motives of action. What in one
ethical system can be a
% --- p. 153 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{153}motive of action is perhaps in another a motive of valuation, and conversely.\footnote[1]{In an essay on my work as an author, reprinted in ``Religiøse Tanketyper'' (1927), I have made use of the above characterization of what I aimed at in my ``Etik.'' But I do not consider it unnecessary to let it stand here. [Later note.]}


Later I have more often sought to make this clear, thus in ``Etiske
Undersøgelser'' (1891) and in ``Den menneskelige Tanke'' (1910). And I have
found a similar way of regarding the position of ethics in various scholars
who do not seem to have known my work, thus in Georg Simmel, Heinrich Maier,
Henri Poincaré and Alexander Shand. In my eyes it is a remnant of dogmatism
when one does not see the matter in this way. ---

When I had thus gained clarity about the position of ethics with respect to
the theory of knowledge, I proceeded to the final working out of my Ethics
on the basis of psychological, historical and economic material that I had
collected over the years. I went into the particular conditions of human life
as far as was possible for me. Yet it was mostly my general conception of
ethics that attracted the attention of my critics. As a rule they took the
matter lightly and found it reprehensible in itself that I denied the
possibility of a single rational ethics that alone brings salvation. Or my
ethics was called a morality of feeling, without heed to the more precise
determinations I gave, and had already given in my Psychology, of the
relation between idea and feeling and of the dependence of the life of
feeling on social and historical conditions. There is still so much dogmatism
in the air that people thought they could make ethics rational merely by
saying ``Reason!'' or ``Society!'' or perhaps, if one was especially learned:
``Clan!'' As if reason could not enter the service of the most widely
differing standpoints, and as if there were not many clans and many
societies which, as experiences of the most recent date prove, do not always
get on well together! --- In wider circles it was presumably above all the
even and thoroughgoing treatment of the
% --- p. 154 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{154}different spheres of life in the light of one leading idea that
has won this book so many readers here and abroad.

An ethics, even if it seeks to go the way of justification as far as is
possible, is not merely a theoretical work. It acquires practical
significance both by what it denies and by what it asserts. The account I
had given denied that a supernatural confirmation or a metaphysical
justification was necessary, since human nature itself, as we can come to
know it from experience, furnishes motives both for acting and for judging
the action. It was therefore regarded in certain quarters as an ungodly
book, and I know of young people who were severely taken to task because it
was found among their books. From another side too, people held to this
negative aspect. There were those who said: here, after all, there is no
sanction, no confirmation by a higher power; why then should we live by this
ethics? Let us rather abandon ourselves to all our desires and not care a
damn what the moral philosopher says! --- Theologians and anti-theologians
often agree like brothers on the conclusion that if the traditional dogmas
do not hold, and if there is no supernatural sanction for ethics, --- ``then
let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die!'' ---

Unlike many other ethicists, I deny moreover that any proof can be given of
the very foundation on which ethics is built. Here several starting points
are possible. But the point then is to draw the full consequences of the
starting point one acknowledges. The demand for serious intellectual work
holds for every standpoint that is to be called ethical at all, whether it
takes egoism or altruism as its basis. If someone then says that he will not
work at all and does not care about being consistent either, all discussion
ceases, and there can then be question only of education, --- of education by
human beings, or of education by life.

In opposition to the current freethinking I pointed out
% --- p. 155 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{155}that serious and positive work was precisely what was required,
both in theory and in practice, when one had given up the old faith. Greater
demands are made precisely both on using one's understanding and on
exercising self-discipline when one no longer leads one's life under the
guidance of authority. ---

Nearly 30 years have now passed since my Ethics came out, and I still
acknowledge its essential thoughts. On particular points I have made changes
or additions in later editions. Possibly, if I were to write it now, I would
lay it out differently. In an outline I prepared for lectures at the Folk
University (1901) (reprinted in the third volume of my Mindre Arbejder), I
have indicated a somewhat different turn in the exposition, a more analytical
line of thought.

\secrule

Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson was much taken with my Ethics and wrote a review of it
in a Norwegian paper, which certainly did a great deal for its spread. I had
several times met him at meetings and festive occasions here in town. I came
to know him more closely through my eldest brother, in whose house I often
saw him. His vigorous and fresh nature, his tremendous eloquence and his
enthusiasm for everything human made it a refreshment to be with him, even
if one came to feel his desire to rule and to have the last word. Of his
works I value his poems most; among the dramatic works it seems to me that
the first part of ``Over Evne'' stands highest. In his novels (especially
``Det flager'' and ``Paa Guds Veje'') I have found much that refreshed me,
though the moralizing tendency came out rather strongly there. Norwegian and
Danish intellectual life owes him an extraordinary amount through the fresh,
bold manner in which he asserted his humanism. Without mockery and goading,
also without learned theorizing, he let an independent human side of life
% --- p. 156 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{156}find expression and become accessible to large circles in images
full of feeling. Without the fresh breath he brought, narrowness and
dogmatism would have ruled even more than they do.

A little clash between us came in the year 1893 on the occasion of my essay
``Filosofi som Kunst'' (printed in the first series of ``Mindre Arbejder'').
I came there to speak of how little a purely theoretical formula is able to
express the right relation between self-assertion and self-surrender, and
how art in its images can express what theory cannot. On this occasion I
referred to Ibsen's ``Bygmester Solnes.'' There the ruthless self-assertion
in Solnes's personality is depicted, and it is shown how this ruthlessness
makes him powerless and barren, but also how through Hilde's intervention he
feels young again, and now commands such strength that he can do justice,
which he could not do before. As a counterpart, morbid self-surrender and
sense of duty are depicted in Mrs.\ Solnes, and it is shown how she would
have been able to be more for others, and better able to fulfill the duties
she talked so much about, if the need for self-assertion had stirred more
strongly in her. I had made the express reservation that I did not
understand everything in this poetic work, and did not approve of everything
either, but took what I could use. And I had expressly remarked that a poet
as such cannot decide whether what he depicts is the rule or the exception.
Bjørnson now wrote me a letter on the occasion of this essay (from Aulestad,
10 May 1893), in which he did find ``many striking things'' in it, but was
indignant that I had praised Ibsen's psychology and in particular praised
``Bygmester Solnes.'' One ought not to admire so irresponsible a person as
the Master Builder! Nor Hilde, who brings her dirty linen with her and finds
a touchstone of the Master Builder's greatness in whether he gets dizzy or
not! The letter ends with the words: ``Hvad fan har vi filosofer til, naar de
gør
% --- p. 157 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{157}tilværelsen ugrejere ved at gøre de ugrejeste Digterbilleder til
Love for os?'' --- and it was signed ``Deres vrede ven Bjørnstjerne
Bjørnson.''

I did not feel touched by these objections, since I had expressly stated
that a poetic image in and of itself can just as well be the exception as
the rule. What had interested me was the contrast between the two
characters. In my reply I tried to make clear what I had praised in Ibsen.
But Bjørnson stuck to his own view. The same summer he was down here, and I
met him at a festive gathering at Klampenborg. When I came into the hall, he
was standing with a number of guests in the opposite corner and shouted, as
soon as he saw me: ``Yes, you are wrong!'' I thought that we should have to
have it out over that. But the discussion was not continued. And it left no
sting.

In the following years I met Bjørnson more often in Copenhagen. I remember
once, at a party at the home of one of our politicians where Hørup was
present, that the conversation at table came to turn on the folk high
schools, and that Hørup spoke of them with scorn and indignation. As often
on such occasions, he went quite white in the face with exasperation.
Bjørnson shouted across to him: ``You must look happy, Hørup, you must look
happy!'' --- But it did no good all the same. ---

When Bjørnson was working on his cantata intended for the University of
Kristiania (``Lyset''), he asked my advice regarding the content, which was
to be a depiction of the triumphal progress of thought and enlightenment. I
lent him books and went through his first draft, and also got several things
in it corrected. There were some lines that I did not understand. The
darkness of the Middle Ages and the longing for light were depicted. Then it
said: ``\textit{One} found a way, --- the greatest means of light the world
has known!'' I did not know for certain who was meant. Bjørnson answered
that it was Guttenberg; --- but, he added, there was after all one more
% --- p. 158 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{158}who invented the art of printing at the same time, --- should one
not then write: ``\textit{Two} found a way'' ---? I advised against it,
however, since it sounded comic. The cantata itself I found magnificent, and
I wished that we had its like at our University.


Later I had points of contact with Bjørnson through his interest in the
Danish cause in North Schleswig. ---

His friendship was an honor to me, and I was very glad of a telegram from
him on my 60th birthday, which ran as follows: ``Thanks for faithful
friendship, thanks for what you taught me.'' ---

I must also mention that the only review of a poetic work that I had written
up to then concerned Bjørnson's ``Poul Lange og Thora Parsberg.'' This drama
had caused a great stir in Kristiania immediately on its appearance, because
Bjørnson was said to have made very detailed use of the character and fate
of his late friend, Minister of State Richter, as a model. I then received,
like others down here, a telegram from ``Verdens Gang'' asking me to write a
review as quickly as possible, so that it could be seen how the drama
affected those standing further off. I wrote this review quite con amore,
since the depiction of character interested me. (It is reprinted in the
second series of ``Mindre Arbejder''). --- A rather interesting piece of
information about Bjørnson's relation to this drama came to me some years
later. A rich American by the name of Young, living in Minneapolis, was
assembling a large library consisting of works by authors from various
countries. He paid for the works himself, but the author concerned was to
write something at the front of each book. When Mr.\ Young now applied to
me as well, he sent me a list of Nordic authors who were already represented
in the library, citing what they had written about their books. Bjørnson had
written at the front of ``Poul Lange'': ``Written in hours of emotion, in the
presence, so to speak, of my late friend.'' ---

\secrule

% --- p. 159 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{159}Henrik Ibsen I came into contact with only a few times. For a
number of years it was an event for me when Ibsen's books came. As in
families where things go regularly, they came every second year, and one
knew then that one had to be prepared for problems that could put a knife
to one's throat. I remember especially the evening I read ``Gengangere.'' It
was a few years after my wife's death, and I was not yet quite used to
solitude. The terrible eeriness of Oswald's death scene, which on a first
reading (as at the first performances) came to determine the main
impression, I do not forget. The room grew clammy and cold for me. What
occupied me on later readings, and especially in Mrs.\ Hennings's
performance of the role of Mrs.\ Alving, was the retrospective understanding
of her own and her son's fate that one gained through her conversation with
Pastor Manders (one of Peter Jerndorff's best roles). Several times I have
had occasion to stress the great art with which Ibsen, through the
conversations of his characters, opens the way to an understanding of their
present through their past. One evening in the early days of the
``Students' Society'' Brandes had succeeded in getting Ibsen up there. It had
evidently been hard going, and it looked as though Brandes had to pull him
into the hall. It was the first time I saw Ibsen. He looked most like a
boatswain; broad and heavy-limbed, brown in the face, he sat motionless and
with half-closed eyes. I had been asked to say a few words, and I dwelt then
precisely on Mrs.\ Alving's character and fate, developing how Ibsen,
through the backward glance, is able to make his figures clear to us. I
would have liked a little word from Ibsen as to whether I had understood him
rightly. A little word did come. He held out his hand to me across the table
and said ``Thank you!'' --- Some ten years later I was together with him in
Kristiania, where by invitation I gave a lecture in the ``Students'
Society.'' The figure I met when I (after he had looked for me in vain at
the hotel)
% --- p. 160 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{160}visited him at his home seemed to me very different from the
boatswain of former days. A dainty little gentleman with the ribbon of an
order in his buttonhole showed me his elegant apartment and his fine
paintings. In conversation between the two of us he was very talkative,
only avoiding any mention of his writings. Yet it was surely on this
occasion that he told me that he had been asked to write the history of his
works and explain how they came into being. I answered that he should not
do so, since his readers were best served by solving for themselves the
riddles his works posed. My real opinion, though, was that his explanations
would be somewhat artificial and keep especially to particular impressions
and moods whose significance could be understood only if more information
were available than he could or would give. Nor, I suppose, did he ever
seriously think of it. --- At a farewell dinner that was given for me he
was present, and I had him on my right. Here too he was in very high spirits
and communicative, and in the course of the evening I noticed that he was
constantly in conversation with someone or other. At table I proposed a
toast to Norway, making use of the scene in ``Lille Eyolf'' where the
Norwegian flag is hoisted to full mast. Afterward I heard that Ibsen had
liked the speech.

The last time I saw Ibsen was when he visited Copenhagen in 1898, where his
70th birthday was celebrated, after it had first been celebrated both in
Kristiania and in Stockholm. He was childishly glad of the fuss that was made
of him, not least of the Grand Cross of the Danebrog which the King had
presented to him. At the Students' Society's celebration I gave one of the
speeches for him. He came from the ``Kvindelig Læseforening'' and was very
pleased with the homage of which he had been the object there. ``And how
they could speak!'' he repeated several times. In my speech (which is
printed in the second series of ``Mindre Arbejder'') I dwelt on his
threefold struggle: to satisfy the demands of art, --- to look the problems
of the time in the face, --- and to overcome the resistance of the
% --- p. 161 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{161}reader and the spectator. I made use of some lines of his poem
about his visit to Egypt (``Ballonbrev''), where he tells of temple ruins
and overturned images of gods which jut up out of the sand like the
skeletons of perished caravans, and says that this culture went under
because it lacked personalities. On this understanding he builds a hope for
the future:

\begin{quote}
Paa begravne Karavaner\\
bygger jeg vor Fremtids Baner!
\end{quote}

It is one of the few places in Ibsen where a hope surfaces, and I would
gladly have heard a word from him about it. But he only said: ``Thank you,
--- you applied that well!'' Whether I had also applied it ``rightly,'' I
was not told. --- After that Valdemar Vedel spoke, and it was now expected
that Ibsen would take the floor. There was great suspense when he rose ---
but it was only to say: ``Thank you for this evening!'' And then he left.
The mood in the overcrowded hall was somewhat flat. But Marcus Rubin broke
the gloom by jumping up on a chair and saying:

\begin{quote}
It was but a feast!\\
before the black night;\\
He was but a guest ---\\
and now he is gone!
\end{quote}
% Det var en Fest kun!\\
% før Natten den sorte;\\
% Han var en Gæst kun ---\\
% og nu er han borte!

A full-throated laugh let the evening end in a conciliatory mood. How,
indeed, could one have expected that the great eccentric should have
unburdened his heart to a whole assembly and solved riddles for us which he
himself surely struggled with, --- insofar as the main thing for him was not
that these riddles gave him motifs for depictions of human characters and
human destinies. Only through such depictions did he know how to speak.

\secrule

When I was putting the last touches to my ``Etik,'' of which I have spoken
here, I suffered from stubborn attacks of gallstones, by which
% --- p. 162 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{162}I had also been troubled now and then before. It got better for a
while, though, and in the spring of 1887 I lived for a time with my sons in
Tisvilde, which at that time did not have the fashionable stamp it has now.
I went about daily in the splendid forest, which with its hills and valleys,
