its dunes and its ravines, reminded me of my dear Jutland. After that I had
a strenuous examination and then went out to Jyderup, where there was also
glorious Danish countryside to wander in. But out there the attacks came
back, and they recurred when I came to town. Julius Petersen then insisted
that I should take a cure at Carlsbad. So I set off, visited Friedrich
Paulsen in Berlin and then steamed through Saxon Switzerland down into
Bohemia. When we had crossed the border, the train became a local train
(Bummelzug), and in the end I was left alone in the compartment with a
pale, fat, sickly and despondent-looking gentleman. I myself did not feel
well and had all sorts of forebodings of new attacks. After my fellow
traveler had long sat staring at me, he said at last: ``Haben Sie auch
extravagiert?'' In spite of my indisposition I chuckled inwardly at this
``auch,'' but I rejected his hypothesis with cold superiority, explaining to
him that my case came from too much diligence and sitting still.

The cure at Carlsbad was not strict, but very dulling. In the end I was not
able to read four lines in a newspaper, and I was horrified when I thought
that in a month or so I was to lecture in Copenhagen. The cure did me good
above all through the complete rest, the constant walks and the strict diet
that was enjoined. I was not free of the attacks, however, until several
years later. For many years I never traveled away to stay overnight without
taking with me the morphine syringe that my doctor had entrusted to me. I
felt no temptation to become a morphine addict. Only in a few cases did the
injections call up beautiful dream visions before I fell asleep; and almost
always there were very unpleasant after-effects.

\secrule

% --- p. 163 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{163}In the eighties, besides my Psychology, psychological works by my
colleagues Kroman and Lehmann had appeared, and since rather considerable
divergences between our views became apparent on various points, I set
about in the winter of 1888---89 giving a fuller account of my
psychological standpoint and meeting the objections that had been raised
against it. The result was a treatise which in 1889 was printed in
Videnskabernes Selskabs Skrifter under the title ``Psykologiske
Undersøgelser.'' Here I have developed, more thoroughly than could be done
in the ``Psykologi,'' the doctrine of the different kinds of recognition, of
the association of ideas, of the different stages of the will and of the
relation between mind and body. On several points this work also became a
preparation for a work on the theory of knowledge which was completed only
20 years later, but whose foundations I had already begun to lay, at the
same time as I was preparing a connected account of the history of modern
philosophy.

\secrule

The autumn of 1889 brought me into a polemical stance toward Georg Brandes,
on the occasion of his unlimited and, in my eyes, uncritical praise of
Nietzsche's theories of the Overman and of the opposition between the great
men and the great mob. Against his essay ``Aristokratisk Radikalisme'' (in
``Tilskueren'') I wrote (likewise in ``Tilskueren'') an essay which I called
``Demokratisk Radikalisme.'' I do not deny that there was something in
Nietzsche's views, as well as in the overvaluation of which they were the
object, that aroused my indignation. If it could really be shown historically
that the individual, scattered great men constituted the only thing that
could give life and history value, then one would have to resign oneself to
it. One cannot fight against a fact. Then ``the great mob,'' as Nietzsche
said, would be only ``copies, means or hindrances'' in relation to them. But
that we
% --- p. 164 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{164}should admire this fact and find existence significant because of
it, that was in my eyes just as absurd a demand as when it is demanded from
the theological side that we should admire the divine world order with its
heaven and its hell. Now I denied first of all that the fact was there.
Experience and history show us a whole series of degrees of independence and
originality, and in such a way that the difference of degree is often
succeeded by a difference of quality. There are greatnesses of different
kinds, and it will be difficult here to establish an order of rank.
Independence is moreover required in order to understand and to acknowledge
greatness. Without this understanding and acknowledgment greatness has no
significance for development, nor for the development of the great ones of
the future. The value of the great rests on their influence as founders,
originators and models. One may well say with Schiller that noble natures
signify something by what they are, not by what they do. But precisely by
what they are, they act to strengthen, to advance and to give direction.

What not least repelled me in Nietzsche was the presupposition that an
essential aspect of superiority and greatness should consist in a feeling of
power conditioned by the distance at which one sees the others moving about
below oneself. Nietzsche entangles himself here in a curious contradiction:
if this feeling of distance is to be a necessary element, then the great
become dependent on the small, since they must have someone to look down on.
Nietzsche expressly ascribes to the mob the reactive feelings, that is to
say, such feelings as are determined by the relation to others and exclude
living one's life out of oneself alone. But his Overmen too, after all,
become reactive.

The controversy was continued through a series of articles from both sides
all winter long. A whole series of side questions (on the significance of
science, on the principles of ethics, on the origin of morality) were
discussed. The whole thing came together for me, as I sought to establish in
my ``Epilog,'' in
% --- p. 165 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{165}the question whether any human being can be said to be an end
without at the same time being a means, or to be a means without at the
same time being an end. It was Kant's old formula that I took up, after I
had sought in my Ethics to give it a new justification. ---

It was no small thing for me to come forward against Georg Brandes. In
liberal circles his standing was overwhelming, and he was regarded as a
symbol or a prophet who must not be touched, not criticized. In particular
the circle in which I moved, apart from those closest to me, regarded him as
sacred and inviolable. Marcus Rubin, when he heard of my intention to write
against Brandes, wrote me a long letter in which he urgently begged me to
refrain. He admitted that there was much to dissociate oneself from, but
ended with the words: ``Of Brandes I say: quand même!'' I could not see that
because Brandes was the object of much hateful, stupid and unjust criticism,
he should therefore not be open to criticism at all. I began the article
with a warm acknowledgment of his significance for Danish intellectual life:
``I will not [begin my criticism] without first and foremost, and in all
sincerity, stating what our literature and our intellectual life owe to this
man's brilliant gifts and great ability to awaken and inspire. I do not
think that his significance can be expressed by saying that he has put
problems up for debate; for he has never really wanted to be a thinker
himself; --- what has been his strength has been his great ability to point,
with energy and warmth, or, to use an expression he seems to favor of late,
with violence, to such intellectual and literary phenomena as he considers
it worth occupying oneself with and letting oneself be influenced by. Even
those who in their own field have learned nothing from him, and who in many
respects have perhaps felt themselves at a distance from him, cannot but
follow his activity with sympathy and be grateful to him for the life and
the movement he has awakened. I here
% --- p. 166 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{166}even leave aside the wonderful gift he possesses for evocative
characterization, which makes his works of literary history so
attractive.''

It was, moreover, my sincere opinion that the ill treatment he had been
subjected to here at home had not affected him so much that he could not
well bear a criticism coming from an entirely different side from the one
from which he had hitherto been attacked almost exclusively. Ardent
Brandesians naturally could not see the matter in this way. In the coverage
our controversy received in the press, there was not much engagement with
the very question at issue, --- in my eyes a testimony to how superficial a
purely literary or aesthetic culture can be, even if for a time it has as
its program ``to put problems up for debate.'' --- Marcus Rubin wrote in
``Politiken'' a so-called account of the controversy, with many fine-sounding
words, with the obligatory homage to Brandes and a benevolent pat on the
shoulder for me, but without understanding of what it was about. And this
article was regarded by many as a word in season. I would rather he had
attacked me, for Bacon is surely right that truth emerges sooner from error
than from confusion.

The press of the Right naturally claimed me for its own, but when Brandes,
in one of his later articles, in the heat of the controversy, reduced me to
a mere nonentity, it turned around and used him against me, and we then came
to stand as two zeros who had nevertheless got into a fight with each other
as though they were real quantities.

It is correct, what Brandes says in his Levned, that the controversy was
conducted ``with unnecessary sharpness on both sides.'' It is no doubt also
correct, what he adds, that for his part he let himself ``be led into
teasing mockery.'' And I admit that I felt hurt by several of his
utterances. But I never failed to recognize his superior gifts and his
flaming enthusiasm for a free intellectual life. It is not easy to reckon up
what we owe him. And as will be
% --- p. 167 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{167}seen from the foregoing, I owe him much, also as regards the form
of my exposition. The very controversy that I had now carried on with him
became of significance for my development.


A couple of years later some of his friends and admirers wished to celebrate
the 25th anniversary of his first book. I confess that I wavered a great
deal as to whether I should take part or not. The issue was decided by the
enthusiasm with which my sons followed his lectures on Shakespeare. I signed
up, and then received a request from the festival committee to speak, which
I promised, only I would not give the main speech of the evening. Once the
decision had been taken, it came easily to me to bring out what for me was
the main thing in Brandes's work, and even to look back on the controversy
with humor. The speech, which is printed in the second series of my
``Mindre Arbejder,'' fell on good ground. I was myself moved in giving it,
and I saw Brandes shed tears while I spoke. Later in the evening he said to
me, what he has repeated in his Levned, that I had heaped coals of fire on
his head.

Shortly afterward he wrote to me: ``Strange is what has become of the
subject of our controversy. Since I first drew attention to Nietzsche in
1887, he has become the fashionable philosopher the world over.'' --- It was
indeed also the case that the followers Nietzsche got, especially in Germany,
were rather dependent imitators (``copies''); but that agreed precisely with
his own theory.

In the year 1902 I went through Nietzsche's philosophy in a series of public
lectures on modern philosophers. By now his writings and drafts were
available more completely, and his letters had begun to appear. I sought to
show that what had been most striking from a purely literary point of view,
the doctrine of master and slave morality and of social dualism, together
with the contempt for the great mob, --- that this was, in Nietzsche's whole
line of thought as one could now survey it, something derived, not something
fundamental. His fundamental idea was
% --- p. 168 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{168}the welfare of the species (not of individuals, not even of the
great), and he thought --- admittedly inconsistently --- that social dualism
was a condition for it. Brandes and I had agreed in regarding Nietzsche as an
opponent of the morality of welfare, and now it turned out that it was his
fundamental idea\footnote[1]{I take the opportunity to correct a slip of memory. It is not (as is said in ``Moderne Filosofer'' p. 145) the ``Midnight Song'' (in Part 4 of Zarathustra) that Nietzsche calls ``the loneliest song that has ever been written''; it is the ``Nachtlied'' (in Part 2) of which this is said. In the foreign editions of ``Moderne Filosofer'' I have had this error corrected.}.
Nietzsche's personality has interested me greatly, not through his sister's
at once idolatrous and self-satisfied account, but through the Swiss
Bernouilli's book on his relation to the two people who were probably closest
to him, the Basel professor Overbeck and his wife.

\secrule

Through all this I had continued my studies, which now concerned especially
the history of modern philosophy, on which I also gave public lectures for
several years. After the completion of my Psychology and my Ethics, the next
task I set myself was to give a reasonably full account of the history of
philosophy in modern times. This task was naturally connected with the plan
for an account of the main problems of philosophy in their mutual relation,
a plan which, as mentioned earlier, dated from 1874, and which constantly
occupied me.

The history of Greek philosophy I had lectured on in the winter of 1885---86.
Later I went through Aristotle's Ethics in special seminars, which were
repeated when the Laboratory for the History of Philosophy was established.
Here I have also repeatedly gone through Plato's ``Republic.'' Greek thought
has continued to be of great significance for me, as it already was at my
first acquaintance with philosophy. I sometimes made forays on particular
points, as will be seen from my ``Mindre Arbejder.'' It is my conviction that
for the study of philosophy an orientation in
% --- p. 169 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{169}Greek thought is indispensable. It should always be the case that
at least one of the University's teachers of philosophy is able to conduct a
seminar on subjects from Greek philosophy in such a way that he himself
relies on the original text, even if most of his hearers must use
translations. That is something I have energetically stressed during the
deliberations on filling vacant chairs of philosophy. Greek thought lies to
such a degree at the root of all European philosophy that a many-sided and
unprejudiced study of the latter must go back to it. There should always be
forces at the University that are able to go back to it. Even if there are
classical philologists who take an interest in this side of their subject, as
I too have had the pleasure of experiencing, it is nevertheless only
independent philosophical study that can say the decisive word here. For my
own part, it was not for lack of desire that I gave up working out an account
of the history of Greek philosophy, but because I had to limit myself, and
the philosophy of the last three centuries was naturally of the greatest
direct significance for the position of the problems in the present. But the
limitation was not carried through without resignation.

In my treatment of the history of modern philosophy I laid more weight on
problems than on systems and sought more to characterize than to report.
Through the characterization the criticism then comes out of its own accord.
To the characterization there belonged also an investigation of the relation
between the philosopher's personality and his doctrine, and several of the
small biographies I wrote con amore. Besides this, I laid great weight on the
relation of philosophy to other sciences, especially natural science, and in
my account Kopernikus, Galilei, Newton, Darwin and Robert Mayer therefore came
to stand in prominent places, because, whether one will call them
philosophers or not, through their research they gave the impulse to
significant changes in the way philosophical problems were posed. On
particular points I first worked out monographs. To these belongs a treatise
in
% --- p. 170 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{170}Videnskabernes Selskabs Skrifter on ``Kontinuiteten i Kant's
filosofiske Udviklingsgang.'' My book on Kierkegaard, and the later book on
Rousseau, also belong here. The writing of the work took place at various
times, not in chronological order. The last part to be written, and perhaps
the best shaped, is the section on the Renaissance.

The book came out in parts in the years 1894 and 1895 and was soon afterward
translated into German, French, English, Spanish and Italian. Next to my
Psychology, it is the one of my books that has been most widely circulated.
It amused me to hear various expert readers each single out a different
section. Dilthey singled out, in a letter to me, the section on German
philosophy from Kant to Hegel as testifying to thorough understanding. The
Scottish philosopher Pringl-Pattison singled out the section on English
philosophy in the 19th century as understanding and critical. The Italian
ambassador in England, San Giuliano, to whom I was introduced in Cambridge in
1909, thanked me for the account of the Italian Renaissance, which he meant to
make use of in a lecture he was to give in Oxford. --- From the German
accounts of the history of modern philosophy my book differs, among other
things, by its detailed treatment of French and English philosophy in the
19th century. Even those Germans who do not adhere to the speculative school
are inclined to regard the development in Germany as the main thing and to
treat the philosophy of other countries in an appendix.

\whiteline

If the section on the Renaissance should be more successful than other
sections, it is perhaps because I made the draft of it during an idyllic
summer stay in Finland. The summer vacation of 1893 I spent, that is, with
my second-youngest brother Theodor Høffding, who in the spring of 1869, as a
young polytechnic graduate, had gone to Russia, where he worked first as a
railway engineer, later as a factory manager and as a contractor. In the
summer of 1893
% --- p. 171 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{171}he lived with his family at a country house in eastern Finland,
near Wiborg, by a lake that was connected with the great Lake Saima. It was a
glorious summer, which was spent on walks and sailing trips, on one occasion
on a trip up through Lake Saima with its thousand islands to Wilmanstrand and
Punkoharja, and from there to the Imatra Falls. Since I have never been able
to take a summer vacation without work, I had Giordano Bruno's works with me
over there and spent some hours each day with this enthusiastic thinker, who
stands as the prophetic herald of the world-view of the modern age.

The visit to Finland, with which a few days' stay in Petrograd was combined,
acquired a special value for me through the life I shared with my brother and
his family. He had been my playmate in my childhood, but had now long lived
away from his native place. He had become a Russian citizen, and his way of
thinking had become entirely Russian. But just as on a later visit to him,
and on his visit to me, when we had both passed 70, I felt the brotherly
bond and experienced the understanding that can exist between close
relatives, even if their work and their homes have come to lie in the most
widely different regions.

\secrule

Roughly from the time I have spoken of here, a beginning was made of some
regular gatherings which I have had, and have, much joy of. The first
occasion was that after the meetings in the Academy I often walked along
with the physiologist Chr.\ Bohr, and that we then often continued the
conversation at a café, where we had supper. I had already come into contact
with Bohr earlier. When he heard, in his time, that I was working on a
Psychology in which I wished to take as much account as possible of
physiological viewpoints and results, he offered his help in going through
the relevant sections. The evening visits thereby occasioned brought many
later ones in their train, and in his and
% --- p. 172 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{172}his wife's beautiful home in the stately residence of the
professor of physiology I have spent many interesting and pleasant evenings.
As a physiologist he belonged, being a disciple of the Leipzig researcher
Ludwig, to the school that would carry through strictly the application of
physico-chemical methods in physiology. Outside his laboratory he was an
ardent devotee of Goethe. When he expressed himself on practical matters or
on views of life, it was usually in the form of paradox and as a rule
improvised. The conversation often took on new life through his
intervention. At our café visits after meetings of the Academy the physicist
Christiansen soon became the third man. He and Bohr had many interests in
common, since Bohr's physiological method led him to thorough studies in
physics. I had, as told earlier, known Christiansen from his very young days,
and our friendship had stood its test in spite of the different ways we went
where the limits of scientific thought lie. He loved literature and
biographies and is still, in his old age, an enthusiastic reader of Homer.
Like Bohr he is fond of paradoxes, which he often holds on to with Jutland
tenacity, and he likes to go against the current. He retired when he turned
69, on account of illness, and then spent a year abroad, especially on the
Riviera. From this stay he came back with renewed interest in experimental
work. In a letter to me from Italy he says that he wishes for a task in
which he can be wholly absorbed. In this too he has succeeded, and he works
steadily and eagerly some 4---5 hours a day. The rest of the time he reads
Homer or some good biography or other. In general there are several examples
of how one can, as professor emeritus, get just as much to do as before. New
tasks come along besides the old ones one wants to put the last touches to,
and there is still so much that one would after all like to become acquainted
with before it is over. --- But I must get back to our gatherings.


The trefoil that had formed grew tired of
% --- p. 173 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{173}café life, and it was then arranged that we took turns going home
with one another on the Friday evenings when there was a meeting in the
Academy. At the same time we now acquired a fourth man in the famous
linguist Vilhelm Thomsen. I had made his acquaintance when we were for a time
teachers together at Maribo School. Later I met him again when he taught my
brother Theodor Russian before the latter's journey to Russia, and later
again when we became colleagues at the University. A closer friendship began
when for several winters we did gymnastics together at a school on Mynsters
Vej. We usually walked together from there in pleasant morning
conversations, and I soon began to be a guest in his home. And I have come
to be deeply fond of him and feel closely bound to him. He is a quiet man,
but he takes part gladly in all kinds of conversation, and his mild eyes and
warm-hearted manner make one want to speak out. I once said in his home, on
a festive occasion, that there was no place where I talked as much as in his
house. Of his own works he seldom speaks. Yet I remember that one Monday
morning, as we walked from gymnastics, he said in his quiet way: ``I rather
think I made a discovery on Saturday evening.'' And then he explained to me
how he had found the key to the alphabet in which an old inscription on the
border between Siberia and China was written, and had thereby also
discovered an Old Turkic dialect hitherto unknown. During our gatherings he
was always eager to investigate every linguistic or historical detail that
came up, provided he did not have the explanation ready to hand. His wife
and daughter often joked about his eagerness to ``look it up.'' The evenings
in his home were not the least pleasant among the many good evenings I owe to
the company of the three friends I have spoken of here.

When the Academy moved into its new premises in the splendid building in
which the Carlsberg Foundation has given it meeting rooms and offices, it
became the custom that the
% --- p. 174 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{174}members drank tea together after the meetings and spent an hour
or so in conversation in the pleasant rooms. Our little club was then moved
to the Friday evenings when no meetings were held. The gatherings are still
held as I write this. But Bohr has passed away, and we miss him greatly. ---
A change has been introduced in the very last few years on my (somewhat
egoistic) proposal, namely that the ladies also take part in the gatherings
outside their homes, just as they had always given the gatherings in their
own homes coziness and charm.

% --- p. 175 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\chapter*{V}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{V. 1894--1904}
\markboth{V. 1894--1904}{V. 1894--1904}
\opage{175}In the autumn of 1894 a change took place in my
domestic arrangements. As mentioned before, after
my wife's death I had not wanted to have any ``lady of the house''.
I wanted no intermediary between myself and my children,
and I could not imagine anyone who, without being
my wife, could take a mother's place. There
was no lack, from time to time, of remonstrances from my
family in that direction. They thought that I was doing
my sons a wrong by letting them go without a real
hearth, a center that would always be ready when they
needed conversation or comfort. I was, after all, always taken up
with work and was not so seldom out in the evening. Yet I
believe that we often had a good time together. When hypochondria,
or other, more agreeable guests, did not present
themselves, we read together, especially Homer and Shakespeare,
whom I know my sons learned from me to know and
to love. And often dinner or supper went on long because of
conversations that had got under way. But perhaps it was
not often enough. I believe that my youngest son in particular felt
a want here. He often spoke with enthusiasm of the comfort
there was in the homes of his friends, where the mother at
her lamp in the living room was always available to anyone who
had something on his mind or simply wanted a little chat.
A living room was lacking in my house. We each had our own
room, and then a dining room. Only work and eating, no
hearth, had their place.

My sister-in-law Elisabeth (married to my eldest brother,
the wholesale merchant Victor Høffding) had often reproached me with this,
% --- p. 176 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{176}and at the beginning of 1894 she came with a regular declaration of war
on the subject. Elisabeth was a remarkable
personality, clear and all of a piece, finely cultivated and with many
interests. She lived in an exceedingly happy marriage.
She and my brother were, even in their old age,
like two young people engaged. They kept a fine and hospitable house,
but at bottom they were happiest when they were alone. They
enjoyed the evenings in their cozy and tasteful home, and the summer
at their country house near Frederiksdal, and they got a great deal
out of their travels. I always had great respect for her,
even if I did not always understand her rightly. She was one of those
who did not much need others, and therefore she believed that
others did not need her either. There was therefore always
a certain reserve in her manner. All the greater the impression
made by a letter I received from her on 17 January 1894.
She wrote that I lacked comfort in my home, but that in
any case my sons, especially the youngest, did. ``I
think,'' she wrote further, ``that one need not talk
long with Hans before one notices what an undercurrent of
longing runs through him for a cozy home \ldots{}
To have in the house a kindly being who cares
for one, who in an hour of dusk or in the evening,
when one needs to rest a little, will listen to one's chat,
to whom one can read aloud or show a little attention in some other way,
is for the young a well-being that he consciously
or unconsciously feels the need of. But tell me, where is
Hans to go with his need? Emil is, after all, not like
others; he seems to be sufficient unto himself, though one cannot
really know. But Hans? When he comes home, you three
have a meal, and whether it turns out lively or empty presumably depends on
what humor you are in. Then he presumably sits down
to read, and reads until evening, if a friend does not
drop in on him, or he has to go out \ldots\ldots{} I do not know
what your reasons may have been for so stubbornly refusing
a woman to bring up your children; they
may have been many and perhaps justified; but I
% --- p. 177 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{177}know that for a number of years I have looked up to you as the least
egoistic person I knew; only here did I find egoism
in you. I believe you have thought more of yourself
than of your sons in this. If you do not now draw a line through it
altogether, then let me, or your sister, or whomever
you like, have leave to seek out someone. If there is
one who seems to fit, you can always decide for
or against. Only I think that if a change is to be made,
the time is now, since it is your intention in the near future
to part with your housekeeper, and the longer
time goes on, the harder it becomes for the young ones to
grow used to living with a stranger.''

For many days and nights I thought over what had here
been laid so urgently on my heart. I could not
overcome my reluctance to take a stranger into my
house, who would come to stand in a strange intermediate position between
myself, my children and my servants. I know that other
widowers have overcome this difficulty; but I
could not. Nor would I be able to marry for my
children's sake; nor, to speak frankly, do I believe that any
widower has done it, even if it was put down to the children's
account.

Then one night I had an idea, and it concerned another
sister-in-law. --- The same year that my wife died,
my second eldest brother Valdemar had also passed away.
He died suddenly of a heart attack. He had been
a merchant captain, but after father's death had entered
the firm as cashier. His widow, Maria, née Bøving,
now lived with two grown-up daughters, and it had now been settled that
the elder of these should travel to America to marry
her fiancé, the engineer Nissen, who a couple of years before had
gone over there and had found himself a position there.
My sister-in-law and her younger daughter were then thinking of
moving into a smaller flat. My thought was that I
would propose that we combine our households, so
that she with her daughter and I with my two sons
% --- p. 178 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{178}made up one household. The proposal was accepted, and in the four
years the life together lasted, my sons and I had a truly
cozy home. We lived in Christianshavn, first in Brogade,
later in Strandgade. My sister-in-law Maria was lively
and quick, independent in her way of thinking and receptive
to everything beautiful, careful and loving as mistress of the house. We
got on well together. Daily life now took a
less monotonous shape than before. The lamp burned in the living room
as a sign of unity for old and young. We read together, and
a pleasant young circle gathered around us. Now and
then I could now see friends and colleagues at my home
in a more festive way. More propriety and order came into my
household, and this had its effects beyond the
time the life together lasted. That it came to an end was due partly to my
sister-in-law's nervousness, which made the housekeeping weigh
on her as a heavy burden, partly to the circumstance that
her elder daughter with husband and child was now returning
from America, and that she would rather live with them. The
younger daughter, Jenny, later married an Italian painter
and died in Sicily of pneumonia.

\secrule

In the year 1896, at the invitation of others, I took part in a
holiday course in Zurich, at which lectures were given on
ethics, pedagogy and political economy. I was to give
lectures on the principles of ethics.

On the journey I spent some days in Berlin, where I renewed
my acquaintance with the museums and visited Friedrich
Paulsen in his villa in Steglitz. In Dresden too there was
great art to renew my acquaintance with. From there I made
an excursion down into Bohemia to visit Professor Friedrich
Jodl, who was staying in the country there. I had come
into contact with him through Gizycki, and he had written
a very fine review of my Ethics in ``Deutsche Literaturzeitung'',
one of the reviews that have pleased me
most. He had for some years been professor in Prague, but
% --- p. 179 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{179}had now been appointed professor in Vienna. What was
interesting in this was that I too had been under discussion in
the Vienna faculty, as Theodor Gomperz, the well-known
author of ``Griechische Denker'', had told me
after the matter had been settled. Even if I had been asked,
I would not have accepted the invitation. In the first place
I could not imagine any sphere of work outside Denmark,
and in the second place conditions in Vienna were very difficult
because of the sharp national and religious antagonisms.
Jodl was well suited to work under these
conditions, and he had a significant career
there right up to his death at a relatively young age. He is
the author of a Psychology and of a History of Ethics, both
very able works. I spent an interesting day
with him and his wife at their summer residence. During our
walks we discussed various problems, and there turned out
to be great agreement between us as regards direction of thought
and the way of posing problems. A somewhat different position
we took toward the religious problem, as became apparent especially
later. Jodl really did not recognize any
problem here at all, but thought that Feuerbach had once and for all
settled the matter. I always saw both a psychological
and an ethical problem here, which it was important to get
formulated in the right way.

From Dresden I went by way of Stuttgart to Switzerland. There
were still a few weeks before the lectures were to begin,
and so I went by Lucerne and Stanz up to Engelberg, where
I stayed a couple of weeks. Around the old monastery, which
was still inhabited by monks, a hotel town had grown up here, high up in a mountain valley,
from which one could really enjoy
the mountain air and take splendid walks. I here made
the acquaintance of a lawyer, Alscher, from Königsberg and
his wife, two lively and interesting people, with whom I
often went walking and could talk about everything under the sun, right
from Dante to the political questions of the present day. For several years
afterward we kept up a correspondence. Now they are both dead,
% --- p. 180 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{180}and I know from a daughter's letter that they had not forgotten their
Danish companion on the mountain walks. A small characteristic
scene from the table d'hôte I must relate. I sat opposite
a family from Dresden and often talked with a young
lady who belonged to it. They were mostly joking remarks
that passed between us. But one day she had
found out that I was a professor, and asked with great interest
how often I had fought duels. When I answered that
I had never taken part in that, she exclaimed in the highest
degree astonished: ``Aber, mein Herr, sind Sie dann ein Streber
gewesen?'' (``Streber'' means in German student language
a swot who curries favor with the professor and
thinks only of getting a good examination, for which reason he does not
take part in student life.) I answered: ``Nein, mein Fräulein,
es gibt noch ein Drittes!'' And I explained what
the ideal of a student was with us, an ideal one could strive
for without fighting duels. The people at the table were indignant
with the young lady, and she looked very unhappy. Then
I took my glass and said: ``Nun, Fräulein, last uns anstossen
und immerfort gute Freunde bleiben!'' At that she became
enthusiastic and cried: ``Ja, mein Herr, die grossen Geister,
sie begegnen doch immer wieder einander!'' --- This
the old ladies found the height of impudence, and I
had to defend my young friend, with whom I also
had a pleasant time in the period that followed during the long
table d'hôte hours. ---

In Zurich I came to live in a boarding house up on the Zürichberg,
where from my room I had a view over Lake Zurich
and in clear weather could see the Bernese Alps. I gave up
this room, however, after a few days to Tönnies,
whose acquaintance I made in Zurich, where he too
was to give lectures. I knew him as the author
of some excellent studies of Hobbes, and of a very
interesting work ``Gemeinschaft und Gesellschaft'', which
I had reviewed in ``Tilskueren'', and which gives an excellent
characterization of the transition from the old ``community'', built on
% --- p. 181 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{181}family ties, custom and usage, to
the modern ``society'', which is built on the acquisitive drive,
and where an external social mechanism takes the place of
the natural bonds of connection. Later on, when the book came out
in a second edition, he did me the honor of dedicating it
to me. I had imagined Tönnies as a powerful Frisian
(he came from the same district as Friedrich Paulsen), broad
and solid, partly because of the energy of his style, partly because
of his Marxist radicalism. But I saw before
me a fine and slight man, soft-spoken and nervous, also weak
in health. He was unhappy about the room he had
been given; he could not sleep there because of the noise all
around. So I let him have mine --- but the next morning he complained
again: ``Ich bin ein Pechvogel!'' For a gentleman had
moved in that same evening into the room next
door, and he snored abominably! --- Tönnies and I became
good friends and are still in touch. He has repeatedly
visited me, and I have also visited him in
Eutin, where he lives.

It was a very pleasant boarding house we lived in. The
old lady, who had charge of the kitchen, one did not see
much of during the day, but as I was up early, I usually saw
her at morning coffee, and we had many a good
chat. She said on that account: ``Ach, ich mag so
gern mit dem Herrn Professor philosophieren!'' --- Among
the residents I became better acquainted with two married couples
from Berlin who had come for the sake of the lectures,
the lawyer Bieber and his wife and Medicinalrat Schwerin
and his wife. Bieber was a liberal man in the best sense of the
word, who had made a name for himself as defense counsel
for Social Democrats at the time when the Prussian government
was proceeding harshly against them. Of the ladies I came to set
great store by Frau Jeanette Schwerin. This finely cultivated
lady, who read her Dante in Italian and translated Leo
Hebræo, took an eager part in philanthropic endeavors in Berlin.
She learned there time after time how difficult it
% --- p. 182 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{182}was to help women who were treated brutally by their
husbands, because they were without rights against them. And that was
the reason she became an ardent champion of woman's
economic and social independence. She is one of the
noblest and most gifted women I have met in my
life. She died only three years later, so that I did not come
to see her again. In the later editions of my Ethics I have
mentioned her and her work.

A remarkable man I met in Zurich was the old
Colonel Egidy, who had resigned his commission in order to work for
a free and purely human religion. He was in decided
opposition to many things in the German character. When
one day at the boarding-house table, where he and several participants
in the lecture work also ate, I remarked that I
could not bring myself to address German ladies as ``Gnädige
Frau'', because it was so servile, he rose in enthusiasm
and came over to me and said: ``Herrlicher Mann,
lass mich Sie umarmen! Das ist ganz aus meinem Herzen
gesprochen!'' --- Also speaking in Zurich was the well-known
economist Werner Sombart, who in a brilliant
series of lectures set forth the ideas of Marxism in a
somewhat dogmatic way. In the discussions that were held
after the close of each series of lectures, I came forward
with a criticism of Marxism along the same lines as the one
I have given in my Ethics. Later this gifted man has
taken up a more critical standpoint. Both him and Tönnies I met
some years later in America. --- In the discussion that
was held after my lecture, I had especially to defend
my theory of the different, logically irreducible ethical
types.

I had an enjoyable evening in Zurich on a visit to
the Scandinavian workers' association. I turned up
without further ado on a meeting night and was received very kindly.
There were speeches and singing, and the young journeymen who were
gathered had a bright and cheerful spirit. They were mainly journeyman painters
who had work in Zurich, where in those years there
% --- p. 183 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{183}was much building. I gave a contribution to the association's
funds and received an emblem with the Scandinavian colors.
It was a Nordic evening in the midst of the German-speaking land. ---
The next New Year I received a telegraphed greeting from ``the traveling
journeymen in Zurich''.

I had been happy in Zurich and had come to know worthy
and interesting people, and it was with sadness
that I left. According to what was later written
to me, several young people had turned up at
the station to bring me a farewell greeting, but they
had mistaken the time.

\secrule

It was in the spring of 1898 that my sister-in-law, who now for
four years had run my house and created its comfort, felt
she was no longer strong enough for it. Besides, she now wanted
to move to her elder daughter, who was returning home from America.
% print: De var (misprint)
It was a great disappointment to me, but I resolved
to make use of the good running order she had brought my household
into, and simply try to maintain it. She had engaged
two capable maids who were glad to stay with me. And this
led to the household order I have lived under since.

There had gradually formed a circle of young people
who regularly visited us. They were mainly friends of my
youngest son, but some young ladies also belonged to
the circle. I now arranged it so that they came every Thursday
to dinner, and that the afternoon and evening were spent in
music, singing or reading. I had much joy from
these evenings. I owe to them a closer acquaintance with
music, with which I would otherwise not have become familiar.
I took especial delight in Beethoven's Fifth Symphony, which
two young people played for me as a piano duet. These Thursday gatherings
continued until the little circle
was scattered by the dispensations of life.

\secrule

% --- p. 184 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{184}For a number of years I had followed with interest the conditions
in North Schleswig, where the Danish population with
steady firmness worked to assert its language and its
national culture, and I had often been glad to meet
outstanding men from over there. In a lecture
I gave in the autumn of 1898 in Kolding, later repeated
in Copenhagen and had printed in ``Tilskueren'', I sought to
show that much of what Fichte in his famous ``Reden an
die Deutsche Nation'' emphasizes in order to strengthen his people's
courage under oppression fits the struggle of the Danish Schleswigers
nowadays. The lecture was attacked in German
papers, and I answered the attacks in ``Kieler Zeitung''.
Shortly before, I had written some articles in ``Frankfurter
% print: Etische (misprint)
Zeitung'' and in ``Ethische Kultur'' on the language situation
in North Schleswig. On that occasion I received a letter from the well-known
philosopher Rudolph Eucken in Jena, of which I quote a
part, because it bears witness that there are excellent men
in Germany who see clearly and courageously in this matter. It says
in the letter (which is written 3 April 1898): ``Auch ich
empfinde solche Beeinträchtigung des natürlichen Rechtes
einer Bildung in der Muttersprache peinlich und kann
darin nur eine Überspannung der Nationalitätsprincipes
erblicken. Wir ereifern uns heute über das `cujus regio,
ejus religio' der 16. u. 17. Jahrhunderts; --- heute scheint
man fast überall nach dem Grundsatze zu handeln, `cujus
regio, ejus natio', und darüber werden spätere Jahrhunderte
kaum günstiger urtheilen''. Eucken finds an excuse
in the fact that most Germans have no idea of the conditions
in North Schleswig, and ends by saying: ``Nach meiner
Überzeugung wäre es im wahren Interesse Deutschlands,
das Gebiet, dessen Grundstock anerkannterweise dänisch
ist, Dänemark freiwillig abzutreten.'' He thinks that from this
would spring a cordial relation and a fruitful interaction
between Denmark and Germany.

\secrule

% --- p. 185 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{185}In political life, after I had moved from
Frederiksberg, I took part only as a nominator at Folketing elections. Slowly
but steadily the old Højre party was dissolving; it wore
out all its significant men in the hopeless struggle and by
the hopeless means that were used in the struggle. Meanwhile
conditions within the Opposition were not pleasant.
It suffered from the long period of waiting, in which all objective
interest threatened to fall away, and in which a brisk and teasing
newspaper article stood as the only possible feat that
could be spoken of. The alliance between the new literary
movement and oppositional politics, which I had in my time
been so much against, had indeed not quite answered to
the great expectations some had cherished, but it was still at work
through its consequences. The paper ``Politiken'' had in
its time been founded precisely on this alliance. The consequence
of this was that those who held to the paper as the Left's
chief organ also had to take its literary reviews
as sound goods, or in any case had to put a good
face on the game, even if they found the game ever so bad. And
the paper's literary articles now became more and more marked by
a wantonness and a frivolity that could not but arouse both
sorrow and indignation. It was especially Edvard Brandes who
let himself go in a way that even made men who stood close to him
say that he must be suffering from a monomania. I
had on one single occasion protested against the tone of the paper, where
it was directed at a man for whom I had reverence, however
far from him I otherwise stood. It was a scandalous article
about Bishop Kierkegaard that I objected to, naturally
with the result that I was taken to task in an editorial postscript.
I had not, however, broken off relations with the paper.
Shortly before the episode I shall now speak of, I had
written a review in it of my late friend Johannes
Fibiger's autobiography. All the more was I indignant to read, in
those same days, a literary review (of ``Damen paa
Natkaféen''), in which the height of frivolity was
reached. At this point two men came up one day to
% --- p. 186 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{186}me, the author Alfred Ipsen and the journalist Mads Jepsen,
and appealed to the duties I had toward Danish
youth to protest against this abuse by
being one of the conveners of a public meeting at which there
was to be a protest against the tone that had spread in
the press, first and foremost in ``Politiken'', but also in other
papers. The two gentlemen did not exactly inspire me with much confidence
as regards impartiality and freedom from prejudice, and I
was not much inclined toward that kind of meeting. But I had
long been vexed, also at the fact that I myself did nothing, and
I therefore gave my signature, thinking that I otherwise
need have nothing to do with the meeting. That
I signed was due in part to my being told that
Valdemar Vedel, whose literary judgment I trusted more
than my own, had given his support. It turned out
afterward that Vedel's support had been obtained only on
condition that I would take part. In a not entirely
honest way two half assents had been made to
count as two whole ones. The invitation to the meeting was signed
by 15 men (the University teachers Vilhelm Thomsen, Gertz,
Viggo Bentzon, Vilhelm Andersen, Vedel, the author
Niels Møller, the painter Viggo Johansen and others). Several University teachers
declared privately that they agreed with the judgment
on the literary articles of ``Politiken'', but that for political
reasons it was indefensible to weaken the position of ``Politiken''.
Here the misfortune of the union of literature and politics
really showed itself. I did not think further about the matter,
but the day before the meeting Valdemar Vedel and Niels
Møller came out to me and told me that some reactionary
hotheads intended to give the meeting a very fanatical
character, and they therefore begged me earnestly to
chair it and thereby give the meeting the character it
in our opinion ought to have. So I came to have a more
prominent position than I had at first imagined.
I then prepared to speak at the meeting as
the opening speaker, though I was not happy about it, especially after I had
% --- p. 187 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{187}heard more closely how the signatures had been brought
together.

On the morning of the day on which the meeting was to be held,
Professor Viggo Bentzon came up to me and told me that
the Minister of Justice was going to bring a case against Edvard Brandes
as the author of the novel ``Ungt Blod'', which had come out
some time before. We now both agreed that
the matter had taken on an entirely different character. In the first place
we had been thinking chiefly of the tone of the newspapers, not of book literature.
In the second place we did not want to meddle in a matter
that was being taken up from a purely legal side. We therefore decided
to have the meeting called off, and drove out to Valdemar Vedel and
Alfred Ipsen to get their agreement to this. With some
hesitation they consented, and I then drew up an
announcement for Ritzau's Bureau.

In fact the demonstration had its effect all the same.
The scandalous articles did not appear again.

The same morning that the meeting had been called off, I went up to
Hørup to explain the connection to him. I had
expected that he would take the story with scorn and irony.
But instead he began to explain to me why
he had at the time had to take Edvard Brandes as literary
editor of the paper. I interrupted him with the remark
that he owed me no account of that, but
that I simply wished to tell him both the reason why we
had planned the meeting and the reason why we now gave
it up. He was evidently much taken up with the whole affair. I
have at any rate never seen him so defensive and so
nervous. I believe in fact that his whole way of thinking
was very different from the one that had lately
come forward in his paper's literary articles, and he must
also have noticed that these articles were harming him and
the paper politically. --- He soon recovered
himself, however, for in the following days it rained in the paper
with taunts and distortions directed at the signatories.
Some of these attacks were of so impudent a
% --- p. 188 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{188}character that I wrote to the editors and canceled my subscription,
with the request that the cancellation take
effect at once. --- In another way too Hørup now took
his revenge. In a letter to Bjørnson a short time after he gave
a highly distorted account of the whole episode
and on occasion represented Vedel and me as sneaks and
hypocrites. This letter ``Politiken'' saw fit to publish
some years later. I had by then begun again to
take ``Politiken'', but now I canceled it again, and since then
it is only occasionally that I see this paper, which with all
its stylistic merits has done our country so much
harm at home and abroad.

Bjørnson disclaimed in a letter to me any part in the letter's
appearing. After Hørup's death he had sent all
the letters he had from him to Edvard Brandes, whose
hand was also evident in the lines that introduced the publication.
That the letter came out was a return of an old favor
(by the way not the only one). Edvard Brandes cannot forget.
And it seems moreover to be --- or to have been ---
a trait of his that he cannot imagine anything but selfish
motives behind any action that goes against him.
Several years after the episode spoken of here, the Supreme Court advocate
Frederik Salomon told me that Edvard Brandes
had complained that people on several sides were out to get him.
``What have I, e.g., done to Professor Høffding?''
he had asked. He has not been able to imagine that one
could come out against him on objective grounds. It was in fact
so far from my having anything against him personally
that I actually liked him very much and had myself felt
the winning and amiable quality in his nature that those
who knew him at close quarters spoke of. I particularly remember
that once, at the time we used to meet in ``Bogstaveligheden'',
he believed that I had felt offended by
some remarks of his at a larger gathering, and
in the friendliest way gave me an explanation of his
statement. His many-sided gifts I have admired.
% --- p. 189 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{189}After writing plays, some of which have artistic
value, he has published fine translations of
Old Testament writings and in recent years has shown himself
an able Minister of Finance and has, by all accounts,
done his country great services by his influence
on the policy that has been pursued during the war. ---

My break with ``Politiken'' brought me into contact with
``Socialdemokraten''. Since I would not write in the papers of the Right,
I was journalistically homeless. But I made use of an
occasion that was given by one of the serious and able
literary articles (by C. E. Jensen) that appeared in those years
in ``Socialdemokraten''. The reviewer had said that the lewd
literature came chiefly from circles that belonged
to the pampered youth of the bourgeoisie. In a letter to the paper I
agreed with him on this, saying that I thought the people of hard work
did not look upon life so frivolously. --- When
I had thus come into contact with the paper, its
editors invited me to write, in the number for 1 May
(1899), an article on the eight-hour working day.
This I did with pleasure; I had already expressed myself in that direction in my Ethics.
--- The offprint I was sent
of the May number is the finest copy I have of any
of my works, since it is printed on silk. --- Otherwise
my relation to ``Socialdemokraten'' had not always been
so friendly. When in the autumn of 1883 I gave lectures
on social ethics, the criticism I made
of the existing economic order was greeted with joy
in the paper, but it was added that if I did not draw socialism
from this criticism as its consequence, it must
be because with me, as with several of my colleagues,
other motives than the purely scientific were at work.
When I protested against this, the paper interpreted
its statement to mean that it had merely meant that I,
as coming from a bourgeois family, could not with the best
will in the world see the matter with the workers' eyes. The interpretation
was somewhat forced.

\secrule

% --- p. 190 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{190}My studies in these years, after the completion of ``den
nyere Filosofis Historie'', concerned the theory of knowledge and the philosophy of religion.
One of the preliminary studies for a theory of knowledge
is to be found in the treatise ``Det psykologiske Grundlag for
logiske Domme'', which was printed in the Skrifter of the Royal Danish Academy of
Sciences (1898). As regards the religious problem, there had
been a long time when it did not interest me
particularly, and when I did not expect to discuss it
beyond the treatment it had received in my Psychology and
in my Ethics, where, by the way, the view I later developed in detail
is already hinted at. Reading biographies
had more and more become my favorite reading, and I came
by this route also to occupy myself with Augustine's
``Confessions'', which interested me greatly from a purely
psychological and historical point of view. And when I came to the tenth
book, where the great Father of the Church raises the question:
``What is it that I love, when I love God?''
(Quid est qoud amo, quum deum amo?) --- then it stood clear
to me that an important source for the understanding
of religious phenomena must be found in the self-testimony of
personalities who, while they live wholly and fully in
their religion, have the ability and the need to make clear to themselves,
in the form of reflection, what they experience in a state of religious
rapture. I then collected a series of similar utterances
--- from Indian literature, from the mysticism of the Middle Ages, from
Luther and Pascal, from Pietism --- and analyzed them
psychologically. It naturally did not occur to me (as people
have taken it on a superficial reading of my writings)
that one could by this route learn anything about the
origin of the positive religions, or about the first
origin of all religion. But one could learn something about what
it is that keeps religion up once it has
come into being, and that is for the philosopher quite as important as the
purely historical question of the origin of dogmas and forms of worship.
And I saw besides clearly that the study of religion's
subjective and individual side must be combined

% --- p. 191 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%

\opage{191}with an objective study of the history of religion. Here I sought
especially to trace what standard the historians of religion
by profession apply when they call one religion
higher, another lower. By both these routes I sought
to form a hypothesis about what is the fundamental thing
in religion in its various forms. And thereby I thought
I could then find a basis for understanding religion's
position in our day and for conjectures about its
future. In a speech at a University celebration in the autumn of
1897 I gave a preliminary characterization of my standpoint.

It was my wish, before I proceeded to the final
exposition of my thoughts on the philosophy of religion, to go through
the problem in detail in lectures. And this gave
occasion for a change in my University work
which also later benefited me. Since I became professor,
I had every year, alongside Professor Kroman,
given a propaedeutic course for the young students,
and besides that held laboratory exercises for a narrow
circle and public lectures for larger circles. Since
the preparation of a course of lectures on the philosophy of religion, intended
for students of all faculties, would demand a great deal of
work, I proposed to Dr. Wilkens, who had become professor
extraordinarius, that he take over the propaedeutic course
in my place. This proposal was accepted and was sanctioned
by the authorities concerned, and it led to the
arrangement that each of the three professors of philosophy every
third year could have more time to give free lectures
or to undertake new works.

To shed light on my standpoint in the philosophy of religion I shall use
some statements in letters that were occasioned by
it.\footnote[1]{A short characterization of my view in the philosophy of religion will be found in the essay on my work as an author, which is reprinted in ``Religiøse Tanketyper'' (1927). [Later note.]}

From a certain quarter people saw in my philosophy of religion something
that smacked of theology, or that the theologians could in any
% --- p. 192 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{192}case could use. I had on that account an exchange of letters
with Dr. Anton Thomsen and set down here a couple of
fragments of two letters from me to him from February 1906.

On 17 February 1906 \ldots{} ``On several points, after all,
the differences between our ways of seeing came out during our
discussion the other evening. Such there will naturally be;
I need only think of my own relation to Brøchner
in my day. But I confess that it seems to me
you suffer from an antitheological anxiety. What is antitheological
is not therefore philosophical. We must look without bias at the
possibilities that present themselves when we come to the boundary points.
Precisely as positivists we can here go quite
calmly and leave it to the prophets of the various parties to
carry on. Perhaps I feel more secure because I
have gone through the various stages and know that for
me they are left behind.''

On 23 Feb. 1906 \ldots{} ``By antitheological anxiety in my
previous letter I meant precisely what you call political
anxiety. I want us to philosophize without tactics. And according to
my view of philosophy and its significance it is our
duty to examine all possibilities when they really come forward
with an attempt at justification.''

On 28 Feb. 1906 \ldots{} ``A working principle is the proposition
of the conservation of value, in that, at an essential
change in the conditions of human life, it leads one to
ask whether equivalents come in place of what has disappeared.
So in particular at the transition from positive religion
to free humanity --- precisely the phenomenon that has led
me to my hypothesis. I take a different attitude toward
`free thinking' when I am convinced that it will provide
ample equivalents than when I am convinced of the
opposite or at least have doubts about it. (I confess that I
still belong among the doubters --- that is, I doubt my own
hypothesis!) And the hope of finding equivalents (which
I will not give up) can lead to a labor of finding
or producing them.'' ---

% --- p. 193 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{193}In the letters quoted here I sought to give an answer to objections
from a quarter that thought it was speaking on behalf of science
and was guided by fear of giving theology
a little finger. From an entirely different quarter came an objection
that I answered in the letter I shall now quote very nearly
in its entirety. A couple of years after the ``Religionsfilosofien''
had come out, I received a letter from a man I
did not know personally, but who was well known in the political
and journalistic world. He wrote that he had
read my book at once when it came out and had thought he
could agree with its main ideas. But after a great
sorrow (the loss of his wife) he had read the book again,
and then things looked different, particularly as regards faith in
a personal immortality. It was a very fine,
serious and well thought-out letter. My reply to him (of
28 October 1903) ran as follows: ``It must be my first
word in reply to your letter to thank you for the confidence
you have shown me by approaching me. I am glad
that my book has placed me in such a light for
you that you could and would write to me, the stranger,
as openly and personally as you have done. Your
letter has both moved me and interested me. As you
will see from my book, I distinguish between the leading fundamental thought
in all religions and religious views of life, and the
special form it takes among different peoples and at different
times. It has been my interest as a philosopher
to attempt a conceptual determination of religion. But in
such a determination not all special features can be included. Belief in immortality,
e.g., occupies a very different place and is motivated
in very different ways in the different religions.
What interests me as a philosopher is really
only that \textit{where} a decisive place is assigned to it,
this happens through a motivation that leads in the direction of what
I in my terminology call `the conservation of value'. And
so it happens, too, in your letter. I myself personally
could not maintain that the conservation of value necessarily
% --- p. 194 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{194}requires the persistence of the individual personality. I stand
on the whole (a fruit of hard personal and theoretical struggles)
skeptical toward any more specific working-out of the
religious principle, fully convinced that such
a working-out necessarily has the character of poetry, valuable for
the mood that carries it, but not an adequate expression
of objective truth. But I see clearly that here is a point
where personal differences will make themselves felt until the end of days,
and I have the deepest respect for
every truly personal settling of life's accounts
on this point. Only I must object when one makes
one's personal need a standard for the emotional life of others.
As, e.g., when someone would conclude that he who has
lost a person he loved, and does not believe in immortality,
must have loved the departed less than he
who \textit{believes} in immortality has loved the one \textit{he} lost.
That conclusion is inadmissible, and here I can set experience
against experience. Yet --- there is no use quarreling about this.'' ---

In ``Forord og Efterskrift til min Religionsfilosofi'' (printed
in the second series of ``Mindre Arbejder'') and in ``Den store Humor''
I have in several respects sought to shed light on my position
on the religious problem as a philosopher and as a human being.
As a philosopher I have to do with the general principles of science
and of life; as a human being I have to do
with the special shading and application of these principles
to which my course of life and my personal experience have
led me. But I believe that in my case the
philosopher and the human being have drawn closer and closer to each other
--- I hope that it has not been to the detriment of
either of them. --- I would particularly refer to the chapter ``Tragik
og Humor'' in the book ``Den store Humor'' as the clearest
and most deeply reaching expression I have been able to give of the
domain where my philosophy and my personal experience of life
meet. ---

My Philosophy of Religion came out in 1901 and was soon translated
into various languages (German, French, English, Russian,
% --- p. 195 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{195}Spanish, Japanese). The best and most understanding review
of it I saw in ``Literary Times'' (24 August 1906).
Under the heading ``A Danish Thinker'' an excellent
résumé of the book's line of thought is given here, something with which
a philosophical author is as a rule not spoiled. It is emphasized
that a thinker from a small country suffers from the fact that he
writes in a little-known language, but that one will in return
rather find in him freedom from prejudice and a universal outlook
(a more unbiased cosmopolitan outlook). The book's personal
character alongside its investigative method
is stressed, and it is remarked at the end that even if the book
might seem to diminish the content of religious faith, ---
to say too little for fear of saying too much, --- yet its strict
honesty refreshes like a spring of cold
water (its austere sincerity refreshes like a spring of cool
water). I do not deny that I was very glad of this
review, and that is why I have quoted it here.

\secrule

On the last lecture day of the nineteenth century
(19 December 1900) I gave at the University a
speech which I published under the title ``Ved Aarhundredskiftet''.
I emphasized here some features in the characterization of the century just
ended. The spiritual antagonisms, and
in particular the national antagonisms, had become sharpened in
the course of the century. In scientific respects
the nineteenth century had to be described as the age of empirical confirmation
and of historical research, whereas the greatest thoughts,
the really fundamental ideas, had appeared in the
seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. In the practical sphere it got
its character from the mighty workers' organizations
and the class struggle conditioned by them, through which for the
first time in history the worst-placed strata of the people, living in the meanest
circumstances, themselves began to take an active part in
the work that can lead to a progressive solution of the
social questions.

\secrule

% --- p. 196 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%

\opage{196}In the autumn of 1901 I received from the University of Uppsala, through
the dean of its humanistic section, an invitation to
come up there in the course of the winter and give lectures there for a month.
I gladly accepted this invitation
and so spent the month of February 1902 in the classic Swedish
university town. For me it was above all Benjamin Höijer's
and Erik Gustaf Geijer's town. These two Swedish thinkers
I had come to take a great interest in, and especially Geijer's rich personality,
his writing of history and his philosophical development
(which forms an analogy to that of Sibbern and Kierkegaard
among us) I occupied myself with then and later, in that I
not only studied his works but also used the
extensive literature in which the personality and development of this
brilliant man are investigated and presented. From
my lectern at Uppsala University I looked out on Geijer's
statue and farther away, out over snow-covered fields and woods.

In preparation for these lectures I had, on the
basis of many years' studies and notes on the main
philosophical problems, worked out a short account of
the present state of these problems, as I conceived
it. As already in the introduction to ``Den
nyere Filosofis Historie'' I distinguished four main problems
--- the psychological, the epistemological,
the ethical-religious and the metaphysical. Or, as I have sometimes
put it, philosophy discusses four main subjects:
personality, science, the conduct of life and the world-view.
I found in Uppsala a good and interested audience,
which admittedly fell off when I came to the
more abstract investigations, but grew again when toward
the end I came back to more accessible questions.
After my return home I worked through anew
the content of these lectures and used it as
the subject of the University program which it was my turn
to write for the University celebration in the autumn of 1902. This
program is regarded by some as the clearest and most concise
account of my main philosophical ideas. It has not
% --- p. 197 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{197}been published through the book trade, but has been distributed on a large scale
by the University and by myself. It has been translated into
German, and as William James liked it so much, he had
it, by arrangement with me, translated into English.

Besides the series of lectures mentioned, which extended
through the whole month of February, I gave in Uppsala and in
Stockholm popular lectures on Holberg and Kierkegaard,
and on more recent epistemological points of view
I spoke in Uppsala's natural science society and at
Stockholms Högskola.

After the close of the lecture series I was honored by
the Uppsala student choir, who turned out with banners, song and a speech
in the entrance hall of the University. And on the journey home I was invited
to a celebration in Lund, which a circle of students there gave for
me. --- I was glad and proud of the honor that was thus
shown me in our neighboring country, and that I had been able
to contribute my mite to the interaction between the universities
of the North.

During my stay in Uppsala I lived in a hotel garni,
but I was hospitably received by several colleagues and felt
at home in their families. At the home of Professor Reinhold Geijer
and his amiable wife I had several pleasant evenings.
The famous linguist Noreen, the dean of the faculty,
also opened his home to me, and I came and went
at his house. His warmth of heart captivated me, and it was
a particular honor to me that he brought me a fine farewell greeting
on behalf of the faculty. All the more ashamed I am to
remember that I could not recognize him when, 10 years
later, I met him in the street in Stockholm and he very
kindly came up to me. My two closest Swedish friends,
both during the stay in Uppsala and later, were Frants and Hanna
v. Schéele. Frants v. Schéele was a knowledgeable and enthusiastic
philosopher who, since he obtained no University appointment,
followed his interest in pedagogy and accepted an appointment
as head of Stockholm's ``elementary school system'', a
position that involves a great deal of work, and to which he has devoted
% --- p. 198 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{198}his best powers. Hanna v. Schéele was my faithful
Swedish correspondent, whose letters gave me a vivid impression
of Swedish moods, and whose sympathy and understanding
have been and are of great value to me.

\secrule

In the summer of 1902 I made a journey with my youngest son
in Germany and Switzerland. In Berlin and Dresden we visited
the glorious museums. We stayed for a time by Lake Lucerne
and later on the Wengernalp.

In the autumn of 1902 I was elected Rector of the University
for 1902---03, succeeding my dear friend Vilhelm Thomsen.
The constitution of the University had shortly before been changed,
in that the Teachers' Assembly got greater influence, and the Consistory
was to be filled exclusively by election, whereas
formerly most of the seats were seats by seniority, where seniority
as professor was what decided. Since I had only
become professor at the age of 40, and since I therefore stood
far back in seniority behind several colleagues of the faculty,
I had never got into that high assembly. I have always
had an interest in the affairs of the University, and it had
therefore grieved me that I had not belonged to the circle
that made decisions about them; the Teachers' Assembly had before
the constitutional change little influence. Some years before
my election as Rector I had, however, been put up as
a candidate for one of the few seats in the Consistory that under the
older arrangement were filled by election. But my opponent
was my friend Vilhelm Thomsen, and I found it natural
that he should go before me. In his gentle way he said
to me that if it had been anyone other than me who had been
put up against him, he would have taken it
amiss. On the very day the election was to take place, he lay
in bed with one of his frequent attacks of illness. I visited
him in the morning and asked for his authorization
to give thanks for the election on his behalf if he were elected,
which I did not doubt. It caused much merriment in
% --- p. 199 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{199}the Teachers' Assembly when, after Thomsen had been elected by
a majority of ten votes, I stood up and gave thanks for the election
on Professor Thomsen's behalf.

My rectorate was then remarkable in that it was the first
time that a man was elected Rector who was not already
a member of the Consistory and thereby familiar with its business.
It was therefore, especially at the beginning, no easy matter to act
as leader toward the men who ``had sat in the Council
for so many years''. I believe, however, that I came off reasonably
well, although it was not always easy to conduct the proceedings in
the Consistory and especially in the Teachers' Assembly, in which certain
members had a tendency to make long
speeches out of season and to come forward with formalistic objections.
I remember a meeting at which rules of procedure were to be adopted,
and at which at the last moment an
objection was raised to the method of voting I had proposed.
As I foresaw that this objection would give rise
to a long discussion, and as the hour was late, I made use
of the right the Rector had to adjourn a meeting
and fix a new meeting a week later.

Besides signing the current documents and
conducting the proceedings in the Consistory and the Teachers' Assembly,
the Rector also has the task of representing the University
to the outside world. In this respect the most interesting thing I came
to attend was the festivities at the German Emperor's visit
to Copenhagen at the beginning of April 1903. After having
been present at the Emperor's landing at the Toldbod
I took part in the evening in a great gala dinner. King Christian
the Ninth proposed the Emperor's health in a German speech, which
he read out with great dignity. The Emperor replied in a
flowery speech, which ended with the wish that the King
might for many years yet stand ``am hohen Mast, von den
Falten des alten Dannebrogs umgeben''. The speech was delivered
in a powerful voice and without the help of paper. After the dinner
the Majesties held a reception. The Emperor showed all evening the
greatest deference to the old King. As soon as the latter
% --- p. 200 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{200}approached, the Emperor stood at attention, like a young lieutenant
before his colonel. With great liveliness and amiability he conversed
with those present. Our democratic
ministers were not all skilled in languages. I heard the Emperor
put a question to the Minister of Agriculture of the time
(O. Hansen), but when the latter only stammered: ``I
regret, --- --- I regret --- ---'' the Emperor looked at him for a moment
and then moved on. When I was presented to
him, he asked in which faculty there were the most students,
and when I answered that it was the medical one, he
said: ``Nun, das ist gut, denn es gibt in der Welt allzu viele
Juristen.'' I permitted myself a little joke on the subject,
whereupon the Emperor began to talk about the glorious student days,
which he looked back on with pleasure, and which his
sons were now enjoying. He spoke with much energy and with
large, shining eyes, which for a while made one forget
the stiff and dry appearance he could otherwise have.

Later in the evening Queen Alexandra, who was
on a visit, came up to me and said that she had heard from her
brother (the Crown Prince) that I had been in touch
with the Dowager Empress Friedrich of Germany (``my poor
sister-in-law'', as she called her). The fact was that the Dowager Empress
had read my Ethics and had sent me greetings
both through the King and through the Crown Prince; I
had also had to send her an autograph. Queen
Alexandra talked with me for a long time and wished to have one of my
books. Some time after I then sent her my Ethics with
a letter to the effect that I was glad to present the book
to the Queen of the country to whose literature and science
I owed so much.

The next evening there was a soirée at the Crown Prince's. Here
a great crowd of people from various circles was gathered,
who were arranged in groups in the various rooms. University,
Academy of Fine Arts, administration, etc., stood ready, and
the Emperor went around and addressed a few winged words
to the various groups. I heard him talk with
% --- p. 201 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{201}Krøyer about academies of art, which Krøyer thought were
an evil, and I heard him say, when Marcus Rubin was
presented as a statistician: ``Statistik --- die schwierigste
aller Wissenschaften!'' (On the other hand I did not see that he got
any more ``lines'' out of this difficult science's Danish representative.)
--- That evening, besides the Rector, the deans too
were present, and I then told them the Emperor's remark
about the lawyers from the previous evening. The dean of law
then said that fun must always be made of the lawyers;
but the physician thought that the doctors were usually the most
roughly handled, and so each dean complained on
his faculty's behalf; only the theologian (Professor Jacobsen)
stood silent until all had spoken, and then said: ``The worst is
after all what is said about theology, and it is only a single
