little word: leider! (in Goethe's Faust).'' ---

\secrule

About a month before the Emperor's visit I had turned 60
(on 11 March). On that occasion I unexpectedly came to
celebrate my first jubilee. I had probably always had a
feeling that the students on the whole liked
me; but I was surprised and overwhelmed by the devotion
and goodwill that now surged toward me. Even if
part of it was owing to the zeal for celebrating jubilees (even where
the person celebrated does not himself think of it), still there was, of this
I was and am convinced, genuine feeling in what met me
on this occasion and on various occasions in
later years. I was heartily glad of the many proofs of
sympathy I received from older and younger, although I often
deep down had the feeling that I was being overrated.
What I knew and know about myself is that I have taken
life and my work --- the work it has been my
good fortune to carry on --- seriously. I have been a diligent man,
and my personal development and my intellectual work have gone
hand in hand, although there are slack places in my personality
which the intellectual work has not been able to master.

% --- p. 202 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{202}The Students' Union and the Students' Society jointly invited me to a celebration, which was held on the
evening after my birthday. It was a great joy to me that Professor Kroman took on the office of toastmaster on
this occasion, --- that Valdemar Vedel gave the main speech, --- and that later Georg Brandes gave the brilliant
speech which he has reprinted in his writings. Among the songs I am especially glad of Sofus Michaëlis's splendid
poem. In addition, friends and listeners brought forth characterizations and words of tribute in prose and in
verse. I especially keep in fond memory Saxild's characterization in ``Tilskueren'', and Niels Møller's poem in
the same place.

When I was about to drive home late in the evening, a crowd of students unharnessed the horse from the cab and
pulled me at a gallop the whole way from the Hotel ``Kongen af Danmark'', where the celebration had been held,
over Knippelsbro to Strandgade, where I lived at that time. Several teams relieved one another during the drive;
those who were not pulling ran alongside the carriage or behind it, and after the whole procession rode the
cabman on his astonished horse. There was a police station in the building where I lived, and the constables came
out to see what was going on. When I had got up to my room, I opened the window and gave one more word of thanks
to my young friends, who answered with a hurrah that rang through the quiet street.

The next day I met the police assistant and asked him to excuse my having been the occasion of a disturbance in
the street. He answered jokingly that the police so often caused a disturbance in the building by bringing drunken
people to the station; --- it might just even out! ---

The summer of 1903 I spent in Jutland, partly in Ebeltoft, where my eldest son was then staying, partly in
Viborg, with Archivist Saxild, partly at Tyborøn with Engineer Munch-Petersen. They were three genuinely Jutlandic
regions.

\secrule

The following winter an invitation came to me to give a lecture on the present position of psychology at
% --- p. 203 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{203}a general scientific congress which was to be held in the late summer of 1904 in St. Louis in North
America, on the occasion of its being a hundred years since Louisiana had been united with the North American free
states. About a hundred European scholars of various disciplines were invited to this congress, besides a good
many Americans. It was mostly the desire to see America that moved me to say yes; but a kind letter from William
James with an invitation to visit him during my stay over there did much to strengthen me in my decision.
Besides, I would meet many interesting people. The prospects for the journey became still more attractive when my
friend and colleague Otto Jespersen came up to me one day and told me that he too had received an invitation. We
then agreed to make the journey together. We two and the physicist Arrhenius were the only Scandinavians who were
invited.

Travel allowance and fee were so ample that I could make a plan for a stay in England and Holland on the return
journey.

Among the preparations for the journey was also that of learning to speak English tolerably. I had not studied
English at all at school, but had later taught myself to read it, and had also had a few lessons; but my
pronunciation was very deficient. I had words enough for household use, especially for philosophical household
use, but was not practiced in finding them in a hurry. It helped a good deal that I now took some lessons from a
capable woman teacher; but it was only after some weeks' stay in America that I could really get my tongue going.
Several Americans, among others William James and Morton Prince, declared my letters ``quite idiomatic''; but my
pronunciation was poor, and I have not succeeded in getting beyond this imperfection. When I once asked Jespersen
what he thought of my English, he answered: ``Well, you can manage to say everything you want to, and you can be
understood; --- but it is not English!'' --- I was fairly well satisfied with this testimonial, although it would
of course, if I were to speak to an audience that was interested not only
% --- p. 204 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{204}in the content but also in the form, be an essential shortcoming that my spoken language was not
``idiomatic''. This was one of the reasons why I have twice declined invitations to come to Scotland and give the
so-called Gifford Lectures. ---

At the end of August, then, Otto Jespersen and I set out on our American journey on the ``Hellig Olaf''. It was a
lovely clear summer evening when we went up through the Sound, and the next morning we had a glorious sail up
through the Kristianiafjord. The ship lay for a day at Kristiania, and we used the time for an excursion to
Holmenkollen. After we had lain for some hours at Christianssand the following day, the voyage went across the
North Sea, north of Scotland, out into the Atlantic. It was a strange thing, for some eight days, to come up in
the morning and see sea around one on all sides. We did not meet many ships on our way. In the distance we often
saw whales sending their spouts high into the air. Sometimes we were accompanied by shoals of dolphins that wanted
to race the ship. It was an amusing sight when in their eagerness they leapt from wave crest to wave crest. But a
sailor who stood beside me said: ``Well, that is just plain stupidity. They want to get round the ship; but then
they could just lie still until the ship has gone past!'' This animal psychology was no doubt quite correct.

Of actual seasickness I had only, one evening up by the Orkneys, a slight attack, which Jespersen cured with a few
drops. But for several days I felt best on deck in an easy deck chair, and there I was given my meals. Here I had
as my neighbor a young, pretty German lady, with whom I had good conversations. My main reading during the voyage
was Shakespeare (in the small, dainty English editions). Later on I could again take part in the social life on
board. In the evening there was sometimes dancing, and I practiced the minuet with a young Danish woman student
who was traveling to America on a visit. A couple of years later she came up for the philosophicum with me, and
% --- p. 205 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{205}when she came and sat down opposite me, I said: ``Well, Miss, let it go as well now as on the
Atlantic!'' This riddle the audience evidently could not guess.

Otto Jespersen was a good, steady traveling companion. We shared a cabin and got on excellently with each other.
In his younger days he had taken part in student gatherings at my home, introduced by his friend Knud Ipsen. He
had a fine scholarly career; it was indeed a great honor to be invited to an English-speaking country to speak on
the history of the English language. I teased him that he studied phonetics at night, not only by day, for when we
sailed at night in fog, the ship's steam whistle sounded constantly: ``Boom---boom---boom!'' and I then heard
Jespersen in the bunk above mine imitate it in a somewhat weaker key, just as he was in the habit of training his
tongue in imitating foreign languages or dialects.

It was a joy to me to get to know Jespersen and to learn what life and what warmth there was behind his somewhat
dry and awkward manner. An old politician who was on board, Commodore Bluhme, said to us: ``Well, now you gentlemen
are setting out as good friends and colleagues; but before the journey is over, you will be so sick and tired of
each other that you cannot bear the sight of each other.'' He was presumably relying on his experience. But his
prophecy did not come true. We had set out saying ``De'' to each other, but came home saying ``du'', and him and
his charming wife, Fru Ane Marie, I still count among my good friends.

Besides Danes, our traveling company also included Americans. A doctor from New York traveled back and forth
across the Atlantic in summer because there were no telephones there. An American lady with her daughters
belonged to the sect that gathers around the so-called ``Christian Science'', whose main tenet is that there is no
evil, no pain in the world. Her confession ran: ``We are glad and happy, and why should we not proclaim that
% --- p. 206 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{206}this is the meaning of the whole?'' --- For a couple of days, however, she had disappeared --- on
account of seasickness. Presumably she then had to admit that there were realities of another kind than the one
she had proclaimed. But I did not get round to asking her about it.

The Congress committee had sent us two tokens (badges), which we were to wear on landing. On arrival we were met
by two envoys who wore similar badges, and with their help we got quickly through customs. We were taken up into
New York and had lunch at a restaurant. Then Jespersen left at once for Philadelphia to visit his wife's brother.
He brought with him on a record his father-in-law's voice, which his brother-in-law had not heard for 20 years. I
was put up in a hotel and introduced into a club which had its rooms on the 13th floor of the same building as the
hotel. The next day I traveled via Boston up into New Hampshire to James's country place in a splendid wooded
region by ``the White Mountains''. From that region, when the land sales in the West began, a whole emigration had
taken place. One saw round about many abandoned farmsteads. It was such a farm that James had bought and made into
a cozy summer home.

When I arrived at the farm, I found only Mrs. James, who sat on the veranda darning stockings. Her husband had
rowed across the lake to the station to meet me, but had arrived too late. I was shown to a spacious room, and a
little later the author Henry James, William's brother, came to bid me officially welcome in his sister-in-law's
name. When I came over to the veranda again, a small man came along in knee breeches and shirtsleeves and with two
oars over his shoulder. He had a fine, intelligent but nervous face with beautiful eyes. And so I stood face to
face with a man of whom I had gained, through his writings, so fine and vivid an impression, one of the finest
descriptive psychologists of the age. It has been said of the two brothers that Henry was the best psychologist
among poets, William the best poet among psychologists. In the course of the conversations we had
% --- p. 207 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{207}in the following days, we discussed both the points where we met and those where there were
divergences. The year before, I had given an account of my relation to James in a University program of 1903 (on
some attempts in the philosophy of religion in recent times), which is reprinted in the second series of my
``Mindre Arbejder''. The portrait of James was later included in the foreign editions of ``Moderne Filosofer'',
and I know that James valued this characterization. As regards his religious views, he thought he could call
himself a Christian, but he belonged to no church (denomination) and did not like hearing sermons, whereas he
often went into a chapel in the morning to hear hymn singing. There was in his way of taking up theoretical and
practical questions something original and personal that had a highly refreshing effect. He belonged to a type
which many would not expect to meet in America, a quiet, gentle and inward spirit, with a sense for the inner life
wherever it is found and whatever forms it may clothe itself in, a type that stands in curious contrast to the
restless type, absorbed in the toil of business, which one often regards as the truly American one. James's
nature suited the nature by ``the White Mountains''. One day, when the forest ``stood still and was silent'', not a
wind stirring, and a wonderful calm and a deep mood rested over the landscape, James said: ``This is an American
day.'' Yes, such days there are in America, and in the circles in which I moved during my two months' stay in
America, I often had occasion to experience such days and to meet the human type that corresponds to them.

James's gentleness and peace of mind were not simply a gift of nature. In an earlier period of his life he had
suffered from violent attacks of neurasthenia accompanied by feelings of anxiety. Everything in life appeared
uncertain and full of danger. He had to cling to the most exalted biblical words he knew so as not to go insane.
He has himself
% --- p. 208 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{208}described this case in his famous book ``Varieties of Religious Experience''. For the case he describes
on p. 160 f. (in the Danish popular edition p. 86 f.) is in reality his own, which I did not know at the time, but
which he has declared in a letter to a French friend, in which he also describes the case as ``acute neurasthenic
attack with phobia''.\footnote[1]{See on this \textit{Th. Flournoy: La Philosophie de William James} (1911), p. 149.}
Whether it was during this attack of illness that he made use of the so-called mind-cure, which consisted in what
he regarded as telepathic influence, I do not know. He has described this cure in ``Varieties'' p. 123 ff. (not
included in the Danish popular edition).

James's previous history I did not know fully when I visited him. If a good and thorough biography of him should
one day appear, it will be extraordinarily interesting to see what he has had to struggle with and how it has
influenced his way of thinking. He himself belonged to what he calls ``the sick souls''. And it was his conviction,
founded on experience, that such a sick soul has the right to seize upon whatever proves to have the power to hold
it up in the moments of crisis. This explains both his deep religious disposition, borne by the need for peace and
for mastery over the inner darkness, and his great impartiality and freedom from every dogmatic formulation. His
position toward the religious problem is that of a physician of the soul, who uses the means that experience
points to, without systematic scruples. His ``Varieties'' is, although he does not conceal his own personal
standpoint, one of the most undogmatic books there are.

He was never free of the neurasthenia. When I was with him, he was suffering from severe depression. Only for a
few hours in the morning could he work. In the afternoon he liked to drive about in a small one-horse carriage.

After a stay of 4---5 days with James I traveled back to New York, where I was invited to stay a couple of days
% --- p. 209 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{209}with one of the gentlemen who had received us on landing, an Anglican clergyman, Mr. Carstensen, a
Danish-born man, son of the founder of Tivoli. He was minister of a small church out in a pleasant residential
district. He lived in a large and handsome house, and he and his wife showed me much kindness. This visit ended
with Mr. Carstensen taking me to the express train by which I, together with a score of participants in the coming
Congress, was to make a circular tour to various places before and after the Congress, under the direction of one
of Cook's agents. It was a mixed traveling company, Frenchmen, Germans and Italians. Among the participants were
the mathematician Darboux, the archaeologist Enlart (who had a thorough knowledge of Danish medieval architecture
and was particularly taken with the Marieklostret in Helsingør), the philosopher Dessoir (a German), the historian
Ettore Païs and the linguist Pio Reina. With Païs I came into closer contact and have also heard from him several
times in the following years. Our first station was Niagara. We arrived there toward evening, and I went at once
--- together with Jespersen, who joined us here --- out to the Falls. We came out right at the edge over which the
mighty masses of water plunge down like fiery horses that rush forward at a furious pace and hurl themselves into
the abyss. The mass of water gliding evenly above suddenly turns into the violence of the fall, just as an
overwhelming emotion can suddenly well up from the ground of a calm disposition, where nothing seemed to presage
such a transition. When some years before I visited the waterfall at Imatra in Finland, where the great masses of
water from Lake Saimaa are pressed out through a narrow cleft in the rock, it was also the image of furious,
onrushing horses that arose at the sight. --- The next day we saw the Falls from below, as we, dressed in
oilskins, came down by elevator to the foot of the cliff. Here it was a splashing and thundering world we entered;
but the impression did not have the sublime character it had above.

Our next station was Chicago, where we spent a couple of
% --- p. 210 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{210}days. A banquet was given for us, paid for by some millionaires (who, however, were not themselves
present). The various nationalities were toasted, and Jespersen replied in a brief, lively speech on behalf of
the Scandinavians.

In St. Louis we were quartered in a new building that was to be used as a student residence, corresponding to our
Regens. There were a great many small apartments, each for two students, with two bedrooms and between them a
common sitting room. Jespersen and I came to live together, and as Arrhenius lived close by, we three took our
breakfast together. Arrhenius was usually in radiant spirits, and his wit and liveliness gave us a cheerful start
to the day. Tönnies, whom I met again here, was often a fourth, quieter participant.

The Congress lasted a week, with lectures and accompanying discussions both morning and afternoon. I spoke on
general psychology, with James Ward from Cambridge in England as co-speaker. Of the discussion after our lectures I
remember nothing. On the other hand I remember other discussions in which I took part, especially the one on
pathological psychology, which was opened by Pierre Janet, whose acquaintance it was very interesting to me to
make. He had written a preface to the French edition of my Psychology, and there was a certain kinship in our
psychological points of view. --- I also made the acquaintance of the chemist Ostwald, who now appeared as a
philosopher with a classification of the sciences which, he had no idea, had already been set up by Comte.
Personally I liked Ostwald; he was hearty and naive, --- in his speculations, though, perhaps too naive.

When one took part in meetings both morning and afternoon, one's time was well taken up. I did not go to
festivities, except to the great closing banquet. There I sat beside a very charming German colleague, Benno
Erdmann of Bonn (now in Berlin). He asked me whether a more conciliatory feeling was not now cherished in Denmark
toward
% --- p. 211 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{211}Germany. I answered that I believed the feeling would become good if new examples did not keep coming
of how the Prussian government suppressed the language and national culture of our countrymen in Schleswig. To
this he said that the State must after all have the same language and culture everywhere. I then said: ``Ja, Herr
Kollege, das ist eben die Nemesis der Eroberung. Man kann die Herzen und die Geister nicht bezwingen, und wenn man
doch Einheit auch auf dem geistigen Gebiete haben will, muss man die rohe Gewalt anwenden.'' After I had explained
the circumstances to him more fully, it was as though a light dawned on the honest man for the first time, and he
answered: ``Ja, ich sehe, man muss ja aus seiner Haut ausgehen, um diese Sache gerecht zu beurteilen.''

After the close of the Congress we came again into Cook's care. We traveled first to Washington, where we stayed a
couple of days. Here we were presented to President Roosevelt, who addressed a few words to each of us. When he
heard that I was from Denmark, he asked whether I knew Jacob Riis, and when I said that I hoped to make his
acquaintance in New York, he said: ``I hope, You will do so, because he is one of our best American citizens, and
at the same time still a good Danish patriot.'' To this I replied that I knew that from one of the President's own
magazine articles, in which he had described his and Riis's work to reform New York's municipal affairs. Roosevelt
made a very energetic impression. When he spoke, something of the beast of prey could come over him, or he looked
as though he were about to charge in as a cavalryman.

During the stay in Washington we were one evening at a soirée given by the President of the St. Louis Congress. On
this occasion there was nothing to be had but oranges and lemonade. That was not enough for Germans and
Scandinavians, and so when we went home, we sought out a beer hall, which we went down into. The famous historian
of dogma Harnack, who was wearing all his
% --- p. 212 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{212}decorations, hesitated a little, though, before he went down with us. ``Nur einen Augenblick!'' he
said, and this moment he used to make the decorations disappear into his pockets. Over the beer great conviviality
reigned. But Harnack teased two Austrians who were present by comparing Austria with the old house in Andersen's
tale: it did not know to which side it should fall, and only for that reason did it remain standing! A rather apt
image of the Austro-Hungarian-Slavic state, but one which Harnack would hardly apply with the same merriment now
(after 1914).

From Washington we went on via Philadelphia to Boston, where Harvard University gave a celebration for us.
President Eliot of Harvard presided and spoke to the various nationalities. The speech to the Scandinavians he
addressed to me, and I had to improvise a little speech, which I believe went off quite well. Here in Boston the
Congress was definitively dissolved. I now took up my residence for some three weeks at Harvard University, which
lies outside the city, in Cambridge, which is separated from Boston only by a river. At first I lived in a
boarding-house, later in James's house. In a letter to a young friend I wrote (14 Oct. 1904): ``I am now living
with my friend Professor James in a large and comfortable house in this splendid university town, --- splendid,
not in the sense of magnificent, but in the sense of glorious and interesting. It is like a large park, where
lecture halls, laboratories, student and professors' residences lie among the trees, which now stand in their
autumn splendor. James is an excellent philosopher, especially by his fine psychological sense and his open eye,
and he is moreover a lovable personality. Immediately after I had come to America, at the beginning of September,
I stayed some days with him at his country estate, and now he has lodged me in his house here in a large bright
room with a view of friendly avenues and gardens. Today I gave a lecture for his students. And yesterday I gave a
lecture out at a women's university, which is called Wellesley College and lies some miles from here .... These
% --- p. 213 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{213}days are some of the best I have had on my journey. Mrs. James too is extraordinarily charming, and the
whole family cannot do enough for me.'' --- The two lectures mentioned here I worked together into an article,
which was printed in English in an American periodical and later in Danish in my mindre Arbejder, third series,
% print: insmensily (misprint)
under the title ``En filosofisk Bekendelse''.\footnote[1]{Both of the two lectures I have mentioned here were given in James's presence. But he has certainly interpreted them far too strongly in the direction of his own ideas when, shortly after my departure, he recommends me very warmly (make much of good old Høffding) to a correspondent in Oxford (24 Oct. 1904) on the ground that I was ``a good pluralist and irrationalist''. If one will read the essay in which both lectures are worked together, in the third series of my mindre Arbejder, one will see that this does not fit (as far as pluralism is concerned). I am naturally glad that James liked me (I took to him immensely, and so did everybody), and that in his opinion I made a good impression in America. --- James was very pleased with an anecdote an American lady had told me, and which I used in my lecture for his students. (It is quoted in Mindre Arbejder III p. 26). It was aimed at orthodox theology, but proves nothing for ``pluralism''.}

For some days Pierre Janet and the English psychologist Lloyd Morgan (who had in his time written a fine review of
my Psychology in ``Nature'') were staying with James at the same time as I. The stay with James was thus of
many-sided interest to me. But I was most taken up with James's gentle and deep personality. I know too that James
felt friendship for me. That appeared from his letters to me in the following years. And when he had died, Mrs.
James wrote to me: ``William had a strong affection for You.'' --- Already at the time of my visit he was weak; the
neurasthenia increased in the following years, besides which he suffered from a heart condition. After having
taken a cure in Europe in vain, he died in the year 1910. ---

At the end of October I sailed from New York on one of the Cunard Line's ships, the Lucania. Just outside New York
we ran into a strong storm, and I had to lie four days in my bunk, where I was well looked after by the English
steward, so well that a young South American who shared the cabin with me also felt like staying in his bunk,
which, however, he was not
% --- p. 214 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{214}allowed to do. When the weather had improved, I came up on deck again, but spent the day by myself in
an open hall. I had my food brought up there, since I did not venture to go down into the saloon. Nor was there
the same coziness there as on the Danish ship. There were many more passengers, and it had a somewhat
uncomfortable effect that warnings had been posted against playing cards with unknown fellow passengers, since the
management knew that there were professional gamblers on board. Not that card-playing was a temptation to me; but
one did look around with a certain suspicion. I spent the day reading and looking out at the sea, which now no
longer had the summery look it had had on the voyage over. In the middle of the Atlantic a wireless telegram came
about the tension between Russia and England, occasioned by the Russian fleet in the North Sea having fired in a
panic on English fishing boats. Every morning a small newspaper was printed on the ship and distributed to the
passengers, and one could thus read the latest news in one's bunk. It is said to have been the first time that
wireless telegraphy was used in that way. When we came to Liverpool, we heard that the danger of war was over.

Together with the steamship ticket I had received a railway ticket from Liverpool to London, which gave the right
to stop at various places on the way. I went at once from Liverpool out to the little town of Chester, partly to
rest after the sea voyage, partly because Chester is a historically interesting town, with memories of Roman times
and of the English Civil War. It was a pleasant English provincial town, and I spent the day partly reading in the
beautiful park, partly walking. In the evening I went on to Stratford on Avon, Shakespeare's birthplace, where I
stayed over the next day. It was in a peculiar mood that I walked about here, where one's thoughts could well
dwell on the great poet's youth and again on his plain life there after he had left the stage and literature.
There are no direct memorials of him, except for his
% --- p. 215 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{215}bust in the church, which dates from the time immediately after his death. But the landscape is
characteristically English, and walking along the broad river Avon, where it flows through meadows and beneath
overhanging willows, I was constantly reminded of the description of Ophelia's death.

In London I had been invited to give a lecture to the Sociological Society, and it had been arranged that I should
stay with three of the Society's members, a week in each place, during my stay in London. I went at once, then,
out to my first hostess, Lady Welby, in Harrow on the Hill, a few Danish miles from London. Lady Welby was the
widow of a landowner. She was very much interested in philosophy and has written on what she called ``Significs'',
i.e. the doctrine of the most exact possible correspondence between word and thought. She held that ordinary
language, and in part also the language of science, was full of unclear metaphors and false analogies. I do not
deny that for me there was something exaggerated in the old lady's zeal for this cause, --- the same impression I
have had of one of our natural scientists' doughty battle against false analogies. The figurative expressions of
language are often excellently suited to searching and working thought, which, as it advances, has it in its power
to strip off the figurative through definite formations of concepts. I would rather look for the imperfection of
language at another point, which Bacon already, and in our day Bergson, have pointed out, namely in this, that by
giving the various things and properties each its own special name it comes to emphasize the difference between
them too much. --- But Lady Welby was a tireless worker. Every morning from 5 to 8 she dictated in bed to her woman
secretary, and when she had got up, what had been dictated was copied out fair. Often she then went through it
with me, and I often had to admire her energy and acuteness. In one of the later editions of the Encyclopædia
Britannica she has written the article
% --- p. 216 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{216}Significs. --- But I remember her especially as a solicitous and kind-hearted hostess.

The very morning after my arrival I received a very sad piece of news from home. A young friend of mine, Dr. med.
Harald Munch-Petersen, son of Julius Petersen, had met with an accident on a journey in Savoy. He had, it was
presumed, fallen from a steep mountain near Aix-les-Bains; but a long time passed before his body was found, and
so a sense of dread was added to the great grief that all who knew him felt. I set down here some lines of a
letter that I wrote during my stay in London to one of the deceased's sisters.

``I have often thought of how you were faring under this new great sorrow. [Half a year before, her mother had
died]. For me too it is a great sorrow, and I cannot at all imagine that I shall not see my dear young friend
again. In recent years, especially after he had become Hans's doctor, we had become very close friends, and I had
great confidence in him. It is a fine career that has been broken off here; we had every reason to believe that he
would have achieved something significant ... There are so many ruins in the world, and it is not easy to see why
it must be so.''

The news of my young friend's death (or properly, of his disappearance) I received, as I said, on the morning
after my arrival. We were sitting by the fireplace in the drawing room. Shortly afterward I got up and went into
the library, which had been put at my disposal as a study. A few moments later there was a soft knock at the door,
and my old Lady came in and said that she had been able to see from me that I had received sad news; she only
wanted to say that I must take care not to fall ill, and that if there was anything she could do to relieve and
strengthen me, she would most gladly do it. I was much moved by the old lady's love and tact, and from that moment
I felt at home, as under a mother's care.

% --- p. 217 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{217}Lady Welby's villa was beautifully situated, with a view over grass- and wood-clad hills. A beautiful
garden belonged to it, and the district invited walks. There was an excellent philosophical library in the house,
so that there was everything I could wish for, both for refreshment and for work. The conversations with Lady
Welby and her secretary were lively and interesting. For some days one of my English translators, Miss Ethel
Meyer, also stayed at the villa. The distance from London was no greater than that one could easily spend a
morning there, attend an afternoon performance at the theater and be home for dinner at 8 o'clock. On the very
first evening, when I came up to my room toward dinner time, I found my tailcoat and the rest of my black dress
neatly laid out; otherwise I should hardly have thought of what was the custom in a fine English house. As a rule
we were only three at table, and I took Lady Welby in. At the end of the meal the ladies would then have me remain
seated over the wine, which, however, I had no wish to do. Every morning the lady of the house held prayers, which
consisted in a reading from the Bible and from the liturgy; all the household were present on this occasion. The
first morning I was asked whether I would go in with them, which I had nothing against. But when, according to
Anglican custom, they fell on their knees at a certain point of the liturgy, I could not join in, but remained
standing. The next morning the secretary said to me that I would probably rather be excused from going in. As far
as I could see, it was a patriarchal custom that the old lady faithfully kept up. One noticed nothing whatever of
theology in her way of thinking, although she had a deeply religious mind.

When the time for the lecture to the Sociological Society drew near, I moved in with my next host, Mr. Gooch, a
young English historian and politician. He had written a good book on ``English democratic ideas in the
seventeenth century'', and he has later (1913) written an excellent book on ``History and Historians in the
% --- p. 218 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{218}19th Century''. He was very well off and could live for his studies and his political interests. When I
visited him again some years later, he was a Member of Parliament, belonging to the Liberal Party. He was an
upright and warm-hearted man with much knowledge and many-sided interests. His wife, who was of German descent,
was also handsome and hospitable. I was excellently off in their house. I can still hear his kind words when he
came in to me in the morning: ``Now, Mr. Høffding, have You made Yourselves comfortable? Have You a good fire?''
Whereupon he --- to show me what it was to be ``comfortable'' --- placed me in an armchair by the fireplace and
gave me the Times.

The lecture to the Sociological Society dealt with the relation between ethics and sociology and was very well
received. There was a long discussion afterward, in which, among others, Professor Westermark of Helsingfors, who
also teaches in London for some months every spring, took part.

With Gooch's help I got reasonably well oriented in London. I visited museums, and I was introduced into a club.
When we walked in the street, he led me like a little child every time we had to cross the heavily trafficked
streets. --- One day I received word from the Danish Minister, Chamberlain Bille, that Queen Alexandra wished to
speak with me, and he suggested that I come to him for lunch, after which he would accompany me to Buckingham
Palace. When we came to the palace, he handed me over to a footman, who handed me over to another footman, who
handed me over to a third footman, who showed me into a hall, where the Queen came a little later. She asked me to
sit on a chair beside her sofa and then conversed with me for half an hour or so, very kindly and openly, among
other things about the danger of war that had recently existed.

I had received invitations both to Cambridge and to Oxford. And so one morning I left Gooch's pleasant home to
drive to the station and from there go to Cambridge.
% --- p. 219 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{219}But on the way a heavy fog suddenly came on, brownish and dense, like a veil that settled over all
things. The cabman had to get down and lead the horse. One could not see one's hand in front of one. At the street
corners stood policemen, who gave the necessary topographical information. I had read of something of the kind in
Dickens, but now I experienced it in its most glaring form. I understood what accidents and crimes could happen in
such cases. I arrived too late for the train and had to spend several hours at the station before the next train
went. When we came out of the city, it cleared up, and the sun shone gloriously when I came to the old university
town, where I was kindly received by Professor Sorley and his wife. I had made Sorley's acquaintance in America
and soon felt at home with my new hosts. They lived in a pleasant house with a garden. Sorley is a fine, quiet man.
As an ethicist he belongs to an idealist school, and one of his most important writings is a critique of
naturalism in ethics. The Sorleys had two sons and a daughter, who were all at home now, but who some years later
were each sent to a boarding school of their own. As the youngest son was somewhat dependent and clung a great
deal to his elder brother, he wanted to go to the same school as he did; --- but in spite of all tears they had to
be separated, so that the younger too could learn to become independent. The eldest began his studies at Oxford
with distinction, but when the war broke out, he went with it, rose to captain and fell in October 1915, while
leading his company forward to the attack. All this still lay in the future, and there seemed to be peace and no
danger in the autumn of 1904. I visited the various colleges, which hold so many memories; e.g. Thomas More,
Bacon, Locke and Newton studied here, and Erasmus visited his friend More here. For Sorley's students I repeated
my lecture on the relation between ethics and sociology. The splendid parks invited walks; they still stood in
their autumn splendor.

% --- p. 220 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{220}German influence has been great in England in the philosophical field in the nineteenth century. Many
professors had received their training in Germany, as had Sorley's colleague James Ward, who not infrequently
mentions ``my old teacher Lotze''. Ward is an able psychologist and theorist of knowledge, though, like most
English and American philosophers, rather given to theologizing. I also stayed some days with Ward and then
traveled to Oxford, where I was to give a lecture to the ``Jowett Society''. I stayed with Sidney Ball, tutor at
St. John's College. He was married and therefore did not live in the college, but in a small house next to it. I
was a guest at the Oxford philosophers' annual dinner, and in my reply to a toast I spoke of the strong German
influence on present-day English philosophy and expressed the hope that, just as in its time Hume's influence had
worked toward a new and distinctive development of German philosophy, so German philosophy might now call forth a
new development of that vigorous philosophizing which has contributed much to giving England so considerable a
place in the history of intellectual culture. --- In Oxford I had the honor of being created Doctor of Science.
Clad in a splendid red and gray silk gown, I was led solemnly before the Vice-Chancellor, who was enthroned on his
high seat. After the Public Orator had set out my merits in Latin, and the Vice-Chancellor had obtained the
consent of the assembled colleagues and Masters, he declared me Doctor and member of the University and asked me
to take a seat at his side. It was my second English doctorate. Some years before I had been made Doctor of Law in
absentia at St. Andrews. --- My lecture to the Jowett Society dealt with the concept of analogy and its
philosophical significance and is printed in ``Mind'' and in my mindre Arbejder (second series). --- I insert here
a letter I wrote from Oxford to a younger philosopher in Copenhagen, Magister Herdis Krarup; it gives a summary of
my experiences in America.

% --- p. 221 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%

\opage{221}Dear Miss Krarup!


Thank you for your kind letter. It pleased me very much to hear that your doctoral dissertation seems to be well
under way. Nor have I ever doubted that it would be. Not least it pleased me to see that you are constantly at work
thinking, and that you, as hitherto, unite an interest in the experimental with an interest in the philosophical
problems. There are so many experimental psychologists with whom that is not the case. In America they have large
and good laboratories, but it does not seem that they get much out of them. Pierre Janet (whose acquaintance it
was a great pleasure to me to make in America) once said in his witty way that he was not sure that their famous
laboratories really existed! --- In America there was a frightful amount of metaphysics in the air alongside the
quite specialized experimental investigations that ignored all questions of principle. But on the whole I must
say that I received an excellent impression of the intellectual life; there was much interest among old and young,
and the metaphysical interest itself was combined with great openness and many-sided discussion. As I put it in a
lecture I gave at the women's university Wellesley College (near Boston): philosophy is in the process of becoming
at once more personal and more scientific. I tried to show the connection between these two things in the constant
need for supplementation and for new experience.

It will interest you to hear that in America I met a woman colleague, Professor Mary Calkins, professor of
philosophy at Wellesley. She read a good paper on comparative psychology at the Congress in St. Louis, and she
pressed Ostwald hard in the discussion after his (very thin!) lecture on ``Methodology''. ---

It has been a great joy to me on my journey to come together with American and English students. James, Royce and
Münsterberg gave me access to that at Harvard, and here in England I had in Cambridge an
% --- p. 222 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{222}interesting evening with a circle of young men (Moral Science Society), with whom I had a lively
discussion after my lecture on the relation between sociology and ethics. --- (In Cambridge it was also a joy to
me to spend some days in James Ward's house). --- Yesterday evening I discussed Kant's philosophy here at St. Johns
College with some young men, and this evening I am to speak at the Jowett-club on the concept of analogy. You see,
I am constantly active. Yet I now long for my Danish friends. Around 16 December I shall be in Copenhagen, and I
look forward to seeing you and our common circle again.


\begin{center}Yours devotedly\end{center}
\begin{flushright}Harald Høffding.\end{flushright}
\whiteline

My last week in England I stayed with the third of my sociological hosts, Dr. Stanton Coit. In his younger days Dr.
Coit had worked in the East End of London among the poor population there, as leader of one of the so-called
``neighbourhood guilds'', where university men seek to spread intellectual culture among the destitute, especially
by living among them and acquainting themselves with their conditions. Now he led an ``Ethical Society'' in
Kensington and worked for non-denominational morality. He was a very hard-working man and much absorbed in his
work. Through his marriage he had become very rich. His German-born wife, a gifted and charming lady, once said to
me: ``Yes, we are socialists, but we live in Hyde Park Gate and keep seven servants!'' --- One evening a large
company had been invited ``to meet Professor Høffding''. And Professor Høffding then stood together with host and
hostess at the door of the drawing room and shook hands with everyone who came. There was conversation and music,
and afterward there were buffets in the rooms upstairs. As so often on such occasions, the best part of the evening
came when the guests had gone, and ``we'' were alone and sat in cozy conversation by the fireplace.

% --- p. 223 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{223}From a letter I wrote while I was staying with Coit I quote the following.

``When I look back on my journey, I must say that it has brought me great profit and in many respects refreshed me
and given me new strength, at least a new desire to work on. But now I am, after all, becoming an old man, so I
must be diligent if I am to have accomplished what I still want to have done. --- I am afraid that I have been
spoiled on the journey, especially here in England, where I have gone from hand to hand and have been treated as an
old friend wherever I have come. Since my return from Cambridge and Oxford I have been staying with a Dr. Coit, in
whose very beautiful and elegant house near Hyde Park I have worked every morning, so as later in the day to visit
museums and in the evening either go to the theater or meet people. The greatest impression on me has been made by
the Parthenon frieze, of which large pieces are here in the original, and by Raphael's cartoons. But a modern
English painter, Watt, with his grand symbolism, has also occupied me. And then I have found good things by my dear
Dutchmen (especially Ruysdael and Hobbema).'' ---

I took the way home through Holland and stayed some ten days in The Hague and in Amsterdam in order to develop and
deepen my knowledge of Dutch painting. In The Hague I performed an inward devotion at Spinoza's statue, which stands
outside the place where he lived in his last years, those years in which we know his daily way of life so well
through the account of a worthy clergyman who later lived in the same house. Otherwise it was the museums I
frequented, and especially the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam brought me many happy hours. I spent the mornings out
there, and in the evenings I read or was at the French comedy.

In the middle of December I came home to Strandgade again after a journey rich in content and in enjoyment.

% --- p. 224 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
% print: V (misprint)
\chapter*{VI}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{VI. 1904--1914}
\markboth{VI. 1904--1914}{VI. 1904--1914}
\opage{224}Shortly before I left for America, my youngest son
had married; the eldest had already left home earlier;
and from that time on I lived alone. Solitude was not
disagreeable to me. I had enough to do, and I have always
had difficulty in breaking off my work and my train of
thought and becoming absorbed in family life and its
interests. In my hypochondriac periods this difficulty was
especially great. At such times it was mostly those closest to
me who suffered for it. With strangers one can, after all,
control oneself more easily, or the strange element is a
positive help in getting beyond one's entanglement in oneself,
the heaviness and the strange sensations of faintness. I have
often been ashamed of this. But I have also again and again
had reason to feel grateful because those closest to me have
borne with me. Now that I had become entirely alone, there
was no one for my hypochondria to fall on. It has faithfully
followed me into my old age too. --- On this I quote a passage
from a letter (from 1902) to a young friend, now dead.

``Even if I had not believed that a definite cause lay behind
your so often depressed mood, I would still have been able to
sympathize with it. For I know from my own experience how
vague, dark and foggy moods can get the better of us, and they
are often precisely the worst adversaries we can have, --- those
that take no firm shape, so that we could look them in the
eye, but which, like figures of fog, are indeed scattered for
the moment when we strike through them, but only to clump
together again.
% --- p. 225 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{225}I can have quite terrible attacks of hypochondria, to
the astonishment of those closest to me, and I by no means
have the evenness and calm that is often ascribed to me. By
contrast, I feel all the more glad when I am together with
people I am fond of and who can set me going. --- Then I have
also had worries and sorrows. No one escapes them. --- But now
I have come to talk about myself, and that was not the
intention.''
---

In an autobiography, on the other hand, it is precisely the
intention that one should talk about oneself, so that no
apology is needed when I dwell a little longer on this
subject and in particular bring forward a single experience.

In states of the kind I have mentioned here, it could be as if
no thought could arise, no hope endure, no light appear, no
work be done. Sometimes such a mood faded away of itself, just
as it had also come ``of itself''; at other times an external
event could act as a diversion; but now and then the bull had
to be taken by the horns. I will tell of a small experience
from the years I am speaking of here, which was very
instructive for me both as a philosopher and as a human being.
It was some years after the journey to America that a very
severe attack came. I did not know what to turn to; it was as
if I were dying of thirst. How it then came about that I took
out Shakespeare's King Lear, --- whether it had perhaps been
lying on the table, --- I do not know. But I stood at my desk
and read, and read. Before the passion, the sorrows and the
clashes I was reading about, the inner fog drew back, and when
I came to the mighty ending with the moving scene where the
old man stands bent over his daughter's body, while the few
faithful ones close in a circle around him, I burst into
heartfelt weeping. I had a feeling as when a storm has raged
and the light begins again to dawn through fog and rain. ---
It is not the only time that the great master's deep
% --- p. 226 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{226}humanity and great art have brought me strength and
peace. Another time it was ``Stormen'' that helped me,
especially Prospero's relation to Caliban, --- when I saw
Prospero, however violently he was torn out of his festive
visions by the thought of the dark and bestial power that was
not yet overcome, nevertheless hold fast to the clarity of his
thought and to his exalted humanity.

When one reads Shakespeare in moods like the one I have
indicated here, one benefits from his art without knowing and
understanding it. But the main thing is still what he himself
has one of his characters say, that above the art that helps
nature there stands an art that nature itself has created. It
is this deep, creative nature whose saving power one comes to
know in such experiences.

Carlyle has said: close your Byron and open your Goethe! A
Danish author wanted in his youth to turn it around: close
your Goethe, and open your Byron! I would say, finally, and
precisely when things are hard: close first your Byron, then
your Goethe, and then open your Shakespeare!

Only the human can help us beyond the human, the all too
human.

\secrule

I still lived in the big old house in Strandgade for some
years after the journey to America. The rooms were large and
comfortable, somewhat low-ceilinged, but appealingly
old-fashioned. And a splendid staircase led up to them. For
walks I had Kristianshavns Vold, and when I wanted to go
farther, Langelinie, having myself rowed across from the end
of Strandgade to Nyhavns-Hoved. But soon the apartment became
too big for me, and I wanted an apartment that would not be
too expensive for me when I retired. I then moved out to Carl
Bernhards Vej, into a small apartment where I had difficulty
finding room for my books and my large worktable, but where I
nevertheless soon felt comfortable and at home. I had more or
less
% --- p. 227 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{227}room for the gatherings I held at home now and then
with the participants in my laboratory exercises. The pleasant
Friday gatherings with Vilhelm Thomsen, Christiansen and Bohr
also went on. To Frederiksberg Have and Søndermarken I had only
a few minutes. My walks in these years, moreover, often
stretched out into the country, to Hvidovre and to Damhussøen
and its surroundings.

In political respects the change had taken place that the
victorious Left had split. I could not bring myself to join
either of the two new parties, and from that time on I have
been a political free agent. In elections I voted according to
the question most immediately at hand. In many things I could
agree with the Radical Left and with its allies, the Social
Democrats. What separated me from the Radicals was especially
their short-sighted and indefensible position on the question
of defense. In the Social Democrats' proposal, complete
disarmament, there was at least consistency, and to that
extent sense; but in the Radicals' position, or hint of a
position, there was absolutely no sense. --- But political
life on the whole took such a form that it could not awaken
any desire to occupy oneself with it. And gradually I followed
so little in this field that I often did not understand at
all what set minds in the high Rigsdag in such strong
commotion.

I had, besides, enough to do. Once in these years, in answer
to an enquête, I gave a description of my working day which
fits more or less the whole later part of my life. A morning
person I have never been. Often, especially in my youth, I
tried to begin my work early in the morning; but it never
succeeded. In my student years it was the time from 10---2 at
night that was my best time; then I had the most peace of
mind. Later, on the other hand, it was the morning hours from
10---2 that became my best working time. The day was then
naturally divided by the lectures, which in later years were
mostly held
% --- p. 228 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{228}from 3 to 4. And I could then still have 5---6 working
hours in the evening. One winter (1909---10) I worked for
several months 11 hours a day.

My written works rest on a mass of drafts and attempts, which
are constantly reworked, and even the continuous fair copy I
have often completely reworked. My Religionsfilosofi was thus
written 4 times, the program on the problems 3 times. When
reading scientific literature I like to work pen in hand; it
sharpens the attention both to what is right and to what is
wrong in the books one reads. And remarks are often born that
must be caught on the wing. I have collected large quantities
of excerpts from books on philosophy, natural science and the
history of religion; unfortunately they are of no use to
anyone but myself (and I myself cannot always read my own
handwriting).

Besides the propaedeutic course two years out of three, I
constantly held laboratory exercises and lectures for larger
circles. Some winters I also gave lectures at the
Folkeuniversitet and took much pleasure in it. There came,
moreover, new editions of my books, which gave much work in
keeping them up to date (which I have not succeeded in doing in
every detail); translations into foreign languages had to be
looked through. Some correspondence was also unavoidable. And
amid all this I was occupied with a work on knowledge and its
main tasks on the basis of the sketch I had given in my
University program of 1902. Before this sketch there were
various preparatory studies in papers I had had printed over
the years in the Skrifter of the Royal Danish Academy of
Sciences. In the winter of 1909---10 I undertook the final
editing of the planned work, which then appeared in the autumn
of 1910 under the title ``Den menneskelige Tanke, dens Former
og dens Opgaver''. (In words of foreign origin it would have
run: The Functions of Thought, Its Categories and Its
Problems). The winter months in which I put the
% --- p. 229 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{229}last touch to this book stand in my memory as a
particularly good time. I worked with zeal and without tiring,
and with a confidence by which I have unfortunately not always
been animated\footnote[1]{[On the content of this book I may refer to the essay on my work as an author, which is reprinted in ``Religiøse Tanketyper'' (pp. 29---33).]}.

I go back some years in time. --- In the summer of 1906 I
lectured at a summer course in Lund for elementary-school
teachers, men and women, from all over Sweden. It was a fresh
and delightful audience, and I was very glad of this guest
appearance, which took place under pleasant circumstances,
since I stayed with my friend Professor Axel Herlin and his
excellent wife. At a small closing celebration I spoke, after
``Der er et yndigt Land'' had been sung to applause. It was,
after all, the year after the separation of Norway and Sweden,
and there was in Sweden some ill feeling over Denmark's
attitude in that matter. I declared that Denmark's position in
this conflict was to be compared with Antigone's in the
conflict between her brothers: she could join in loving, but
not in hating! ---

That same autumn I represented the University at the 400th
anniversary of the University of Aberdeen. I had a hard
journey with much seasickness across the North Sea, and a
young Englishman who was on board felt very sorry for ``the
poor old gentleman'', who was so ill. After a good night's
sleep in London I met my friend Otto Jespersen at the station
the next morning; he too was going to Aberdeen, where he was to
represent the Academy. At the ceremony the representatives of
the various countries walked forward in alphabetical order,
led by a student as herald, while the national anthem
concerned was played. And so Jespersen and I marched forward
to the stately ``Kong Christian''. In the three minutes each
deputation had, I declared that there were two things Danish
students especially valued in Scottish thought, the broad
Common Sense and the keen sense for problems. I received on
this
% --- p. 230 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{230}occasion my third English doctorate. There were great
festivities, both official and private. And on this occasion I
also came to know pleasant English home life, since I stayed
some two miles outside the town with a colleague, Dr.
McIntyre. In the same house stayed the German philologist
Diels, whom it was a joy to me to get to know. In Aberdeen I
also met the French philosopher Boutroux, whom I was with
again some years later in Geneva, and who later again gave
guest lectures in Copenhagen. I learned to admire his gift for
brilliant characterization of philosophical types, and his
open-mindedness and personal amiability have made him dear to
me.

\secrule

Several times I have mentioned how much I love the nature of
Jutland. For a number of years I have spent my summer holidays
in Jutland. I have mentioned the holiday in 1903. But I must
also mention that I lived two summers (1898 and 99) on a farm
by Salten Langsø, some five miles south of Silkeborg, in a
glorious district with heath, lakes and woods, which truly
invited long walks. To Himmelbjerget it was no farther than
that one could walk there and back in an afternoon. From 1907
on I have for a number of summers (with the exception of 1909)
lived on a farm between Hobro and Aalborg, in a true Jutland
district with hills and stream, heather and wood. The
excellent family I stayed with as a paying guest later moved
to Moesgaard near Aarhus, and I have found the same comfortable
home there, while the nature is somewhat different, more
idyllic and more akin to that of Zealand.

\secrule

On 1 September 1908 it was twenty-five years since I had been
appointed professor, and on that occasion I was presented with
an address from men in various walks of life and from a number
of former students, in which I was at the same time asked
% --- p. 231 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{231}to sit for my portrait. Since the collection for this
purpose had produced a large surplus, they wanted to have me
painted twice, so that one picture should be given to the
University, the other after my death pass to the National
Museum at Frederiksborg. On the occasion of the day I received
various other tokens of kind thoughts. I did not myself
celebrate the day, but it did me good to notice that my work
had met with understanding. When I began my lectures the day
after, I was received with loud applause by older and younger
students.

To paint the two portraits I chose Viggo Johansen and Herman
Vedel. I confess that I cannot really recognize myself in
either of the two pictures, although each of them has surely
caught something characteristic. Of portraits of myself I
value most the bust which the sculptor Brandstrup made some
years before, and which is in the Statens Museum for Kunst.
--- But I have sufficiently experienced how difficult it is to
know one's mental self, and something similar probably holds
as regards the bodily self as well.

\secrule

That I, as mentioned above, worked particularly well in the
winter of 1909---10 was perhaps because the previous summer I
had made a longer journey which cheered and refreshed me
greatly. I had received from the University of Cambridge in
England a request to write an essay on ``Darwin og
Filosofien'' for a Festschrift to be published on the occasion
of the centenary of Charles Darwin's birth, --- and with it an
invitation to come over for the celebration and become an
honorary doctor. I had also received from Geneva an invitation
to take part in a celebration on the occasion of the
University's 350 years of existence. And finally I had been
asked to open a discussion on the psychology of religion at a
psychological congress that was to be held in Geneva a month
after the University celebration. I now combined all these
various invitations and
% --- p. 232 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{232}planned a round trip via Esbjerg to England and from
there through France to Switzerland and home through Germany.

In fine summer weather I traveled, then, together with my
zoological colleague Jungersen and his wife, two most amiable
traveling companions, over to Esbjerg and from there across
the North Sea to Harwich. This time the North Sea was
comparatively gentle; in any case the lively conversations
with the Norwegian meteorologist Mohn and his daughter kept
the swell from making me sick. In Cambridge I stayed, as five
years before, with Professor Sorley. On the very first day my
host invited me for a row on the river Cam. He himself stood
in the stern and sculled us forward with his oar; we others,
gentlemen and ladies, sat on comfortable cushions, and so we
glided down the river through the splendid grounds belonging to
the various colleges. On the banks young people could be seen
lying about in conversation or reading. We met other boats with
students or with the University's guests. In the brilliant
sunshine it was a glorious trip, which has left a vivid picture
in my memory. On one of the following days the solemn conferring
of doctorates took place. We were 21 who were created at this
Darwin commemoration. One by one we stepped forward before the
Chancellor, Lord John Rayleigh, who sat in his chair clad in
the magnificent chancellor's robe. At his side stood the Public
Orator and read out a characterization in Latin of each of us.
I was much moved and glad at mine, since in it I could
recognize the understanding and kind view of English friends.
After this reading I gave the Chancellor my hand, and he
admitted me to the number of doctors with a Latin formula in
the name of the Trinity. It was a collision between old and
new to hear this formula pronounced at a ceremony in Darwin's
honor. Otherwise the occasion of the day was celebrated by a
speech by Balfour and, on behalf of the foreigners, by
Arrhenius, and also in the following days by garden parties in
various colleges. A special joy was the time spent with the
good and warm-hearted Sorleys.
% --- p. 233 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{233}Their happy home was not yet darkened by the sorrow
that six years later was to be caused by the fall of their
eldest, gifted son.

From Cambridge I went to London, where I first stayed for a
day or so with a young Danish friend, the engineer Thomsen,
and his wife. Both had often visited me in Copenhagen as quite
young people, and I had followed them on their way with
interest. Then I stayed some days with Lady Welby, who had grown
old but still pursued her studies with zeal, and then with
Gooch, who had now become a member of Parliament. Through him I
obtained admission to a sitting of Parliament, and although
nothing of greater importance took place, I still got an idea
of the proceedings in the world's first and most famous
parliament, and it was with historical reverence that I looked
out over the chamber from my box. Some days later the journey
went on to France. I had a glorious crossing from Dover to
Calais. The white cliffs of Dover shone in the sunshine, and
the blue sea sparkled. For an ardent reader of Shakespeare
poetic memories were awakened here. And some lines of
Wergeland's ``engelske Lods'', which Professor Mohn had
enthusiastically reminded me of as we approached the English
coast, came to my mind again:

\begin{quote}
``Det, som skinner vester hist\\
mellem Sky og Havsens Vover,\\
Det er England, solbelyst,\\
Klipperne ved Dover.\\
Shakespeare cliffens hvide Hvælv\\
vesterud er Marmorfoden,\\
hvorfra Sejrens Dronning selv\\
stolt behersker Kloden.''
\end{quote}

The deck was full of travelers from every possible country,
who were now making the crossing between the two countries to
which world culture owes so much. To my bodily well-being there
contributed, besides the sunshine and the life around me, the
excellent lunch Mrs. Gooch had provided me with.

% --- p. 234 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{234}In Paris I stayed four days. A joy of recognition rested
over them; it was forty years since I had been there. The
bright, beautiful summer days now were very different from the
wintertime in which my stay had fallen the previous time, and
cast a new light over the familiar places. And how much had not
changed in Paris; the previous time it was under the Empire.
And how much had not changed in and for me? --- But I enjoyed
life in those days, drove around in a cab to look about, was in
museums in the mornings and at the theater in the evenings. I
visited Professor
% print: Brunschwicg (misprint)
Léon Brunschvicg and his wife, who some years before had been
in Copenhagen and been my guests. To the well-known, much
disputed philosopher Henri Bergson I paid a long visit and had
an interesting conversation with him. I admired the subtlety
and open-mindedness of his thinking. He knew that on various
points I took a critical stance toward his philosophy, and we
came at once to the decisive questions. He gave a nervous
impression, but above all the impression of a man who lives in
his work of thought without any other consideration than how
the thoughts can rightly unfold and find their clearest
expression. It is quite unjust to think one can dispose of him
by shouting fashionable philosopher after him or by making
jokes about the vitalism he shares with a number of biologists.
--- Some years later I published a little book on his
philosophy, which was translated into English, and when Bergson
had read it, he wrote me a longish letter in which he
acknowledged the chivalry of my criticism and made a number of
counter-remarks. It pleased me to see that he too kept a good
memory of our conversation. When the book was translated into
French, the letter was included as an appendix.

In Geneva I took part in the University celebration and
received here a new doctorate (the sixth!); this time it was
Docteur ès lettres, motivated by my book on Rousseau, on the
recommendation of the Société Jean Jacques Rousseau. It pleased
me to meet the philosopher Boutroux here again, this time
% --- p. 235 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{235}accompanied by his lively and gifted wife, a sister of
the mathematician and philosopher Poincaré and a cousin of the
President of the French Republic. Some years later I had the
pleasure of seeing them both in Copenhagen, where he gave two
brilliant lectures at the University, and where I also had
them as guests at my home. --- On my last day in Geneva this
time I was together with the Boutroux at the home of the
literary historian Bouvier, chairman of the Société Jean
Jacques Rousseau. Here I also met the well-known historian
Gabriel Monod, a brother-in-law of Bouvier, an exceedingly
attractive man, refined and gentle in his manner and his
judgment. He pleased me by telling me that in his lectures on
the history of culture he had made good use of my book on the
history of modern philosophy. --- The Monod family, to which he
and Bouvier belonged, had connections with Denmark, since the
grandfather of these two had been a French Reformed pastor in
Copenhagen. And so here too I was given a Danish national dish,
namely rødgrød, but in a very refined form, as a jelly with
cream; it did, however, come from Copenhagen.

That same evening I sailed from Geneva across the Lake of
Geneva to Montreux. The weather was rainy, and I kept to the
cabin, where I met a Dr. Forel, brother of the well-known
psychiatrist. When the next morning I opened my balcony door
at the Hotel Suisse in Montreux, the glorious blue Lake of
Geneva lay before me. I now had some paradisal days, which were
spent on walks partly northward to Clarens, known from
Rousseau's ``Nouvelle Héloïse'', partly southward past Chillon,
known from Byron's poem on the prisoner of Chillon. Later I
moved up the mountain, to Glion, whose pure, strong air did me
good. I here made the acquaintance of an elderly English lady,
Mrs. Rufford, a clergyman's widow, with whom it was very
pleasant to talk and discuss. She was free and open in her
views. Her husband had belonged to the critical school in
theology, and she was in high degree free of prejudice. We
corresponded for several years afterward.

From Glion I went via Aigle up to Ormont dessus, in
% --- p. 236 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{236}the vicinity of the Diablerets glacier, where an
American colleague, Professor Leuba, had booked a room for me.
I spent a week or so here and was often together with Leuba
and his family. Then I went down again via Aigle to Martigny,
where I spent the night, so as to make the next day the
magnificent trip by mountain railway from Martigny to
Chamounix. It is one of the most glorious things I have
experienced. The line runs right along the edge of a mountain,
and one looks down into deep valleys and across to mountain
heights on the other side. There was great enthusiasm among the
travelers too. A French father, who was making the trip with
wife and children, cried out time after time: ``Oh, ça vaut
bien l’argent! Ça vaut bien l’argent!'' I liked this
exclamation better than the Germans' ``Famos! Furchtbar
schön!''

In Chamounix I met my friend the chemist Karl Meyer with his
wife and daughters, and we had a pleasant time with one
another, all the while that in this great nature, with Mont
Blanc right before us, we received unforgettable impressions.
After the Meyer family had left, I put the last touch to the
lecture I was to give at the psychological congress in Geneva.
And on solitary walks I experienced something of what Kant has
said, that the great in nature as it were bends us back into
ourselves to find an inner greatness as a counterpart to the
outer. Alas, it was not pure greatness I could find. There was
so much that was petty that came out at the same time. But it
went through a purgatory, and as the conclusion of the whole
movement in my mind there arose the confidence that there was
after all a striving to be worthy to behold so mighty a
nature, --- a striving for kinship, however distant, with what
is great in the world of the spirit. ---

In Geneva I came to stay with the psychologist Th. Flournoy,
who had long since sent me a very kind invitation. He met me
at the railway station, and I now spent a good full week in
his beautiful and comfortable home in the suburb of
Florissant. His wife was a stately
% --- p. 237 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{237}and gracious lady, independent in her way of thinking
and in her way of taking life, like her husband a descendant of
the old strict Calvinists who founded Geneva's freedom and
culture. Of orthodox Calvinism there was certainly not much
left, but as a heritage there prevailed a consistency of
thought that cuts through the half-measures characteristic of
Lutheran theology. Théodore Flournoy himself is an excellent
psychologist of the experimental school. He has written on
visions of colors and figures, but has occupied himself quite
especially with somnambulistic phenomena, which he has treated
from a scientific point of view in several books and papers.
Alongside that and in connection with it he has a keen sense
for the involuntary movements of mental life. His religious
standpoint is akin to that of James, whose friend he was.

The days were spent with lectures and discussions. I had
planned my opening lecture so that with the help of the
history of religion I would find out what I called the
psychological place of religion, that is, which region of
mental life religion most nearly belonged to. In a similar
direction went the lecture of the other opener, Leuba, though
with a decidedly polemical tendency. In the discussion several
theologians spoke, not exactly with great clarity. As not
seldom, the Catholic theologians here too were sharper and more
consistent than the Protestant ones, and I remember with
pleasure a discussion I had with Abbé Pacheu from Paris, author
of several works on religious mysticism. At the closing banquet
he gave a speech in which he said that he too was ``un
chercheur comme Monsieur Høffding''. Several years later I
received greetings from him through Danish travelers who had
met him. It was a shortcoming of both opening lectures that no
account was taken of the pathological phenomena that so often
accompany religious states of mind. In the discussion the
psychopathologists could not get a word in at all for the many
theologians.

% --- p. 238 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{238}An interesting debate was provoked by the
German-American physiologist Jacques Loeb's lecture on
``Tropisms'' (roughly the same as reflex movements). Loeb
maintained with great sharpness the necessity of seeking purely
mechanical explanations of all animal and human movements, in
contrast to the current spiritualistic explanations. From my
Spinozist standpoint I could support him in the debate from the
philosophical side. --- I had already met him in America, but
now became better acquainted with him in Geneva. When Flournoy
one day suggested that I invite some of the participants in the
congress to lunch at his house, I chose Loeb and the American
psychiatrist Morton Prince, whom I had likewise met in America.
On one of the last days of the congress Morton Prince presented
to a quite small circle a female patient whom he had cured of
double consciousness. After hypnotizing her, Morton Prince
could by suggestion call forth her earlier states again, and
one thereby gained an interesting insight into the course of
the illness and of the cure. It is the lady who in the
psychopathological literature is known under the name B. C. A.
(A was a very depressed state; it was relieved now and then by
B, a very frivolous state; but there appeared now and then,
especially under hypnosis, a more harmonious state, C, which
Morton Prince cultivated in pure form through constant
suggestions). She was a very intelligent lady, who declared
that out of gratitude to Prince, and so that others might
benefit from her case, she gladly submitted to hypnosis again.

Best of all in this whole stay in Geneva, though, were the
summer evenings out in Florissant with my dear host and his
family. I felt quite at home with them. I had the same good
fortune here as I had had at Harvard, in London, in Cambridge,
in Oxford and in Aberdeen. To judge from these experiences,
philosophers must be well suited to founding good homes. Yet I
am inclined to give the wives the
% --- p. 239 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{239}main credit, so that the philosophers' merit becomes
that of winning good wives. Madame Flournoy was indeed a
mistress of the house without equal, both by her spiritual
superiority and by her at once energetic and gentle management
of everything in the house.

A Swedish friend and colleague, Sidney Alrutz from Upsala, was
also staying with the Flournoys. We meant to leave immediately
after the close of the congress, but were asked in the kindest
way whether we would not stay over the next day, which was a
Sunday. It was a very hot day, which we spent in the garden in
all sorts of good conversation. The next day we left, each in
his own direction. I had no idea that the excellent woman I
had come to know was soon to go on the journey from which one
does not return. A couple of weeks after my return home to
Copenhagen I received a letter from Flournoy in which he told
me that his wife, during a stay in the mountains, had caught
pneumonia and had died after a short illness. Later he
published in her memory a biographical sketch, which contained
some of her poems and gave a characterization of her religious
standpoint. She was a deeply religious nature and held
essentially to Christianity; but she was to such a degree
convinced that God could not be the cause of evil that she
could not believe that he had created the world. God works
constantly to alleviate and prevent the evils that the laws of
matter bring with them. But if he were really present in the
world, he would have to be victor everywhere! It was her own
experiences and her own reflection that had brought her to this
stage, which she embraced with great seriousness, without its
preventing gentleness and a bright mind from prevailing in her
conduct. In his little book Flournoy quotes some sentences from
a letter of mine, which I had written immediately after the
news of her death; I said in it that there were few people
toward whom I felt such a desire and need to open myself and
communicate myself as toward her. --- I have not lost all
connection with the family in Florissant in
% --- p. 240 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{240}later years. They have always sent me news of the more
important family events. We also have, after all, one beautiful
memory in common. ---

From Geneva I traveled through Savoy to Grenoble. On the way I
stopped at Aix-les-Bains, where five years before my young
friend Harald Munch-Petersen had lost his life. His body had
been found half a year later and buried in the town's
cemetery, on ground given by the municipality. Danish friends
