had had a monument designed by Bindesbøll and Jerndorff erected
on the grave, which I now wished to visit. It was painful to
stand there at the grave of broken hopes. I had the grave put
in order and arranged with the gravedigger how it was to be
kept up. Then I traveled to Chambéry, the residence of the old
dukes of Savoy, which interested me most, however, because Jean
Jacques Rousseau had lived there for several years. I drove out
to Les Charmettes, a country house outside the town, where he
spent the time that in his ``Bekendelser'' stood before him as
an idyll, and where he pursued the studies that made his gospel
of nature more than a mere matter of feeling. In Grenoble I met
a number of Danish students who had made a journey through
Germany and Switzerland, and who were staying there to take
part in the vacation courses the University of Grenoble holds
every year for foreigners. How diligently they studied I shall
leave unsaid; but they enjoyed themselves splendidly, and I
enjoyed myself well with them for a couple of days. We made an
interesting trip up to the Chartreuse, where the empty
monastery buildings stood as memorials of the violent struggle
between state and church that had recently raged.

Via Lausanne and Frankfurt I traveled home to Copenhagen, and
in the first while felt very tired from the journey and the
irregular way of life. My eldest brother invited me to stay
some weeks with him at his country house near Frederiksdal, and
I recovered so well there that I could begin my work after the
vacation with fresh strength.

% --- p. 241 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{241}It was in the following winter (1909---10) that I put
the last touch to the above-mentioned rounding-off (not
concluding) account of my studies of human thought and its
relation to existence and its riddles. That I could now publish
this account (``Den menneskelige Tanke'' 1910) was naturally a
major event for me. I thought that I could speak of ``langer
Jahre redlich Streben'' and moreover add: ``Nun, man kommt doch
eine Strecke!'' --- Yes, but how long this stretch is, I
naturally can myself have no opinion about.

\secrule

The following three years (1910---12) take their character for
me partly from interesting lecture journeys to Sweden, Finland
and Norway, partly from deaths in my nearest circle. Light and
darkness contend sharply in my memory of these years.

In the summer of 1910 I gave a series of lectures on social
ethics at the summer course in Stockholm. As in Lund in 1906, I
had here a good audience of teachers, men and women, and I felt
quite at home among them. And here too I delighted in the
full-toned Swedish singing. None of the Nordic peoples sings its
national anthem as powerfully and proudly as the Swedes. Prince
Eugen of Sweden was president of the course, and I was glad to
meet him here again, after I had made his acquaintance some
years before in Copenhagen at the home of his friend the
painter Viggo Johansen. Together with several of the speakers
at the course I spent a beautiful summer evening at his villa
by the ``inloppet''. --- The stay in Stockholm was very pleasant
for me, since I stayed with my friends
% print: Scheéle (misprint)
Frants and Hanna v. Schéele. After the close of the lectures I
spent some time with them at their beautiful summer residence
in Sødermanland.

The next year (1911) I accepted an invitation to give
% --- p. 242 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{242}lectures in Helsingfors. At the end of March I went
via Stockholm to Finland. I lectured every day for a week on
``Personlighedsprincipet i Filosofien''. On request the lectures
were later printed both in Finnish and in Swedish. The
expression ``principle of personality'' I had often used before
without knowing that it was Erik Gustaf Geijer who first used it
(1838) to designate the right the individual has to initiative
as well as to independent appropriation. It signifies a
reaction against Romanticism and the ``historical school'', a
luminous reaction, which within Danish intellectual life came
some years later through Sibbern and Kierkegaard. My lectures
aimed to show the psychological possibility and the ethical
justification of this principle, its significance for the
philosophy of religion, and for the right understanding of the
relation between science and life. The little book
(Personlighetsprincipen i Filosofin, Stockholm 1910) I
deliberately did not let appear in Danish, because I think that
Swedish and Danish should not be regarded as two entirely
different literatures. I have a certain fondness for the little
book, because in it I have tried in concentrated form to shed
light on a subject that I have come upon here and there in my
various writings in more special contexts. --- One evening I
also gave a lecture in which I drew a comparison between
Kierkegaard and Nietzsche, two thinkers who could illuminate
each other both by their mutual contrast and by various points
of likeness. The lecture was printed in ``Svensk Tidsskrift''
and later in Danish (in ``Mindre Arbejder''. Third Series).

During the stay in Helsingfors I enjoyed great kindness and
hospitality from the Rector, the philologist Heikel, and other
colleagues. After the close of the lectures I went to
Petrograd, where I stayed some days with my brother, the
engineer Theodor Høffding. It was a joy to me to live these
days with him and his wife and to renew acquaintance with his
sons, as well as to make the acquaintance of
% --- p. 243 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{243}his Russian daughters-in-law. (The youngest son and his
wife I did not meet, however, as they did not live in
Petrograd). --- On the journey home I stopped some days in Åbo,
where I lectured in the Pedagogical Society. Here too I had an
excellent and attentive audience and met interesting people.
When on a Sunday afternoon I was to sail from Åbo to Stockholm,
and so say farewell to Finland, a number of my listeners had
gathered on the shore, and as the ship put out, they sang
``Suomi's Sang''. It was a moving farewell from a country for
which I had already beforehand come to feel love, for its
nature, for its poetry and for its tragic fate. --- The voyage
through the sounds of the Åland Islands was very beautiful.
There was still ice between the islands, and only a narrow
channel had been made for the steamer. The sun shone on the
white ice and on the green spruce forests on the islands. In
several places people were going from one island to another,
and often, as soon as the steamer had passed, a rolling bridge
was run out to get across the shipping channel. It was a
peculiar winter picture. ---

In the spring of 1912 I was invited to lecture in Kristiania. I
stayed there two weeks. In the first week I lectured every
other day to a larger circle (1100 listeners) in the
University's great festival hall on ``aandelig Kultur''. (The
lecture is printed in Mindre Arbejder. Third Series). In the
second week I gave three lectures on questions in the theory of
knowledge. In addition I spoke in the Students' Society and in
the Philological Society. It was a joy to me to become better
acquainted with Norwegian colleagues. After the close of the
lectures I spent some days up at Voxenkollen, where deep snow
still lay, which in the brilliant sunshine and under the blue
sky made a splendid sight. ---

When I think of the three years 1910---12, it is --- when the
bright memories prevail --- especially the visits to Stockholm,
Helsingfors and Kristiania that come to mind. It was a
% --- p. 244 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{244}joy to me, now, as earlier in Upsala and in Lund, to
take part in working for a community of intellectual life in
the Nordic countries.

\secrule

But these three years have also left memories of a sad kind.
Through deaths in my nearest circle I began to learn that to
live long is to outlive many with whom one would gladly have
gone on living.

My brother Otto Høffding, who lived at Strandegaard on Præstø
Bugt, was an able and highly respected farmer. In his later
years he held the post of chairman of the United Agricultural
Societies of Zealand. In his tenant farm his family felt at
home. This was due not only to the many memories that through
three generations were now attached to the idyllic place, but
also to his and his wife's hospitality and their clear and
sound view of life. Since for several years I had lived in the
summer near Strandegaard, namely at Vemmetofte Strand and at
Strandegaard Dyrehave, I had had the opportunity to grow close
to them.

My brother was a handsome and stately man. Not without reason
was he called, in the funeral address given by one of his
friends, a noble nature. He did not easily open up his
innermost self. And yet he was a gentle and loving man, easily
moved to tears. He was much loved in his district by high and
low. It therefore caused much grief when in the spring of 1910
he suddenly collapsed. After a walk across his fields he was
seized with violent pains and had to be taken, sedated with
morphine, by automobile to Copenhagen, where some days later he
was operated on. It then turned out, as the doctors had
probably suspected beforehand, that a cancer had burst the
intestine. A few days later he died. It was sad down at his
farm to hear the church bell calling to his funeral on the
quiet spring day. The gentle chime that so many times in my
% --- p. 245 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{245}childhood and later had been part of the idyll down
there now brought the last farewell to one of those closest to
me.

A couple of months later my eldest brother, the wholesale
merchant Victor Høffding, died. He had continued with great
ability and in honorable fashion the business founded by our
father (chiefly in seeds and iron) and was highly respected in
the commercial world. After the death of his wife, Elisabeth
Høffding, some years before, he had wasted away. She had been
very ill for several years, and in his care for her he had
neglected an abdominal complaint, which now spread more and
more. In these years of his infirmity he had a touching need to
have his brothers and sisters around him. My sister and I often
had to be with him at his comfortable country house near
Frederiksdal. He liked best to talk of old days and dwelt on
the memories we had in common. After great suffering he died in
June 1910. I lost in him a friend who followed me on my course
with brotherly interest. I often looked in on him at his office
(the corner of Gammel Torv and Nørregade) when I walked to the
University. --- His children, of whom the son has continued the
family's fine tradition in the commercial world, show on every
occasion their affection for the old uncle, who is now the
eldest of the family, and of whom they know that he was their
father's friend.

The only brother I still have left lives in Petrograd, where
--- as mentioned earlier --- I have visited him twice, just as
he in the autumn of 1915 stayed for a month or so with me at
Carlsberg. Besides him, of my brothers and sisters I have only
my sister left. In her gentle nature, which has stood its test
through hard times, I find again the best that could be
inherited from our mother. She and I are now alone with the
old memories from home. She takes part with heartfelt sympathy
in everything that concerns me. And gentle as her mind is, she
still has her clear and definite view of life, won through
experience and independent reflection. --- I cannot at all
imagine that she should go before me. ---

\secrule

% --- p. 246 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{246}The year after (shortly before my journey to Finland) I received one
morning in the spring word by telephone of the death of my friend
Christian Bohr. He had died suddenly the night before. It was not long
since he had taken part in one of the pleasant Friday gatherings I have
mentioned before, where his life and wit contributed so essentially to
what the evenings yielded. He had, to be sure, recently suffered a
disappointment, in that one of his works proved not to lead to the result
he had expected. But the main thing was that his somewhat heavy
constitution could not endure the strenuous work he lived in. He had come
home from the laboratory at about ten in the evening, apparently well and
cheerful; but then he had a heart attack, which after a couple of hours
ended in death. It was a great sorrow for those closest to him and for his
friends, and a great loss for Danish science. For my own part I owe him
much, and I felt it a joy and an honor to stand close to him. At the wish
of his family I gave an address at his funeral in the Crematorium, and I
set down here some portions of the characterization of my departed friend
that I attempted on that occasion.

``This man was torn away in his full strength. The news struck with
violent and overwhelming force. A happy death it was, to be sure; he came
straight from his work and lay down on the deathbed of a few hours. To fall
asleep thus after the day's work is a manner of death that many wish for
themselves. But here, after all, the poet's words do not fit: `He fell
asleep, as the sun goes down at harvest-time.' For it was not harvest-time,
not yet autumn for him. He did not yet belong among the veterans. He stood
in the rich summer of his searching genius and his energy for work, in the
first rank among Denmark's men of science, and still had fruitful years of
work in prospect.

If it has fallen to my lot to speak here, it is not because I was one of
his colleagues in his field. But I have followed him through a long series
of years with instruction and admiration. It was a helping hand he gave me,
when my work had to
% --- p. 247 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{247}seek help from his field, that first brought us into closer
connection, and later I have been able to follow his work through the years
in the Royal Danish Academy of Sciences. It was a festive evening when he
took the floor, absorbed by the new things he had found, by the
difficulties he had overcome, and by the new problems that arose before
him. And his investigations moved, over that long series of years, along
one single definite line. It was his task, in one of the most central
domains of organic life, to trace the boundary between life, and the laws
of inorganic nature, --- to see whether there was a fixed boundary, and
where in that case it lay. And for this the physiology of respiration was
quite especially suited. Bohr stands as an independent collaborator in the
great period in the history of physiology that was founded by Johannes
Müller and his disciples in Germany and by Claude Bernard in France, and
whose program was to follow the working of the general forces of nature as
far into the processes of organic life as possible. Bohr found a
provisional limit to their working in the fact that respiration was not
wholly determined by the influence of external conditions. The riddle
proved to lie further back than the contending parties had supposed. There
was a time when Bohr complained that his position was often misunderstood,
as if he wished to return to so-called vitalism. But his meaning was only
that a new line of investigation had to be undertaken, chiefly of the
influence of the nervous system on the processes in the cells of the lungs.
His position here was characteristic of his character as an investigator,
and he expressed it clearly and aptly in his last University program. His
mastery of thought shows itself in the critical holding fast to the reach
of the problems, with reference to the great horizons that open up behind
each single line of investigation for the true investigator, --- but at the
same time in the firm conviction that there is only one way by which
progress into the new regions can be achieved, steady, faithful work in the
spirit of strict
% --- p. 248 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{248}science. His work could have had as its motto Lotze's words:
enthusiastic only for the great, but faithful in the small! He stood for us
all as an instructive example, not only through the results his research
brought, but above all through his whole scientific bearing.

He has done his country honor. If our flag cannot wave victorious in the
strife of the world powers, it can wave proudly over many a deed of the
spirit, many an exploit of thought, and it is lowered at this bier! ---

For those who had the joy of standing close to him outside collegial
intercourse as well, his personality presented basic features similar to
those that distinguished him as an investigator. His free and energetic
mind often played with paradoxes, and he let his wit have its play; his
friends could often feel as if they were in a purgatory before his
criticism; but behind it there always lay respect for serious work and a
great faithfulness in friendship. He was not one of those who easily let
feeling run away with them, and who gave or expected declarations of
friendship, but all the more did his hearty glance and his firm handshake
tell. Nor was he one of those who talked much about his view of life and
its fortunes. In the background, however, there stood for him an outlook
that could recall Goethe's great, at once naturalistic and ideal view of
life, in which the small and the bitter things faded away against a great
horizon. Few knew their Goethe as he did. He perhaps most often quoted
Mephistopheles' speeches; but behind them lay a striving like Faust's, only
he did not, like Faust, give up the work with retorts, lever and screw
(Hebeln und Schrauben); it was not by going around the place of scientific
work that the way to truth lay for him. ---

Now we shall no longer see his bright gaze and clear, spirited brow, which
gave his whole powerful figure its stamp, or listen to his instructive
exposition or to his wit and his sharp criticism!

He leaves a great void in science at home and
% --- p. 249 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{249}abroad, and in the circle of friends and colleagues. But we, to
whom he was so much, now turn nonetheless to the one and to those to whom
he was most. In his beautiful home he was the soul through his life and his
interests, and those for whom he opened it will understand how great the
void there must be. He found understanding and love there. In this as in
other things he was a happy man. Not least was his joy in the young, able
talents that he saw unfolding in scientific works, precisely in such
domains as had special interest for him. There had, after all, been every
reason to believe that he would have a fine evening of work together with
his aspiring sons, and warmed by all the love that surrounded him in his
home. It was not to be so.

But from the thought of the suddenness of the loss and of all that the loss
contains, we turn back again to the remembered image of his personality and
of his figure as an investigator.


Honor and peace be with the memory of Christian Bohr!'' ---

A year or so later I stood again in the Crematorium to speak at a friend's
coffin. Julius Petersen had been ailing for a number of years, and, odd as
he was, and skeptical toward his own science, or at any rate toward his own
profession, he would not let himself be examined by any physician. He
literally withered away, often in great suffering. But again and again his
warm heart could stir and his soulful eyes bear witness that the old
friendship still lived in him. Of his death I give an account in the
address I gave at his funeral, in which I also attempted a characterization
of him. I set down this address here, roughly as it was delivered.

``So our old, dear friend has found rest after the long time of pain. And
he had a beautiful death. Toward the morning hours on the day that was to
be the day of his death, a greater and greater restlessness came over him,
which was first stilled when his faithful nurse asked whether he
% --- p. 250 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{250}wanted to get up. He nodded eagerly; speak he could not. He was
then carried over to the window and saw the sun shining on the water, a
sight he had always been very fond of. His youngest son supported him. The
nurse now asked whether she should sing a lullaby he had always been very
fond of, and to this he answered eagerly Yes, Yes! So there was singing for
the old man, as there was singing for him in his childhood, and when the
song was over, he was dead.

As in the hour of his death, so during his whole illness there was a
wondrous spiritual clarity about him, together with the advancing
decrepitude. A struggle went on between his need for thought and speech and
the darkness that the illness, as well as the melancholy which was his
companion through life, kept spreading anew over his mind.

And this struggle between light, vigorous work and zest for action on the
one side, melancholy, bitterness and passive sinking down on the other
side, runs through his whole life, right from the young years. He was a man
of strife, and a brave man. It was within him that the strife took place.
When we met as comrades in the last years at school, more than half a
hundred years ago, it was the oscillation between light and darkness in his
mind, between zeal and languor in his activity, that first gave me an
understanding of him. One had to hold fast to the fact that both belonged
to his nature, and those who became his friends learned to bear with him in
the heavy and dark hours, in contrast to which the real and hearty sympathy
and the clear, lively thought worked all the more strongly in the good
times. The way in which he then came to meet us with his warm glance, his
friendly handshake, made his friends, like himself, forget the hours when
the `mjeltsjukans svartalf' that Tegnér has depicted held sway. There was a
fire within him that often threatened to consume himself, but that could
give light and warmth when the dark mists did not prevent it from becoming
a pure and clear flame.

His work came in fits and starts. It could not be otherwise
% --- p. 251 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{251}under his changing life of moods. At school he was periodically
considered lazy, because for long stretches he neglected everything. But he
could then, in a short time, by violent concentration and intense
diligence, work his way up to a place among the first. Our old Rector had
great goodwill and also a certain understanding of him; but he nonetheless
felt toward him like the hen toward the swimming ducklings it has hatched.
And his friends often fared the same way.

He finished his University studies with feverish haste and soon after began
to practice out in the poor quarters of Nørrebro, and he quickly acquired a
large practice. His warm feeling for the needy and the suffering animated
his activity, but often made it hard and painful for himself. The want and
suffering he saw so much of increased the low spirits that so easily
mastered him, and his modest home often seemed to him too luxurious when he
returned to it from the wretched rooms in which so many of his patients
lived. In other circles too than those of the poor he won a large practice,
which returned to him when, after some years' absence as a country doctor,
he came back to Nørrebro.

As a physician he worked above all through his warmth of heart and
sympathy, through the immediate beneficial impression of his personality,
through the mysterious influence that is not the least essential part of
the effect the physician produces at the sickbed. Everyone whose physician
he has been will have experienced how calming it was merely when he came
and sat down. Not everyone discovered that behind this calming presence the
strongest inner discord was often stirring in himself.

Something tragic came into his whole position through his slight faith in
medicine as a science. He himself had no faith in the remedies he used, and
which most of his patients would not do without. What had his heart was
medicine as an art, Hippocratism
% --- p. 252 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{252}with its great respect for the organism's self-help, which
required the physician's activity only to keep hindrances away, to relieve
and strengthen, to individualize, to treat each case and each single
patient in its own particular way. It is a great ideal for the
practitioners of the healing art that he draws at the end of his book on
the historical development of the medical art of healing. It seemed to him
that many of the practitioners of the more recent medical science did not
have sufficient understanding of this ideal, and it aroused in him an
antipathy to the new tendencies that became more pronounced with the years.
He himself belonged to a period of transition, in which the old art of
healing was more and more replaced by a technique built on medical science,
and what is tragic in such a period of transition worked strongly in his
inmost being and increased the bitterness that the mjeltsjukans svartalf
had beforehand so often instilled in his mind.

It was the history of the healing art that he treated in his work as an
author and as University teacher of the history of medicine. His
considerable literary talent and the eloquence he commanded in his inspired
moments made it possible for him to give brilliant and sympathetic
portrayals of the heroes of the healing art. Here both his interest in and
his sense for personalities and his skeptical attitude toward modern
theories and methods found expression.


Those were his happiest years, in which his literary work really flourished
and won recognition. It was also a great help to his soul to be able to
immerse himself in research and exposition. Then he could more easily
overcome the darkness of despondency and subdue the inner unrest. His
strength found an outlet in production instead of being wasted in
hypochondria and melancholy.

The one who of all understood him best, his wife, saw this clearly. As his
and her old friend I must here express my great admiration for this
faithful and wise woman, who in her own nature also had her own share to
struggle
% --- p. 253 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{253}with, but who was wholly absorbed in him and his doings and had
a clear eye for the core of his nature and great faith in it. She held fast
to the center about which the strong oscillations took place, always sure
that the pendulum would swing back into the old path, and patiently waiting
for it. She saw clearly that salvation for him lay in work, and never grew
tired, despite all his resistance, of keeping him at it. After her death he
began to decline. The long dreadful illness by which she wasted away, the
great emptiness the loss caused, and the loss of a young son, on whom he,
like the rest of us, set great hopes, wore on his vital strength, and to
this was then added the long illness that has now led to his passing. But
even now his lively spirit and his warm heart broke forth again and again
through the shadows that illness and melancholy caused.

As a relief it is now felt by us all that his sufferings are ended. But
then there comes also the wistful thought of what we have lost in him. Not
only his children and nearest kin, his friends too feel that here a life
has closed which, in its personal singularity, its depth, its faithful
endurance in life's inner and outer struggles, must fill a great place in
the minds of all who had attached themselves to him and gained an insight
into what moved within him. I personally am not among those who have least
to be thankful for, and I must be allowed here to thank the friend of my
youth, on whose faithful heart I could always rely, and who, tossed about
in many ways in the course of life, always preserved the sacred fire within
him, the sacred fire of ideal striving, of understanding and of compassion.

And so we all say farewell to our friend. Weary of days as he was, he might
well have deserved a gentler evening than the one the wasting and
tormenting illness permitted. But a beautiful death was granted him; he
went away, after all, greeting the rising spring sun. What moved within him
in the last moments no one can say. But
% --- p. 254 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{254}I am hardly mistaken, judging by everything, when I believe that
it was something like what the poet has expressed in the line: `Yet the
spring of life wells up, as ever it welled!'

Honor and peace be with the memory of Julius Jacob Petersen!''

\secrule

In March 1913 my seventieth birthday was approaching. I was thinking a
little of being away from town that day. I felt I had had jubilees enough.
I had made a whole plan for a solitary excursion to North Zealand, from
which I would return home in the evening to drink tea with my son and
daughter-in-law in Hellerup. Inquiries were made privately whether I would
accept an invitation to a festive dinner; but it was warded off. But then I
was surprised and much moved by an invitation from the three children of my
eldest brother, the wholesale merchant Aage Høffding and his sisters Mrs.
Schierbeck and Mrs. Dyrhauge. They wished to gather family, friends and
colleagues in my nephew's beautiful home in Nørre Farimagsgade. I gladly
accepted this invitation, and we drew up a list of about 40 participants
for this family celebration. Besides some Danish colleagues who were close
to me, my Swedish friend Professor Axel Herlin and his wife were also
invited, and at the last moment my German friend Professor Ferdinand
Tönnies came as well. And to this was added one more thing that made the day
a radiant event for me. The Students' Council had obtained permission from
the Rector of the University and from the Director of Police to greet me
with a torchlight procession, and had then arranged with my nephew that the
procession should go to his home, which lay not far from the University.

And so the day dawned that was in so many ways to bring me joy through the
overflowing kindness that met me from so many sides. In the morning, having
been summoned, I was in audience with the King, who with a few kind words
presented me with the Commander's Cross
% --- p. 255 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{255}of the First Class. On several occasions it has been a joy and an
honor for me to learn that King Christian X followed my activity at and
outside the University. Later in the day flowers, congratulations and
deputations streamed in, and I had just time for a short rest before I was
to drive to my brother's children's celebration for their old uncle.
Speeches and songs (among them a fine cantata by Niels Møller) alternated
right up to nine o'clock, when the torchlight procession was to come, and I
stepped out on the balcony facing Ørstedsparken. It was a splendid sight
when the torchlight procession appeared on the other side of the park and
moved around it up Nørre Farimagsgade, which was black with people. I was
much moved to see this mass of people, which stood quite still and waited.
I may say that what stirred in me was indeed joy and pride at being the
object of all this homage, but that the thought nonetheless stirred in me
especially that it was as one of the teachers of our old University that it
was accorded me, so that it could bear witness to the good relation that
prevails between teachers and students when both parties are absorbed in
serious striving. Now the long procession came up in front of the house,
and after the singing of a fine song the student Skat Hoffmeyer stepped up
onto a platform and gave a speech in which he dwelt on my work and my
relation to the students, especially to the individuals who had confided in
me. The essential content of my reply was that for me these torches cast
light back on the happy years in which I had worked at the University and
had there met so much fresh youth and so much serious striving. I had
especially been gladdened by the trust that so many had shown me by asking
my advice on purely personal matters. I hoped that the torches would also
cast their light forward, and that our University might always find
faithful sons and be the home of a fine collaboration between older and
younger in the service of truth. I closed with a cheer for the
% --- p. 256 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{256}University. Then the procession filed past amid hurrahs and
disappeared on the other side of the park.

When the last torches disappeared my emotion got the upper hand, and I went
and sat in a solitary room, where I burst into tears. What had met me on
this day was so overwhelming that I could not understand that it really was
me it all concerned. I had to think of the many dark hours, the many doubts
about myself I had gone through, the sour work I had many times had to do.
There must, after all, if I could trust what had met me today, be some for
whom I had meant something. I do not let my judgment of my works depend on
the judgment of others; but it does warm one to the innermost when signs
come that one believes one can rightly interpret as an expression of
understanding.


Before and after the birthday there were celebrations in the Students'
Society and in the Students' Union, and finally the participants in my
laboratory exercises gave a party for me. It was an eventful week. ---

\secrule

A year after 11 March 1913, on 12 March 1914, the chairman of the Board of
the Carlsberg Foundation came out to me and informed me that the Board
intended to propose to the Academy that I be chosen to occupy the main
building of Old Carlsberg, which under J. C. Jacobsen's will was to be used
as a residence for the Danish man or woman whom the said Academy might
select for it. This provision was now to take effect, since the testator's
son Carl Jacobsen had died.

This came as a complete surprise to me. There had been much discussion in
some papers, from what I had heard, and I too had been mentioned. And I had
seen myself in Klods-Hans as Diogenes, who in the end, however, for
economic reasons preferred his tub to the Carlsberg Honorary Residence. But
I had, like all the
% --- p. 257 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{257}members of the Academy, been convinced that the choice should and
must fall on Vilhelm Thomsen. But then Thomsen's physician had firmly
advised him against moving from his present home, which in every respect
suited his frail health, out to Carlsberg, which did not suit him so well,
besides the fact that the change itself could be risky. And so it was that
they turned to me.

I had never seen the house from inside, and the first visit out there on a
fine day in early spring was overwhelming. I still harbored some economic
misgivings; there had been so much talk of how expensive it was to live in
such a residence, --- and the Diogenes of ``Klods Hans'' therefore had to go
out and beg once he had got the Honorary Residence! Although I was not
badly placed financially, there were nonetheless considerations I had to
take into account, especially when I thought of my approaching retirement
from the University. These misgivings were overcome, however, and a few
days later I wrote to the Board and accepted the offer. The week after
(20 March) the matter came before the Academy. I had been asked not to
appear in the meeting room until I was called in, and I waited a quarter of
an hour or so in a side room. When I had been called in, the President,
Vilhelm Thomsen, informed me in a few kind words that the Academy had
unanimously chosen me as occupant of the Honorary Residence. In my reply I
began by saying that the President knew me so well that he knew it was not
in me either to dissemble or to flatter. It was not dissembling when I said
that it grieved me that his health did not permit him to accept the offer.
And it was not flattery when I said that the Honorary Residence was his due
as our country's foremost man of science, and when I added that, if he
could not accept the offer, there was still a great leap before it could be
directed to me. Turning then to the Academy, I expressed my heartfelt
thanks for the election and added thanks for the many years in which I had
had the honor of being a member. It was, I
% --- p. 258 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{258}said, of great importance particularly for the philosopher to be
able to follow at first hand what goes on in other sciences, by hearing
their representatives speak about methods and results within their field.

A couple of months later (11 May) I moved in at Carlsberg. And with this I
have reached the point at which I had in mind to close these memoirs. Only a
few things more will I mention.

For the time being I continued my University activity in its full scope,
with the propaedeutic course for the young students, laboratory exercises
for a narrower circle and evening lectures for a wider circle. From a
certain quarter in the press there are said to have come, right from my
seventieth birthday, frequent hints that I ought now to withdraw --- I felt
myself still fit for work, and the expressions of sympathy I had received
from the students I did not take as a farewell greeting. Still, 72 years
stood before me as a fitting limit. And out here in the beautiful natural
surroundings, where at any moment one could refresh oneself after the work
in the study by a walk in the glorious park or in the antique colonnades,
the urge awoke to put the last hand to various planned works and to take up
various sketches for working out. I also began to grow tired of the
preparatory work that must precede every lecture, although the lecture
itself was as a rule a joy to me. I therefore decided at New Year 1915 to
submit my application for retirement, to take effect from the following
first of September. The rest of the semester was taken up in part by very
tiring and painful faculty deliberations about who should be my successor.
I will not go further here into these deliberations, any more than into the
new deliberations and the competition that became necessary when my first
successor died. I do not conceal that my desire for continued University
activity dwindled greatly because of a good deal that I experienced on this
occasion.

% --- p. 259 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{259}Since I have been accused of voting against Dr. C. N. Starcke on
both occasions for reasons other than the merits of the case, I shall
explain more fully what my position was in these deliberations. At the
first vacancy the choice stood between Dr. Starcke and Dr. Anton Thomsen. I
had earlier been close to Dr. Thomsen, but I had had to subject one of his
writings to a very sharp criticism, which in turn led to a mocking attack on
his part. I nonetheless supported his election because of the talent and
independence I found in him. Dr. Starcke had in my view at one time fallen
into hasty production, in which the stream of words covered over a lack of
sharp grasp of the problems. Later, because of school work and political
work, he had had to put philosophy on the shelf. That he had criticized my
Etik (a criticism I had answered) naturally played as small a part with me
on this occasion as that Thomsen had criticized and mocked my
Religionsfilosofi. --- After Thomsen's death several applicants came
forward, and a competition was held. The works Starcke produced on this
occasion had in my eyes very serious defects, and I cannot deny that
% print: nægte, at / var baade (misprint)
I was both astonished and indignant at the way in which the discussion of
them was conducted in the assessment committee. I held to my view and,
together with the Dean, formed a minority in the vote. --- Within the
majority too, however, misgivings made themselves felt. One of the foreign
members said to me: ``I cannot vote against the old man.'' He would have
preferred to vote for one of the younger men, but gave it up, presumably
under the influence of the deliberations conducted within the majority
between the meetings. I myself spoke only in the meetings themselves, and it
is untrue when a son of Starcke has spoken in a newspaper of the
``activity'' I was supposed to have exerted to exclude his father. --- The
day after the close of the competition I wrote to Professor Alfred Lehmann,
who had voted for Starcke, and urgently asked him to use his personal
relation
% print: foreløbig Lehmann (misprint)
to Starcke to dissuade him from publishing anything whatever for the time
being. Lehmann answered that he had already put it to Starcke that he must
submit to strict work if he was to give satisfaction, especially as regards
exercises with older students. He had moreover dissuaded him from publishing
``the written work (in the competition), with which everyone thought he had
come off very badly.'' It turned out, unfortunately, that this warning did
not help.

When Starcke's appointment was settled, I wished him in friendly words good
fortune and success in his new position.

It is possible that I have underrated his latest writings. But in any case
it did not happen from such motives as a son of Starcke has attributed to me
in ``Politiken'' (3 July 1926). --- What I have set out
% --- p. 260 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{260}above I did not wish to put forward in an article of reply, partly
because I felt that the tone of the attack ruled out a reply, but partly
also because it went against me so soon after Starcke's death to drag up
these unpleasant matters. (July 1926).

\whiteline

Now I could live solely and wholly for my studies and my production. Every
morning I feel glad at the thought that I have the day at my disposal for
work of my own choosing. In the morning hours I work on philosophical
subjects, and in the evening I write at my biography, --- yes, and now that
this is finished, other tasks will no doubt come. Besides, I read what I can
manage of general literature. I cannot boast of keeping up in this field,
but it may perhaps interest readers of my biography to see what of newer
and older literature has especially been nourishment to me in recent years,
and I therefore set down here a part of an article that I dated 11 March
1916.

\secrule

A living and colorful mood of nature I have found in Ludvig Holstein's
poems. They enrich feeling through the fresh breath from soil and field,
from garden and wood, from life together with nature through the changing
of the seasons. One is called out of the study to move about in free and
rich nature. It is not nature's great scenes, not heights and expanses, that
are brought before us here, but it is the small things, the details, that
are presented in their peculiarity, revealing to us a whole world where the
dull sense could formerly see nothing. Stuckenberg too leads us out into
nature, but only to lead us at once into a series of delicate and deep
moods, which in the poet have now sought nourishment in images of nature,
now been called forth by them. And to these two poets Sofus Michaëlis joins
himself as the poet of thought, for whom the fundamental laws and
fundamental forms of existence are the great sources of mood. In mighty
images he sees, when he stands above the strata that a
% --- p. 261 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{261}cutting has laid bare, the history of the earth and of mankind
pass by.

I confess that, much as I owe to Danish poetry, Swedish poetry has
nonetheless for a number of years given me still greater refreshment and
rest. Gustaf Fröding's Vermland poems, his images of nature, the clash of
humor and bitterness in his mind, the pith of his language, borne up by the
dialect of his home district, the strength and depth of his thoughts, sprung
as they are from the fortunes of a tossed life, --- all this has given me
the greatest poetic joys, ever since I bought his poems in Uppsala 14 years
ago. And Verner v. Heidenstam leads us into the enigmatic inmost of the
human heart, to which no one has the key, not even man himself, for

\begin{quote}
i menniskans öden en gåta bor gömt,\\
som aldrig tyddes, hur lärd och berömd\\
hun läste sin filosofia.
\end{quote}

It does the philosopher good to hear this in the urgent language of poetry,
even if he knew it beforehand from his own experience, after he has for his
part put honest work into finding out what the riddles are and what they
mean.

Selma Lagerlöf, with her incomparable Gösta Berling, forms a transition from
lyric poetry to narrative prose. It is a great pleasure to take up anew a
single chapter of this book, fresh as nature, by itself, or to follow a
single one of its characters through the vicissitudes of his fate. Swedish
landscape, Swedish folk poetry and Swedish life of mood meet us here, at
once with the strength of reality and with the splendor of imagination. ---
If I go from Selma Lagerlöf to Danish storytellers, I come, for my part,
first upon Henrik Pontoppidan, whose ``Muld'' is the most Danish book I
know. It is not the construction of Pontoppidan's books that I admire, but
it is the clear and striking characterization of the individual scenes and
of the
% --- p. 262 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{262}characters in the particular situations. His latest book [Torben
og Jytte] has, with all its lack of unity in what has so far appeared,
greatly engaged me through its individual portrayals, which have enriched me
with a series of pictures of life that I will not forget. I wait with
suspense for the last part, to see how the different regions of life here
at home may after all prove to form a whole. And I do not deny that I am
still waiting for a better fortune for poor Jytte than the one that has so
far fallen to her lot. She is drawn so vividly and naturally, with all her
wavering and in all her dividedness, for which the author makes her pay
dearly, that toward her there must stir the sympathy that what is truly
alive involuntarily calls forth, however it may behave\footnote[1]{[Later note.] The hope was (see the last part) not to be fulfilled. But Pontoppidan is right, with the right of tragedy.}. And from Pontoppidan himself I
still expect many a good account of human beings and human fates. ---
Andersen-Nexø leads us into a wholly different world from the one in which
Pontoppidan moves. We follow in his ``Pelle'' the proletarian boy, who
begins life with two bare hands, and whose labor for a place at life's table
nonetheless leaves him time and strength to spare to see, in great fantasies
of the future, possibilities of brighter conditions for his class, and to do
a work of organization that leads him through great catastrophes. What one
remembers most is probably the childhood on Bornholm and the strike winter
in Copenhagen. But there are many who, like Charles Darwin, in their old age
like best books that end well, and for me too the idyll with which the book
ends stands as something I take joy in imagining, and in whose lasting
possibility I hope.

Though it is not the very newest present whose literature I have spoken of
here, the forces that have produced the literature I have lived in are
nonetheless for a great part still at work. But I cannot close without
naming what I owe to books by older French and English authors.
% --- p. 263 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{263}Mme Staël-Holstein's ``Corinna'', Dickens' ``David Copperfield''
and George Eliot's ``Mill on the Floss'' I read again and again and with
ever new joy. And then, last of all, the confession that my highest moments
are still given me by Shakespeare's ``golden song'' and by the great and
clear images of fate of the Greek tragedians. In this great art I especially
like to immerse myself when the inadequacy of psychological analysis for the
understanding of human characters becomes clear to me again and again, both
as philosopher and as human being. It is not only intuition that here
yields a fullness that thought cannot exhaust; here too the consoling
assurance of the sublimity of greatness in its very downfall wins a victory
over despondency and doubt.

\secrule

When I was little, my family lived in summer at a farm in Valby (which has
now been replaced by a four-story building). Here I saw the main building of
Old Carlsberg and the beautiful garden with the pergola come into being.
Little did I suspect that I would come to live in that splendid house, and it
is strange to think back on the days when as a little boy I went about in
these parts. I remember especially how I often rode along up to the brewery
(in a one-horse carriage, drawn by ``the little black one'') to fetch beer
for the use of the farm, and then now and then could see a little of the
splendor. It is far from the case that I feel like Aladdin when I think of
the time when I walked here as a little boy. If there is anything I am not,
it is an Aladdin. I pride myself on diligence and honesty, on a certain
perseverance that astonishes me now in retrospect when I think of my
hypochondria and of the slight interest that for many years (perhaps because
of the hypochondria) I believed I could detect for what I myself was
absorbed in. I have had the good fortune to bring out what I had at heart,
and to point to the paths that, according to my experience and my
reflection, one must take for the life of the spirit to unfold freely and
healthily. And a greater
% --- p. 264 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{264}good fortune the gods cannot bestow. The gods cannot help it that
the ability was not greater in the one on whom they bestowed this good
fortune. It is also a good fortune for me that I have completed this
autobiography. Through the work on it, which has extended over more than a
year, I have in several respects learned to know myself better. But above
all I have been glad to write it, because during the work I came to live
again in the memory of people I have loved.

I do not think much about death. I know that I am best prepared for it when
I collect myself around what has made life valuable for me. And I hope to
keep the ability for such collectedness. Most of all I would wish the end to
come in the middle of an hour of work.

\secrule

It has been strange to walk out here in the idyllic quiet while the World
War, which began shortly after I had come out here, rages throughout Europe.
It was a good thing for me when a young friend, Vilhelm Sloman, got me to
take part in his fine work of procuring books for prisoners of war. But it is
so little that can be done. --- On some men of science the war has had the
effect that they cannot work in their field. For my part it has rather led
to deeper absorption in my philosophical work. Nor have I felt any misgiving
about occupying myself with my own individual course of life while millions
of people clashed against one another and the whole future of Europe was at
stake. Serious work and honest self-reflection keep their value
nonetheless, however things go in the world.

Nor had I been one of those who were so optimistic in their view of human
nature and in their belief in how gloriously far we had come that the war
and its brutality must shake them in their innermost faith. I know from
myself and from others the opposition
% --- p. 265 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{265}between Prospero and Caliban. Both belong to human nature, and
the bright view of life must always prove its right by taking up the fight
with the bestial anew. The bestial has many forms. It can spread in
peacetime as well as in wartime. I do not give up the hope that the powers
of light will assert themselves, even if the victories must always be
confirmed through new struggles.

\whiteline

Finished 21 December 1916.

% --- p. 266 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\chapter*{VII}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{VII. 1914--1922}
\markboth{VII. 1914--1922}{VII. 1914--1922}
\opage{266}The preceding sections of these memoirs were concluded
in December 1916, and I did not then imagine that there would
be a continuation. But the years that have passed since
have in many outward and inward respects been eventful
for me. Here in my idyllic home at Carlsberg, where
better than in my earlier dwellings I can follow the fixed course of the sun
and the stars and the capricious drifting of the clouds, I have
followed the great events of the world with suspense,
while I nevertheless found rest in the work that I still
thought I had before me, and also once more immersed
myself in the thought of what had given life value for
me. Of this I feel a need to write down one thing and another.
I am just now (January 1922) in the mood that follows
the completion of a piece of work, while a new one has not yet been
planned. Then one's own experiences naturally press forward
again.

\secrule

Not only through the newspapers did I follow the course of the
world's events. Through letters from both of the warring parties
I gained an impression of how people understood, and were moved
by, what was going on. For my own part, as
for the very great majority here at home, my sympathy was unreservedly on
the side of the Western Powers. Not only because of the encroachments
from Germany that we ourselves had suffered under, but also because
of the reactionary and militaristic attitude in
the policy of Germany and Austria, we could not make their
cause ours. Those were therefore terrible times when the Germans
repeatedly threatened Paris, and when their swelling
% --- p. 267 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{267}sense of power and victory found clear expression. They had
won so many times; should they not win this
time too, since they had used the time since the last war so well! And
then world dominion would be theirs. A German friend of mine who died before the war,
the poet Arthur Pfungst in Frankfurt, a
radical man who felt himself in decided opposition to Prussian
government and the Prussian character, had nevertheless stated, as
something that in his eyes was self-evident, that if they again
won a war with France, they would not be content as
last time, but would take the whole French north coast right up to Havre
in order to have free access to the ocean and a better hold
on England. Even Danes living in Germany were seized
by the idea of power and by the certainty of its victory. My
cousin the poet Karl Gjellerup, from his youth ``the Germans'
pupil'' and for many years at home in the German
way of thinking, wrote to me shortly after the outbreak of the war that
now Denmark's day of visitation had come. He addressed an
urgent appeal to me to do what I
could to influence the mood here at home, which in
his opinion was going in a ruinous direction. Our outwardly
correct attitude could not help us, since our press was decidedly
anti-German. And when the war that has now begun
is ended, Germany and Austria will be able to do with Europe
as they will. Germany is now taking note of its friends and its
enemies, never again to forget them. The sovereignty of small states
will soon be over; they must seek attachment to
a great power. A friendly attitude on the Danish side could
lead to a more liberal government in North Schleswig --- though
not to a frontier adjustment, which is hardly desired in
North Schleswig either, ``whose sons from every farm and house have, on
the mightiest battlefields of world history, mingled blood
with all the German tribes for Germany's culture!'' --- Yes, the
fine and truly idealistically minded poet had indeed
become the Germans' pupil! How little he knew the
spirit in which the Danish South Jutlanders went into the struggle!
They thought only that they had the choice between fleeing from
% --- p. 268 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{268}their native region, whereby they would ease German immigration,
and doing their duty as citizens in the state they had been forced into.
And they thought besides that if they did their duty as citizens, it would
become morally impossible for the Prussian government to
rob them of the land their forefathers had inhabited
from time immemorial. And how the Germanized
Danish poet confuses German culture, which all honor, and German
militarism, which is a danger to the culture of the world --- and in the end
to the true German culture itself!

Especially as regards this last point, his thoughts coincided
with those of many German authors and scholars.
The excellent and liberal-minded educator Rudolph
Penzig implored me ``im Namen der uns teuren ethischen
Kultur der Menschheit'' to counteract the false reports
about the war that the French and the English press
were spreading, and that were leading whole peoples astray. The distinguished
philosopher and fine critic Georg Simmel, professor in Strassburg,
wrote to me no less urgently, so that I
(and through me others up here) might get the right understanding
of what was taking place. Germany has not begun the war;
every German knows that in advance (von sich aus)!
Germany has no need of expansion: we have, after all, everything a
nation can wish for! Against its opponents' long-prepared
conspiracy Germany stands united, and this
unity is the mightiest manifestation of ethical-political energy
that world history has yet seen. The Germans are accused
of barbarism because in the utmost self-defense they have had to
damage some old buildings. But what is that compared with
the barbarism France and England show in making it possible,
through their alliance with Russia, for the Cossacks
to destroy the cities of Kant and Goethe, of Humboldt and Hegel!
The Muscovites' horses are to be allowed to trample the
soil where the highest scholarship and the most magnificent
organization have seen the light! For a hundred years
Germany will not forget this. ---

I answered my German colleagues quite briefly that we
% --- p. 269 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{269}up here had better access to reports from both sides,
and that we used our best judgment to find out
who was telling the truth, though well aware that here history
would in the end speak the decisive word. To Simmel, with whom
I had earlier carried on a philosophical correspondence, I said
besides that I looked forward to the time when we could again
continue our discussions with free minds. ---

Later in the autumn of 1914 I was drawn more directly
into the strife of opinions. The correspondent of the ``Vossische Zeitung''
in Copenhagen came out to me and asked me
to write an article in his paper in which I would express
myself on what we here at home owed to German scholarship. I
answered that I could do this only if I could at the same
time express my great astonishment at the
manner in which 93 German scholars and artists
had recently come forward.

In an appeal addressed ``to the civilized world,'' these
men, for the most part scholars and artists of
high rank, had protested against ``the lies and calumnies with
which the enemies seek to sully Germany's pure cause in the
hard struggle for life forced upon it.'' The appeal (which
is said to have been composed by the poet Sudermann) sets out 6
propositions: 1) It is not true that Germany is guilty
of this war. 2) It is not true that Germany has wantonly
violated Belgium's neutrality. 3) It is not true that the life and property of a
single Belgian citizen has been violated
by German soldiers, except where the bitterest self-defense required it.
4) It is not true that German troops have raged against Löwen
(Louvain) in a brutal manner. 5) It is not true that
German warfare has disregarded international law. 6) It is not
true that the struggle against so-called German militarism is not
a struggle against German culture, as the enemies hypocritically
say. --- For these 6 propositions the signatories vouched
with their names and with their honor.

It was sad to find among the signatories names
such as Felix Klein, Nernst and Planck, Harnack and Hermann,
% --- p. 270 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{270}Brentano, Liszt and Schmoller, Eduard Meyer and Wilamowitz,
Riehl, Wundt and Windelband.

In my article in the ``Vossische Zeitung'' I spoke from
a sincere heart of what we owed to German scholarship. But
I added that we up here had been all the more surprised
that a number of distinguished scholars could vouch on their
honor for things of which they could have only imperfect
and one-sided reports. I said further,
as I had said to my correspondents, that we up here
had better opportunity to test the reports in an
impartial manner, but that in the end only history could
judge.

On the occasion of this article I received a letter from a German
district judge (Landgerichtsrat) in Berlin wholly unknown to me
(his name was Eugen Meyer), in which he began
by declaring that with people who could express themselves as I
had done one could no longer meet in ``the temple of the seekers
of truth.'' Next he states that the question of
who had begun the war could be settled neither by
``Presslügner'' nor by ``Gelehrte unserer Zeit,'' but must
be cleared up with the help of the state archives.

I answered quite briefly that the content of my article had
after all been precisely to dispute the right of ``the scholars of our time'' to
declare what had and had not happened at the beginning of the war and in the
conduct of the war, and to maintain that only history
could settle this. That must have struck the man, for in a
following letter ``he regrets his sharpness.'' But he declares
that the German scholars have only defended their people's
cause. And Germany, he continues, is a national state. Only
the most pressing self-defense has compelled it to incorporate
elements with foreign languages (among others ``140,000
Westjüten und [!] Dänen''). As for militarism,
it was (this must be said in German) ``eine Teilerscheinung
des Pflichtlebens, des reinen Opfers, das reine Sittlichkeit
von uns fordest.'' For Germany has so many enemies,
and in the struggle against them it stands alone. Perhaps it will
% --- p. 271 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{271}perish! It is spat upon like Jesus before the Council! (Bespien
werden wir wie Jesus vor dem hohen Rat!). But the day of victory
will come again, the day of the German people and of truth!

I did not continue the correspondence. --- In Germany itself
there were protests against that appeal, and it has since been
made known that many of the signatories had given their
assent by telegraph and without knowing the wording! When the occasion
arose, many of them declared after the war that
they regretted their signature, indeed some even that they looked back
on this affair with horror, after they had come to
know how matters stood with the attack on Belgium
and with the conduct of the German troops there. Dr. Hans
Weberg (lecturer in international law), who has thrown light on the whole affair in a
small pamphlet (Wider den Aufruf der 93! 1920), says rightly
that the 93 had in fact declared themselves in solidarity with
the conduct of the imperial government, and that the document betrays
the same spirit of the policy of blood and iron that in 1899
made the German Foreign Office reject the idea of a
court of arbitration at The Hague. ---

In England and France the conduct of the 93 had a violent
effect. A quiet man, hitherto very well disposed
toward Germany, Professor Sorley in Cambridge, expressed
himself in a letter to me in the following way: Military and industrial
success has changed the national direction of the German people.
Some Germans, e.g. Eucken, see this, but hope that
a new idealism will develop. But, to judge by the conduct of Eucken and the
other professors, this new
idealism must be of a strange kind. Arrogance is the most
prominent trait of the Germans of our time. It appears,
e.g., in their judgments on the philosophy of other countries. If Europe
is to be fit to live in, German militarism must be struck down.
The future of the small states depends on the victory of the Allies. Finally
Sorley says that he does not believe that international intercourse
with the Germans will become possible in his lifetime. --- My
French translator Madame de Quirielle wrote to me on
the occasion of the manifesto of the 93 that its only
% --- p. 272 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{272}interest was to show that there were not \textit{two} Germanies, a military one and
a cultural one, and that one therefore cannot give the military the whole
blame for the war. But, she added, even if the intellectuals
would not separate their cause from that of the army and the people,
they ought nevertheless to have waited until the facts were
clearly established.

From letters from French and English friends that I have lying
before me, I see that I, as is only natural,
did not conceal my interest in the cause of the Western Powers.
An English lady, Mrs. Alice Rufford, whose acquaintance I had
made at Glion in 1909 and with whom I had since carried on a
lively correspondence, was glad that I wished England
success in this terrible war. She had feared
that I would believe what the German newspapers said about her
country. She speaks with admiration of the wounded Belgian soldiers
who had come over to England, --- ``these brave people,
who had saved both England and France from a sudden
attack for which they were not prepared.'' --- The correspondence
with Mrs. Rufford stopped before the end of the war. My
old, wise and liberal-minded friend has probably passed away. On
our walks in the mountains above Montreux we had
exchanged our opinions and experiences of life (especially when her
very orthodox friend was not with us).

The profound philosopher Herbert Bradley wrote to me in March
1915: ``Some years ago it became clear to me that
war was almost inevitable, but nothing could make my
countrymen realize this and prepare for it.
It is bitter to think that if they had prepared
for the war, they might perhaps have prevented it.''

Of the sacrifices the war brought, the harvest of young gifted
men that it reaped, many of the letters tell. Thus
Émile Boutroux writes that he has lost many relatives
who have fallen with honor. The Fondation Thiers, a kind of scholarly
college of which he was director, he has turned
into a hospital, which is run by Madame Boutroux. Sorley tells
of the death in battle of his young son in Belgium, after he had, as
% --- p. 273 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{273}so often, gone gladly to meet danger. The young captain
(20 years old) was leading his men forward to the attack when death
struck him. His father says of him: ``In soul and body
he was among the fairest of the fair, and he
understood the secret art of making everyone who came
near him glad.'' The young man had already won
a fine name as a poet and had begun his studies
at Oxford in a brilliant manner. A collection of letters
from him, especially during a stay in Germany (Schwerin and
Jena) before the war, shows his fresh and independent way of thinking.
I myself saw him only as a boy in his parents'
pleasant home, where I stayed several times.

For many good Germans the defeat, and what followed
it, was a grief of the heart. Thus my friend Ferdinand
Tönnies writes (April 1919) that he grieves deeply over the dissolution of his
people. He himself, however, suffers less than others, since
he had never had an overstrained faith in Bismarck's
German Empire (which, though, in his opinion was the least
imperialistic of the great powers). Despite all his sympathy with
the working class, he was by no means glad of the revolution,
but would rather have seen a calm development.

\secrule

During the war my spacious and secluded residence
at Carlsberg was often the place for gatherings that, because
of the circumstances, had to take place quietly.

The famous physiologist Richet had come up here to
give a lecture on the war from a French point of view at
the ``Alliance française.'' But since all public lectures by
foreigners were forbidden by the government, he was invited
to speak here at Carlsberg to a narrow circle. Before
the lecture I addressed the following words to him:

``It is a great honor for me to receive you in this house,
which was built by a man who was a good Danish patriot
and loved France. When I moved in here I found
two flags, the Dannebrog and the Tricolor. I hope that the day
% --- p. 274 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{274}will come when I shall be able to hoist the Tricolor to celebrate
a peace that is truly a peace for all Europe. When
the founder of Carlsberg loved France, it was not
purely a matter of feeling. On your way in here, Monsieur Richet, you have
come along Pasteur's road and past a bust of Pasteur.
Carlsberg's great industry, whose profits are applied to the good of the sciences,
owes an extraordinary amount to the genius of Pasteur.

Our gathering here this evening is entirely private and must
not be mentioned in the press. We thought that Monsieur Richet would
like to have an opportunity to speak freely about the events of the time
to a circle that feels sympathy for his country
and for himself. But this gathering also has
another purpose. We have heard, to our very great regret, that
in France our painful position during
this war is not always understood, in which we are obliged to hold back expressions
of sympathy and antipathy. Fifty years ago we had to
fight alone against the two great powers against which three
great powers are now fighting. That has made us cautious. But our
heart has not grown cold. We hope that what will be
said this evening by representatives of our political, commercial
and scholarly life will give our French guest
a clear idea of our position and our feelings.

You, Monsieur Richet, do not come to us as a stranger. Our
physicians honor you for your scientific works and discoveries.
Several of us greeted you on your return journey
from Stockholm, where you had received the Nobel Prize. I
myself have profited greatly from your psychological writings.
And we know that you are not only an eminent scientist,
but that your heart beats for all that is great
and beautiful. You must have suffered under the events of the time, which
went against all that love of mankind could hope for.
But you feel always the need to work for your country,
this glorious country, which has rendered mankind such great
services.''

Some years later Richet recalled this gathering with a few kind
% --- p. 275 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{275}words in a letter he wrote to me on
the occasion of a preface which I, at the request of the Flournoy
family, had written for a new edition of the early work of our common
sick friend Théodore Flournoy.

\whiteline

The misunderstandings of which Denmark's position and mood during
the World War were the object in France also gave occasion
later to secret gatherings at Carlsberg,
where men of all parties met to deliberate on
what could be done by private means to bring clarity
to the matter. Owing to the course of events it did not become
necessary to take any step in that direction.

\secrule

I came into closer touch with the World War and its effects
through taking part in the work of the Danish Red Cross. While in the summer of 1915 I was staying at Moesgaard
near Aarhus, the librarian Vilhelm Slomann asked me
by telephone for a conversation. As I was just about
to drive to Aarhus, I made an appointment with him there, and he now came forward
with a request that I be chairman of a committee
that was to be formed to procure books for prisoners of war
from the various countries. Slomann's idea was that each
belligerent country should procure books for its captive
countrymen, and that the Book Committee in Copenhagen should be
the intermediary through which the books were sent to the prison camps.
I readily agreed to the proposal and thereby entered
upon an activity that extended through all the war years
and brought me into touch with people and conditions that
would otherwise have lain far from me. But first and foremost
it was a relief after all to help lessen the distress
during the great world catastrophe. The spiritual distress
could be quite as serious as the material. --- It
was a great joy to me to come to know Vilhelm Slomann more closely.
His warm temperament, great enthusiasm and wealth
of initiatives gave the work a swing that led to fine
% --- p. 276 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{276}results. We worked well together, even if his zeal
and restlessness at times burst the forms that it was
the chairman's duty to uphold. When I look back on the
activity of the Book Committee, ``Bellibria'' (as it was called after its telegraphic address),
it is not only with joy
at having taken part in the fine work, but also
with joy at having won a friend.

In the first year we met the great expenses of arranging
and dispatching the books out of a capital quietly collected
(50,000 kroner). But after that all the aid to prisoners of war,
``Bellebria'' too, was supported by the state, in recognition
that this was an activity that did the country
honor and awakened sympathy for it. We no longer needed constantly
to make collections. From the very beginning we had
obtained permission to use the Red Cross emblem and
had come into contact with the International Red
Cross in Geneva. Now we became a special department of the Danish
Red Cross's prisoner-of-war work, alongside the departments
that worked for correspondence between the prisoners
and their home countries, for the sending of clothes and food,
for visits to prison camps, etc. On that occasion I was
admitted as a member of the central board of the Danish Red Cross.

Because of the geographical situation it was especially the prisoners
on both sides of the Eastern Front that we could work for.
We procured German books for German prisoners of war in Russia and
Russian books for Russian prisoners of war in Germany. Director
Vagn Jacobsen showed us the kindness of letting us have
splendid premises at Carlsberg for storing books and
for an office. At times we might have a collection of
several hundred thousand volumes waiting to be sent
off. It cannot be denied that Germany provided in a magnificent
way for its captive sons, among whom there
were many students. All the way to Siberia we sent scholarly
and literary works. A few times I personally received
requests for particular works for captive philosophers,
% --- p. 277 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{277}and I then used what I could spare from my own library.
Moving were the letters of thanks we received from prisoners
whose spiritual hunger we had been able to relieve. At the beginning
of the war there also came many Russian books,
which were sent to captive Russians in Germany. But many
Russians could not read, and because of the unsettled conditions
in Russia the shipments therefore stopped later on. We
had, moreover, an envoy skilled in the Russian language, who visited
prison camps in Germany to hear the wishes of the Russian prisoners.
We attempted something similar in Russia, but
it did not succeed. On the other hand we could make use of Danish officers
and physicians who accompanied German sisters of the Red Cross
on visits to prison camps in Russia and Siberia. We also got some
Turkish books sent to Turkish prisoners in Russia,
whereas it was not possible to procure a Tatar translation
of the Koran for a captive Russian Tatar in Germany
(A Turkish delegate explained to me, moreover, that the Koran
must not be translated at all from the holy Arabic
language in which it was originally written). On a single
occasion we were able to send a splendid English collection of books to English
prisoners in Germany; but otherwise it was nearer at hand for England
to let its shipments go through Holland, just as
it was for France to send its own through French Switzerland.

Our work meant that we received a good many visits from
Russian and German envoys, and the festive rooms of Carlsberg
were often taken into use. In the spring of 1917 there came a deputation
from the German universities with the famous philologist
Wilamowitz at its head, to give thanks for the book aid to
captive German students. The summer before, ten Russian
sisters of the Red Cross came to Copenhagen in order to go from there,
accompanied by Danish officers, to visit Russian prisoners in Germany.
I visited them at their hotel to talk with them about
the book matter. There were several highly cultivated ladies of high station
among them, with whom it was of great interest to talk.
Despite the seriousness of the times they had not lost their good spirits. I
invited them to visit me in the evening at Carlsberg, and
% --- p. 278 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{278}when, before I left, I asked how many of the ladies I
might then have the pleasure of seeing, one of them answered:
Tout le regiment, Monsieur! It was a glorious June evening in
the season of roses. In their long gray costumes they skipped about
in the rose garden, and later, at the supper table, they gave
speeches in French and English. It is one of the most beautiful
memories I have from the war years; but it is darkened by the thought
of how things have gone with the ladies during their country's
defeat and dissolution. To one of them a moving story
attaches. She was a general's wife, and her husband
had fallen in the Russian defeat in East Prussia. She
had entered the Red Cross and had joined this expedition
in order, if possible, to find traces of her husband. She is said
in fact to have reached the battlefield, and nearby she came upon
a peasant who, after being questioned by the German officer who
accompanied her, produced a locket in which
her own picture was found! The body was then found nearby.
--- The visit of the Russian ladies had a little epilogue. One
of them had, during the stay in Germany, written down diary notes
about the visit to Copenhagen, and so also about
the evening at Carlsberg. These papers were confiscated on
the return journey at Warnemünde. The president of the German care for prisoners of war,
General Friedrich, when he later visited
me, was curious to see the place where the Russian ladies
had enjoyed themselves so much, and asked about everything he
had read of in the papers (--- und wo wurden die Reden
gehalten? etc.).

Most (not all) of the German envoys who came up here
in connection with the aid to prisoners of war were tactful and chivalrous
men. General Friedrich was especially well liked. Of several
of these men I have the impression that long before the catastrophe they
sensed that their country would succumb. This applies especially
to General Friedrich. When he was here for the last time
(in the late summer of 1918), he was quiet and dejected.
He died before the end came.

% --- p. 279 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{279}In the summer of 1917 a new constitution came into force for
the Danish Red Cross. Previously a board in Copenhagen
had had the direction, and the branches outside Copenhagen
were regarded merely as subsidiaries. Now the branches became more
independent and took part in the election of the central board, which
no longer co-opted its own members. They were at a loss for
a new chairman and turned (after having turned in vain
to various others) to me. (From a letter left behind in the chairman's
portfolio I came to know the preceding
negotiations. --- Outgoing chairmen should never
leave that kind of letter in their portfolio). It was by
a kind of surprise attack that I was taken. But I have not
had reason to regret it, and I hope that the Danish
Red Cross has not regretted it either. I now combined
the special position as chairman of Bellibria with the position
of chairman of the Danish Red Cross. Besides the
various prisoner-of-war departments, each of which had its own management
and its own offices, I now came into relation with the great
domestic work. (Nursing, ambulance transport, the Samaritan Society,
etc.). Much here was foreign to me, at any rate in
the beginning, but an executive committee, which consisted
of able men and women, lightened the work and the responsibility.
