I learned much about the practical conditions of life, and
I gained much experience of people through the
position I had come into. On the whole I look back with pleasure
on that time. I came out well from the responsibility, and
I have taken part in a significant activity.

In the autumn of 1917 a conference was held in Copenhagen, under the formal direction
of the Danish Red Cross, to discuss
the treatment of prisoners of war. The two groups of enemies of the Eastern Front
met here in the midst of the war. Prince Valdemar, who
was honorary president of our prisoner-of-war departments, presided;
in his absence I presided. But the negotiations
were conducted with superior skill by the then
head of department in the Foreign Ministry, Herluf Zahle. With
a certain suspense the Danish members of the conference assembled
% --- p. 280 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{280}at Amalienborg (in Christian IX's palace) for the
first meeting between the enemies. With strict etiquette
it had been arranged that the delegates of the belligerent countries
(Russians and Rumanians on the one side, Germans, Austrians
and Turks on the other) at one and the same moment, at
a given signal of a bell, entered the hall through different
doors and sat down, each delegation at its own table. A few
times there threatened to be a clash, when one party accused
another of mistreating prisoners of war; but the chairman
always managed to get the negotiations
going again. In the small committees things gradually became quite
genial. Many cigarettes were smoked in Queen
Louise's old sitting room. The negotiations led to a real
result, in that certain humane measures were adopted
that were to be observed in the treatment of prisoners of war.
From what was forbidden one could, moreover, infer how
terrible things have often been, as when, e.g., it was forbidden
to use degrading punishments (especially by fastening mocking
placards on a prisoner who had committed an offense). The rules adopted at the
conference have been of importance
for later negotiations between the enemy groups of the Western Front.

Although one could negotiate together despite the enmity,
one could not, however, celebrate together. The Foreign Ministry, at
whose expense the conference was held, proposed to me that
the festivities be held at Carlsberg. An emissary from the ministry
then took over the supreme command out here for two days. He saw
to everything, and my household helpers and I had nothing
to do with any of it, except that I had to dress in full dress,
preside at table two days in a row, and give two French
speeches. One day there was a festivity for the Germans, the Austrians
and the Turks, the next day for the Russians and the Rumanians.
It turned out that several of the Russian, Rumanian and Turkish
delegates had used my books in their student years (in
French translation), and on that occasion
many kind words were addressed to me. Later the foreign ministers concerned
% --- p. 281 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{281}each gave festivities of their own, so that in
this respect too it was a rather strenuous time.

\secrule

It was, as already said, especially the belligerents of the Eastern Front
that the Danish Red Cross had to do with. But we also tried to help French
prisoners of war in Germany, by collecting
books and in other ways. And in the last year of the war
Slomann had the brilliant idea that in the prison camps
examinations of a preparatory kind could be held, so that
candidates for the preliminary examination, training-college students and future university entrants could
have their examinations behind them when they came home
after the conclusion of peace. To carry this out
Danish examination commissioners were to be sent to Germany and France,
with authority from the French and the German government respectively,
and to arrange the examinations, at which
captive professors and senior masters were to be examiners.
Dr. Louis Hammerich had been chosen to travel to
Germany, Rector Otto Zahle to travel to France, for this
purpose. When the matter seemed to be coming into order, I went to the
French minister, M. de Conti, to present Rector
Zahle; Dr. Hammerich was already in Berlin. On this visit
to the French legation a scene took place which I
must describe here, since I have heard that incorrect accounts
of it are in circulation.

While Count de Beaucaire, who before the war was French
minister here, was a very attractive and sympathetic personality,
this can hardly be said of M. Bapst and M. de
Conti, who were here during the war. They had evidently been
imbued with suspicion of Denmark, or at any rate
of Danes who did not belong to a small, tenacious, hypernational
clique that knew how to encapsulate the French ministers and
make them unreceptive to whatever did not bear the clique's
stamp. Slomann and I once went to Bapst to
talk about the book matter, but although a time had been agreed, the
minister had forgotten it, and we had to wait over an hour before
% --- p. 282 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{282}he came. (The time passed, moreover, very pleasantly and interestingly,
since the lively and gifted military attaché Colonel
Taylor, who afterwards fell at the Chemin des Dames, entertained
us in a captivating manner). When Monsieur Bapst finally came,
we did not succeed in interesting him in the book matter. Later,
when he saw how eagerly the German side took up the matter,
he came rushing out to Carlsberg to ask whether the matter
had been put before him; he had forgotten it! With his
successor M. de Conti it went with me in the following way.
Shortly after his arrival in the early summer of 1918 he invited
me to dinner on 14 July, but when I learned that there
would be French demonstrations which, in my capacity
as chairman of the Danish Red Cross, I could not attend,
I sent my regrets. I then waited to pay a call
on him until I could present Rector Zahle to him, which
for various reasons dragged on until the autumn. As soon as we now
came in, he flew at me. ``Yes, now you come, now that
we have won! Before, I saw nothing of you! We distinguish
between true and false friends!'' I was undeniably somewhat
taken aback at this greeting, but answered that my French and
English friends knew where my sympathies had been
during the war, and that I had waited to come until
I found an occasion. It was a very unpleasant
situation, since I must not provoke the testy man
more than he had provoked himself, lest he should
put obstacles in the way of Rector Zahle's journey\footnote[1]{Rector Zahle, moreover, got as good as no access to the prison camps guarded by the French themselves. A head of department in the French Ministry of War declared that toward the German prisoners they would indeed show humanité, but not générosité! On the other hand Zahle received a hearty welcome in the German prison camps guarded by American soldiers (with c. 50,000 prisoners) and accomplished much there for the benefit of the prisoners. The corresponding activity for French prisoners in Germany came to nothing.}. When
I came home, I wrote a letter to Conti, which for safety's
sake I put before Herluf Zahle, the head of department, who corrected
some expressions that seemed to him too strong. I stated
in this letter, first, that the men who without remuneration
devoted their time and their strength to the service of the Danish Red
% --- p. 283 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{283}Cross do not approach the ministers of the belligerent countries
except when they have an offer to make, and that
I had therefore waited until the examination matter had been put in order,
--- and second, that the leaders of the Danish Red Cross were
obliged to observe the strictest neutrality in order to be able
to carry out their work. To this letter I received no
answer. Later he once sent me congratulations on
a Danish honor that had been conferred on me. In the meantime
he is said, from what has reached my ears, to
have said: ``Yes, he \textit{had} received the Commander's Cross of the Legion of Honor;
so he had no reason to come!''
(I had received this decoration a year before the war, on the grounds
of my work as an author).

Of course this conduct on the part of one of France's representatives
has not in any way impaired my admiration for
France and my gratitude toward the country that contributed
so much to Danish North Schleswig's being able to come
back.

\secrule

The three Scandinavian Red Cross societies worked together during the war as far
as possible, which among other things gave occasion for
the chairman of the Norwegian Red Cross, Supreme Court Advocate Heyerdahl,
and me to be guests for a week or so in February 1920 of the chairman of the Swedish
Red Cross, Prince Carl of Sweden. They were pleasant
and lively days that we spent with Prince Carl and Princess
Ingeborg in their beautiful home at Djurgården. Our
negotiations turned mostly on the possibility of aid
in the return of the prisoners of war; but there was also an opportunity
to get one's bearings with regard to the three Red Cross societies'
very different positions within their countries. The Swedish
Red Cross stood in the front rank through its rich means, its
close relation to the state and its excellent organization.
Besides, we also discussed our conduct at a conference
which the so-called League of Red Cross Societies (consisting essentially
of representatives of the Entente Powers) had convened for
the beginning of March 1920 in Geneva. At this conference
% --- p. 284 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{284}I represented the Danish Red Cross and had excellent
support in the director of the Serum Institute, Dr. Thorvald Madsen,
who represented the Danish government. The yield of
this conference was not great, although the speeches (and the dinners)
were many. My philosophical colleague at the University
of Geneva asked me to give a lecture at
the University, which, despite the short notice, I also undertook.
I chose a subject I had just treated in
Danish, trying to give ``an intellectual characterization
of the 19th century.'' The lecture was given in
the great hall of the University, which was quite full. I was in good form,
and in the course of the week I had got so much French
into my ear and brain that I managed reasonably well to bring it
forth on my tongue. A question hour which, on request, I
held immediately after the lecture went off very lively,
and a good many sensible questions came up. I
felt like an old cavalry horse that hears the trumpet.

Both on the way out and on the way home I spent
some days in Heidelberg with my niece Ellen and
her husband, the engineer Nissen, who lived in a glorious villa
on the hillside above the town. There, on
the way home, I celebrated my 77th birthday. In the morning I was
awakened with song by the young people of the family.
--- Otherwise it was very dismal and troublesome to travel
through Germany at that time. In Hamburg I was stopped
on the way home by a general strike, but together with two
other travelers I hired a motorcar and then drove through
Mecklenburg to Warnemünde, where I caught the Danish
ferry.

In February 1921 negotiations were held at Carlsberg
between the three chairmen of the Scandinavian Red Cross societies, each
accompanied by a member of the board. My assistant was
Chief Physician Svendsen of Odense, one of the Danish Red Cross's
most eminent men. The most important matter here was agreements
on a common stand at the conference that the International
% --- p. 285 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{285}Red Cross was to hold in Geneva in the spring of 1921.
At this conference the Danish Red Cross was represented
by Chief Physicians Svendsen and Videbech. The negotiations
were this time fruitful in several respects.

One of the last acts I had to perform as chairman
was the formal direction of a congress for combating
venereal diseases, which the ``League of Red Cross Societies'' had
asked the Danish Red Cross to hold. I had, with
the full support of the central board of the Danish Red Cross,
made it a condition of our taking on the responsibility for
this congress that it should consist exclusively of specialists.
I opened and closed the congress, but the meetings
were held under the direction of Professor Rasch. At the congress
envoys from England, Holland and Germany met with
envoys from the four Scandinavian countries. According to the specialists'
statements the congress was successful. Apart from the practical
yield, it offered the interest that Englishmen and Germans
met here both for negotiations and for festive
gatherings. The language of the proceedings was English, but
a fair amount of German was spoken too. ---

In the spring of 1921 the four years for which I had been
elected chairman had expired, and at my age (78) I would
not accept re-election. I keep many good memories
from my Red Cross time, both from abroad and at home, of
personalities I came to know and of serious work
for the welfare of human beings.

\secrule

Now that I am to speak of the great, joyful event
that the Reunification was for all Danes, I must first look
back a little to show my position on the South Jutland question,
which has not been spoken of connectedly in the foregoing.

Among my first childhood memories, as I have mentioned in
its place, is the mood of 1848, as it
was awakened in me by the remarks of my parents and my brothers.
I also remember clearly that, on a
% --- p. 286 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{286}journey by carriage down into Zealand with my parents, I saw a
detachment of troops on the march over to ``the war'' and heard
the bugle calls when it set off after a halt. I knew
that the war was against ``the Germans,'' but otherwise I of course understood
nothing of it all. The patriotic feelings awakened early
(most strongly awakened when I saw my parents weep after
the Eckernförde disaster) held through the years of childhood and youth.
When I began to read newspapers, it was not the
``internal'' politics of the Kingdom that interested me, but the constant
effort to obtain a constitution that could make
a united whole out of all the Danish and German elements of the realm.
The details I naturally could not follow at that time.
But I entered in good faith into the National Liberal,
``Eider-Danish'' standpoint with its strict adherence to
what was then thought to be the correct constitutional view.
When I now think back on that time, it stands
before me as a barren time, in which many good forces
were wasted in attempts to fill a vessel of the Danaids. And now
(through Krieger's diaries) the cover has indeed been drawn away from
the relations among the National Liberal leaders, so that their
petty jealousy and their common helplessness, when the catastrophe
came, are no secret. The defeat in
1864 had the effect that one was led from the supposed formal
right over to the real right, which lies in a
people's inward adherence to its language, its memories and
its way of taking life. And this transition was favored
in a gratifying way by the growing feeling of Danishness
in North Schleswig, just as it also received a natural
support from the fact that the internal politics of the Kingdom led
to the center of gravity coming more and more to lie in democracy.
In the Students' Society the idea then arose of
founding an association that was to work, according to its ability and quietly,
for the Danish language and culture in North Schleswig. It was the present
Prime Minister Neergaard who brought this matter
forward at a meeting in the Students' Society in the year 1887, and on
his proposal I became chairman of the new association, which
% --- p. 287 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{287}got the odd name 4 S (i.e. the Students' Society's South Jutland
Society), by analogy with a previously founded North Jutland
association named S S (i.e. South Jutland Society),
which worked especially for visits by young North Schleswigers to Danish
folk high schools. Already just after '64 a
secret association named ``Danebrog'' had been founded, chiefly by
old National Liberals. It had good funds at its disposal
for the support of national life in North Schleswig. The association
4 S never got many members and had no great income.
In the Students' Society the soil for its work was
not unreservedly favorable; people feared new conflicts
with Germany and a repetition or continuation of '64.
It came especially to lack an influx of young forces.
Moreover, 4 S did not come forward as agitators and shunned exaggerated
patriotic statements and proclamations, whereas
in other similar associations, which issued from other
groups within the student world, one could even hear a
cheer raised for ``the third Schleswig war.'' From 4 S there issued
a special association which on Sundays sometimes
gathered South Jutland pupils from the folk high schools and
agricultural schools of the surrounding district, arranged museum and theater visits for
them, and gatherings with speeches and songs. This association
was given, at my proposal, the name Vidar (the silent god of the Æsir),
in contrast to other associations, which were rather loud-voiced,
although they undeniably did a great work.

My own activity in the service of 4 S was not of importance.
But this association commanded some of the
best forces that have worked in the service of the national cause.
There were men like H. V. Clausen, the quiet but inwardly
enthusiastic man, who knew North Schleswig inside and
out, was informed about the sentiments and economic position in
every district and on every farm over there, and with his statistics
and his maps gave a sound basis for work and for
hope. There was the historian Mackeprang, himself born over there,
author of an account of the condition of Danishness in
North Schleswig from '64 on. And there was Niels Hjort, who
% --- p. 288 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{288}conceived the idea of a fund that could save the Danish
soil over there from German colonization and from the German
government's attempts (as in Poland) to drive native,
nationally minded men from their farms; in the course
of one winter he collected in all quietness \textonehalf{} million kroner,
which was deposited in the Haderslev Bank and served to support
farms whose mortgage situation might make it easy for German
buyers to get in. The work of these men has made
the history of 4 S an honorable one, and it was a joy to me to work
with them and win their friendship.

For a number of years we worked together with the association
``To Løver,'' which had issued from the Students' Union and
found a better soil there than 4 S found in the Students' Society.
The link between the various groups that
worked for the national cause in North Schleswig was the Keeper of the Public Records
A. D. Jørgensen. It was of interest to me to come
into closer relations with this fine historian, whose inner
glow did not often break through a certain stiffness and coolness outwardly.
After late meetings we often walked together at night
to our homes in Frederiksberg, and then his
innermost thoughts could sometimes find expression, and they went, both in military-political
and in religious respects, in other directions
than the National Liberal and conservative circles that claimed
him for their own would have been able to approve. When he spoke
in favor of developing the armed forces, it was, he explained to me,
because a small people, in his conviction, ought not
to withdraw from taking part in the great events of history,
but seek attachment to a great power, which, as the
geographical conditions were, could be none other than
Germany. In religious respects his sympathy was with Catholicism,
which, by the way, is clearly noticeable in his portrayal
of Steno. --- After Jørgensen's death Supreme Court Advocate
Nellemann took, with great amiability, ability and expert knowledge,
his place as the link between the various
South Jutland associations. Clashes now came about not infrequently.
On the whole I had, with regard to ``To Løver,'' the
% --- p. 289 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{289}impression that here I stood face to face with the National Liberal view
that I myself had lived in during my uncritical young days.
What I have occasionally experienced after the war (sometimes
in a rather insolent form toward me personally) has confirmed
me in this. There are, after all, many in our country
who have learned nothing and forgotten nothing.

Every year there were larger gatherings, at which the
various South Jutland associations here met with
men from South Jutland. It was festive to come together
with men like Gustav Johannsen, Hanssen-Nørremølle,
Jessen, Reimers and many more of the best South Jutland
men. Among these I felt especially drawn to
Hanssen-Nørremølle. After several years' stay at Danish
folk high schools he had studied here at the University and at
several German universities, and it was a rich and comprehensive
culture that he had acquired. He had, and has, a
remarkable ability to see what is essential in a matter and to
find the ways by which it can come into its own. When
he expressed general points of view, it was always in such a way
that one felt how they had grown up out of personal
experience and out of an eye for realities, and how they had
their significance for him as guiding stars in continued
work. In a multitude of practical and local matters in South Jutland
he became the understanding leader, and this he became
gradually in high politics too, as North Schleswig's
representative in the German Reichstag. Of him one can say
that he had learned what was to be learned and forgotten what
ought to be forgotten. His great enthusiasm for his people's cause
he did not vent in empty phrases and in quixotic attempts,
but in manly work on tasks whose necessity
sprang from the given conditions. Even when things looked darkest
for our cause, it was strengthening to have his clear
stand and untiring course before one's eyes.

A little episode from these years I cannot pass over, since
it throws light on the Prussian regime in North Schleswig. In
the summer of 1889 I made a journey to South Jutland. In
% --- p. 290 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{290}Sønderborg I visited Hanssen-Nørremølle, who had then recently
married. One Sunday afternoon he drove me round
in Sundeved to visit the large farms where
he had relatives and friends. Everywhere we were hospitably received,
and I got a strong impression of how solid a foundation
Danishness was building on here. This glorious land must
above all not be lost. A new school system had recently been introduced,
according to which in the elementary school too, not
only in the higher schools, teaching was to be only in German,
with the exception of a few hours of religion. A little girl
wept because she did not know ``what she should say when
she came to school.'' Besides, there had been eager spying
on the German side; there had been talk of a
larger visit by Danish students, and the police wanted to
know whether the population itself had had anything to do with the matter.
On one farm the gendarme had even hidden himself
in the bedroom to hear whether husband and wife might not in private
talk about the matter.

One day I drove about on Als with some young students
I had met in Sønderborg. Old Reimers
drove with us. The young people sang Danish songs when
we were in a district where Reimers thought there were no spies.
It was a splendid trip. Als is indeed like a garden.
But the day after we were summoned to the town hall, where
the mayor held up to us that we had behaved ``in einer
Weise, die der Staat schlechterdings nicht vertragen
kann,'' and that he would therefore be obliged to expel us.
It was a critical situation. But by paying closer
attention to the mayor's statement I realized that
what was complained of must have happened the day before our
drive, and that it must therefore have been another party
that had committed the terrible crime against
the Prussian state. Since some of the young people had
return tickets stamped with the day of arrival, we could
prove that they had not come until the evening of the
day the crime was supposed to have taken place, and we now played
% --- p. 291 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{291}injured innocence. The mayor now asked us to go back
to our hotel, where we would be informed in an hour.
We waited in some suspense, but then the police clerk came
and asked me for a private conversation. He informed me that
we did not need to leave, but added that the reason for our
summons was that we had been seen together with Herr Reimers.
I answered: ``Ich kenne Herrn Reimers als einen
sehr braven Mann,'' to which he said: ``Ja, so kennen
wir ihn auch, aber er ist ein dänischer Agitator.'' I: ``Ja,
so nennen Sie ihn; wir haben einen anderen Namen für
ihn.'' --- The clerk, who is said to have earlier been on the
Danish side, was evidently very embarrassed by the matter. ---
When I came home to Copenhagen, the story had been improved:
I was supposed to have been seen being transported through
the town between two gendarmes! ---

I also visited Flensburg and was the guest there of the editor
Jessen, whose wife, née Fibiger, I had met in her young
days in her uncle Johannes Fibiger's
vicarage. There was a breath of energy in everything Jessen
said. Together with the Jessens and two Danish ladies I visited
the Isted grave in the Flensburg churchyard, where we sang
``Slumrer sødt i Slesvigs Jord.'' Jessen was convinced
that Germany was heading toward its dissolution, so that we could get
Denmark to the Eider (and ``we shall see to it that the South Schleswigers
become Danish''), --- and that the Duke of Cumberland
would then become King of Hanover and Duke of
Holstein. I did not know whether to laugh or weep on
hearing this. Flensburg gave the impression of an overwhelmingly
German town. Five years before, Gustav Johannsen had been
defeated here in the Reichstag election, and it had proved
impossible to keep the Low German-speaking part of the population
on the Danish side. --- From Flensburg I made a
walk to Sankelmark together with H. V. Clausen, who
explained to me with expert knowledge how the honorable
fight here had been fought. At Bilskov Inn (where in its time
the plan for the battle of Isted had been laid) the innkeeper's wife was
% --- p. 292 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{292}Danish-speaking, but could not be got to say anything in
Danish, since the Germans had made her believe that it was a
language of the rabble she spoke. ---

The years went by, and the World War, which had long threatened,
drew near, and with it the great suspense as to how
our country would fare in the mighty reckoning
that must be at hand.

But still in the spring of 1914 all seemed quiet, and we celebrated
in this country the 50th anniversary of the brave fight
at Dybbøl on 18 April 1864, the last fight on South Jutland's
mainland. A commemoration was held at the
Royal Theater in the presence of the royal family and the old veterans.
After a cantata, rich in thought and weighty in word, by
Niels Møller, I gave the address. After having spoken of the course
of the war and dwelt on the fight at Dybbøl fifty years ago,
I said:

``As after an earthquake new vegetation covers the
masses that had collapsed, so has life unfolded
in our country in the last half-hundred years. It is a large
question whether despondency and the feeling of impotence would so
easily have been overcome if the heroic fight had not been
fought. We do not boast, but we have shown that we have the right and
feel the duty to maintain our place and lead our own life.
The work of peace and the memories of war give us the right to it.''

I closed with the following address to the veterans,
who filled all the floor space in the theater and now rose:

``And now I speak to our veterans to bring them
our thanks.

You did not come home with victory. You came home despondent to a
despondent people. One veteran writes: `Quietly we marched
out, and quietly we marched in. We brought no victory with us, but
each of us nevertheless had the conviction of having done
his duty.' Another veteran writes: `The troops were not allowed
to march into the city by the main streets, but had to
steal quietly and unnoticed along the ramparts to their
% --- p. 293 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{293}barracks, as if they had not fully done their duty, but
had reason to be ashamed and to hide themselves!'

What was neglected then, in the time of despondency, shall
today be made good. We salute you, you brave, steadfast and
undaunted men! But the best amends you will receive if
you have the feeling that the country and the people you fought
for were indeed worth striking a blow for. Courage and work will be required
of our people if it is to maintain its place in
the ranks of the nations. But there your tenacious fight and your
love of the fatherland will stand as testimony to the spirit
and the strength that dwell in our people.

What held you up in the time of danger and toil,
that was the innermost of our people's soul, love of the land,
faithfulness to its memories, the wish that it may
keep the freedom to live its own life. What the poet
says of memory --- that it seems as nothing, yet is a
hidden spring --- holds also of love of the fatherland.
It may often seem to have vanished; it is
not always noticed in the busy, scattered course of the day. And yet
it stirs in all honest work, in everything in which we live with
our whole soul, --- so as then to rise with might in the decisive
hours.

So we greet the men who half a century
ago, in dark and heavy days, fought for Denmark's honor and
right! We ask them to keep up their courage with us for a bright
and honorable future for our people, such a future as
they staked their lives to secure!

Honor to the heroes of '64! Honor to the land they fought
for!'' ---

\secrule

Four months after this commemoration had been held, the
World War then broke out, the war that in its effects was to
lead to so joyful an event as the return of South Jutland.
But while the war lasted, hope and fear alternated.
Possibility stood against possibility. Could not Germany's
% --- p. 294 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{294}victory lead to its now, when the motive could not be interpreted
as fear, using the opportunity to come into a conciliatory
relation with its nearest neighbor to the north? There were Germans
who had long and eagerly wished for this. Or were
those right who thought that Germany would now use the
good opportunity to incorporate into itself the neighbor which had indeed
behaved formally correctly during the war, but about
whose real sympathies there could nevertheless be no
doubt? --- If, on the other hand, the Western Powers won, would they
then be eager for us to get South Jutland back, and would
this eagerness have its ground in the principle of nationality or
rather in an arrangement of affairs favorable to these powers
at the Eider Canal? A French journalist who, on an official
mission, traveled through Sweden and Denmark during the war
and had visited me several times, had declared outright
that France did not care at all about the principle of nationality
(it wanted, after all, German-speaking Alsace for itself), but
that the main thing was that the Kiel Canal should pass out of Germany's
dominion. Here at home there were not a few who held fast to
a Denmark to the Eider as the goal; that it would
require extensive use of military force had nothing deterrent
for their way of thinking. There were others who,
since the South German Schleswig had originally been colonized from the south
and had always been nationally German, wished for the Danevirke line,
inspired by the many memories attached to
it, and trusting that there was still a ``subconscious''
Danishness among the population between Flensburg and the Danevirke
that could surface after some time of calm and reflection.

All these possibilities stood against one another. But besides,
the question naturally came up whether Denmark could
accept South Jutland from one of the warring parties
without thereby making itself suspect to the other.
At a meeting at Carlsberg, to which, by arrangement with
colleagues from 4 S, I had invited men of various parties,
the question was discussed whether any Danish
% --- p. 295 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{295}government whatever could refuse to accept South Jutland,
from whichever side it might be offered. The mood was decidedly
for accepting an offer in any case,
especially after H. V. Clausen had shown statistically
that a line could be drawn north of which the population
was overwhelmingly Danish. That was the famous
Clausen line, which indeed was afterwards also taken as the basis,
adopted by the government and the Rigsdag and approved by the victorious
Western Powers. For the time being, however, it was only hopes that
were in question. Then came the November day when Germany
collapsed, and when in its distress it accepted Wilson's
14 Points, among which the self-determination of peoples
also had a place. The consequence of this was drawn in Berlin
at once as regards North Schleswig and Poland; there were to be
no more ``Musspreussere.'' Wilson was a
dreamer, but woven into his dreams was a principle American in the best
sense, the same on which in his
time the brilliant Alexander Hamilton had founded the
American constitution of the Union, and which already lay at
the basis of the American Declaration of Independence: that the state
must have its ultimate foundation in the free choice of the people. Since now
Wilson himself belonged to the Allies who were fighting Germany,
a possibility had here come forward that let the return of South Jutland
by plebiscite stand as
recognized by both of the warring parties. The South Jutland
question itself had also long since passed from
being a question of constitutional law to being a purely national question,
a question of the sentiments of the South Jutland people.

Of course the principle of sentiment would not have been recognized
without the victory of the Allies. But America, which proclaimed
this principle, itself contributed decisively to the victory.
Had America not sent its millions of well-equipped
soldiers across the ocean in the greatest haste,
Marshal Foch could not have gathered the masses of troops with
which in July 1918, to the complete
% --- p. 296 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{296}surprise of the Germans, he broke out of the woods of Villers-Cotterets and thereby
brought about the decisive turn.

True enough, not all Schleswigers of Danish sentiment came
along. That is a sting that remains, even in those
who consider the solution accomplished to be the only possible
and the only just one. Had the plebiscite boundary been set
farther south, such a majority as was desirable would not have been
reached. Here we suffer for the sins of our forefathers.
They were more taken up with supposed constitutional law than with
what is really decisive in the life of a people. Now
it was a matter of salvaging the part of the old Danish duchy
of Schleswig that had remained Danish and would continue
to be so. In a plebiscite the will of the majority must, after all,
be decisive. North of the boundary drawn
there is a German minority that will strive to preserve
its nationality, essentially by using, under the mild Danish
rule, the means the Danish Schleswigers
used under German pressure. And south of the boundary there is
a Danish minority, practiced in living under foreign rule,
which now, under the German republican constitution,
has better conditions than before. ---

I have wished here to set out how the matter stood
for me after the many years of observation and work. With
deliberate purpose I supported, as far as I could, the work of Hanssen-Nørremølle
and H. V. Clausen. Great recognition these men
did not exactly receive for their work. With many
here at home it had become an article of faith that Denmark should reach
to the Eider, or at any rate to the Danevirke. What one
should then do with the hundreds of thousands of Germans one would
get along with it, one heard nothing about. For my part
it had long been clear to me that all we could and
ought to wish for was to get Als and Sundeved along with it. And even
here I had, as I expressed it in a statement to the press, had
a hope indeed, but not really a faith in the fulfillment of the wish.
But there is here at home, in both national and religious
respects, a superstition about faith. Accordingly, when
% --- p. 297 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{297}the statement to the press had appeared, I received an anonymous letter (from a
lady),\footnote[1]{If one could get statistics on anonymous letters, it would surely turn out that they are predominantly written by women. They have more need than men to vent their feelings in this way. When I had been chosen for the ``Honorary Residence,'' I received an anonymous letter which ``in the name of all Danish women'' called on me to decline the election, --- because I was not a ``believer.'' One of the anonymous letters I received during the political strife of the eighties had, however, a decidedly masculine tone; I was threatened that I ``would get a thrashing some evening, all right.''} which began thus: ``Poor Professor Høffding,
how poor you must be!'' --- As if hope were not
rich when it inspires to serious endeavor (which faith,
which easily becomes fatalistic, does not always do).

Before the plebiscite I was chairman of two meetings in
the Town Hall, where the main speakers were Hanssen-Nørremølle
and Nis Nissen, those two stout leaders of the South Jutlanders.
There was an excellent mood at these meetings.
Various interruptions from one particular quarter were answered
with great quickness, schooled as both speakers were through
meetings with Pan-Germans. The morning before the first meeting
I received a letter from a lady (this time, however, not anonymous),
who wondered that I, who had hitherto had nothing
to do with the South Jutland question, should now come forward. This
gave me occasion to state in my introductory words
that I had now for 33 years seriously occupied myself with
this question. --- Later I chaired a meeting in Grundtvig's
House, where Nis Nissen also spoke. My introductory words
there gave Kloppenborg-Skrumsager (an excellent
man, but inclined to confuse himself with Uffe
the Meek) occasion to say (in Flensborg Avis) that now
I had stood there and disowned the fine thoughts I had expressed in
my youth, --- and that merely to please the Germans!
--- On the whole that side has denied itself nothing.
But I ought not to have mentioned such things here at all,
when I see how men like Hanssen-Nørremølle
and H. V. Clausen have been treated. And then
all this pettiness vanishes before the great experience these
% --- p. 298 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{298}years have brought all Danes. Not least for the old, who
remember the pain of the separation, it has been a glory
to live to have this experience.

\secrule

When I left the University, I had plans and drafts
for various works, which I now meant to use my
leisure to carry out. Alongside my activity in the Red
Cross it was this that occupied me in the following
years. I found at Carlsberg a good place to work, where
there were not only glorious rooms and a splendid garden, but
where it was as if it lay in the air that work should be done. I
gave up the thought of continuing my laboratory teaching,
since I was reluctant to put my special work entirely
aside a few days a week in order to be able to prepare
for the classes. For the same reason I declined an invitation I
received in February 1915 from the University of Glasgow to give
lectures on the philosophy of religion for two semesters (the
so-called Gifford Lectures). I excused myself on the ground of my
72 years and of my wish for full otium. The most
weighty reason, however, was that I had in my time published my
philosophy of religion, which had been translated into a whole series of
foreign languages, English among them, and that I now had more
inclination for psychological, epistemological and historical-philosophical
subjects. In addition, although in the deed of foundation of
the Gifford Trust no dogmatic conditions whatever had been laid down,
most Gifford lectures had nevertheless been
given in a more so-called ``positive'' direction than I, from
my psychological-historical point of view, could take.
Finally I was also doubtful about my English, which
could pass tolerably in a single lecture, but could hardly
be offered to an audience over several months. ---
I missed a fee that was almost a small fortune.
But then I could sit in peace at Carlsberg, where
I was indeed well provided for. ---

The works I have completed here at Carlsberg fall
% --- p. 299 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{299}into three groups: psychological (Den store Humor. 1916; Oplevelse
og Tydning 1918), epistemological (Totalitet
som Kategori. 1917; Relation som Kategori. 1921) and historical-philosophical
(Spinoza's Ethica. 1918; Om Platon's Parmenider.
1920; Ledende Tanker i det 19. Aarhundrede 1920).
Only on the occasion of ``den store Humor'' will I here make
some remarks.

In the book I have sufficiently indicated for a careful reader
(especially at the end of ch. 6) that I do not dare to regard
myself as a humorist in the sense in which I
take the word. I can only say that I wish I were
one. And by a reference to an earlier passage in the book
I have indicated where the essential hindrance for me
has lain, namely in the hypochondria (Acedia) which in
Dante is punished by wallowing in the mire of Hell. Nevertheless I believe
that it is not without connection with my nature that the subject
has had so great an attraction for me. A striving
to unite the great and the small in life in the way that lies in the concept of humor
has perhaps lain in my
nature. My friend from youth Hans Skovgaard writes from his
vicarage (March 1915): ``Now that you are writing your
memoirs, you must regard yourself as something valuable
and at the same time have your amusement in finding
it comic that such a one as you should really belong
to the totality. Humor is for you something genuine
and familiar, so that you need not explain it with effort,
but can paint it from the bottom of your heart as a
totality that is also glad of small things.'' --- In the same
letter he himself jests in a humorous way about his
legs, worn by hardening of the arteries, and adds: ``I now hobble
about in wooden shoes here in Kettinge village, or rock along
the snowy road in my old carriage and blink at the sun and
find that it is a sublime idea heaven has had when it
hit upon turning water into the pure white snow and
making the whole landscape a residence of honor.'' The year after, when
the book on humor had come out, he writes: ``The book is
% --- p. 300 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{300}written out of yourself, so that I know you well in
the book.''

I think I have the right to use my old friend's
testimony, even if it goes further than I myself would and
could express myself. --- Things went downhill, moreover, for this same old
friend. For my birthday in 1918 he writes: ``I can hardly
hold on to a pen, nor to a thought.'' --- Skovgaard
retired in 1919 and moved to Copenhagen. And
in February 1920 he died, while I was at the Red Cross
meeting in Geneva. He did not have so good an old age as
I. But his faithfulness and his understanding he kept
to the last. ---

Another friend, whom I count among the old ones, although his
friendship is of much later date than Skovgaard's, Professor
Valdemar Vedel, wrote on the occasion of the book on humor,
among other things: ``There is, after all, a need to keep the multiplicity
and the oppositions unresolved, unleveled --- a
feeling of richness and freedom, a feeling of openness; one wants to
let existence play freely.'' This significant remark
points to a danger that is present in every
formation of wholes within mental life, in the sphere of feeling as well
as of thought. But I think that the book itself
makes all the necessary reservations. Humor itself presupposes
precisely that there is a multiplicity that cannot be overcome,
and that one must essentially let stand as it is. But
in order to be able to assert oneself against it --- in order to be able to
``let existence play freely'' --- one must, as in great
humor, have a deep and serious background, a stronghold that
keeps one from being split. I have even required that humor
should take itself humorously, namely by
realizing that it is not the only competent way of taking
life. ---

On the occasion of the book on the leading ideas of the 19th century
I had an interesting letter from Georg Brandes,
who after some appreciative words stated that in his
sphere he had come to a result similar to mine in
% --- p. 301 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{301}mine: ``Although the world of thought is not foreign to me, I am
not at home in it, and my interests and endeavors
have had to gather around art, where the century
does indeed also stand out with a clear distinctive character, even if perhaps
it has not reached the very highest heights there either.'' --- He
closed with the following statement: ``The World War has driven
a good deal of confidence in what has been achieved out of its entrenchments.
We, like the insect, crawl up a wall, fall down
when the top edge is reached, and begin all over again. Fortunately
you have not (any more than I) lost your zest for work and
your resilience.''

\secrule

In one of the last years in which I lectured at the University, a
young woman student, Agnete Bertram, came out to me after
a lecture I had given on Spinoza. She was
much taken with Spinoza's thoughts, which for the first time
came before her. Quietly her own thoughts had
moved in the same direction, but she now found a
clear expression for the union of a sense of reality and an
ideal view that she was longing for. I offered to go through
Spinoza's chief work with her, she using
an English translation. Later we read some of
my own books, and she also took part in my laboratory classes.
She was a great help to me in preparing
my works, not least the book on humor, through her
apt and independent remarks. Philosophy, however, was
not her chief interest; this was concentrated for the time being
on Danish literature, which she studied under Vilhelm
Andersen. Danish she had chosen as her main subject; her
subsidiary subjects were English and gymnastics. But she was a
Renaissance nature, with a great need to develop her powers,
although she was not yet clear in which direction
her gifts lay. From her earliest youth her
interest went in an artistic direction, and she sometimes regretted
that she had not taken the way of art. I owe
her an extraordinary amount, because she opened my eyes to
% --- p. 302 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{302}nuances of color and form to which I had hitherto been blind.
Both on walks and before works of art she taught
me to observe and enjoy quite differently than before. She
also developed my sense for poetry, especially while I
read together with her some of the English poetical works
she had set down for her examination. More and more, however, her
interest gathered around gymnastics, especially through Professor
Lindhard's lectures, in which he demanded that
gymnastics, namely women's gymnastics, be built up on a
strictly physiological and anatomical basis. Previously
there had been only one kind of gymnastics, the masculine, which
was without further ado regarded as applicable to women. Agnete
Bertram's need to unite the artistic with
the rational could here find satisfaction. She
worked out Lindhard's theory, when her examination studies were finished,
practically and artistically, and she soon found
much support among young women, who with enthusiasm
took part in exercises that at once satisfied
the need for healthy muscular functions and the need for harmony
and plasticity in movement. It was a joy to me to
give room in Carlsberg's colonnade hall (``Pompeii'') for such
exercises, on one occasion also for a public display.
The fresh and perfectly formed movements and the participants'
beautiful antique costumes suited well the Greek columns of
``Pompeii.'' And the life that on exercise days filled the
otherwise so quiet Honorary Residence, when the young ladies moved about
upstairs and down, with jest and laughter, was refreshing for an
old professor.

More and more Agnete Bertram has since extended her teaching,
so that it takes all her time. She is wholly
absorbed in her art, and she is also working on setting forth
its theory.

I shall never forget what she has been to me in the
years when she could give me a part of her time, and I follow
her on her way with its sense for the demands of nature and
of harmony, which I owe it to her to have gained.

% --- p. 303 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{303}Now that I, in my eightieth year, conclude these
memoirs, it is with conflicting feelings that I look back
on what I have set down in this book. Was it
worth writing all this down? Have I not talked too much
about myself? And on the other hand, have I managed
fully to express my gratitude for what life
has brought me, for the people I have known and loved,
for the world of thought that has opened itself to me, and
in which it is an honor to be merely the humblest servant?

Were I to answer these questions, I should never
be finished, and the answer might perhaps lead me
to discard the whole thing. So I set them aside, trusting
that perhaps one or another may yet find interest, and perhaps
instruction, in following how I have worked in the face of
the problems of life and of thought.

My philosophical development will, I hope, be understood
through what I have related of my youth and then of
my later studies.\footnote[1]{I have given a fuller account of this in the essay on my work as an author, reprinted in \textit{Religiøse Tanketyper} (1927).} I find two decisive points of departure,
Søren Kierkegaard's principle of personality and
the positivism of Comte and Spencer. Here lie the most significant
influences I have received. (I take the occasion
to state that Comte in his time worked more strongly on
me than Spencer). Through these two influences the
task was set me on which I have worked through my
principal works (Psykologi --- Etik --- Religionsfilosofi ---
Den menneskelige Tanke). I myself find less and less
any irreconcilable opposition between personal striving
and scientific thinking.

In recent years my philosophy has several times been made
the subject of doctoral dissertations (I know of two French and one German).
It is especially my philosophy of religion that has been discussed.
And sometimes the authors concerned have tried to
construct my development, without my quite being able
to recognize myself in it. The most significant attempt
% --- p. 304 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{304}has been made by the Swiss Jean de la Harpe, who has undertaken
a critical investigation of the relation between my philosophy of religion
and my philosophy as a whole. (La Religion comme
conservation de la valeur dans ses rapports avec la philosophie
générale de Harald Høffding. Lausanne et Paris.
1920). In a longish letter to the author I had every reason
to thank him for his interest in my writings
and for the clear and accurate exposition of my fundamental ideas,
while I could not agree with him that there was
a ``dualism'' between my doctrine of the possibility of religion
in the sense of faith in the persistence of value and my
philosophy as a whole. But in particular I had to object
to his construction of my development. I wrote
to him as follows: ``You confuse the kinship with other philosophers,
after my development was essentially complete, with
influence from these philosophers during my development itself.
I conceive the history of philosophy as a great dialogue,
and when I myself attempted to interject a reply
into this dialogue, I naturally had to take account
of earlier replies in the same direction (especially Spinoza
and Kant, from whose influence the authors thought they could
derive two opposed tendencies in my philosophy). But it does not
follow from this that these earlier replies motivated
my reply from the start. As regards Spinoza in particular, I have
always stood critical toward him. I saw early that on
essential points he ends in a faith. (On this see Den menneskelige
Tanke. p. 140). My `monism' I have not from
Spinoza, but from a purely psychological investigation of
how we convince ourselves of reality (see the section
in my Psykologi on `Opfattelsen af det Virkelige'). All
science begins with, and is at bottom throughout,
only a consistent extension of the practical criterion of reality.
My `monism' consists in my assuming
lawlike connection as the expression of reality;
but my monism is `critical', because the work of finding
and carrying through such a connection has not been
% --- p. 305 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{305}completed and probably never will be. As regards my philosophy of religion
in particular, you seem to overlook that on my view
all scientific study of religion is psychological
and historical. My special theory is that all social and individual
religion and religiosity, on closer analysis, proves
to be a faith in the persistence of value, and that
such a faith can in fact persist even if the time of the positive religions
should be past ..... In my doctrine of categories (in
`Den menneskelige Tanke' 1910) I have sought to show
how concepts of value relate to the other categories.
Especially the connection between the two concepts
totality and value is of great importance here, which I have later
developed further in a treatise on the concept of totality
(1917).'' --- This last treatise Dr.~la
Harpe did not know, since it was only later translated into German.
But a connection between totality and value in fact
underlies all my writings on ethics from
1876 onward, although only in ``Den menneskelige Tanke'' have I expressly
demonstrated it. I cannot go further here
into this question. I fear that this autobiography
already contains too much philosophy. ---

People in daily life owe more than they suspect
to the philosophers' labor of thought. But it is through many
intermediate links and essentially indirectly that the significance of philosophy
makes itself felt. Philosophy has, as my old teacher
Sibbern puts it, an ``intermediary'' (mediate) significance
for life. Every human being has his philosophy of life, whether
he knows it or not. For no one, whatever faith or
unbelief he may otherwise have, can do without thoughts that order
his experiences, guide his actions and awaken new
striving. Such thoughts arise under the influence of
all sides of mental life and are determined partly by tradition,
partly by one's own experiences. Through many intermediate links
such a philosophy of life stands in interaction with philosophy in the stricter
sense. Even in the greatest and strictest philosophers
one will be able to demonstrate the influence of their involuntarily
% --- p. 306 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{306}formed philosophy of life, besides the fact that this itself is altered through
their work on giving their thoughts scientific form.
It has made a strong impression on me to see that
even Plato (in the seventh Letter) has declared that there is a difference
between his philosophy, accessible to all and scientifically formulated,
and ``that which his striving really concerns''.
Perhaps, though, Plato, vexed at dilettantes' boasting
of insight into his fundamental thought, stresses this difference more strongly
than is right. But it is true that here we in the end stand
before something incommensurable, because it is at once
inexhaustible and complex. Here the old saying can be applied,
that from the gods we learn to be silent, from men to
speak. And the gods are right in the end. ---

At bottom it is hard going to live. I sympathize with
Schiller's words: ``Herb ist des Lebens innerster Kern''. There
is so much that is heavy and sluggish in us and outside us, and in
the struggle to overcome it one cannot always sing.
Yet --- there are other elements in the drink that life pours out
than the bitter ones, and I praise life because I too have
had them mixed in. When all is said, it is a
strengthening drink that is handed to us, precisely through this mixture.
Perhaps there are also elements in the drink
that we have not yet been able to distinguish.

In my personal faith I go straight to that which, from all
I have been able to understand, underlies all faith,
to the assurance that Ingemann has expressed in ``Sangen om
Livet'' thus: ``Yet the spring of life wells up where eternally it
sprang.''
% Dog Livets Kilde springer, hvor evig den sprang.
All conceptions of gods and of an existence other
than the one we know from experience are in the end only
symbols of the assurance that the sources of value in existence
will never dry up. I do not feel alone in this faith,
but in inward communion with all earnest and inward
souls, even if many of them cannot find their dogmas again
in me. I understand well that many find only in the inherited
religious conceptions that on which they can
lay their head.

% --- p. 307 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{307}I can best express my relation to such people
by setting down here a letter I once wrote to a lady
I was very fond of, and who was much taken with the religious
movement called the Inner Mission. She had
had much to struggle with in her life and had shown herself
a brave little person. My acquaintance with her came
from her being married to a brother of my late wife.
Both have long since died. The occasion for the letter was
that she had sent me an edifying book that had made
a strong impression on her, and with lovable naivety she hoped
now that it would have an effect on me that was good in her eyes.
--- The letter, whose draft I have found among
my papers, ran as follows:

\whiteline

``Dear Laura, It is out of your loving disposition, which you have so
often shown toward me, that you sent me the book I
now send back, and especially that you sent me the good letter
that came with it. I confess that the letter was dearer to me than
the book. It is not easy for me to explain myself, but since you
are fond of me and have confidence in me, you must believe me
when I say that if I have come away from so many
thoughts that are so much to you and also \textit{have been} so
to me, I dare confidently say that it has happened because
truth, so far as I could see it, has always been
sacred to me, and that I, if I would not deny what is innermost
in me, had to go the way I have gone. It is simply so
that the ways are different for different people. I do not take
life lightly, and I see clearly the dangers that threaten
many souls when doubt comes. I never awaken
doubt when it is not in the sacred service of truth.

As things have gone, I dare say that life has become greater
and richer for me, and that courage and the desire to take it up and
work not only for myself but also for others have
grown in me.

But, dear Laura, wherever I feel that a sincere
mental life is stirring, there is my sympathy. And perhaps in
% --- p. 308 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{308}no one have I felt it as in my little sister-in-law in Aarhus,
whose striving I have followed through the years. Can we
not meet here, even if our striving after truth leads
us along different ways? That hope I never give up with regard to
those I am fond of.''

[The letter must have been written around 1900].

\secrule

A philosophy of personality is very well possible without dogmas.
This holds especially of the dogma of personal immortality.
Very early the conviction dawned on me that there
could be much of value in existence even if my
personal immortality did not belong to what is valuable,
and I have not noticed that my zeal to find, develop
and spread values in the world, my work for what
is true, beautiful and great, has thereby been weakened. I know
dead times; but should not those who have all the rubrics of dogmatics
filled in also know them? My position
here is expressed in what, according to Johannes Fibiger's autobiography,
I am supposed once to have said in a conversation with him: if
there is a personal immortality, we will of course come to experience
it. Whether there is, we know just as little as we know how
old we shall become. In any case we cannot form any
conception whatsoever of it. On this point I make
Wilhelm von Humboldt's words my own: ``Human
conceptions of immortality I will not form; and
others I cannot form.'' --- Modern belief in immortality
has, not only outside the Church, gradually become a
meager conception, most often built on a slender spiritualism.
I better understand the mighty visions of primitive Christianity
of judgment and the end of the world. But if they are to hold,
the whole of life must be laid out quite differently from how it is now led
inside and outside the Church. --- A longing or need in the direction
of immortality I have never felt. Nor, when
it fell to my lot to close the eyes of people
I had loved, had I felt the need for a reunion, which for many
% --- p. 309 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{309}is the essential motive for believing in an immortality.
There is, after all, a tragedy of life. Losses are suffered, an
emptiness is left behind that only work and striving forward
can remedy. --- In the hope of reunion an unsavory
coziness often asserts itself. It affects me
as when people in the theater chat together at the most moving
places in the play. Far better do I understand the
great Scholastic Thomas Aquinas when he says that
in the other world there will be such glory to behold
that one is wholly absorbed in it and cannot think of oneself
or look to see whether one has got all one's good friends along
up there.

\whiteline

Let us really bring forward the idea of personality, and let us then
have testimonies about life and about spiritual need that are really
founded on independent experience of life and not
on adaptations to old traditions, which yet themselves
in the end arose in this way!

\whiteline

There has been no lack even of rather pressing appeals
from younger people to raise a storm against Church and theology.
But precisely because I adhere to the principle of personality,
that is in my eyes not the way to go. What matters,
rather, is indirectly, in Socratic fashion, to get people to
think for themselves. Besides, the history of religion shows,
not least the history of Christianity, that reinterpretations
of the religious traditions are constantly going on, so that
the actual and personal faith involuntarily becomes another
than the official one. And here it is personal experiences that
determine the reinterpretations. Spiritual changes take place
slowly when they are to be thorough. Many inconsistencies
and half-measures follow from this in particulars; but
when life does not stand still, a need to get beyond them
will stir again and again.

Nevertheless many things may suggest that a
prophet is needed, a great, free human being who can teach us courage and
% --- p. 310 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{310}honesty and integrity in our thoughts about life. He will
surely not pull his punches. I for my part
have, as I once had occasion to say in a polemic concerning great
men, only been a poor
professor, not a prophet. And big words are ridiculous
in the mouths of small men.

\secrule

Every morning I sit in one of the large rooms at Carlsberg
facing three of Thorvaldsen's most beautiful works: Morning,
Hebe and Night. ``Morning'' does not make much impression
on me. Of the roses she scatters it holds for me
that their time is past. To Hebe I devote my daily cult,
hope for a drink from her cup, and promise to be
true to her as long as there is life in me. ``Night'' I look
toward as to a woman friend who at last arranges the pillow
on my bed. As yet I know only one of the children
she carries in her arms, but when the other child's lot
becomes mine, I hope to find rest like it.

\hfill{\footnotesize Finished 15 March 1922.}\par

% --- p. 311 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\chapter*{VIII}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{VIII. 1922--1924}
\markboth{VIII. 1922--1924}{VIII. 1922--1924}
\opage{311}More than two years have passed since I wrote what I thought
was to be the conclusion of my memoirs. I cannot
say that since that time I have lived in the thought of the
motherly embrace on which, according to Thorvaldsen's relief, even
Death can lean, and which I mentioned in the last words
I wrote then. Brighter moods have made themselves felt,
productive moods too. One of our authors,
who in his somewhat older days believes he has won
an infallible religious standpoint, declared last year that ``the old
man at Carlsberg'' must now be full of days, and,
as was delicately hinted, of spiritual striving as well. I
by no means feel hit by such words. Already when
I concluded the preceding section of the memoirs in March 1922,
I had in mind a continuation of the works on the theory of knowledge
in which I had sought to develop further
some points of view in my principal work ``Den menneskelige
Tanke''. And my subject this time was a concept
that had long underlain my thoughts on
life and science, on religion and poetry, without my having
seen it as clearly as it now presented itself to me. It was
the concept of analogy, which I now undertook to investigate in
earnest, with regard to its significance in the various
domains and in the relation between these domains. I
had long been aware that, not only in religious
conceptions, but also in natural science, in philosophy
and in so-called common sense, a confusion of identity and analogy
occurs again and again. But of
% --- p. 312 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{312}special significance to me now were Niels Bohr's electron physics
and Hjelmslev's geometrical investigations. Through
these works I got the best possible examples of the role of analogy
in science too, where the relation
between observation and interpretation is concerned, or where the
relation of scientific domains to one another is concerned. I
had long ago been led to the conviction that
the relation between the physiological and the psychological conception of
human nature could, strictly speaking, only be called
analogy. Likewise it was clear to me that the relation between
examples of the same concept was a relation of analogy.
Finally it was a fundamental idea in my philosophy of religion that
all religious conceptions are due to analogies that the human
mind is led to form under the influence of its
experiences of life. In a treatise on the concept of analogy, which
I presented to the Royal Danish Academy of Sciences shortly before my eightieth
birthday, I have sought to develop these
points of view, besides others I had become aware
of. This treatise, which appeared in Danish in 1923 and in
German the following year, will form the conclusion of
my work in the theory of knowledge. At any rate no ideas have
so far turned up that could lead to a continuation
of this work. --- In June 1923 three
hundred years had passed since Pascal's birth, and Xavier Léon, the editor
of ``Revue de Métaphysique et de Morale'', asked me
on that occasion to write an essay on Pascal and Kierkegaard
for the Festschrift his Revue was to publish. The subject
was not new to me. I had often immersed myself in Pascal,
especially once the splendid edition of his works that Brunschwicg
and others had produced was available. Likewise what is
analogous in the positions of the two great religious thinkers had struck me.
I had often, when I had to explain Kierkegaard's standpoint
to a Frenchman, called him le Pascal danois. On
renewed investigation the parallels between the two
men in their relation to the religious problem increased, and I came
through this back once more to my own conception of the
% --- p. 313 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{313}relation between religion and human culture, which had
developed chiefly under the influence of Kierkegaard. The essay
was printed both in Danish (in ``Tilskueren'') and in
French. It is perhaps the one of my works with which I have most
right to be satisfied from a purely literary point of view (which
perhaps does not mean much).\footnote[1]{Reprinted 1927 in ``Religiøse Tanketyper''. [Later note].}

In recent years I have also been rather occupied with
translation of my works. The essay ``Oplevelse
og Tydning'' (the first of the essays in the Danish
book of that name) was translated into German by a German
man of letters who for some time was staying in this country. On the other hand
I myself translated the analogy treatise and, at the request
of the Societas Spinozana, the essay published in 1918,
``Spinoza's Ethica''. It has especially pleased me
that under the title ``La Relativité philosophique'' a French
translation of my essays on totality
and on relation is now being printed. Here I stand in a debt of gratitude to
the French philosopher Emile Meyerson, with whom in
recent years, by reason of my works on the theory of knowledge,
I have come into lively and constant correspondence.

In general it has been a joy to me in recent years
to notice interest in my philosophizing in France and to make
the personal acquaintance of excellent French thinkers.
In 1906 I made the acquaintance of Emile Boutroux in Aberdeen,
where we were both guests at the University jubilee.
Afterwards in 1909 I met him and his charming wife
(the sister of the mathematician Poincaré) in Geneva, likewise at
a University jubilee, and finally he was, accompanied by his
wife, in Copenhagen in 1913, invited by the University to
give lectures. Later I was in contact with
him right up to his death. Even earlier I had come to know
Léon Brunschwicg (now Professor at the Sorbonne)
and continued to be in fruitful contact with him. He
has visited me in Copenhagen, and I him in Paris. The closest
relation I have come to have with Émile Meyerson, whose works in the
% --- p. 314 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{314}theory of knowledge are the most significant to have appeared
in recent years. He wrote to me for the first time in
the year 1918, when he had found points of contact between
his conception and mine. It is owing, as I said, to his interest
in my works that two of them can now appear in
French. The correspondence with Meyerson in recent years has
been and is a great encouragement to me. We have discussed
several important points where our views went in somewhat
different directions. In my essays of recent years
one will find more information about this. Common to us was
that we had an eye for the irrational remainder that, however far
knowledge advances, is left over, precisely when
one applies a strictly rational standard. The great
warmth with which Meyerson in his letters speaks
of the impression he has got of me through my works
has pleased me quite exceedingly.

Meyerson comes from Poland, lived his youth in
Germany, but has since lived in France for over 40 years.
In Germany he studied natural science; only in France
did he begin to philosophize. His rich knowledge of natural science
makes it easy for him to illustrate his ideas in the theory of knowledge
by apt examples, which he analyzes
in masterly fashion. He finds it interesting that
he and I agree to so high a degree in our views,
since we have yet come to philosophy from very different
sides, he essentially from natural science and its
history, I from psychological and ethical-religious problems.
He has never been a teacher of philosophy, but has held an
official post, from which he retired in 1921 at the
age of 63. His health has been weak in recent years,
and there is unfortunately not much prospect that he,
as he has repeatedly announced, will be able to come to
Copenhagen to continue our written discussion through conversation.
It would be a very great joy to me to see
him here.

With much interest and understanding he expressed himself last year
% --- p. 315 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{315}about my essay on Pascal and Kierkegaard. Only
he did not quite agree with me when at the end I pointed
to Plato's harmonious concept of personality as the point of departure
we should hold to. He sympathizes most
with ``philosophers who, like Kant, have been influenced by
the Bible''. He feels a spiritual kinship with Deutero-Isaiah.
This he himself explains by his being a Jew; but
he thinks that those who have come from Christian families
will feel something similar toward the New Testament. Our
connection with the Greeks is, he thinks, purely intellectual,
but our moral nature leads back to Judaea. Yet
he remarks in conclusion that the difference between him and
me is not great on this point either, since I hold that
the Greek spiritual tendency had to be deepened and widened through
later spiritual currents, among others Christianity.

The friendship this thorough and spirited scholar has
shown toward me has been a good support to me
in recent years.

\secrule

The preparatory work for the essay on Pascal and Kierkegaard
renewed for me the problem of my youth, which, however,
had not in the meantime been out of my thoughts. Even
after I had found and worked through the position
on this problem that I, according to my experience and my understanding,
had to take, there was still always occasion to
think about what it could be that held most
people fast in the established Church. Here I could naturally
reach only an indefinite estimate. The main thing for me was
that there constantly stirred a need to live in great images,
in which the fundamental mood that experience of life and its
great contrasts awakened found expression, a need that one
did not feel satisfied by what science and art
could bring. This need expresses itself in many forms
and degrees and can seek expression in many different
ways. But for most people there is laid down in the church tradition,
into which they are led early, a great poetry of life,
% --- p. 316 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{316}beside which all that they can find themselves pales. At the same time
there stirs, especially in times like ours, a need to have
something to hold on to amid the swell of life, and such a
hold was easiest to find in the church's dogmas and
the church's cult. Much suggests that cult (especially
hymn-singing), even in Protestantism, plays a greater role
than preaching.

For me myself the problem had from my youth essentially
been determined by the conflict between the ethics of primitive Christianity
and modern Christianity's attempt to
fuse cultural and social interest with religious
ethics. The so-called People's Church meant, from this point of view,
a great compromise, which the Church's representatives would not
face. In the correspondence between Otto Møller
and Skat Rørdam this comes out in a particularly naive
way. --- Studies in the history of religion show that the same
problem makes itself felt within all great positive religions
in the relation between a founding time, which constantly
stands as the ideal, and later times, in which people have
accommodated themselves to the demands of a life constantly advancing.
This holds for Buddhism and Mohammedanism as well as
for Christianity. This historical consideration,
which neither Pascal nor Kierkegaard entered into, made it
easier for me to understand what went on within
church life.

I had, however, sometimes thought of withdrawing from
the People's Church. Especially when a gifted and deeply religiously moved
lady was declared by the Supreme Court not entitled to take part
in elections to the parish council because she was a Unitarian,
I felt it as an inconsistency that on the census list
I still entered myself as belonging to the People's Church, since
my standpoint was further from the People's Church's than the Unitarian one.
But I could not put up with the ridiculous custom
that one had to appear in person before the parish priest to
withdraw. --- A couple of years ago the question came
up again for me in a somewhat different form. The proceedings
% --- p. 317 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{317}before the elections of bishops were not edifying, and through
the parish councils and the way in which they were
elected the road must necessarily be barred for many young,
independently inquiring men to become teachers within
the Church. Orthodoxy is, according to an observation many have
made, stiffer among laymen than among theologians. I then made
the decision to withdraw, and informed in writing
the parish priest in my parish of this. It went simply enough.
On the back of my baptismal certificate it was merely written that I no longer
belonged to the People's Church. The step I here took, I took
as a Danish citizen, out of dissatisfaction with a Danish
institution, not really for religious reasons. ---

I cannot refrain from mentioning a small example of
how the Church, as someone has put it, drags along the
impossible so as not to lose the necessary. A couple of years ago
two little girls (aged 12---14) came out
to me. I did not know them, but presumably they had
heard that at Carlsberg there lived a man who had among other things
speculated about religion. On two fine slips of paper
with gilt edges they brought a series of questions that the school's
religious instruction had raised in them. They
were friends; the one was visiting the other during the holidays,
and they had now lain awake at night discussing the problems.
When I had talked with them a little, I was struck by
the seriousness, partly indignation, with which they regarded
the doubts that had arisen in them. I shall not go through
all the questions here; there were some I did not go
into. Most of the questions came from Bible history. How
could, e.g., Cain fear that people he met
would kill him: there were of course no other people than
Adam and Eve! The teacher had merely said to this that it
stood in the Bible and so one must believe it. Nor, indeed, has
the Church said definitely when the content of the Bible is to be taken
literally and when it is poetry. My answer was that
the biblical stories were the old legends of the Jewish people,
in which one still found so much that is beautiful that one constantly
% --- p. 318 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{318}returned to them. With this answer the younger of my
guests was not satisfied, however. We too have old forefathers,
she said, so why do we keep to the legends of the Jews
instead of using our own? --- The elder of the
young girls, who seemed to have a poetic mind, while the
logical was more developed in the younger, was especially dissatisfied
with the story of creation. It was too mechanical for her;
things were created from outside. Was it not more beautiful to
think that things developed, just as a flower
grows, so that one form unfolds from the other?
--- The conversation showed me how religious instruction
can crush both the child's logical sense and its poetic sense,
when it is carried on as, on the Church's official presuppositions,
it really must be carried on. --- I was much taken up
with the conversation with the young girls and tried to manage as
well as I could on Socratic principles. Later
I had several visits from the elder (the younger
had come down with a long illness). She told me that they now
had got a new teacher who did not take things so heavy-handedly,
and besides, she had now realized that
