many of the questions that had troubled them they must
leave alone until they could discuss them on their own.

\secrule

Now and then the memory of the time when I read with the
young students has come up in me, and when Professor
Frithiof Brandt a couple of years ago proposed that I
give a lecture to his audience, the desire for
a repetition was awakened. I used a part of a work I
had in hand, and spoke about the relation between natural science
and the human sciences. I was well received and
had great joy of this attempt. I repeated it the year
after and spoke then on ``Videnskab og Livsanskuelse'', a
lecture that will be printed in ``Vor Ungdom''. But
on other occasions too I came to speak to the young. Two
years running I have taken part in the meetings that the association
% --- p. 319 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
``\opage{319}Norden'' held at Hindsgavl for young students or for
teachers, men and women, from the Nordic countries. Hindsgavl
is one of the most beautiful places in Denmark. The glorious garden
goes down to the Little Belt with its wood-wreathed shores, and
here it was a joy to me to move among the young people
and get an impression of what occupied them. My
subjects at these gatherings were: ``Søren Kierkegaard'',
``Holberg som Populærfilosof'' and Troels Lund's
book ``Bakkehus og Solbjerg''. This last subject gave me
a welcome opportunity to speak about the poetry of life
in which, I believe, the attempts at a concentrated
conception of life must in the end issue. Later (in the autumn of 1923)
I received from some students a request to give a
series of lectures on the philosophy of religion. I then gave
lectures on this subject in the garden room at Carlsberg
for a circle of some thirty-odd young listeners. One of
the hours was used to answer questions put
orally by listeners, and the last hour was used
to answer written questions (of which one was especially
acute and penetrating). After the end of the
last hour refreshments were taken and there was strolling in
the winter garden. ---

The student meeting at Hindsgavl in 1922 was the occasion of
an acquaintance that came to be of special significance for me. I
fell into conversation with a woman student from Stockholms
Högskola, Greta Ellstam, about the mysticism of the Middle Ages, which
from different points of view interested us both, in her
case both from the religious and from the purely
historical side, in mine especially from the psychological
side. In the course of our conversations I noticed that
she was on the way to Catholicism. I took good care not
to intervene directly in what was moving in her mind,
but tried by various routes to stress the importance of
the step she seemed about to take. Besides
the history of religion she also studied the history of literature and
spoke with enthusiasm and understanding of poetic works
% --- p. 320 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{320}she had immersed herself in. During our continued friendship
she has been exceedingly much to me through
the two great interests she thus cherished, and which both
have deep roots in her personality. We could meet
in spirited poetic works, even if we still interpreted them
each in our own way. This was so, e.g., with Geijer's little
poem ``Nathimlen'', where the poet speaks of how, of the love
that passes through the world, a ray has fallen into
his soul. She could well sympathize with my interpretation
of this glorious poem as an expression of the often so
narrow stream of values of life; the ray we both believed,
each for ourselves, that we experienced, but about the stream we were of different
faith. My young friend's religious interest soon carried
her over to Catholicism, and she even entertained
thoughts of entering a convent. In the following winter she took part
with great zeal in the Catholic service in Stockholm.
In spite of her bodily weakness she went fasting every morning
to Mass. This had to stop when one morning she fainted
in the church. I had thought that I should never see
or hear anything of her again after her conversion.
But then at Christmas 1922 I received a letter from her, in which
she tells of the course of her studies, and in which it
also shone through that she was beginning to feel the conversion
as an unsatisfying step. Her studies in the history of religion
had led her to immerse herself in the
Indian Upanishads, those remarkable works in which
inward mysticism and keen thinking met in so peculiar
a manner. By this route thoughts had come
into her mind that could not be reconciled with the Church's
cult and dogmatics. She also thinks that the study of my
Religionsfilosofi in the course of the autumn has had an influence
on her mind. There was a clear change to be
noticed when she visited me at Easter 1923, and especially when
she spent her summer holidays at Carlsberg the following summer.
After she had taken her degree at
Stockholms Högskola in the autumn, she followed my invitation to
% --- p. 321 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{321}take up residence at Carlsberg, in order there, as far as her
health permits, to continue her studies. I have thus
gained in her a dear housemate, whose open sense and
fine understanding for what is great and beautiful enrich
my life. Under her influence (although she herself has
her dark moments) my old tendency to hypochondria has
almost vanished. We sometimes pursue common studies.
Thus I have gone through Spinoza's Ethica with her
in Latin (under constant criticism from her side of Spinoza's
bad Latin), and since a general philosophical orientation
is a part of her plans for the future, I have been able to be
of help to her in various ways. Conversely she has,
both through her knowledge of the history of religion and through her
fine sense of language, been a good help to me in preparing
the third edition of my Religionsfilosofi. Poetic works too,
Swedish and Danish, and from foreign literatures
especially Shelley, we have pursued together. --- As regards my personal
view of life, I feel understood by her
as by no one else. ---

I have the hope that the stay here at Carlsberg will not
be without fruit for her continued development, from which
I expect much, although in the nature of things
I shall not live to see it. When these lines after
my death come to light, they shall bring her
a greeting from her old friend with heartfelt thanks for
what she has been for him in his last years.\footnote[1]{On 3 October 1924 Greta Ellstam became my wife. [Later note].}

\secrule

In later years I have often called myself an over-jubileed
man. It is perhaps a fault that I have never in time withdrawn
from a jubilee celebration that could be expected. But I
have never had any wish to travel without special reason, and I
have not always been able to, even if I wished. When now the 80th
birthday approached, and I heard of preparations to
celebrate it, I was so childishly glad that people wished to show
% --- p. 322 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{322}me kindness that I did not think at all of withdrawing.
The Students' Society held a fine gathering, at
which I read from my ``Erindringer'' what concerned
my relation to the political and literary movement of
the '70s and '80s. A circle of my personal friends
held a party that was splendidly opened with a quartet
by Mozart and continued with a supper at which
many warm words were addressed to me. On the birthday
itself I received in the morning a visit from the King. He
came from the Lucasstiftelse, where the Queen at that time lay ill,
and he brought me flowers and a written greeting from her.
He himself congratulated me in his warm and
simple way. In the course of the day I had visits from many colleagues
and friends. The Rector of the University, Professor Bock,
brought me, in an exceedingly warm manner that deeply
moved me, a greeting from the University. The chairman of the Carlsberg
Foundation, National Archivist Erslev, brought a greeting from the Foundation's
board and presented me with a beautiful silver bowl, on
which were set both my birthplace on Gammel Torv
and the main building at Carlsberg, where I shall probably
die. For dinner a few relatives and friends were
gathered at my home. It was a special joy to me that Vilhelm
Thomsen and his wife could be present.

The University had invited me, on the occasion of my 80th
birthday, to give a lecture in the University's
ceremonial hall, and I had chosen the 15th of March for it. It
became for me a high point of the festivities, and it
was with great emotion that I once more mounted the lectern,
after the Rector had again spoken to me in his warm and
heartfelt manner. It pleased me especially that in his characterization
of my activity at the University he quoted
the following closing words of a speech I had given in the year 1897
at the University festival: ``He whose position in life entails
that he must not only occupy himself with the problems in the
quiet of his private chamber, but must also set the young on their way
in their striving to find their bearings in the
% --- p. 323 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{323}world of thought, will seek in all his conduct to unite the sense for the
striving personality with the conviction that the personality
must be purified and ennobled through the work of
winning the truth and bowing to its demands.''\footnote[1]{The lecture is --- under the name of ``Filosofiske Synspunkter'' --- printed in ``Religiøse Tanketyper'' (1927). [Later note].}

\secrule

Shortly after my birthday I wrote to Meyerson that I
now felt myself at the end of my production and in future
would keep to a receptive attitude. He protested against this in a way
very flattering to me. But the only work
I have done since is to write, on the basis of notes
for use in my laboratory exercises, a treatise
on Plato's books on the State.

[Later (1925), however, came my philosophical testament: ``Erkendelsesteori
og Livsopfattelse''.]

A couple of days after I had presented the Plato treatise
to the Academy, I fell seriously ill. It
was a bronchitis that threatened to turn into pneumonia.
For some days an intestinal complication was also feared,
and there is said to have been talk of an operation. Pain
I did not really have, but I lay in a state of exhaustion
the like of which I have never known. When I was asked
how I was, I am said to have answered: ``I
am not at all.'' My condition was like a zero. Anxiety I did
not feel. I was excellently nursed by my physician Einar Hall
and later, during convalescence, by Greta Ellstam. When
I was on my feet again, a few weeks' stay in the Jyderup
woodlands gave me fresh strength. Out there I experienced so
sudden and splendid a breaking-through of spring as
I have never seen the like of.

But now I feel myself in earnest an old man.
I used to be a brisk walker, but now I prefer to go from
bench to bench in the Carlsberg garden or in Søndermarken.
Larger works are out of the question; the initiatives are
% --- p. 324 ---
\setcounter{footnote}{0}%
\opage{324}gone. But I busy myself daily with something or other. A special
rest it is for me to read Greek, the language I have loved
most. This summer I have thus again taken up Herodotus
and Sophocles, after Plato had occupied me
the previous year.

All around me my old friends and colleagues are dying. Only
Vilhelm Thomsen still keeps up, especially with the help of his
faithful wife, and I look forward to these two,
in whose home I have had such good hours for so many years,
moving now in the autumn --- if all goes well --- out to Valby
Bakke into a villa that belongs to the Carlsberg Foundation. I still hope
sometimes to meet his mild, loving gaze.\footnote[1]{Vilhelm Thomsen died 12 May 1927. [Later note].} ---
But otherwise it grows empty in the circle of my contemporaries. I
sometimes feel like the Greenlander who, on Mylius
Eriksen's monument, tells how his comrades die,
one after the other. But like him I have kept on
writing my diary.

And should these lines be the last I come
to write, they shall end with a thanks to life for what
it has brought me, thanks that it has made possible for me a work in
the service of thought, however modest it may be,
thanks for the understanding and the love I
have met.

\whiteline

{\small 10 July 1924.}
